## “And the Dead Spake—” / 死者发声——

===Original===
There is not in all London a quieter spot, or one, apparently, more withdrawn from the heat and bustle of life than Newsome Terrace. It is a cul-de-sac, for at the upper end the roadway between its two lines of square, compact little residences is brought to an end by a high brick wall, while at the lower end, the only access to it is through Newsome Square, that small discreet oblong of Georgian houses, a relic of the time when Kensington was a suburban village sundered from the metropolis by a stretch of pastures stretching to the river. Both square and terrace are most inconveniently situated for those whose ideal environment includes a rank of taxicabs immediately opposite their door, a spate of buses roaring down the street, and a procession of underground trains, accessible by a station a few yards away, shaking and rattling the cutlery and silver on their dining tables. In consequence Newsome Terrace had come, two years ago, to be inhabited by leisurely and retired folk or by those who wished to pursue their work in quiet and tranquillity. Children with hoops and scooters are phenomena rarely encountered in the Terrace and dogs are equally uncommon.

In front of each of the couple of dozen houses of which the Terrace is composed lies a little square of railinged garden, in which you may often see the middle-aged or elderly mistress of the residence horticulturally employed. By five o’clock of a winter’s evening the pavements will generally be empty of all passengers except the policeman, who with felted step, at intervals throughout the night, peers with his bull’s-eye into these small front gardens, and never finds anything more suspicious there than an early crocus or an aconite. For by the time it is dark the inhabitants of the Terrace have got themselves home, where behind drawn curtains and bolted shutters they will pass a domestic and uninterrupted evening. No funeral (up to the time I speak of) had I ever seen leave the Terrace, no marriage party had strewed its pavements with confetti, and perambulators were unknown. It and its inhabitants seemed to be quietly mellowing like bottles of sound wine. No doubt there was stored within them the sunshine and summer of youth long past, and now, dozing in a cool place, they waited for the turn of the key in the cellar door, and the entry of one who would draw them forth and see what they were worth.

===Chinese===
全伦敦再没有一处地方，比纽瑟姆台地（Newsome Terrace）更清静，或者更显然与生活的喧嚣火热两相隔绝。这是一条死胡同：在上首那一端，两排方正紧凑的小宅之间的马路，到头被一堵高高的砖墙堵住；而在下首这一端，要进去的唯一通道，是穿过纽瑟姆广场（Newsome Square）——那一片小巧而幽隐、呈长方形的乔治王朝式宅第，是肯辛顿（Kensington）尚为郊野村落、与京城之间隔着一片直抵河边的牧场时遗留下来的旧物。无论广场还是台地，对于那些心目中的理想环境须包括门前正对一排出租汽车、街上有成群的公共汽车轰隆驶过、以及几步开外便有座车站、因而有一列列地下火车震得餐具和银器在餐桌上叮当作响的人来说，都是再不方便不过的所在。正因如此，两年以前，纽瑟姆台地便已被清闲的退隐之士、或那些想在清静安宁之中做事的人所占据。手里推着铁圈、脚底下踩着滑板的孩子，在台地上是难得一见的景象，狗也同样不多见。

这条台地由二十来所宅子组成，每一所宅子前头都有一方围着栏杆的小花园，你常常可以看见宅子的女主人——人到中年，或已届暮年——在里头莳花弄草。冬日的傍晚，一到五点钟，人行道上通常便再没有别的行人，只有那警察踱着软底的步子，整夜里每隔一会儿便提着他的牛眼灯朝这些前花园里探望一眼，而在那里头所能找到的最可疑之物，也不过是开得早的番红花或乌头罢了。因为天一擦黑，台地的居民便都已回到了自家屋里，在拉拢的窗帘和闩好的百叶窗背后，度过一个家居的、无人惊扰的夜晚。在我所讲的那个时候以前，我从未见过有出殡的从台地上抬出去，也未曾见过办喜事的人往人行道上撒彩纸屑，婴儿车更是闻所未闻。台地和它的居民，正像一瓶瓶上好的葡萄酒那样，静静地酿熟着。毫无疑问，他们心里贮藏着的，是早已远去的青春的阳光与盛夏，如今，他们在阴凉处打着盹，只等着地窖门上的钥匙一转，等着那个进来把他们取出、瞧瞧他们到底值几个钱的人。

===Original===
Yet, after the time of which I shall now speak, I have never passed down its pavement without wondering whether each house, so seemingly-tranquil, is not, like some dynamo, softly and smoothly bringing into being vast and terrible forces, such as those I once saw at work in the last house at the upper end of the Terrace, the quietest, you would have said, of all the row. Had you observed it with continuous scrutiny, for all the length of a summer day, it is quite possible that you might have only seen issue from it in the morning an elderly woman whom you would have rightly conjectured to be the housekeeper, with her basket for marketing on her arm, who returned an hour later. Except for her the entire day might often pass without there being either ingress or egress from the door. Occasionally a middle-aged man, lean and wiry, came swiftly down the pavement, but his exit was by no means a daily occurrence, and indeed when he did emerge, he broke the almost universal usage of the Terrace, for his appearances took place, when such there were, between nine and ten in the evening. At that hour sometimes he would come round to my house in Newsome Square to see if I was at home and inclined for a talk a little later on. For the sake of air and exercise he would then have an hour’s tramp through the lit and noisy streets, and return about ten, still pale and unflushed, for one of those talks which grew to have an absorbing fascination for me. More rarely through the telephone I proposed that I should drop in on him: this I did not often do, since I found that if he did not come out himself, it implied that he was busy with some investigation, and though he made me welcome, I could easily see that he burned for my departure, so that he might get busy with his batteries and pieces of tissue, hot on the track of discoveries that never yet had presented themselves to the mind of man as coming within the horizon of possibility.

My last sentence may have led the reader to guess that I am indeed speaking of none other than that recluse and mysterious physicist Sir James Horton, with whose death a hundred half-hewn avenues into the dark forest from which life comes must wait completion till another pioneer as bold as he takes up the axe which hitherto none but himself has been able to wield. Probably there was never a man to whom humanity owed more, and of whom humanity knew less. He seemed utterly independent of the race to whom (though indeed with no service of love) he devoted himself: for years he lived aloof and apart in his house at the end of the Terrace. Men and women were to him like fossils to the geologist, things to be tapped and hammered and dissected and studied with a view not only to the reconstruction of past ages, but to construction in the future. It is known, for instance, that he made an artificial being formed of the tissue, still living, of animals lately killed, with the brain of an ape and the heart of a bullock, and a sheep’s thyroid, and so forth. Of that I can give no firsthand account; Horton, it is true, told me something about it, and in his will directed that certain memoranda on the subject should on his death be sent to me. But on the bulky envelope there is the direction, “Not to be opened till January, 1925.” He spoke with some reserve and, so I think, with slight horror at the strange things which had happened on the completion of this creature. It evidently made him uncomfortable to talk about it, and for that reason I fancy he put what was then a rather remote date to the day when his record should reach my eye. Finally, in these preliminaries, for the last five years before the war, he had scarcely entered, for the sake of companionship, any house other than his own and mine. Ours was a friendship dating from schooldays, which he had never suffered to drop entirely, but I doubt if in those years he spoke except on matters of business to half a dozen other people. He had already retired from surgical practice in which his skill was unapproached, and most completely now did he avoid the slightest intercourse with his colleagues, whom he regarded as ignorant pedants without courage or the rudiments of knowledge. Now and then he would write an epoch-making little monograph, which he flung to them like a bone to a starving dog, but for the most part, utterly absorbed in his own investigations, he left them to grope along unaided. He frankly told me that he enjoyed talking to me about such subjects, since I was utterly unacquainted with them. It clarified his mind to be obliged to put his theories and guesses and confirmations with such simplicity that anyone could understand them.

===Chinese===
然而，在我将要讲的那个时候以后，每次我从台地的人行道上走过，总不免要纳闷：这一所所看似如此安宁的宅子，会不会都像某台发电机那样，正轻柔地、不着痕迹地孕育着庞大而可怖的力量——一如我曾在台地上首那一头最后一所宅子里所见正在运转的那样的力量，而那一所，你会说，是整排房子里最清静的一所。哪怕你一连整整一个夏日目不转睛地盯着它看，很可能你所能看见从它里头走出来的，也不过是早晨一位上了年纪的妇人——你会一猜便中她是这里的女管家——臂上挎着买菜的篮子，过一个钟头又走了回来。除了她以外，那一整天往往可以既无人进、也无人出。偶尔会有一位清瘦而精干的男子，顺着人行道快步走出来，但他出来绝非每日都有的事；事实上，每逢他露面的时候，他都打破了台地几乎人人遵守的惯例，因为他出现——倘若有所出现的话——总在晚上九点到十点之间。到了那个时辰，他有时会绕到我在纽瑟姆广场的家里，看看我是否在家、有没有心思过一忽儿聊聊。随后，为了透透空气、活动活动筋骨，他便到灯火通明、喧嚷热闹的街上大走一个钟头，到十点光景再折回来——仍是那样面色苍白、不带一点血色——于是便开始我们之间那些谈话，而那些谈话之于我，渐渐地生出了一种令人沉醉的吸引力。更少见的时候，我会在电话里提议由我上他那儿去坐坐：这事我不大做，因为我发现，只要他自己不出来，便意味着他正埋头于某项研究，而虽然他待我客气周到，我却一眼便看得出他恨不得我早点告辞，好去摆弄他的电池和那些组织切片，急切地追踪那些迄今从未进入过人类心智、被认为有丝毫实现可能的发现。

我上面这一句话，大概已让读者猜到，我所讲的不是别人，正是那位隐居的、神秘的物理学家詹姆斯·霍顿爵士（Sir James Horton），随着他的辞世，一百条向那生命所从出的幽暗森林里半砍半辟出来的通路，都只得等着哪一位和他一般果敢的拓荒人，重新拿起那把迄今除他之外无人使得动的斧头，才能继续开通。世上恐怕再没有一个人，受惠于他的人类对他亏欠如此之多，而知之如此之少。他似乎完全独立于他所献身（诚然，那献身并无一丝爱的服侍）的那一族类：多年来，他孤身独处，蛰居在台地尽头的那所宅子里。在他眼里，男男女女就好比地质学家眼中的化石，是些供敲打、锤击、解剖、研考的东西，其目的不仅在于重构往古的世代，更在于为将来的构筑铺路。譬如众人皆知，他曾用刚宰杀的动物身上尚有生命的组织，拼造出一个造物来——以猿的脑、公牛的心、羊的甲状腺，等等凑合而成。此事我不能提供任何第一手的记述；诚然，霍顿曾对我略略说过一点，并在遗嘱里吩咐，他身故之后，将有关此事的几份备忘录寄交给我。然而在那只鼓鼓囊囊的信封上，却写着「1925 年 1 月方得启封」。他谈起这事时颇为有所保留，并且——我是这么觉得——略带几分悚然，那是在那造物完成之际所发生的种种怪事。显然，谈论这事使他颇为不快，也正因如此，我猜想他才把他那份记录到我手中的日子，定在当时看来还相当遥远的某一天。最后，作为这一番开场白的一点补充：战前最后那五年里，为了作伴，他除了自己家和我的家以外，几乎没有进过任何别家的门。我俩的交情始于学生时代，他始终不曾让它完全中断；但我看在那几年里，除了谈正经事务之外，他跟其余五六个人说过话。他早已从外科诊务中退了下来——在那行当里，他的技艺无人能及——如今更是彻底回避与同行们有任何些微的往来，他把他们看作既无胆识、又无起码学识的冬烘学究。偶尔他会写出一本划时代的小册子，像扔一根骨头给一条饿狗那样扔给他们，但大半时候，他全神沉溺于自己的研究之中，任他们在黑暗里独自摸索。他曾坦白告诉我，他喜欢和我谈这些题目，因为我对他那些题目一窍不通。要把他的理论、揣测和印证说得连外行人也一听就懂，反倒能叫他的思路理得更清楚。

===Original===
I well remember his coming in to see me on the evening of the 4th of August, 1914.

“So the war has broken out,” he said, “and the streets are impassable with excited crowds. Odd, isn’t it? Just as if each of us already was not a far more murderous battlefield than any which can be conceived between warring nations.”

“How’s that?” said I.

“Let me try to put it plainly, though it isn’t that I want to talk about. Your blood is one eternal battlefield. It is full of armies eternally marching and countermarching. As long as the armies friendly to you are in a superior position, you remain in good health; if a detachment of microbes that, if suffered to establish themselves, would give you a cold in the head, entrench themselves in your mucous membrane, the commander-in-chief sends a regiment down and drives them out. He doesn’t give his orders from your brain, mind you—those aren’t his headquarters, for your brain knows nothing about the landing of the enemy till they have made good their position and given you a cold.”

===Chinese===
我清清楚楚地记得，1914 年 8 月 4 日那天傍晚，他来看我。

「这么说，仗到底打起来了，」他说，「街上挤满了激动的人群，简直走不通。古怪，是不是？倒好像咱们每一个人自身，还不已经是一个远比交战两国之间所能想象的更为惨烈的战场似的。」

「这话怎讲？」我说。

「我尽量说得明白些吧，虽然我要谈的本不是这个。你的血液，便是一座永恒的战场。里面满满当当地驻扎着大军，永恒地进军、永恒地反进军。只要与你为友的那几路兵马占了上风，你便康健无恙；可倘若有一队原本会害你伤风的微生物，在你黏膜上盘踞下来、站稳了脚跟——只要放任它们盘踞——总司令便会派一团人马下去，把它们赶出去。你要知道，他并不从你的脑部下达命令——那可不是他的司令部，因为你的脑子，要等到敌人登陆成功、占了位置、害得你伤风之后，才会对敌人的登陆有所知觉。」

===Original===
He paused a moment.

“There isn’t one headquarters inside you,” he said, “there are many. For instance, I killed a frog this morning; at least most people would say I killed it. But had I killed it, though its head lay in one place and its severed body in another? Not a bit: I had only killed a piece of it. For I opened the body afterwards and took out the heart, which I put in a sterilised chamber of suitable temperature, so that it wouldn’t get cold or be infected by any microbe. That was about twelve o’clock today. And when I came out just now, the heart was beating still. It was alive, in fact. That’s full of suggestions, you know. Come and see it.”

The Terrace had been stirred into volcanic activity by the news of war: the vendor of some late edition had penetrated into its quietude, and there were half a dozen parlour-maids fluttering about like black and white moths. But once inside Horton’s door isolation as of an Arctic night seemed to close round me. He had forgotten his latchkey, but his housekeeper, then newly come to him, who became so regular and familiar a figure in the Terrace, must have heard his step, for before he rang the bell she had opened the door, and stood with his forgotten latchkey in her hand.

===Chinese===
他停了停。

「你身体里头并非只有一个司令部，」他说，「是有好多个。比方说，今早我杀了一只青蛙；至少大多数人都得说我把它杀了。可我当真杀了它吗——尽管它的头搁在一处，断了的身子搁在另一处？一点也不：我不过是杀了它身上的一块。因为我后来剖开它的身子，把它的心取了出来，放进一只温度适宜、消过毒的小室里，免得它变凉、或沾上什么微生物。那是今天十二点钟光景的事。而刚才我出来的时候，那颗心还在跳。它是活的，千真万确。这里头大有文章，你知道。来看看吧。」

台地被开战的消息搅得像火山一般活动起来：卖号外的小贩钻进了它那清静之地，六七个客厅女仆像黑白花的飞蛾一般扑来扑去。可一进了霍顿的家门，一种恍如极地长夜般的孤寂便仿佛把我合拢了起来。他忘了带弹簧锁的钥匙，可他的女管家——其时刚到任不久，后来在台地上成了这么一位循规蹈矩、人所熟见的身影——想必是听见了他的脚步声，因为他还没按铃，她已开了门，手里拿着他落下的那把钥匙，站在那里。

===Original===
“Thanks, Mrs. Gabriel,” said he, and without a sound the door shut behind us. Both her name and face, as reproduced in some illustrated daily paper, seemed familiar, rather terribly familiar, but before I had time to grope for the association, Horton supplied it.

“Tried for the murder of her husband six months ago,” he said. “Odd case. The point is that she is the one and perfect housekeeper. I once had four servants, and everything was all mucky, as we used to say at school. Now I live in amazing comfort and propriety with one. She does everything. She is cook, valet, housemaid, butler, and won’t have anyone to help her. No doubt she killed her husband, but she planned it so well that she could not be convicted. She told me quite frankly who she was when I engaged her.”

Of course I remembered the whole trial vividly now. Her husband, a morose, quarrelsome fellow, tipsy as often as sober, had, according to the defence cut his own throat while shaving; according to the prosecution, she had done that for him. There was the usual discrepancy of evidence as to whether the wound could have been self-inflicted, and the prosecution tried to prove that the face had been lathered after his throat had been cut. So singular an exhibition of forethought and nerve had hurt rather than helped their case, and after prolonged deliberation on the part of the jury, she had been acquitted. Yet not less singular was Horton’s selection of a probable murderess, however efficient, as housekeeper.

===Chinese===
「多谢，加布里埃尔太太（Mrs. Gabriel），」他说，门便无声无息地在我们身后合上了。她的名字和脸，仿佛在哪份带插图的日报上登过，倒有些面熟——熟得相当叫人害怕；可我还没来得及去寻思这是从何而来的印象，霍顿便替我接上了。

「半年前因谋杀亲夫受审过，」他说，「一桩古怪的案子。要紧的是，她是独一无二、十全十美的管家。我从前用着四个佣人，样样事都一塌糊涂——咱们上学那会儿就是这么说的。如今只一个佣人，我过得舒舒服服、规规矩矩，简直不可思议。什么活儿她都干。她又是厨子，又是贴身侍仆，又是女佣，又是管家，并且不肯要任何人帮手。毫无疑问，她是杀了她丈夫的，可她筹划得天衣无缝，没法给定罪。我雇她的时候，她坦坦白白地把她是谁告诉了我。」

当然，此刻我一下子把那场审判的始末记得清清楚楚。她的丈夫是个阴郁、爱吵架的家伙，醉的时候和清醒的时候一样多；按辩方的说法，他是刮脸时割断了自己的喉咙；按控方的说法，则是她替他下了手。关于这伤是否可能是自己所致，照例有证词上的出入，而控方还力图证明：是在喉咙被割断之后，那脸才被打上肥皂沫的。如此不寻常的一份深谋远虑与镇定的展示，于他们的案情反而有害，而非有益，陪审团经过长久的商议之后，宣告她无罪。然而同样不寻常的，是霍顿竟选了一个十之八九的杀人凶手——无论她多么能干——来当管家。

===Original===
He anticipated this reflection.

“Apart from the wonderful comfort of having a perfectly appointed and absolutely silent house,” he said, “I regard Mrs. Gabriel as a sort of insurance against my being murdered. If you had been tried for your life, you would take very especial care not to find yourself in suspicious proximity to a murdered body again: no more deaths in your house, if you could help it. Come through to my laboratory, and look at my little instance of life after death.”

Certainly it was amazing to see that little piece of tissue still pulsating with what must be called life; it contracted and expanded faintly indeed but perceptibly, though for nine hours now it had been severed from the rest of the organisation. All by itself it went on living, and if the heart could go on living with nothing, you would say, to feed and stimulate its energy, there must also, so reasoned Horton, reside in all the other vital organs of the body other independent focuses of life.

===Chinese===
他猜到了我这一层心思，便先我一步说了出来。

「除了拥有一个十全十美、绝对安静的家所能带来的那种舒坦之外，」他说，「我把加布里埃尔太太看作是我自己不遭谋杀的一道保险。一个人要是曾为一条人命受过审，便会格外小心，再不肯让自己重又陷入与一具尸首近在咫尺的可疑境地：只要躲得开，自家屋里就再也不能有死人了。到我的实验室来吧，看一看我这小小的死后犹生的例证。」

眼见那一小块组织依然在以不得不称之为生命的力量搏动，实在令人惊叹；它确是在微弱地、却又是可以察觉地一缩一张，尽管此时它与其余的躯体分离已经九个钟头了。它全凭自己活着，而一颗心若能在外人看来毫无凭借以滋养、刺激其能量的情况下继续活着，那么，霍顿如此推论道，身体其余所有重要器官之中，也必各自另有一些独立的生命焦点存在着。

===Original===
“Of course a severed organ like that,” he said, “will run down quicker than if it had the cooperation of the others, and presently I shall apply a gentle electric stimulus to it. If I can keep that glass bowl under which it beats at the temperature of a frog’s body, in sterilised air, I don’t see why it should not go on living. Food—of course there’s the question of feeding it. Do you see what that opens up in the way of surgery? Imagine a shop with glass cases containing healthy organs taken from the dead. Say a man dies of pneumonia. He should, as soon as ever the breath is out of his body, be dissected, and though they would, of course, destroy his lungs, as they will be full of pneumococci, his liver and digestive organs are probably healthy. Take them out, keep them in a sterilised atmosphere with the temperature at 98.4, and sell the liver, let us say, to another poor devil who has cancer there. Fit him with a new healthy liver, eh?”

“And insert the brain of someone who has died of heart disease into the skull of a congenital idiot?” I asked.

“Yes, perhaps; but the brain’s tiresomely complicated in its connections and the joining up of the nerves, you know. Surgery will have to learn a lot before it fits new brains in. And the brain has got such a lot of functions. All thinking, all inventing seem to belong to it, though, as you have seen, the heart can get on quite well without it. But there are other functions of the brain I want to study first. I’ve been trying some experiments already.”

===Chinese===
「当然，这样一个被割下来的器官，」他说，「要比它与其余器官协力合作时衰竭得快些，过一会儿我便要给它通上一点温和的电刺激。倘若我能让那只罩着它的玻璃钵，在消毒的空气里保持着青蛙体温的温度，我看不出它为什么不能一直活下去。养料——当然，还有喂它的问题。你可看得出这在外科上头打开了怎样一扇门？你想象一下，有一家铺子，玻璃柜里陈列着从死者身上取下的健康器官。比方说，有一个人死于肺炎。他的气一断，便该立刻加以解剖；当然，两肺是要毁掉的，因为里头满是肺炎球菌，可他的肝脏和消化器官多半是健康的。把它们取出来，搁在消毒的大气里，温度维持在 98.4 度，再把那肝脏，比方说，卖给另一个肝上长了癌的可怜虫。给他换上一只崭新、健康的肝，呃？」

「把一个死于心脏病的人的脑子，装到一个天生的白痴的头盖里？」我问。

「是的，也许成；可是你知道，脑子在它那些连接和神经的接合上，麻烦得很。外科还得学上许多，才能装得成新脑子。况且脑子又有那么多功能。一切思考、一切发明似乎都属于它，虽然你也见到了，心没有它也照样过得挺好。可脑子还有些别的功能，是我更想先研究的。我已经做了几样实验了。」

===Original===
He made some little readjustment to the flame of the spirit lamp which kept at the right temperature the water that surrounded the sterilised receptacle in which the frog’s heart was beating.

“Start with the more simple and mechanical uses of the brain,” he said. “Primarily it is a sort of record office, a diary. Say that I rap your knuckles with that ruler. What happens? The nerves there send a message to the brain, of course, saying—how can I put it most simply—saying, ‘Somebody is hurting me.’ And the eye sends another, saying ‘I perceive a ruler hitting my knuckles,’ and the ear sends another, saying ‘I hear the rap of it.’ But leaving all that aside, what else happens? Why, the brain records it. It makes a note of your knuckles having been hit.”

He had been moving about the room as he spoke, taking off his coat and waistcoat and putting on in their place a thin black dressing-gown, and by now he was seated in his favourite attitude cross-legged on the hearthrug, looking like some magician or perhaps the afreet which a magician of black arts had caused to appear. He was thinking intently now, passing through his fingers his string of amber beads, and talking more to himself than to me.

===Chinese===
他稍稍调了调酒精灯的火苗——那灯烘着一只消过毒的容器周围的水，保持着恰当的温度，而青蛙的心便在那容器里跳动。

「先从脑子那些较为简单、较为机械的功用入手，」他说。「脑子的根本，是一座档案处，一本日记。比方说，我用那把尺子敲你的指节。会怎么样呢？那里的神经自然就给脑子发了一条消息，说——我怎么说得最浅显呢——说『有人在弄痛我』。眼睛又发来一条，说『我看见一把尺子在打我的指节』；耳朵再发来一条，说『我听见了那一敲的声音』。可这些先不去说它，此外又怎样了呢？嗳，脑子把这事记下来了。它把你指节挨了打这件事，记上了一笔。」

他一边说着，一边在屋里踱来踱去，脱去外衣和马甲，换上一件薄薄的黑色晨衣，到这时，他已盘腿坐在炉前地毯上他最爱用的那个姿势里，看起来像个术士，或者像那唤使黑魔法的术士召来的魔神。他正凝神苦思，一面用手指捻着他那串琥珀念珠，与其说是对我说话，不如说是自言自语。

===Original===
“And how does it make that note?” he went on. “Why, in the manner in which phonograph records are made. There are millions of minute dots, depressions, pockmarks on your brain which certainly record what you remember, what you have enjoyed or disliked, or done or said. The surface of the brain anyhow is large enough to furnish writing-paper for the record of all these things, of all your memories. If the impression of an experience has not been acute, the dot is not sharply impressed, and the record fades: in other words, you come to forget it. But if it has been vividly impressed, the record is never obliterated. Mrs. Gabriel, for instance, won’t lose the impression of how she lathered her husband’s face after she had cut his throat. That’s to say, if she did it.”

“Now do you see what I’m driving at? Of course you do. There is stored within a man’s head the complete record of all the memorable things he has done and said: there are all his thoughts there, and all his speeches, and, most well-marked of all, his habitual thoughts and the things he has often said; for habit, there is reason to believe, wears a sort of rut in the brain, so that the life-principle, whatever it is, as it gropes and steals about the brain, is continually stumbling into it. There’s your record, your gramophone plate all ready. What we want, and what I’m trying to arrive at, is a needle which, as it traces its minute way over these dots, will come across words or sentences which the dead have uttered, and will reproduce them. My word, what Judgment Books! What a resurrection!”

===Chinese===
「那么，它是怎么记上那一笔的呢？」他接着说。「嗳，就用留声机唱片录音的法子。你的脑子里有千千万万细微的麻点、凹坑、痘痕，这些无疑记录着你的记忆、你的喜好与厌恶、你的言行。脑子的表面无论如何也大得足够充作信纸，把这一切、把你所有的记忆都记下来。倘若一次经历所留下的印象并不深刻，那麻点便按得不深，记录也就褪去：换句话说，你便渐渐把它忘了。可倘若印象深刻鲜明，那记录是永远不会磨灭的。比方说，加布里埃尔太太在割断她丈夫喉咙之后给他脸上打肥皂沫的那回事，她是忘不掉的。这就是说——倘若她真做了的话。」

「这一下你总明白我要说的了吧？你当然明白。一个人的头颅里，贮藏着他所做过、所说过的所有可记之事的完整记录：他的一切心思都在里头，他的一切言语都在里头，而刻得最深的，是他那些习惯成自然的心思，以及他常常说的话；因为有理由相信，习惯会在脑子里磨出一道辙来，以至于那生命之理——管它究竟是什么——当它在脑子里摸索着、潜行着的时候，便不住地跌进这道辙里。这就是你的唱片，你那张现现成成的留声机底片。我们所要的、而我也正设法弄到的，是一根唱针，当它沿着这些麻点所走的那一道细微的轨迹滑过之时，便会碰上死者生前说过的话、说过的句子，并把它重放出来。老天爷，这是何等的审判之书（Judgment Books）！何等的一场复活！」

===Original===
Here in this withdrawn situation no remotest echo of the excitement which was seething through the streets penetrated; through the open window there came in only the tide of the midnight silence. But from somewhere closer at hand, through the wall surely of the laboratory, there came a low, somewhat persistent murmur.

“Perhaps our needle—unhappily not yet invented—as it passed over the record of speech in the brain, might induce even facial expression,” he said. “Enjoyment or horror might even pass over dead features. There might be gestures and movements even, as the words were reproduced in our gramophone of the dead. Some people when they want to think intensely walk about: some, there’s an instance of it audible now, talk to themselves aloud.”

He held up his finger for silence.

“Yes, that’s Mrs. Gabriel,” he said. “She talks to herself by the hour together. She’s always done that, she tells me. I shouldn’t wonder if she has plenty to talk about.”

===Chinese===
在这一方与世隔绝的境地之中，街上那沸腾的激动，连最遥远的一点回声也透不进来；从敞开的窗口涌进来的，唯有子夜那一片寂静的潮水。可就在更近的某处——无疑是从实验室那一堵墙的那一边——传来了一阵低低的、却又相当执拗的呢喃。

「也许，我们的唱针——可惜尚未发明出来——当它在脑中那言语的记录上走过的时候，说不定还能带出脸上的神情来，」他说。「欢乐或惊恐也许还会从死者的容颜上一掠而过。也许还会有手势，有动作，因为那些话正在我们的死者留声机（gramophone of the dead）里被重新放出来。有些人，每要想得极深的时候，便要来回踱步；有些人——这会儿就有一个听得见的例子——会高声自言自语。」

他竖起一根手指，叫人噤声。

「是了，那就是加布里埃尔太太，」他说，「她一聊就是一两个钟头。她对我说，她向来如此。我看她有的是话可聊，倒也不足为怪。」

===Original===
It was that night when, first of all, the notion of intense activity going on below the placid house-fronts of the Terrace occurred to me. None looked more quiet than this, and yet there was seething here a volcanic activity and intensity of living, both in the man who sat cross-legged on the floor and behind that voice just audible through the partition wall. But I thought of that no more, for Horton began speaking of the brain-gramophone again.… Were it possible to trace those infinitesimal dots and pockmarks in the brain by some needle exquisitely fine, it might follow that by the aid of some such contrivance as translated the pockmarks on a gramophone record into sound, some audible rendering of speech might be recovered from the brain of a dead man. It was necessary, so he pointed out to me, that this strange gramophone record should be new; it must be that of one lately dead, for corruption and decay would soon obliterate these infinitesimal markings. He was not of opinion that unspoken thought could be thus recovered: the utmost he hoped for from his pioneering work was to be able to recapture actual speech, especially when such speech had habitually dwelt on one subject, and thus had worn a rut on that part of the brain known as the speech-centre.

“Let me get, for instance,” he said, “the brain of a railway porter, newly dead, who has been accustomed for years to call out the name of a station, and I do not despair of hearing his voice through my gramophone trumpet. Or again, given that Mrs. Gabriel, in all her interminable conversations with herself, talks about one subject, I might, in similar circumstances, recapture what she had been constantly saying. Of course my instrument must be of a power and delicacy still unknown, one of which the needle can trace the minutest irregularities of surface, and of which the trumpet must be of immense magnifying power, able to translate the smallest whisper into a shout. But just as a microscope will show you the details of an object invisible to the eye, so there are instruments which act in the same way on sound. Here, for instance, is one of remarkable magnifying power. Try it if you like.”

He took me over to a table on which was standing an electric battery connected with a round steel globe, out of the side of which sprang a gramophone trumpet of curious construction. He adjusted the battery, and directed me to click my fingers quite gently opposite an aperture in the globe, and the noise, ordinarily scarcely audible, resounded through the room like a thunderclap.

“Something of that sort might permit us to hear the record on a brain,” he said.

===Chinese===
便是那一夜，我才头一回起了这么个念头：在这些宅子平静的临街门面底下，也许正进行着一种炽烈的活动。哪一所看起来都没有这一所更安静的了，然而这里头却翻腾着一种火山般的活动、一种炽烈至极的生气——既在那个盘腿坐在地板上的男人身上，也在那隔着板壁依稀可闻的声音背后。可我没有再往下想，因为霍顿又开口谈那脑留声机了。……倘若能用一根纤细之极的唱针，描出脑子里那些无穷细微的麻点和痘痕，那么，借助某种能把留声机唱片上的痘痕转化为声音的机括，也许就能从一个死人的脑中，复原出某种听得见的言语来。他向我指出：这一张奇异的唱片必须是新的；必须是新近死去之人的唱片，因为腐败和朽坏很快便会把这些无穷细微的痕迹抹去。他并不认为未曾说出口的心思可以如此复原：他这一番拓荒的事业，所敢指望的至多，不过是能重新捕捉到真实说过的话语——尤其是当这种话语常常萦绕于同一个题目之上，因而在脑子那一处叫做言语中枢（speech-centre）的地方磨出了一道辙的。

「比方说，」他说，「让我弄到一个铁路搬运工的脑子——刚死的、多年来惯于喊出一个站名的那种人——我便大有希望从我的留声机喇叭里听见他的嗓音。再比方说，假定加布里埃尔太太在她那一场场没完没了的自言自语里老是说着同一桩事，那么在同样的情形下，我也许能把她常常说的话重放出来。自然，我的仪器必须是迄今未有的那种精微灵敏：它的唱针要能描出表面极细微的凹凸，它的喇叭又须有极大的放大之力，能把最微弱的一声低语化作一声呐喊。可正如显微镜能给你看肉眼看不见的物件的细处一样，作用于声音的这类仪器也是有的。这儿就有一具放大之力颇为可观的。你不妨试一试。」

他领我走到一张桌前，桌上摆着一台连着一只钢制圆球的电池，圆球的侧面伸出一支构造奇特的留声机喇叭。他调好电池，叫我朝球上的一个孔轻轻地弹一下指头；那声响，平日里几乎听不见，此刻却如一声霹雳，响彻了整间屋子。

「大约就是这一类的玩意儿，可以让我们听见脑子上的唱片了。」他说。

---

===Original===
After this night my visits to Horton became far more common than they had hitherto been. Having once admitted me into the region of his strange explorations, he seemed to welcome me there. Partly, as he had said, it clarified his own thought to put it into simple language, partly, as he subsequently admitted, he was beginning to penetrate into such lonely fields of knowledge by paths so utterly untrodden, that even he, the most aloof and independent of mankind, wanted some human presence near him. Despite his utter indifference to the issues of the war—for, in his regard, issues far more crucial demanded his energies—he offered himself as surgeon to a London hospital for operations on the brain, and his services, naturally, were welcomed, for none brought knowledge or skill like his to such work. Occupied all day, he performed miracles of healing, with bold and dexterous excisions which none but he would have dared to attempt. He would operate, often successfully, for lesions that seemed certainly fatal, and all the time he was learning. He refused to accept any salary; he only asked, in cases where he had removed pieces of brain matter, to take these away, in order by further examination and dissection, to add to the knowledge and manipulative skill which he devoted to the wounded. He wrapped these morsels in sterilised lint, and took them back to the Terrace in a box, electrically heated to maintain the normal temperature of a man’s blood. His fragment might then, so he reasoned, keep some sort of independent life of its own, even as the severed heart of a frog had continued to beat for hours without connection with the rest of the body. Then for half the night he would continue to work on these sundered pieces of tissue scarcely dead, which his operations during the day had given him. Simultaneously, he was busy over the needle that must be of such infinite delicacy.

===Chinese===
自那一夜之后，我到霍顿那里走动，比以前频繁得多了。他既已把我引进了他那一片奇异的探索之地，似乎便乐于我在那里头。一来，正如他自己所说，把想法化作浅显的话，反倒能使他自己的思路清楚起来；二来，他后来也承认，他正沿着一条条全然无人涉足过的小径，走进那样一些寂寥的知识荒原，以至于连他这般最是孤高、最是独立不倚的人，也觉得身边需要有个活人在场。尽管他对这场战争的种种结局漠不关心——因为在他看来，有远比这更要紧的得失正等着他去耗尽心力——他还是毛遂自荐，到伦敦一所医院里去做脑部手术的外科医生，而他的效力，自然是大受欢迎的，因为在这种工作上，没有人能带来像他那样的知识与技艺。他整日忙碌，做出了一桩桩近乎神迹的治愈，凭借大胆而灵巧的切除，那些除他之外无人敢一试的切除。他时常把那些看上去必死无疑的病患救活，而与此同时，他始终在学。他拒收任何报酬；他只要求，凡是切下了脑组织的病例，都让他把那些碎块带走，以便通过进一步的检查和解剖，增长他专用于伤者的那些知识与手术上的本事。他用消毒绒布把这些小块包起来，装进一只箱子里带回台地，箱子里通着电热，好维持人血的正常温度。他这么推论道：这样一来，他这小块组织，也许便能保有某种自身的、独立的生命，正如那从青蛙身上割下来的心，在与身体的其余部分断了联系之后，尚能继续跳动几个钟头一样。随后大半个夜里，他便继续在这些几乎尚未死透的、白天手术所获的离体组织上做工。与此同时，他还忙着那张非有无比的精微不可的唱针。

===Original===
One evening, fatigued with a long day’s work, I had just heard with a certain tremor of uneasy anticipation the whistles of warning which heralded an air-raid, when my telephone bell rang. My servants, according to custom, had already betaken themselves to the cellar, and I went to see what the summons was, determined in any case not to go out into the streets. I recognised Horton’s voice. “I want you at once,” he said.

“But the warning whistles have gone,” said I, “and I don’t like showers of shrapnel.”

“Oh, never mind that,” said he. “You must come. I’m so excited that I distrust the evidence of my own ears. I want a witness. Just come.”

He did not pause for my reply, for I heard the click of his receiver going back into its place. Clearly he assumed that I was coming, and that I suppose had the effect of suggestion on my mind. I told myself that I would not go, but in a couple of minutes his certainty that I was coming, coupled with the prospect of being interested in something else than air-raids, made me fidget in my chair and eventually go to the street door and look out. The moon was brilliantly bright, the square quite empty, and far away the coughings of very distant guns. Next moment, almost against my will, I was running down the deserted pavements of Newsome Terrace. My ring at his bell was answered by Horton, before Mrs. Gabriel could come to the door, and he positively dragged me in.

“I shan’t tell you a word of what I am doing,” he said. “I want you to tell me what you hear. Come into the laboratory.”

===Chinese===
一天傍晚，我做了一整天的事，正觉疲乏，刚怀着一点不安的预期，听见空袭将至的警报汽笛声响起来，电话铃便响了。我的佣人照例已经躲到地窖里去了，我便走过去看看是什么事，已横下心来无论如何不上街。我听出是霍顿的声音。「我立刻要你来。」他说。

「可是警报已经响了，」我说，「我不爱淋一阵弹片雨。」

「哦，那个不管，」他说，「你一定得来。我激动得连自己耳朵听到的话都不敢信了。我要一个见证人。就来。」

他没等我答话，因为我已听见他那头的话筒被咔哒一声挂了回去。显然，他是认定我要来的，而我想，这一点在我心里起了某种暗示的作用。我对自己说我不会去，可不出两分钟，他那股认定我要来的笃定，再加上能关心些空袭以外之事的前景，便叫我坐立不安起来，终于走到街门口张了一张。月光明亮之极，广场上空无一人，远远地传来隐隐的炮声，像是一阵阵地咳嗽。下一刻，我几乎身不由己地顺着纽瑟姆台地空无一人的人行道奔跑起来。我按响他家的门铃，加布里埃尔太太还没来得及来开门，霍顿便先来应了门，他简直是把我拽了进去。

「我做的事，一个字也不告诉你，」他说，「我要你告诉我你听见的是什么。到实验室来。」

===Original===
The remote guns were silent again as I sat myself, as directed, in a chair close to the gramophone trumpet, but suddenly through the wall I heard the familiar mutter of Mrs. Gabriel’s voice. Horton, already busy with his battery, sprang to his feet.

“That won’t do,” he said. “I want absolute silence.”

He went out of the room, and I heard him calling to her. While he was gone I observed more closely what was on the table. Battery, round steel globe, and gramophone trumpet were there, and some sort of a needle on a spiral steel spring linked up with the battery and the glass vessel, in which I had seen the frog’s heart beat. In it now there lay a fragment of grey matter.

Horton came back in a minute or two, and stood in the middle of the room listening.

“That’s better,” he said. “Now I want you to listen at the mouth of the trumpet. I’ll answer any questions afterwards.”

With my ear turned to the trumpet, I could see nothing of what he was doing, and I listened till the silence became a rustling in my ears. Then suddenly that rustling ceased, for it was overscored by a whisper which undoubtedly came from the aperture on which my aural attention was fixed. It was no more than the faintest murmur, and though no words were audible, it had the timbre of a human voice.

“Well, do you hear anything?” asked Horton.

“Yes, something very faint, scarcely audible.”

“Describe it,” said he.

“Somebody whispering.”

“I’ll try a fresh place,” said he.

===Chinese===
待我依言在那张紧挨着留声机喇叭的椅子里坐下时，远处那几门炮又不作声了；可突然间，隔着墙，我听见了加布里埃尔太太那熟悉的呢喃。霍顿正忙着摆弄他的电池，闻声一跃而起。

「这不行，」他说，「我要的是绝对的安静。」

他走出房间，我听见他在叫她。趁他不在，我把桌上的东西端详得更仔细了些。电池、钢制圆球、留声机喇叭，全在那里，还有一支装在螺旋钢丝弹簧上的什么唱针，把电池和那只玻璃器皿连接起来——我曾看见过青蛙的心在那器皿里跳动。此刻那器皿里搁着一小块灰白色的东西。

霍顿一两分钟后便回来了，站在屋子当中听着。

「这就好了，」他说，「现在我要你把耳朵凑到喇叭口上去听。回头有什么问题，我再答你。」

我把耳朵侧向喇叭，便看不见他在做什么了；我听着，直听到那寂静在我耳中变成了一片沙沙声。忽然那沙沙声止住了，因为有一缕低语盖过了它——那低语无疑是从我凝神谛听的那个孔里出来的。那不过是一声极微弱的呢喃，虽然听不清字句，却带着人声的音色。

「怎么样，你听见什么没有？」霍顿问。

「听见了，极微弱，几乎听不清。」

「形容形容。」他说。

「有人在低语。」

「我换一个地方试试。」他说。

===Original===
The silence descended again; the mutter of the distant guns was still mute, and some slight creaking from my shirt front, as I breathed, alone broke it. And then the whispering from the gramophone trumpet began again, this time much louder than it had been before—it was as if the speaker (still whispering) had advanced a dozen yards—but still blurred and indistinct. More unmistakable, too, was it that the whisper was that of a human voice, and every now and then, whether fancifully or not, I thought I caught a word or two. For a moment it was silent altogether, and then with a sudden inkling of what I was listening to I heard something begin to sing. Though the words were still inaudible there was melody, and the tune was “Tipperary.” From that convolvulus-shaped trumpet there came two bars of it.

“And what do you hear now?” cried Horton with a crack of exultation in his voice. “Singing, singing! That’s the tune they all sang. Fine music that from a dead man. Encore! you say? Yes, wait a second, and he’ll sing it again for you. Confound it, I can’t get on to the place. Ah! I’ve got it: listen again.”

Surely that was the strangest manner of song ever yet heard on the earth, this melody from the brain of the dead. Horror and fascination strove within me, and I suppose the first for the moment prevailed, for with a shudder I jumped up.

“Stop it!” I said. “It’s terrible.”

His face, thin and eager, gleamed in the strong ray of the lamp which he had placed close to him. His hand was on the metal rod from which depended the spiral spring and the needle, which just rested on that fragment of grey stuff which I had seen in the glass vessel.

“Yes, I’m going to stop it now,” he said, “or the germs will be getting at my gramophone record, or the record will get cold. See, I spray it with carbolic vapour, I put it back into its nice warm bed. It will sing to us again. But terrible? What do you mean by terrible?”

===Chinese===
寂静又落了下来；远处那隐约的炮声依旧哑着，唯有我呼吸之际衬衣前胸所发出的些微窸窣声，独自打破它。继而，留声机喇叭里的低语又响了起来，这一回比先前响得多——仿佛那说话的人（仍压低了嗓门）向前走近了十来码——可仍旧含糊、听不真切。而那是一缕人声的低语，这一点也更加无可置疑了；还不时地，不知是否出于我的想象，我觉得自己抓住了只言片语。有一阵子它整个沉默下来，继而，我心里猛地一动，隐约明白了所听的是什么，便听见有什么东西开始唱了起来。字句虽仍旧听不清，却有旋律在，那调子是《蒂珀雷里》（Tipperary）。从那支形如牵牛花的喇叭里，传出了它的两个小节。

「这一回你又听见什么了？」霍顿嚷道，嗓音里迸出一声狂喜，「唱歌，唱歌！那正是他们人人都唱的调子。从死人那里传来的好音乐呢。你说再来一遍？是，等一秒钟，他还会给你再唱一遍的。该死，我找不着那地方了。啊！找着了：再听。」

的确，这是世上迄今所曾听见过的最奇异的一种歌声，这一缕从死者的脑子里传出的旋律。恐惧与着迷在我心中交战，我想，一时之间是前者占了上风，因为我打了个寒噤，跳了起来。

「停下！」我说，「太可怕了。」

他的脸瘦削而热切，在搁得离他很近的那盏灯的强光里熠熠发亮。他的手按在那根金属杆上，那螺旋弹簧和唱针便悬在杆下，针尖刚刚搭在我先前在玻璃器皿里所见的那一小块灰白色的东西上。

「是，我这便要停下了，」他说，「要不然细菌就要上来侵犯我的唱片了，要不然唱片就要凉了。瞧，我给它喷上石炭酸气，再把它放回它那张舒舒服服的暖床里。它还会再给我们唱的。可是可怕？你说可怕是什么意思？」

===Original===
Indeed, when he asked that I scarcely knew myself what I meant. I had been witness to a new marvel of science as wonderful perhaps as any that had ever astounded the beholder, and my nerves—these childish whimperers—had cried out at the darkness and the profundity. But the horror diminished, the fascination increased as he quite shortly told me the history of this phenomenon. He had attended that day and operated upon a young soldier in whose brain was embedded a piece of shrapnel. The boy was *in extremis*, but Horton had hoped for the possibility of saving him. To extract the shrapnel was the only chance, and this involved the cutting away of a piece of brain known as the speech-centre, and taking from it what was embedded there. But the hope was not realised, and two hours later the boy died. It was to this fragment of brain that, when Horton returned home, he had applied the needle of his gramophone, and had obtained the faint whisperings which had caused him to ring me up, so that he might have a witness of this wonder. Witness I had been, not to these whisperings alone, but to the fragment of singing.

“And this is but the first step on the new road,” said he. “Who knows where it may lead, or to what new temple of knowledge it may not be the avenue? Well, it is late: I shall do no more tonight. What about the raid, by the way?”

To my amazement I saw that the time was verging on midnight. Two hours had elapsed since he let me in at his door; they had passed like a couple of minutes. Next morning some neighbours spoke of the prolonged firing that had gone on, of which I had been wholly unconscious.

===Chinese===
其实，他这一问，连我自己也几乎说不出个所以然来。我所目睹的，是科学上一桩崭新的奇迹，其奇妙也许不亚于历来曾叫观者瞠目的任何一桩；而我的神经——那一班爱哭哭啼啼的小孩子——竟在那黑暗与深渊之前叫了起来。可经他三言两语地把这一现象的来龙去脉说与我听之后，那恐惧便淡了下去，而着迷却渐渐加重了。那一天他曾出诊，给一个脑中嵌着一块弹片的年轻士兵动过手术。那孩子已奄奄一息，可霍顿原本还存着一丝救他的指望。取出弹片是唯一的指望，而这就得切掉一块叫做言语中枢的脑子，再从中取出那嵌在里头的东西。可这指望终究落了空，两个钟头之后，那孩子便死去了。霍顿回家之后，便把他的留声机唱针触到了这一小块脑子上，从而得到了那几缕依稀的低语——正是这几缕低语叫他打电话给我，好让我给这一奇迹做个见证。我所做的见证，不仅是这几缕低语，还有那一小段歌声。

「而这，不过是这条新路子上迈出的第一步，」他说，「有谁知道它会引到哪里，又会不会是通往某座新的知识之殿的大道呢？好了，时候不早：今夜我不再做了。顺便问问，那场空袭怎样了？」

我吃惊地一看，时间已快近子夜。自他把我让进门算起，已经过去了两个钟头；这两个钟头过得却像两分钟。第二天早上，几位邻居谈起夜里那一阵响了好久的炮声，而我竟全然未曾觉察。

===Original===
Week after week Horton worked on this new road of research, perfecting the sensitiveness and subtlety of the needle, and, by vastly increasing the power of his batteries, enlarging the magnifying power of his trumpet. Many and many an evening during the next year did I listen to voices that were dumb in death, and the sounds which had been blurred and unintelligible mutterings in the earlier experiments, developed, as the delicacy of his mechanical devices increased, into coherence and clear articulation. It was no longer necessary to impose silence on Mrs. Gabriel when the gramophone was at work, for now the voice we listened to had risen to the pitch of ordinary human utterance, while as for the faithfulness and individuality of these records, striking testimony was given more than once by some living friend of the dead, who, without knowing what he was about to hear, recognised the tones of the speaker. More than once also, Mrs. Gabriel, bringing in syphons and whisky, provided us with three glasses, for she had heard, so she told us, three different voices in talk. But for the present no fresh phenomenon occurred: Horton was but perfecting the mechanism of his previous discovery and, rather grudging the time, was scribbling at a monograph, which presently he would toss to his colleagues, concerning the results he had already obtained. And then, even while Horton was on the threshold of new wonders, which he had already foreseen and spoken of as theoretically possible, there came an evening of marvel and of swift catastrophe.

I had dined with him that day, Mrs. Gabriel deftly serving the meal that she had so daintily prepared, and towards the end, as she was clearing the table for our dessert, she stumbled, I supposed, on a loose edge of carpet, quickly recovering herself. But instantly Horton checked some half-finished sentence, and turned to her.

“You’re all right, Mrs. Gabriel?” he asked quickly.

“Yes, sir, thank you,” said she, and went on with her serving.

“As I was saying,” began Horton again, but his attention clearly wandered, and without concluding his narrative, he relapsed into silence, till Mrs. Gabriel had given us our coffee and left the room.

“I’m sadly afraid my domestic felicity may be disturbed,” he said. “Mrs. Gabriel had an epileptic fit yesterday, and she confessed when she recovered that she had been subject to them when a child, and since then had occasionally experienced them.”

“Dangerous, then?” I asked.

“In themselves not in the least,” said he. “If she was sitting in her chair or lying in bed when one occurred, there would be nothing to trouble about. But if one occurred while she was cooking my dinner or beginning to come downstairs, she might fall into the fire or tumble down the whole flight. We’ll hope no such deplorable calamity will happen. Now, if you’ve finished your coffee, let us go into the laboratory. Not that I’ve got anything very interesting in the way of new records. But I’ve introduced a second battery with a very strong induction coil into my apparatus. I find that if I link it up with my record, given that the record is a—a fresh one, it stimulates certain nerve centres. It’s odd, isn’t it, that the same forces which so encourage the dead to live would certainly encourage the living to die, if a man received the full current. One has to be careful in handling it. Yes, and what then? you ask.”

===Chinese===
一个星期又一个星期，霍顿在这条新的研究路上做工，把唱针的灵敏与精微磨得更精，又把电池的功率大加扩充，使那喇叭放大的力量更见增长。其后这一年里，有多少个夜晚，我都在谛听那些在死亡中早已喑哑了的声音；那些在最初的实验里还模糊不清、不知所云的呢喃，随着他那套机械装置的精微日增，渐渐发展成了连贯而清晰可辨的字句。如今留声机开动的时候，已不必再叫加布里埃尔太太噤声了，因为我们所听的那个声音，已升到了与寻常人说话相等的音量；而至于这些唱片的逼真与各具个性，更有不止一次显眼的佐证：某位死者的生前好友，事先并不知道自己将要听到的是什么，一听便认出了说话人的嗓音。也不止一次，加布里埃尔太太端着苏打水瓶和威士忌进来，给我们摆了三只杯子，因为她说她听见了——据她告诉我们——有三个不同的嗓音在说话。但暂时还没有什么新的现象发生：霍顿不过是在完善他先前那项发现的机械装置，一面颇为吝惜时间地草拟着一部专著——不久他便会把它扔给他的同行们——专记他迄今所已获得的结果。而正在霍顿已站在他早已预见到、并曾说过在理论上并非不可能的种种新奇迹的门槛上之时，却来了那样一个夜晚——一个奇异的、紧接着一场急转直下的灾祸的夜晚。

那天我在他家吃饭，加布里埃尔太太手脚利落地把她精心备下的菜肴一道一道端上来。吃到将近末了，她正替我们撤席、好上甜点的时候，我猜是被地毯翘起的一角绊了一下，可她随即就稳住了身形。但霍顿立即把说了一半的句子收住，转身朝向她。

「你没事吧，加布里埃尔太太？」他急急地问。

「没事，先生，谢谢您。」她说着，便继续她的活计。

「我刚才说到哪儿了，」霍顿重新开口，可他的心思显然已经跑了，话头没说完便又沉默下来，直沉默到加布里埃尔太太给我们端上咖啡、退了出去。

「只怕我这家庭的安逸要被搅了，」他说，「加布里埃尔太太昨天发了一回羊痫风，她醒过来之后自己承认，她小时候就常犯这病，自那以后也间或发过。」

「那么，是危险的了？」我问。

「就这病本身而言，一点也不。」他说，「倘若她发作的时候正坐在自己的椅子上，或正躺在床上，便没有什么可忧的。可倘若她发作的时候正给我做着饭，或者正要下楼，那她便可能跌进火里，或从整段楼梯上滚下去。咱们但愿这种可悲的祸事不至于发生。好了，你咖啡喝完了的话，咱们就到实验室去吧。倒不是我又有什么很有趣的新唱片。只是我在我的装置里加进了第二只电池，带着一只极强的感应线圈。我发现，要是把它接到我的唱片上——只要这唱片是一张——是一张新鲜的唱片——它便能刺激某些神经中枢。奇不奇：那般鼓舞死者复生的伟力，倘若一个人受了它的全部电流，便也必定会鼓舞生者去死。摆弄它的时候，是不能不留神的。是了，你又要问，那又怎么样呢？」

===Original===
The night was very hot, and he threw the windows wide before he settled himself cross-legged on the floor.

“I’ll answer your question for you,” he said, “though I believe we’ve talked of it before. Supposing I had not a fragment of brain-tissue only, but a whole head, let us say, or best of all, a complete corpse, I think I could expect to produce more than mere speech through the gramophone. The dead lips themselves perhaps might utter—God! what’s that?”

From close outside, at the bottom of the stairs leading from the dining room which we had just quitted to the laboratory where we now sat, there came a crash of glass followed by the fall as of something heavy which bumped from step to step, and was finally flung on the threshold against the door with the sound as of knuckles rapping at it, and demanding admittance. Horton sprang up and threw the door open, and there lay, half inside the room and half on the landing outside, the body of Mrs. Gabriel. Round her were splinters of broken bottles and glasses, and from a cut in her forehead, as she lay ghastly with face upturned, the blood trickled into her thick grey hair.

Horton was on his knees beside her, dabbing his handkerchief on her forehead.

“Ah! that’s not serious,” he said; “there’s neither vein nor artery cut. I’ll just bind that up first.”

He tore his handkerchief into strips which he tied together, and made a dexterous bandage covering the lower part of her forehead, but leaving her eyes unobscured. They stared with a fixed meaningless steadiness, and he scrutinised them closely.

“But there’s worse yet,” he said. “There’s been some severe blow on the head. Help me to carry her into the laboratory. Get round to her feet and lift underneath the knees when I am ready. There! Now put your arm right under her and carry her.”

===Chinese===
那天夜里极热，他先把窗子大敞开来，然后才在地板上盘腿坐下。

「我来替你回答你那个问题，」他说，「虽然我记得这事我们从前谈过了。倘若我手里并非仅是一块脑组织，而是——比方说——一整颗头颅，或者最妙的，是一具完整的尸首，我想我所能弄出来的，便远不止于从留声机里重放出来的言语了。死者的嘴唇本身也许会——老天！那是什么？」

就在紧贴着门外、就在我们刚才离开的餐室通往我们此刻所坐的实验室的那段楼梯的底下，传来玻璃碎裂的一声巨响，继而是一个沉重之物从一级磕到下一级、咚咚地滚下来的声响，末了砰地一下摔在门槛上、撞在门上，那声响恰似拳头在敲着门，要求放它进来。霍顿一跃而起，把门拉开；只见加布里埃尔太太的身子，一半在屋里，一半在外头的楼梯口上。她周围尽是碎了的瓶子和玻璃杯的碎片；她仰面朝天地躺着，脸色惨白，一道伤口在前额上，血顺着伤口淌进她那浓密的灰发里去。

霍顿已跪在她身旁，用手帕按着她的前额。

「哎呀！这不打紧，」他说，「既没割断静脉，也没割断动脉。我且先把它包上。」

他把手帕撕成几条，打结接起来，灵巧地扎成一条绷带，盖住她的前额下半部，却没遮住她的眼睛。那双眼睛以一种呆呆的、了无意义的凝滞直瞪着，他凑近了细细端详。

「可是还有更糟的，」他说，「头上挨过重重的一击。帮我把她抬进实验室去。你绕到她脚那头，等我说一声『起』，你就从膝盖底下往上抬。起！这就对了。现在把你的胳膊整个伸到她身下，把她抱起来。」

===Original===
Her head swung limply back as he lifted her shoulders, and he propped it up against his knee, where it mutely nodded and bowed, as his leg moved, as if in silent assent to what we were doing, and the mouth, at the extremity of which there had gathered a little lather, lolled open. He still supported her shoulders as I fetched a cushion on which to place her head, and presently she was lying close to the low table on which stood the gramophone of the dead. Then with light deft fingers he passed his hands over her skull, pausing as he came to the spot just above and behind her right ear. Twice and again his fingers groped and lightly pressed, while with shut eyes and concentrated attention he interpreted what his trained touch revealed.

“Her skull is broken to fragments just here,” he said. “In the middle there is a piece completely severed from the rest, and the edges of the cracked pieces must be pressing on her brain.”

Her right arm was lying palm upwards on the floor, and with one hand he felt her wrist with fingertips.

“Not a sign of pulse,” he said. “She’s dead in the ordinary sense of the word. But life persists in an extraordinary manner, you may remember. She can’t be wholly dead: no one is wholly dead in a moment, unless every organ is blown to bits. But she soon will be dead, if we don’t relieve the pressure on the brain. That’s the first thing to be done. While I’m busy at that, shut the window, will you, and make up the fire. In this sort of case the vital heat, whatever that is, leaves the body very quickly. Make the room as hot as you can—fetch an oil-stove, and turn on the electric radiator, and stoke up a roaring fire. The hotter the room is the more slowly will the heat of life leave her.”

===Chinese===
他抬起她的两肩时，她的头无力地往后一仰，他便把它撑在自己膝头上；那条腿一动，那颗头便默默地一颠一垂，仿佛在默默应承着我们所做的事；嘴角边积着一点皂沫的嘴唇则软软地耷拉开来。我去取了一只垫子来垫她的头时，他仍托着她的肩；不一会儿，她已被安放在那张搁着死者留声机的矮桌旁边了。随后，他用轻巧灵便的手指，在她头盖上一寸寸地摸过去，摸到右耳正上方、稍稍偏后那一处，便停了下来。他的手指一遍、又一遍地摸索着、轻轻按着，闭起眼，凝神细察他那训练有素的触觉所告诉自己的一切。

「她的头盖骨就在这儿碎成了几片，」他说，「正中间有一块已与其余的完全脱开，而几片碎骨的茬子，必是正抵着她的脑子。」

她的右臂手掌朝上摊在地上，他用一只手的指尖按住她的腕子。

「脉一点也没有了，」他说，「按寻常的意义说，她已经死了。可你要记得，生命是以一种异乎寻常的方式固执地延续着的。她不可能全然死了：一个人除非五脏六腑都被炸成齑粉，否则不会一下子就全然死了。可我们若不解除脑子所受的压力，她不久便要全然死去了。这是头一桩要做的事。我在这儿忙这个的时候，你去把窗子关上，再把火生旺。这一类的情形之下，那种生命之热——管它是什么——是离开身子极快的。你把这屋子弄得越热越好——去搬一只油炉来，把电暖炉打开，再添上一炉烧得通红的火。屋子越热，她身上的生命之热便走得越慢。」

===Original===
Already he had opened his cabinet of surgical instruments, and taken out of it two drawers full of bright steel which he laid on the floor beside her. I heard the grating chink of scissors severing her long grey hair, and as I busied myself with laying and lighting the fire in the hearth, and kindling the oil-stove, which I found, by Horton’s directions, in the pantry, I saw that his lancet was busy on the exposed skin. He had placed some vaporising spray, heated by a spirit lamp close to her head, and as he worked its fizzing nozzle filled the air with some clean and aromatic odour. Now and then he threw out an order.

“Bring me that electric lamp on the long cord,” he said. “I haven’t got enough light. Don’t look at what I’m doing if you’re squeamish, for if it makes you feel faint, I shan’t be able to attend to you.”

I suppose that violent interest in what he was doing overcame any qualm that I might have had, for I looked quite unflinching over his shoulder as I moved the lamp about till it was in such a place that it threw its beam directly into a dark hole at the edge of which depended a flap of skin. Into this he put his forceps, and as he withdrew them they grasped a piece of bloodstained bone.

“That’s better,” he said, “and the room’s warming up well. But there’s no sign of pulse yet. Go on stoking, will you, till the thermometer on the wall there registers a hundred degrees.”

When next, on my journey from the coal-cellar, I looked, two more pieces of bone lay beside the one I had seen extracted, and presently referring to the thermometer, I saw that between the oil-stove and the roaring fire and the electric radiator, I had raised the room to the temperature he wanted. Soon, peering fixedly at the seat of his operation, he felt for her pulse again.

“Not a sign of returning vitality,” he said, “and I’ve done all I can. There’s nothing more possible that can be devised to restore her.”

===Chinese===
他早已打开了他的外科器械柜，从里头抽出两抽屉亮晃晃的钢器，搁在她身旁的地板上。我听见剪刀铰断她那长长的灰发时所发出的咯吱声；待我在炉边忙着生火、点火，又照霍顿的指点到食物间里去把那只油炉找来点上的时候，我看见他的柳叶刀已在裸露的皮肤上忙起来了。他在她头边搁了一瓶汽化的喷雾，用一盏酒精灯烘着，他一边做工，那嗤嗤作响的喷嘴便把一股洁净而芳香的气味送满空气之中。他不时抛出一两句吩咐。

「把那盏拖着长电线的那盏电灯给我拿来，」他说，「我的光不够。你要是见不得，就别瞧我在做什么，因为你要是被瞧得发了晕，我可顾不上来照应你。」

我想，是对他手头所做的事那一种强烈的兴趣，压下了我本可能有的那一点不安，因为我毫不畏缩地从他的肩头后头看过去，一面把那盏灯移来移去，直到把它移到这样一个位置，使它的光柱直直地照进一个黑洞里去，那洞沿上还耷拉着一小片皮肤。他把钳子探了进去，待抽出来时，钳子上夹着一块血淋淋的骨头。

「这就好了，」他说，「屋子也热起来了。可脉还没有一点。接着烧吧，等墙上的温度计指到一百度。」

待我再一次从煤窖那边走回来一看，我先前所见取出的那块骨头旁边，又多了两块；不久我看看温度计，只见在油炉、熊熊的火和电暖炉的共同作用之下，我已把屋子烧到了他所要的温度。不久，他凝神盯着他施术之处，又一次去按她的脉。

「一点回生的迹象也没有，」他说，「我已经尽了所能。再没有什么别的法子可想了，再想也不能把她救回来。」

===Original===
As he spoke the zeal of the unrivalled surgeon relaxed, and with a sigh and a shrug he rose to his feet and mopped his face. Then suddenly the fire and eagerness blazed there again. “The gramophone!” he said. “The speech centre is close to where I’ve been working, and it is quite uninjured. Good heavens, what a wonderful opportunity. She served me well living, and she shall serve me dead. And I can stimulate the motor nerve-centre, too, with the second battery. We may see a new wonder tonight.”

Some qualm of horror shook me.

“No, don’t!” I said. “It’s terrible: she’s just dead. I shall go if you do.”

“But I’ve got exactly all the conditions I have long been wanting,” said he. “And I simply can’t spare you. You must be witness: I must have a witness. Why, man, there’s not a surgeon or a physiologist in the kingdom who would not give an eye or an ear to be in your place now. She’s dead. I pledge you my honour on that, and it’s grand to be dead if you can help the living.”

Once again, in a far fiercer struggle, horror and the intensest curiosity strove together in me.

“Be quick, then,” said I.

“Ha! That’s right,” exclaimed Horton. “Help me to lift her on to the table by the gramophone. The cushion too; I can get at the place more easily with her head a little raised.”

He turned on the battery and with the movable light close beside him, brilliantly illuminating what he sought, he inserted the needle of the gramophone into the jagged aperture in her skull. For a few minutes, as he groped and explored there, there was silence, and then quite suddenly Mrs. Gabriel’s voice, clear and unmistakable and of the normal loudness of human speech, issued from the trumpet.

===Chinese===
他这一说，那举世无双的外科的热忱便松懈了下来，叹一口气，耸一耸肩，他站起身，抹了一抹脸。忽然之间，那股火一样的急切又在他脸上燃了起来。「留声机！」他说，「那言语中枢就在我刚才动手术的地方旁边，丝毫未受损伤。老天爷，这是多么难得的机会。她活着的时候尽心伺候我，死了也要让她伺候我。而且我还可以用这第二只电池刺激那运动神经中枢（motor nerve-centres）。今夜我们也许能见到一桩新的奇迹。」

我心中不禁涌起一阵恐惧。

「不，别这样！」我说，「太可怕了：她才刚死。你要这样做，我就走了。」

「可我正巧得到了我长久以来所一直想要的种种条件，」他说，「而我实在少不得你。你一定得做见证：我必须有一个见证人。哎，老兄，全国上下，没有一个外科医生或生理学家不愿舍了一只眼睛或一只耳朵来换你此刻这个位置的。她是死了。这一点我拿我的名誉向你担保，而一个人倘若能造福活人，便是死，也死得其所。」

恐惧与最强烈的好奇，又一次在我心中剧烈地交战起来，比上一次更为凶猛。

「那么，就快一点吧。」我说。

「哈！这才对，」霍顿嚷道，「帮我把她抬到留声机旁的桌子上去。垫子也一起；她头稍稍垫高些，我更容易下得着手。」

他打开电池，把那盏可移动的灯拉到身边，将他寻找之处照得通明雪亮，便把留声机的唱针，插入她那头盖上参差不齐的破洞里去。他在那里摸索、探查了几分钟，四下里悄然无声，继而，猛然间，加布里埃尔太太的声音——清清楚楚、绝不会有错、而且响度与寻常人说话完全相同的声音——从那喇叭里传了出来。

===Original===
“Yes, I always said that I’d be even with him,” came the articulated syllables. “He used to knock me about, he did, when he came home drunk, and often I was black and blue with bruises. But I’ll give him a redness for the black and blue.”

The record grew blurred; instead of articulate words there came from it a gobbling noise. By degrees that cleared, and we were listening to some dreadful suppressed sort of laughter, hideous to hear. On and on it went.

“I’ve got into some sort of rut,” said Horton. “She must have laughed a lot to herself.”

For a long time we got nothing more except the repetition of the words we had already heard and the sound of that suppressed laughter. Then Horton drew towards him the second battery.

“I’ll try a stimulation of the motor nerve-centres,” he said. “Watch her face.”

He propped the gramophone needle in position, and inserted into the fractured skull the two poles of the second battery, moving them about there very carefully. And as I watched her face, I saw with a freezing horror that her lips were beginning to move.

“Her mouth’s moving,” I cried. “She can’t be dead.”

He peered into her face.

“Nonsense,” he said. “That’s only the stimulus from the current. She’s been dead half an hour. Ah! what’s coming now?”

===Chinese===
「是呀，我常说我总有一天要跟他算这笔账，」那字字咬清的音节传了出来，「他一喝醉了酒回来就打我，他是这样的，我常常被他打得青一块紫一块。可这一回，我要拿一道红来还他那青一块紫一块。」

那唱片变得模糊起来；从里头出来的不再是字字清楚的言语，而是一阵咯咯的怪响。渐渐地，那怪响清楚了，我们听到的乃是一种可怕的、压抑着的笑声，听着叫人毛骨悚然。它一阵阵地响个不停。

「我钻到一道什么辙里去了，」霍顿说，「她一个人在心里头想必笑了许多。」

好长一段时间，我们没有听到别的，只有先前听过那几句话的一再重复，以及那一阵压抑着的笑声。然后，霍顿把第二只电池拉到跟前。

「我来试一试刺激那运动神经中枢，」他说，「看着她的脸。」

他把留声机的唱针固定在位置上，又把第二只电池的两个电极，插入那破裂的头盖里去，在里面非常小心地挪动着。我盯着她的脸看，只见——怀着一种冷彻骨髓的恐惧——她的嘴唇竟开始动了起来。

「她的嘴在动！」我叫道，「她不会是死了。」

他凑近去端详她的脸。

「胡说，」他说，「那不过是电流的刺激。她已经死了半个钟头了。啊！这一下又是什么了？」

===Original===
The lips lengthened into a smile, the lower jaw dropped, and from her mouth came the laughter we had heard just now through the gramophone. And then the dead mouth spoke, with a mumble of unintelligible words, a bubbling torrent of incoherent syllables.

“I’ll turn the full current on,” he said.

The head jerked and raised itself, the lips struggled for utterance, and suddenly she spoke swiftly and distinctly.

“Just when he’d got his razor out,” she said, “I came up behind him, and put my hand over his face, and bent his neck back over his chair with all my strength. And I picked up his razor and with one slit—ha, ha, that was the way to pay him out. And I didn’t lose my head, but I lathered his chin well, and put the razor in his hand, and left him there, and went downstairs and cooked his dinner for him, and then an hour afterwards, as he didn’t come down, up I went to see what kept him. It was a nasty cut in his neck that had kept him—”

Horton suddenly withdrew the two poles of the battery from her head, and even in the middle of her word the mouth ceased working, and lay rigid and open.

“By God!” he said. “There’s a tale for dead lips to tell. But we’ll get more yet.”

Exactly what happened then I never knew. It appeared to me that as he still leaned over the table with the two poles of the battery in his hand, his foot slipped, and he fell forward across it. There came a sharp crack, and a flash of blue dazzling light, and there he lay face downwards, with arms that just stirred and quivered. With his fall the two poles that must momentarily have come into contact with his hand were jerked away again, and I lifted him and laid him on the floor. But his lips as well as those of the dead woman had spoken for the last time.

===Chinese===
那两片嘴唇咧开来，扯成了一个笑容，下颚骨一松，从她嘴里便涌出了我们方才从留声机里听见的笑声。继而，那死去了的嘴开口说话了，含含糊糊地吐着些听不懂的字眼，像是一串咕噜咕噜、断断续续、上气不接下气的音节。

「我把电流开到最大。」他说。

那颗头一抽搐，竟抬了起来，嘴唇挣扎着要发声，忽然之间，她说得又快又清。

「正当他把剃刀掏出来，」她说，「我从背后走到他跟前，一只手捂住他的脸，用尽全身力气，把他的脖子往他椅背上一折。我又捡起他的剃刀，只一刀——哈，哈，这才是治他的法子。我一点也没手忙脚乱，倒把他的下巴好好地打上肥皂沫，把剃刀塞进他手里，撇下他，便下楼去替他做饭；过了一个钟头，他还不下来，我便又上去看他到底耽搁着什么。耽搁着他的，是他脖子上那一道要命的口子——」

霍顿猛地把那两个电极从她头上抽开，便在她话说到一半，那张嘴也戛然不动，僵僵地张着。

「老天在上！」他说，「这真是死者嘴唇说出来的故事。可我们还能再多听一些。」

下面究竟发生了什么，我始终没有弄明白。在我看去，他仍旧俯身在桌上，手里握着那两个电极，一脚踏空，便一头栽倒，横跌到桌上去了。只听得尖锐地啪地一响，一道蓝得叫人睁不开眼的闪光，他已面朝下地躺在那里，两条胳膊还在微微地动、微微地颤。他这一倒，那两个想必是一瞬间碰到了他手的电极又被弹开了去；我把他从桌上扶起，让他躺在地板上。然而他的嘴唇，同那死去了的女人的嘴唇一样，已经是最后一次开口了。

## At Abdul Ali’s Grave / 在阿卜杜勒·阿里的墓旁

===Original===
Luxor, as most of those who have been there will allow, is a place of notable charm, and boasts many attractions for the traveller, chief among which he will reckon an excellent hotel containing a billiard-room, a garden fit for the gods to sit in, any quantity of visitors, at least a weekly dance on board a tourist steamer, quail shooting, a climate as of Avilion, and a number of stupendously ancient monuments for those archaeologically inclined. But to certain others, few indeed in number, but almost fanatically convinced of their own orthodoxy, the charm of Luxor, like some sleeping beauty, only wakes when these things cease, when the hotel has grown empty and the billiard-marker “has gone for a long rest” to Cairo, when the decimated quail and the decimating tourist have fled northwards, and the Theban plain, Danae to a tropical sun, is a gridiron across which no man would willingly make a journey by day, not even if Queen Hatasoo itself should signify that she would give him audience on the terraces of Deir-el-Bahari. A suspicion however that the fanatic few were right, for in other respects they were men of estimable opinions, induced me to examine their convictions for myself, and thus it came about that two years ago, certain days toward the beginning of June saw me still there, a confirmed convert.

Much tobacco and the length of summer days had assisted us to the analysis of the charm of which summer in the south is possessed, and Weston﻿—one of the earliest of the elect﻿—and myself had discussed it at some length, and though we reserved as the principal ingredient a nameless something which baffled the chemist, and must be felt to be understood, we were easily able to detect certain other drugs of sight and sound, which we were agreed, contributed to the whole. A few of them are here subjoined.

===Chinese===
卢克索（Luxor）这地方，凡去过的大概都会承认，自有其格外迷人之处，并有许多足供旅人赏玩的名目，其中他必会首推一家极好的旅馆——内有台球房，还有一座连神祇也乐于栖坐的花园，再则是各色游客、每周至少一回的游船舞会、猎鹌鹑、如阿瓦隆（Avilion）一般的气候，以及若干古老得令人惊骇的遗迹，以飨好古之士。然而对另外一些人而言——他们人数着实寥寥，却几近狂热地笃信自家那一套正见——卢克索的美，恰如某位睡美人，唯有等上述种种消歇之时方才苏醒：等旅馆空了下来，记分员「去开罗（Cairo）长期休养」了，被射杀得所剩无几的鹌鹑和射杀它们的游客一同北遁了，而底比斯（Theban）平原在那热带的骄阳之下宛如被接纳的达那厄（Danae），化作一面烤架，白日里再无人情愿横越它一道，哪怕哈特谢普苏特女王（Queen Hatasoo）亲自示意要在代尔巴哈里（Deir-el-Bahari）的台地上赐他觐见，他也不肯。然而那寥寥几个狂热之徒在别的事情上见解均属可取，我便疑心他们在这上头也是对的，于是萌生了亲去验证他们信念的念头。如此，两年前的六月初那几天，我便仍逗留在那里，成了一个死心塌地的皈依者。

多量的烟草和夏日的漫长，助我们析出了南方之夏所独具的那种魅力的成分，韦斯顿（Weston）——最早蒙召的几位之一——和我曾就此作过一番相当详尽的讨论。虽说我们把那最主要的成分留作一个无以名之、难倒化学家、非亲感不能领会的东西，却也不难从中辨认出若干诉诸视听的别的药剂，我们一致认为它们共同凑成了这整体。兹附列几条于下。

===Original===
The waking in the warm darkness just before dawn to find that the desire for stopping in bed fails with the awakening.

The silent start across the Nile in the still air with our horses, who, like us, stand and sniff at the incredible sweetness of the coming morning without apparently finding it less wonderful in repetition.

The moment infinitesimal in duration but infinite in sensation, just before the sun rises, when the grey shrouded river is struck suddenly out of darkness, and becomes a sheet of green bronze.

The rose flush, rapid as a change of colour in some chemical combination, which shoots across the sky from east to west, followed immediately by the sunlight which catches the peaks of the western hills, and flows down like some luminous liquid.

The stir and whisper which goes through the world: a breeze springs up; a lark soars and sings; the boatman shouts “Yallah. Yallah”; the horses toss their heads.

The subsequent ride.

The subsequent breakfast on our return.

The subsequent absence of anything to do.

At sunset the ride into the desert thick with the scent of warm barren sand, which smells like nothing else in the world, for it smells of nothing at all.

The blaze of the tropical night.

Camel’s milk.

Converse with the fellahin, who are the most charming and least accountable people on the face of the earth except when tourists are about, and when in consequence there is no thought but backsheesh.

Lastly, and with this we are concerned, the possibility of odd experiences.

===Chinese===
在黎明前温暖的黑暗中醒来，发觉赖床的念头随醒来一并消散。

在寂静的空气里携马横渡尼罗河（the Nile）那无声的开端——那些马儿和我们一样站着，嗅一嗅即将到来的清晨那不可思议的甘美，屡屡如此，分明并不因其重复而稍减其奇妙。

日将出未出之际那一刹那，时长无穷小而感受无穷大：灰幔笼罩的河面忽地被击出黑暗，化作一张绿铜的薄片。

那一抹飞红，疾如某种化学反应里的变色，自东向西掠过天穹，紧随其后是阳光攀上西边群山的峰巅，如某种发光的液体般流淌而下。

掠过整个世界的那一阵骚动与低语：起了一阵风；一只云雀腾起歌唱；船夫高喊「Yallah. Yallah」（走啊，走啊）；马儿甩着脑袋。

随之而来的骑乘。

回来之后随之而来的早餐。

随之而来的，无所事事。

日落时分骑进沙漠，空气里浓稠地满是温热的荒沙气息，那气息与世间任何气味都不同，因为它闻上去什么也不是。

热带之夜的炽白的辉煌。

骆驼奶。

与农民（fellahin）们的闲谈——他们是世上最迷人、最不可解的一群人，唯独游客一近身便不成，那时节他们脑子里除却赏钱（backsheesh）二字再无别的念头。

最后，也是与本题相关的一项：碰上离奇经历的可能。

===Original===
The beginning of the things which make this tale occurred four days ago, when Abdul Ali, the oldest man in the village, died suddenly, full of days and riches. Both, some thought, had probably been somewhat exaggerated, but his relations affirmed without variation that he had as many years as he had English pounds, and that each was a hundred. The apt roundness of these numbers was incontestable, the thing was too neat not to be true, and before he had been dead for twenty-four hours, it was a matter of orthodoxy. But with regard to his relations, that which turned their bereavement, which must soon have occurred, into a source of blank dismay instead of pious resignation, was that not one of these English pounds, not even their less satisfactory equivalent in notes, which, out of the tourist season, are looked upon at Luxor as a not very dependable variety of Philosopher’s stone, though certainly capable of producing gold under favourable circumstances, could be found. Abdul Ali with his hundred years was dead, his century of sovereigns﻿—they might as well have been an annuity﻿—were dead with him, and his son Mohamed, who had previously enjoyed a sort of brevet rank in anticipation of the event, was considered to be throwing far more dust in the air than the genuine affection even of a chief mourner wholly justified.

Abdul, it is to be feared, was not a man of stereotyped respectability; though full of years and riches, he enjoyed no great reputation for honour. He drank wine whenever he could get it, he ate food during the days of Ramadan, scornful of the fact, when his appetite desired it, he was supposed to have the evil eye, and in his last moments he was attended by the notorious Achmet, who is well known here to be practised in Black Magic, and has been suspected of the much meaner crime of robbing the bodies of those lately dead. For in Egypt, while to despoil the bodies of ancient kings and priests is a privilege for which advanced and learned societies vie with each other, to rob the corpses of your contemporaries, is considered the deed of a dog. Mohamed who soon exchanged the throwing of dust in the air for the more natural mode of expressing chagrin, which is to gnaw the nails, told us in confidence that he suspected Achmet of having ascertained the secret of where his father’s money was, but it appeared that Achmet had as blank a face as anybody when his patient, who was striving to make some communication to him, went out into the great silence, and the suspicion that he knew where the money was, gave way, in the minds of those who were competent to form an estimate of his character, to a but dubious regret that he had just failed to learn that very important fact.

===Chinese===
构成本篇故事诸事的发端，发生在四天前：村里最年长的人，阿卜杜勒·阿里（Abdul Ali），猝然离世，年事与赀财俱丰。这两样，有人以为怕都有些夸张，但他的亲属们众口一词地断言，他的岁数和英磅一样多，而且各是一百。这两个数字之浑圆妥帖无可辩驳，事情巧得不由人不信，他咽气不到二十四小时，这便成了定论。至于他的亲属，把这场迟早要来的丧亲之痛，从虔敬的顺受化作了茫然惶恐的，却是这一桩：那些英磅，一也找不见；连它们稍不如人意的替代品——钞票——也找不见。原来在旅游季之外，钞票在卢克索被视作点金石之一种不大靠得住的变体，虽说境遇合宜时确也能变出金子来。年高百岁的阿卜杜勒·阿里死了，他那一个世纪的金磅——它们原也和年金差不多——随他一同死了，而他的儿子穆罕默德（Mohamed），先前便因翘盼此事而享有一种名誉上的头衔，此刻大家却都觉得，他扬起的尘土，未免比一个名正言顺、情真意切的主丧者所该扬起的要多得多。

阿卜杜勒其人，恐怕说不上是那种规矩的体面人；他年高赀丰，却并无多大的令名。他弄得到酒便喝，斋月（Ramadan）里只要食指大动，便照吃不误，且不以此为意；据说他生着一对邪眼（the evil eye）；临终之际侍奉在侧的，又是声名狼藉的艾哈迈德（Achmet）——此人在本地以通晓黑巫术（Black Magic）著称，还因一桩远为下作的勾当而遭人疑心，那便是劫掠新亡者的尸身。因为在埃及，剥古代帝王与祭司之尸的敛衣，是各文明博学的学会竞相逐鹿的特权；而劫取同时代人的尸身，则被视作狗之所为。穆罕默德很快便把往空中抛尘土，换成了更自然的表达懊丧的方式——啃指甲。他私下里告诉我们，他疑心艾哈迈德已探知了他父亲钱财所在；然而眼见他病人奋力想对他交代些什么、却终于归于大寂的当儿，艾哈迈特的脸和别人一样地空白。于是那「他已知道钱财所在」的疑心，在那些有资格品评其为人者心中，便让位于一种颇可怀疑的惋惜——惋惜他刚刚错过了得知那桩紧要事实的机会。

===Original===
So Abdul died and was buried, and we all went to the funeral feast at which we ate more roast meat than one naturally cares about at five in the afternoon on a June day, in consequence of which Weston and I, not requiring dinner, stopped at home after our return from the ride into the desert, and talked to Mohamed, Abdul’s son, and Hussein, Abdul’s youngest grandson, a boy of about twenty, who is also our valet, cook and housemaid, and they together woefully narrated of the money that had been and was not, and told us scandalous tales about Achmet concerning his weakness for cemeteries. They drank coffee and smoked, for though Hussein was our servant, we had been that day the guests of his father, and shortly after they had gone, up came Machmout.

Machmout, who says he thinks he is twelve, but does not know for certain, is kitchen-maid, groom and gardener, and has to an extraordinary degree some occult power resembling clairvoyance. Weston, who is a member of the Society for Psychical Research, and the tragedy of whose life has been the detection of the fraudulent medium Mrs. Blunt, says that it is all thought-reading, and has made notes of many of Machmout’s performances, which may subsequently turn out to be of interest. Thought-reading, however, does not seem to me to fully explain the experience which followed Abdul’s funeral, and with Machmout I have to put it down to White Magic, which should be a very inclusive term, or to Pure Coincidence, which is even more inclusive, and will cover all the inexplicable phenomena of the world, taken singly. Machmout’s method of unloosing the forces of White Magic is simple, being the ink-mirror known by name to many, and it is as follows.

A little black ink is poured into the palm of Machmout’s hand, or, as ink has been at a premium lately owing to the last post-boat from Cairo which contained stationery for us, having stuck on a sandbank, a small piece of black American cloth about an inch in diameter, is found to be a perfect substitute. Upon this he gazes. After five or ten minutes his shrewd monkey-like expression is struck from his face, his eyes, wide open, remain fixed on the cloth, a complete rigidity sets in over his muscles, and he tells us of the curious things he sees. In whatever position he is, in that position he remains without the deflection of a hair’s breadth until the ink is washed off or the cloth removed. Then he looks up and says, “Khalás,” which means, “It is finished.”

===Chinese===
阿卜杜勒就这样死了，下葬了，我们都去吃了丧宴，在六月某日下午五点钟，吞下了比一个人自然而然愿意吃的更多的烤肉。韦斯顿和我因此用不着进晚餐，从骑马进沙漠回来之后便留在屋里，和阿卜杜勒的儿子穆罕默德，以及阿卜杜勒最小的孙子侯赛因（Hussein）说话。侯赛因是个二十岁上下的少年，同时兼做我们的贴身仆役、厨子和女佣。他们两人一同凄然地讲述了那笔曾经有过、如今却无影无踪的钱财，又讲了几桩关于艾哈迈德的丑闻，说他癖好坟场。他们喝着咖啡，抽着烟——侯赛因虽是我们的仆役，那天我们却做过他父亲的座上客——他们刚走，马赫穆特（Machmout）便上来了。

马赫穆特自以为十二岁，却也说不准，他是我们的厨房丫头、马夫兼园丁，并天生一股异乎寻常的、类乎天眼通（clairvoyance）的玄秘本领。韦斯顿是心灵研究学会（Society for Psychical Research）的会员，他平生一大恨事，便是戳穿那个弄虚作假的灵媒布伦特太太（Mrs. Blunt），据他说马赫穆特那一切不过是读心术（thought-reading），并已把马赫穆特的许多次表演记录下来，日后说不定会显得颇有趣味。然而在我看来，读心术并不能将阿卜杜勒葬礼之后的那番经历解释圆全；和马赫穆特一道，我只得把它归之于白巫术（White Magic）——这本是个极能兼容的术语——或归于纯粹巧合（Pure Coincidence），此词更其兼容，把世上一切不可思议的现象、逐个看来，都一概覆盖了。马赫穆特释放白巫术之力所用的法门很简单，便是许多人久闻其名的墨镜法，做法如下。

把少许黑墨倒进马赫穆特的掌心，或者——由于近来墨水紧缺（上次从开罗运我们文具的那班邮船在沙洲上搁了浅），一块直径约一英寸的黑色美国布（American cloth）小片，被发现完全可以替代。他便凝视着它。五或十分钟后，他那精明如猴的表情从他脸上褪去，他双目大睁，定定地凝在那布片上，周身的肌肉陷入一种彻底的僵直，于是他便向我们讲述他所看见的种种奇事。无论他原是何姿势，便一毫不差地保持着那姿势，直到墨被洗去、或布片被取走。然后他抬起头，说一声「Khalás」，意思是：「完了。」

===Original===
We only engaged Machmout’s services as second general domestic a fortnight ago, but the first evening he was with us he came upstairs when he had finished his work, and said, “I will show you White Magic; give me ink,” and proceeded to describe the front hall of our house in London, saying that there were two horses at the door, and that a man and woman soon came out, gave the horses each a piece of bread and mounted. The thing was so probable that by the next mail I wrote asking my mother to write down exactly what she was doing and where at half past five (English time) on the evening of June 12. At the corresponding time in Egypt Machmout was describing speaking to us of a “sitt” (lady) having tea in a room which he described with some minuteness, and I am waiting anxiously for her letter. The explanation which Weston gives us of all these phenomena, is that a certain picture of people I know is present in my mind, though I may not be aware of it﻿—present to my subliminal self, I think, he says﻿—and that I give an unspoken suggestion to the hypnotised Machmout. My explanation is that there isn’t any explanation, for no suggestion on my part would make my brother go out and ride at the moment when Machmout says he is so doing (if indeed we find that Machmout’s visions are chronologically correct). Consequently I prefer the open mind and am prepared to believe anything. Weston, however, does not speak quite so calmly or scientifically about Machmout’s last performance, and since it took place, he has almost entirely ceased to urge me to become a member of the Society for Psychical Research, in order that I may no longer be hidebound by vain superstitions.

Machmout will not exercise these powers if his own folk are present, for he says that when he is in this state, if a man who knew Black Magic was in the room, or knew that he was practising White Magic, he could get the spirit who presides over the Black Magic to kill the spirit of White Magic, for the Black Magic is the more potent, and the two are foes. And as the spirit of White Magic is on occasions a powerful friend﻿—he had before now befriended Machmout in a manner which I consider incredible﻿—Machmout is very desirous that he should abide long with him. But Englishmen it appears do not know the Black Magic, so with us he is safe. The spirit of Black Magic, to speak to whom it is death, Machmout saw once “between heaven and earth, and night and day,” so he phrases it, on the Karnak road. He may be known, he told us, by the fact that he is of paler skin than his people, that he has two long teeth, one in each corner of his mouth, and that his eyes, which are white all over, are as big as the eyes of a horse.

Machmout squatted himself comfortably in the corner, and I gave him the piece of black American cloth. As some minutes must elapse before he gets into the hypnotic state in which the visions begin, I strolled out on to the balcony for coolness. It was the hottest night we had yet had, and though the sun had set three hours, the thermometer still registered close on 100°. Above, the sky seemed veiled with grey, where it should have been dark velvety blue, and a fitful puffing wind from the south threatened three days of the sandy intolerable khamsin. A little way up the street to the left was a small café in front of which were glowing and waning little glowworm specks of light from the water pipes of Arabs sitting out there in the dark. From inside came the click of brass castanets in the hands of some dancing-girl, sounding sharp and precise against the wailing bagpipe music of the strings and pipes which accompany these movements which Arabs love and Europeans think so unpleasing. Eastwards the sky was paler and luminous, for the moon was imminently rising, and even as I looked the red rim of the enormous disc cut the line of the desert, and on the instant with a curious aptness, one of the Arabs outside the café broke out into that wonderful chant﻿

> “I cannot sleep for longing for thee, O full moon
 
 Far is thy throne over Mecca, slip down, O beloved, to me.”

Immediately afterwards I heard the piping monotone of Machmout’s voice begin, and in a moment or two I went inside.

===Chinese===
我们雇马赫穆特来做第二杂役才不过半月，但他来我们这里的头一个晚上，干完活便上楼来说：「我给你演白巫术；给我墨水。」接着便描述起我们伦敦宅子的前厅，说门口拴着两匹马，不久一男一女走出来，各给马喂了一块面包，便上了马。这事听来十分可信，于是趁下一班邮船，我写信请母亲把 6 月 12 日傍晚五点半（英国时间）她究竟在做何事、在何处一一记下。在埃及对应的时刻，马赫穆特正向我们描述、并告诉我们有一位「sitt」（女士）在某间屋里用茶，那屋子被他描绘得相当细致，而我正焦灼地等着她的回信。韦斯顿对所有这些现象的解释是：我心头浮着我所认识的某些人的某个画面，尽管我也许并不自觉——他说，是浮现在我的潜意识之我（subliminal self）之前的罢——而我对被催眠的马赫穆特作了一种无言的暗示。我的解释则是：根本没有解释。因为不论我怎样暗示，总不能叫我兄弟偏在马赫穆特说他正在外头骑马的当儿，当真出去骑马（倘若我们果然查明马赫穆特所见在时刻上分毫不差的话）。于是我宁可心存开阔，什么 都准备去信。然而说起马赫穆特最近这一回，韦斯顿的口吻便不怎么从容，也不怎么科学了；自那事发生以来，他几乎已不再劝我入心灵研究学会，好教我不再为虚妄的迷信所拘。

马赫穆特若自有族人在场，便不肯施这一手，因为他说，他在这等状态之中，倘若屋里有一个懂黑巫术的人，或那人知晓他在修习白巫术，那便可请黑巫术所主之灵，去杀白巫术之灵，因黑巫术更为凶强，而二者本是仇雠。而白巫术之灵偶尔是个有力的盟友——它曾以我以为匪夷所思的方式护佑过马赫穆特——马赫穆特便极盼它能长留己身。好在英国人似乎不懂黑巫术，他和我们在一起便无碍。那与之一语便致死的黑巫术之灵，马赫穆特曾在凯尔奈克（Karnak）大道上见过一回，「在天与地之间、夜与昼之间，」他这样措辞。他说，要认出他来，可凭这几样：他的肤色比他的族人更浅；嘴里两边各生一颗长牙；他的双眼通体皆白，大如马眼。

马赫穆特在角落里舒舒服服地蹲下，我把那块黑色美国布片递给他。他进入幻象初生的催眠状态尚需几分钟，我便踱到阳台上去纳凉。这是我们到此以来最热的一夜，太阳虽已落了三个钟头，温度计上仍将近 100 度。头顶的天该是幽暗如绒的深蓝，此刻却似蒙着一层灰；一阵一阵、一股一股的南风，预示着接下去要有三日叫人难耐的沙尘喀新风（khamsin）。左边街上去不多远，有一家小小的咖啡馆，门前的黑暗里，阿拉伯人坐着抽水烟，烟锅里的小小光点如萤火般忽明忽灭。屋里头传来某个舞女手中铜响板的叩击声，清脆而精准，衬在弦与管的伴乐那种哀号的风笛声之上——正是为阿拉伯人所喜、而为欧洲人所厌的那些动作的伴奏。东边的天色更淡、更亮，月亮将升，我正看着，那巨大的红边圆盘便切入了沙漠的天际线；说时迟那时快，带着一种古怪的应景，咖啡馆外的一个阿拉伯人忽地放声唱起那支奇妙的歌——

> 「因思慕你，我难成眠，啊，满月。
 你宝座远在麦加（Mecca）之上，降临吧，我所爱，到我身边。」

紧接着我便听见马赫穆特那尖细单调的嗓音开始了，过不了一会儿我便回到屋里。

===Original===
We have found that the experiments gave the quickest result by contact, a fact which confirmed Weston in his explanation of them by thought transference of some elaborate kind, which I confess I cannot understand. He was writing at a table in the window when I came in, but looked up.

“Take his hand,” he said, “at present he is quite incoherent.”

“Do you explain that?” I asked.

“It is closely analogous, so Myers thinks, to talking in sleep. He has been saying something about a tomb. Do make a suggestion, and see if he gives it right. He is remarkably sensitive and he responds quicker to you than to me. Probably Abdul’s funeral suggested the tomb!”

A sudden thought struck me.

“Hush!” I said, “I want to listen.”

Machmout’s head was thrown a little back, and he held the hand in which was the piece of cloth rather above his face. As usual he was talking very slowly, and in a high staccato voice, absolutely unlike his usual tones.

“On one side of the grave,” he piped, “is a tamarisk tree, and the green beetles make fantasia about it. On the other side is a mud wall. There are many other graves about, but they are all asleep. This is the grave, because it is awake, and is moist and not sandy.”

“I thought so,” said Weston. “It is Abdul’s grave he is talking about.”

“There is a red moon sitting on the desert,” continued Machmout, “and it is now. There is the puffing of khamsin, and much dust coming. The moon is red with dust, and because it is low.”

“Still sensitive to external conditions,” said Weston. “That is rather curious. Pinch him, will you?”

I pinched Machmout; he did not pay the slightest attention.

“In the last house of the street, and in the doorway stands a man. Ah! ah!” cried the boy suddenly, “it is the Black Magic he knows. Don’t let him come. He is going out of the house,” he shrieked, “he is coming﻿—no, he is going the other way, towards the moon and the grave. He has the Black Magic with him, which can raise the dead, and he has a murdering knife, and a spade. I cannot see his face for the Black Magic is between it and my eyes.”

Weston had got up, and, like me, was hanging on Machmout’s words.

“We will go there,” he said. “Here is an opportunity of testing it. Listen a moment.”

“He is walking, walking, walking,” piped Machmout, “still walking to the moon and the grave. The moon sits no longer on the desert, but has sprung up a little way.”

I pointed out of the window.

“That at any rate is true,” I said.

Weston took the cloth out of Machmout’s hand, and the piping ceased. In a moment he stretched himself, and rubbed his eyes.

“Khalás,” he said.

“Yes, it is Khalás.”

“Did I tell you of the sitt in England?” he asked.

“Yes, oh, yes,” I answered; “thank you, little Machmout. The White Magic was very good tonight. Get you to bed.”

Machmout trotted obediently out of the room, and Weston closed the door after him.

“We must be quick,” he said. “It is worth while going and giving the thing a chance, though I wish he had seen something less gruesome. The odd thing is that he was not at the funeral, and yet he describes the grave accurately. What do you make of it?”

“I make that the White Magic has shown Machmout that somebody with Black Magic is going to Abdul’s grave, perhaps to rob it,” I answered resolutely.

“What are we to do when we get there?” asked Weston.

“See the Black Magic at work. Personally I am in a blue funk. So are you.”

“There is no such thing as Black Magic,” said Weston. “Ah, I have it. Give me that orange.”

Weston rapidly skinned it, and cut from the rind two circles as big as a five shilling piece, and two long, white fangs of skin. The first he fixed in his eye, the two latter in the corners of his mouth.

“The spirit of Black Magic?” I asked.

“The same.”

He took up a long black burnous and wrapped it round him. Even in the bright lamp light, the spirit of Black Magic was a sufficiently terrific personage.

“I don’t believe in Black Magic,” he said, “but others do. If it is necessary to put a stop to﻿—to anything that is going on, we will hoist the man on his own petard. Come along. Whom do you suspect it is﻿—I mean, of course, who was the person you were thinking of when your thoughts were transferred to Machmout.”

“What Machmout said,” I answered, “suggested Achmet to me.”

Weston indulged in a laugh of scientific incredulity, and we set off.

===Chinese===
我们发现这些实验只要一加接触，便出结果最快，这一层越发坐实了韦斯顿的解释——他用的是某种繁复的心灵感应之术，这一点我坦言我弄不明白。我进屋时他正坐在窗前一张桌旁写字，抬头道：

「握住他的手，」他说，「此刻他说的话还全无条理。」

「这你怎么解？」我问。

「迈尔斯（Myers）以为，这和梦话极相近。他方才说了些什么坟啊墓的。你不妨给他一个暗示，看他答得对不对。他异常灵敏，对你的应比对我要快。多半是阿卜杜勒的葬礼引出了那座墓！」

我忽然起了一个念头。

「嘘！」我说，「我要听一听。」

马赫穆特的头微微后仰，那只攥着布片的手举得略高于面孔。他一如既往地说得很慢，嗓音高亢而断续，和他平时的腔调全然两样。

「坟的一边，」他尖声道，「有一棵柽柳，绿色的甲虫围着它作狂欢。另一边是一道土墙。四下里还有许多别的坟，可它们都睡着。这一座却是 那座坟，因为它是醒着的，而且湿润，不是沙的。」

「我料是如此，」韦斯顿说，「他说的是阿卜杜勒的坟。」

「有一轮红月亮坐在沙漠上，」马赫穆特接着说，「就是现在。有喀新风的噗噗声，许多尘土来了。月亮因尘土而发红，也因它低。」

「对外界条件依旧敏感，」韦斯顿说，「这倒颇奇。你掐他一下，好吗？」

我掐了马赫穆特一下；他全不理会。

「在这条街最后一所屋子里，门口站着一个人。啊！啊！」那孩子忽然叫起来，「他懂的是黑巫术。别让他过来。他出了屋了，」他尖叫道，「他来了——不，他往另一头去了，朝着月亮和坟那边。他身上带着那黑巫术，能叫死人复活，他还带着一把杀人的刀，一把铲子。我看不见他的脸，因为黑巫术隔在他脸和我的眼之间。」

韦斯顿已站了起来，和我一样，屏息悬在马赫穆特的字句上。

「我们去那儿，」他说，「这正是个验证的机会。且听他说。」

「他在走，走，走，」马赫穆特尖声道，「仍在朝着月亮和坟走。月亮不再坐在沙漠上了，已跳起来一点。」

我朝窗外一指。

「至少这一点是真的。」我说。

韦斯顿从马赫穆特手里取走布片，那尖细的嗓音便止了。不一时他伸了个懒腰，揉揉眼睛。

「Khalás。」他说。

「是的，是 Khalás。」

「我有没有跟你说英国那位 sitt？」他问。

「说了，哦，说了，」我答道，「谢谢你，小马赫穆特。今夜的白巫术很好。去睡吧。」

马赫穆特乖乖地小跑着出了屋子，韦斯顿随手把门带上。

「我们得快，」他说，「值得去走一遭，给这事一个机会，只可惜他见的不是什么更舒坦的景象。奇的是他并未去送葬，却把那坟形容得分毫不差。你怎么看？」

「我看，是白巫术让马赫穆特看见了一个带着黑巫术的人，正往阿卜杜勒的坟上去，也许是去盗坟。」我毅然答道。

「我们到了那儿，又当如何？」韦斯顿问。

「看那黑巫术施为。就我个人而论，我害怕得要命。你也一样。」

「世上根本没有黑巫术这回事，」韦斯顿说，「啊，有了。把那只橙子给我。」

韦斯顿飞快地剥开橙子，从橙皮上剪下两片如五先令硬币大小的圆片，和两根长长的、白色的尖牙。前者他嵌在眼里，后者嵌在嘴的两角。

「黑巫术之灵？」我问。

「正是。」

他抓起一件长长的黑色斗篷（burnous）把自己裹上。便在明亮的灯光下，这位黑巫术之灵也够叫人望之生畏了。

「我并不信黑巫术，」他说，「可别人信。倘若有必要去阻止——去阻止任何正在进行的勾当，咱们就以其人之道还治其人之身。走吧。你疑心是谁——当然，我指的是，当你的念头传给马赫穆特那一刻，你心里想的是谁。」

「马赫穆特所说的那番话，」我答道，「叫我想到艾哈迈德。」

韦斯顿发出一声科学上的不信之笑，我们便动身了。

===Original===
