The moon, as the boy had told us, was just clear of the horizon, and as it rose higher, its colour at first red and sombre, like the blaze of some distant conflagration, paled to a tawny yellow. The hot wind from the south, blowing no longer fitfully but with a steadily increasing violence was thick with sand, and of an incredibly scorching heat, and the tops of the palm trees in the garden of the deserted hotel on the right were lashing themselves to and fro with a harsh rattle of dry leaves. The cemetery lay on the outskirts of the village, and, as long as our way lay between the mud walls of the huddling street, the wind came to us only as the heat from behind closed furnace doors. Every now and then with a whisper and whistle rising into a great buffeting flap, a sudden whirlwind of dust would scour some twenty yards along the road, and then break like a shore-quenched wave against one or other of the mud walls or throw itself heavily against a house and fall in a shower of sand. But once free of obstructions we were opposed to the full heat and blast of the wind which blew full in our teeth. It was the first summer khamsin of the year, and for the moment I wished I had gone north with the tourist and the quail and the billiard marker, for khamsin fetches the marrow out of the bones, and turns the body to blotting paper. We passed no one in the street, and the only sound we heard, except the wind, was the howling of moonstruck dogs.

The cemetery is surrounded by a tall mud-built wall, and sheltering for a few moments under this we discussed our movements. The row of tamarisks close to which the tomb lay went down the centre of the graveyard, and by skirting the wall outside and climbing softly over where they approached it, the fury of the wind might help us to get near the grave without being seen, if anyone happened to be there. We had just decided on this, and were moving on to put the scheme into execution, when the wind dropped for a moment, and in the silence we could hear the chump of the spade being driven into the earth, and what gave me a sudden thrill of intimate horror, the cry of the carrion-feeding hawk from the dusty sky just overhead.

Two minutes later we were creeping up in the shade of the tamarisks, to where Abdul had been buried. The great green beetles which live on the trees were flying about blindly, and once or twice one dashed into my face with a whirr of mail-clad wings. When we were within some twenty yards of the grave we stopped for a moment, and, looking cautiously out from our shelter of tamarisks, saw the figure of a man already waist deep in the earth, digging out the newly turned grave. Weston, who was standing behind me had adjusted the characteristics of the spirit of Black Magic so as to be ready for emergencies, and turning round suddenly, and finding myself unawares face to face with that realistic impersonation, though my nerves are not precariously strong, I could have found it within me to shriek aloud. But that unsympathetic man of iron only shook with suppressed laughter, and, holding the eyes in his hand, motioned me forward again without speaking to where the trees grew thicker. There we stood not a dozen yards away from the grave.

===Chinese===
正如那孩子所说，月亮刚刚离开地平线；它升得越高，起初那种如远方火警般红而沉的色泽，便渐渐淡成了褐黄。南来的热风已不再一阵阵的，而是带着稳步加猛的势头，沙浓风炽，热得叫人难以置信。右边那家空无人住的旅馆的花园里，椰枣树的树顶在风中剧烈地来回抽打，干叶发出粗厉的沙沙声。坟场在村外，只要我们的路还夹在那条拥塞街道的土墙之间，风来到我们身上便只是关着的炉门后透出的那种热。时不时地，带着一阵低语与尖啸、继而化作一记猛烈的扑打，一阵突如其来的尘卷便会沿着路面扫过二十来码，然后如拍岸即灭的浪头一般撞在某一堵土墙上粉碎，或重重地撞向一所宅子，落下一阵沙雨。可一旦离开遮蔽，我们便正对着那风的全副炽热与冲击，迎面扑来。这是当年头一场夏日的喀新风，那一刻我真愿自己当初也随游客、鹌鹑和记分员一同北去了，因为喀新风能把骨髓从骨头里榨出来，把身体化作吸墨纸。我们在街上没碰见一个人，除了风声，所听见的只有中了月华之毒的狗的嚎叫。

坟场四周绕着一道高高的土墙，我们在墙下避了片刻，商议行止。墓旁的那一排柽柳顺着坟场中央延展下去，只要沿外墙绕过去，在柽柳挨近墙处轻轻翻入，借助风的狂烈，我们便可不被人察觉地挨近那座坟——倘若当真有人在的话。我们刚刚定下此计，正要上前付诸实施，风忽然停了一瞬，在那随之而来的寂静里，我们听得见铲子切入泥土的闷响；还有——令我陡然一阵切肤的战栗的——就在我们头顶那沙尘弥漫的天空里，那只食腐之鹰的叫声。

两分钟后，我们便借着柽柳的荫蔽，向阿卜杜勒下葬之处悄悄摸上去。栖在树上的那些硕大的绿甲虫盲目地乱飞，有一两只带着披甲振翅的呼响撞到我脸上。我们离坟还有约莫二十码时，停了一停，从柽柳的掩蔽后小心地探看出去，便瞧见一个人的身影，已半身没入土中，正在掘开那座新翻的坟。韦斯顿立在我身后，已把黑巫术之灵那几样特征调整就位，以备不时之需；我猛一回头，猝不及防地和那副惟妙惟肖的扮相打了个照面——虽说我的神经还算不得脆弱，那一刻我也险些要放声大叫。可那位毫无同情的铁人只是憋着笑，浑身直抖，手里捏着那对假眼，一声不响地示意我再往前走，走到树木更密之处。我们便立在那里，离坟不过十几码。

===Original===
We waited, I suppose, for some ten minutes, while the man, whom we saw to be Achmet, toiled on at his impious task. He was entirely naked, and his brown skin glistened with the dews of exertion in the moonlight. At times he chattered in a cold uncanny manner to himself, and once or twice he stopped for breath. Then he began scraping the earth away with his hands, and soon afterwards searched in his clothes which were lying near for a piece of rope, with which he stepped into the grave, and in a moment reappeared again with both ends in his hands. Then, standing astride the grave, he pulled strongly, and one end of the coffin appeared above the ground. He chipped a piece of the lid away to make sure that he had the right end, and then, setting it upright, wrenched off the top with his knife and there faced us leaning against the coffin lid, the small shrivelled figure of the dead Abdul, swathed like a baby in white.

I was just about to motion the spirit of Black Magic to make his appearance, when Machmout’s words came into my head: “He has with him the Black Magic which can raise the dead,” and sudden overwhelming curiosity, which froze disgust and horror into chill unfeeling things, came over me.

“Wait,” I whispered to Weston, “he will use the Black Magic.”

Again the wind dropped for a moment, and again, in the silence that came with it, I heard the chiding of the hawk overhead, this time nearer, and thought I heard more birds than one.

Achmet meantime had taken the covering from off the face, and had undone the swathing band, which at the moment after death is bound round the chin to close the jaw, and in Arab burial is always left there, and from where we stood I could see that the jaw dropped when the bandage was untied, as if, though the wind blew towards us with a ghastly scent of mortality on it, the muscles were not even now set, though the man had been dead sixty hours. But still a rank and burning curiosity to see what this unclean ghoul would do next stifled all other feelings in my mind. He seemed not to notice, or, at any rate, to disregard that mouth gaping awry, and moved about nimbly in the moonlight.

He took from a pocket of his clothes, which were lying near, two small black objects, which now are safely embedded in the mud at the bottom of the Nile, and rubbed them briskly together. By degrees they grew luminous with a sickly yellow pallor of light, and from his hands went up a wavy, phosphorescent flame. One of these cubes he placed in the open mouth of the corpse, the other in his own, and, taking the dead man closely in his arms as though he would indeed dance with death, he breathed long breaths from his mouth into that dead cavern which was pressed to his. Suddenly he started back with a quick-drawn breath of wonder and perhaps of horror, and stood for a space as if irresolute, for the cube which the dead man held instead of lying loosely in the jaw, was pressed tight between clenched teeth. After a moment of irresolution he stepped back quickly to his clothes again, and took up from near them the knife with which he had stripped off the coffin lid, and holding this in one hand behind his back, with the other he took out the cube from the dead man’s mouth, though with a visible exhibition of force, and spoke.

“Abdul,” he said, “I am your friend, and I swear I will give your money to Mohamed, if you will tell me where it is.”

===Chinese===
我想，我们等了约莫十分钟，那人——我们看清了是艾哈迈德——在那件亵渎的活计上不停地劳作。他浑身赤裸，棕色的皮肤在月光下因劳作的汗水而闪亮。他时不时冷冷地、诡异地自言自语，有一两回停下来喘气。然后他开始用手扒土，不久又到他放在一旁的衣服里去摸一段绳子，拿着它跨进坟里，不一刻又两手各执一端冒了出来。接着，他跨立在坟上，用力一拽，棺木的一端便露出了地面。他从棺盖上敲下一块，确认自己拽的是对的那一头，然后把它竖起来，用刀撬去顶盖——于是面对着我们、倚在棺盖上的，便是已死的阿卜杜勒那具干瘪瘦小的身形，如婴孩一般裹在白布里。

我正要让黑巫术之灵现身上场，马赫穆特的话却浮上心头：「他身上带着那黑巫术，能叫死人复活。」一阵突如其来的、压倒一切的好奇心油然而生，把嫌恶与恐惧都冻成了冰冷的、无知无觉之物。

「等等，」我低声对韦斯顿说，「他要施那黑巫术了。」

风又停了一瞬，在随之而来的寂静里，我又一次听见头顶那只鹰的啼叫，这一回更近了些，而且我仿佛听见的，不止一只。

与此同时，艾哈迈德已揭去了尸身脸上的盖布，解开了那条裹带——人一死便要缠住下颌、把嘴合上的那条带子，阿拉伯人下葬时总留着它不解。从我们站立之处可以看见，带子一解开，那下巴便耷拉下来，仿佛——尽管风朝我们吹来，带着一股可怖的朽亡之气——尽管这人已死了六十个钟头，肌肉至今未曾僵定。然而一股炽烈而难耐的好奇，要看看这不洁的食尸鬼下一步将做什么，把我心头别的一切感受都扼杀了。他似乎不曾注意，至少是不理会那张歪张着的嘴，只在月光下灵巧地来回走动。

他从放在一旁的衣服口袋里，取出两件小小的黑色物件——如今它们已稳稳地嵌在尼罗河河底的淤泥里——并把它们飞快地相互摩擦。渐渐地，它们亮了起来，发出一种病态的、苍黄的微光，一团摇曳的、磷火般的火焰从他手上腾起。他把其中一个小方块放进尸身张开的嘴里，另一个放进自己嘴里，把那死人紧紧搂在怀里，仿佛当真要与死神共舞一般，从自己嘴里向那紧贴着的、死寂的洞穴一口一口地长长吹气。猛然间他倒抽一口冷气退了回去，那口气里像是惊异，也像是恐惧；他呆立了一会儿，似乎踌躇不决——因为那死人含着的小方块并没有松松地搁在下颌之间，而是被紧咬的牙关死死咬住了。踌躇片刻之后，他快步回到衣服那边，从近旁拾起那把撬掉棺盖用的刀，一手把它藏在背后，另一手费了好大可见的力气，才把小方块从死人嘴里取出，开口说道：

「阿卜杜勒，」他说，「我是你的朋友，我发誓我会把你的钱给穆罕默德，只要你告诉我钱在哪里。」

===Original===
Certain I am that the lips of the dead moved, and the eyelids fluttered for a moment like the wings of a wounded bird, but at that sight, the horror so grew on me that I was physically incapable of stifling the cry that rose to my lips, and Achmet turned round. Next moment the complete Spirit of Black Magic glided out of the shade of the trees, and stood before him. The wretched man stood for a moment without stirring, then, turning with shaking knees to flee, he stepped back and fell into the grave he had just opened.

Weston turned on me angrily, dropping the eyes and the teeth of the Afreet.

“You spoiled it all,” he cried. “It would perhaps have been the most interesting﻿ ﻿…” and his eye lighted on the dead Abdul, who peered open-eyed from the coffin, then swayed, tottered, and fell forward, face downwards on the ground close to him. For one moment he lay there, and then the body rolled slowly on to its back without visible cause of movement, and lay staring into the sky. The face was covered with dust, but with the dust was mingled fresh blood. A nail had caught the cloth that wound him, underneath which as usual were the clothes in which he had died, for the Arabs do not wash their dead, and it had torn a great rent through them all, leaving the right shoulder bare.

Weston strove to speak once, but failed. Then:

“I will go and inform the police,” he said, “if you will stop here, and see that Achmet does not get out.”

But this I altogether refused to do, and, after covering the body with the coffin to protect it from the hawks, we secured Achmet’s arms with the rope he had already used that night, and took him off to Luxor.

Next morning Mohamed came to see us.

“I thought Achmet knew where the money was,” he said exultantly.

“Where was it?”

“In a little purse tied round the shoulder. The dog had already begun stripping it. See”—and he brought it out of his pocket—“it is all there in those English notes, five pounds each, and there are twenty of them.”

Our conclusion was slightly different, for even Weston will allow that Achmet hoped to learn from dead lips the secret of the treasure, and then to kill him anew and bury him. But that is pure conjecture.

The only other point of interest lies in the two black cubes which we picked up, and found to be graven with curious characters. These I put one evening into Machmout’s hand, when he was exhibiting to us his curious powers of “thought transference.” The effect was that he screamed aloud, crying out that the Black Magic had come, and though I did not feel certain about that, I thought they would be safer in mid-Nile. Weston grumbled a little, and said that he had wanted to take them to the British Museum, but that I feel sure was an afterthought.

===Chinese===
我可以确定的是：那死人的嘴唇动了一下，眼皮也如一只受伤之鸟的翅膀般颤动了一瞬。可一见这情景，那恐惧在我心头越发膨胀，以致我肉体上再也没法压住冲到唇边的那声喊，艾哈迈德回过头来。说时迟那时快，完整的黑巫术之灵从树荫里悄无声息地滑了出来，立在他面前。那可怜的人呆立了一瞬，一动不动，然后两膝打着颤转身要逃，一退步，便跌进了他自己刚掘开的那座坟里。

韦斯顿恼怒地朝我转过身来，丢下了那阿非利（Afreet）的眼和牙。

「你把一切都毁了，」他叫道，「那也许会是最有趣的一桩……」可他的目光落到那已死的阿卜杜勒身上——那人睁着眼从棺里向外张望——接着摇晃起来，踉跄着向前一栽，面朝下扑倒在他跟前的地上。他那样躺了一瞬，然后那尸身缓缓地、无可见外因地滚了过来，仰面朝天，瞪着天空。脸上满是尘土，可尘土里混着新鲜的血。一枚钉子挂住了裹尸的布——布下照例是他咽气时穿的衣服，因为阿拉伯人不为亡者沐浴——那钉子把衣料连裹布一齐撕开一道大口子，露出右肩来。

韦斯顿想说话，张了张嘴，却没说出来。然后道：

「我去报警察，」他说，「你留在这里，看着艾哈迈德别叫他爬出来。」

但我断然不肯。我们用那绳子——他当夜已用过一回的——把棺木盖在尸身上，免得它被鹰啄去，然后捆住艾哈迈特的胳膊，把他押回了卢克索。

第二天早上，穆罕默德来看我们。

「我原就想着艾哈迈德知道钱在哪里。」他得意洋洋地说。

「在哪里？」

「在一只小钱袋里，系在肩膀底下。那狗已经动手扒它了。瞧——」他从口袋里掏出它来，「全在这里头，那些英国钞票，每张五镑，一共二十张。」

我们的结论却略有不同，因为便是韦斯顿也肯承认：艾哈迈德原本巴望从死人口中探出那笔钱财的秘密，然后再把他新杀一回、重新埋掉。但这纯属揣测。

另一桩有意思之处，在于我们拾到的那两个黑色小方块，发现上面刻着古怪的字符。某日傍晚，趁马赫穆特向我们展示他那古怪的「读心术」本领之时，我把它们放进他手里。其结果是：他失声尖叫，大喊黑巫术来了。虽说这事我也不敢打包票，我想它们还是放在尼罗河中央比较稳妥。韦斯顿嘀咕了几句，说他本想带它们去大英博物馆的，但我敢肯定那不过是事后一想。

## At the Farmhouse / 在那座农舍

===Original===
The dusk of a November day was falling fast when John Aylsford came out of his lodging in the cobbled street and started to walk briskly along the road which led eastwards by the shore of the bay. He had been at work while the daylight served him, and now, when the gathering darkness weaned him from his easel, he was accustomed to go out for air and exercise and cover half a dozen miles before he returned to his solitary supper.
Tonight there were but few folk abroad, and those scudded along before the strong southwesterly gale which had roared and raged all day, or, leaning forward, beat their way against it. No fishing-boats had put forth on that maddened sea, but had lain moored behind the quay-wall, tossing uneasily with the backwash of the great breakers that swept by the pier-head. The tide was low now, and they rested on the sandy beach, black blots against the smooth wet surface which sombrely reflected the last flames in the west. The sun had gone down in a wrack of broken and flying clouds, angry and menacing with promise of a wild night to come.

===Chinese===
十一月一个日子的暮色正急速地沉落下来，约翰·艾尔斯福德（John Aylsford）从他鹅卵石小街上的寓所里走出，沿着那条沿海湾东岸蜿蜒的道路，迈着轻快的步子走去。趁着天光尚亮，他一直在作画；如今渐浓的暗色把他从画架前支开，照他素来的习惯，总要出去透透气、活动活动，走上个六英里，才回他那冷清的晚饭去。
今夜出门的人寥寥无几，那几个也都是在那一整天呼啸肆虐的强劲西南大风前匆匆赶路，或者弓着身子、迎着风艰难地往前闯。渔船没有一艘开到那发了疯似的海上去，都系在防波堤后头，随着扫过堤头的滔天巨浪退下来的回涌，不安地颠簸摇摆。如今潮水退了，它们便搁在沙滩上，衬着那平滑湿润、阴沉沉地映着西方最后几缕余晖的沙面，像是一块块黑色的污渍。太阳已在一堆破碎飞驰的云翳里落下去了，带着怒色，带着凶兆，预示着夜里将有一场狂风骤起。

===Original===
For many days past, at this hour John Aylsford had started eastwards for his tramp along the rough coast road by the bay. The last high tide had swept shingle and sand over sections of it, and fragments of seaweed, driven by the wind, bowled along the ruts. The heavy boom of the breakers sounded sullenly in the dusk, and white towers of foam appearing and disappearing showed how high they leaped over the reefs of rock beyond the headland. For half a mile or so, slanting himself against the gale he pursued this road, then turned up a narrow muddy lane sunk deep between the banks on either side of it. It ran steeply uphill, dipped down again, and joined the main road inland. Having arrived at the junction, John Aylsford went eastwards no more, but turned his steps to the west, arriving, half an hour after he had set out, on the top of the hill above the village he had quitted, though five minutes’ ascent would have taken him from his lodgings to the spot where he now stood looking down on the scattered lights below him. The wind had blown all wayfarers indoors, and now in front of him the road that crossed this high and desolate tableland, sprinkled here and there with lonely cottages and solitary farms, lay empty and greyly glimmering in the windswept darkness, not more than faintly visible.

===Chinese===
连日来，每到这个时候，约翰·艾尔斯福德便朝东出发，沿着海湾边那条崎岖的海岸路跋涉。上一回的大潮把卵石和沙子卷到了路的好几段上，被风驱赶着的碎海草在车辙里一路滚将过去。巨浪沉重的轰鸣在暮色里沉闷地响着，那忽隐忽现的一座座白色泡沫塔，显出它们在海岬那边的礁石上跃起得有多高。他把身子斜倾着顶住风，沿着这条路走了半英里光景，便拐进一条窄窄的、泥泞的小巷，那巷子深深陷在两旁的土堤之间。它陡峭地上坡，又重新陷下去，与通往内陆的大路汇合。到了这个岔口，约翰·艾尔斯福德便不再往东，而是折向西行，出发半小时后，便到了他所离开的那个村庄上方的小山顶上——其实从寓所只要爬五分钟坡，便能到他此刻站着俯瞰下方零星灯火的地方。风把所有的行路人都赶进了屋，此刻在他面前，那条横穿这片高峻荒凉的高地、零星散布着孤零零的村舍和独门独户的农庄的道路，空空荡荡，在风扫过的黑暗里泛着灰蒙蒙的微光，影影绰绰，几乎难以辨认。

===Original===
Many times during this past month had John Aylsford made this long detour, starting eastwards from the village and coming back by a wide circuit, and now, as on these other occasions, he paused in the black shelter of the hedge through which the wind hissed and whistled, crouching there in the shadow as if to make sure that none had followed him, and that the road in front lay void of passengers, for he had no mind to be observed by any on these journeyings. And as he paused he let his hate blaze up, warming him for the work the accomplishment of which alone could enable him to recapture any peace or profit from life. Tonight he was determined to release himself from the millstone which for so many years had hung round his neck, drowning him in bitter waters. From long brooding over the idea of the deed, he had quite ceased to feel any horror of it. The death of that drunken slut was not a matter for qualms or uneasiness; the world would be well rid of her, and he more than well.

===Chinese===
在过去这一个月里，约翰·艾尔斯福德已经许多回走这长长的弯路，从村东出发，又兜一个大圈回来；此刻，和那几回一样，他在树篱黑黢黢的掩蔽下停住脚，风从树篱间尖啸而过，他蹲伏在阴影里，仿佛要确认身后无人跟随，面前这条路也空无行人，因为他不愿在这些行走中被人瞧见。他停着脚，便任凭自己心头那股恨意熊熊烧起，为他即将要做的事暖暖身子——唯有做成了那件事，他才能从人生里重新讨回半分安宁或好处。今夜他下了决心，要把自己从那块多年来挂在他脖子上、把他溺在苦水里的磨石底下解脱出来。杀念在心头盘桓日久，他早已对它没有半点骇怕了。那个醉醺醺的贱人之死，算不得教人惊惶不安的事；世上少了她只会更好，于他更其如此。

===Original===
No spark of tenderness for the handsome fisher-girl who once had been his model and for twenty years had been his wife pierced the blackness of his purpose. Just here it was that he had seen her first when on a summer holiday he had lodged with a couple of friends in the farmhouse towards which his way now lay. She was coming up the hill with the late sunset gilding her face, and, breathing quickly from the ascent, had leaned on the wall close by with a smile and a glance for the young man. She had sat to him, and the autumn brought the sequel to the summer in his marriage. He had bought from her uncle the little farmhouse where he had lodged, adding to its modest accommodation a studio and a bedroom above it, and there he had seen the flicker of what had never been love, die out, and over the cold ashes of its embers the poisonous lichen of hatred spread fast. Early in their married life she had taken to drink, and had sunk into a degradation of soul and body that seemed bottomless, dragging him with her, down and down, in the grip of a force that was hardly human in its malignity.

===Chinese===
对于那个曾经做过他的模特、二十年来做了他妻子的美貌渔家女，他一丝一毫的柔情也没有，能刺穿他那漆黑的决心。正是在这里，他第一次见到她——那年夏天他出来度假，和两三个朋友一起借住在他此刻要去的这座农舍里。她正从小山上走上来，迟暮的夕阳把她的脸镀成金色，因为爬坡，她微微喘着气，便就近靠在墙头，朝那年青人嫣然一笑、秋波一转。她给他做过模特，秋天接着夏天而来，随之便是他们的婚事。他从她叔叔手里买下了他当年借住的那座小农舍，在那简朴的宅子上加建了一间画室和画室上方的一间卧室；也就是在那里，他眼看着那一簇从来算不得是爱的火苗，熄灭了，在那冷透的余烬之上，有毒的地衣似的恨意迅速蔓延开来。婚后不久她便染上了酒，从此身与心都沉沦到一种似乎深不见底的败坏里去，把他一同拖着，越陷越深，那拽着他的力量恶毒得不像是人力。

===Original===
Often during the wretched years that followed he had tried to leave her; he had offered to settle the farm on her and make adequate provision for her, but she had clung to the possession of him, not, it would seem, from any affection for him, but for a reason exactly opposite, namely, that her hatred of him fed and glutted itself on the sight of his ruin. It was as if, in obedience to some hellish power, she set herself to spoil his life, his powers, his possibilities, by tying him to herself. And by the aid of that power, so sometimes he had thought, she enforced her will on him, for, plan as he might to cut the whole dreadful business and leave the wreck behind him, he had never been able to consolidate his resolve into action. There, but a few miles away, was the station from which ran the train that would bear him out of this ancient western kingdom, where the beliefs in spells and superstitions grew rank as the herbage in that soft enervating air, and set him in the dry hard light of cities. The way lay open, but he could not take it; something unseen and potent, of grim inflexibility, held him back.﻿ ﻿…

===Chinese===
在那之后那些凄惨的年月里，他曾屡屡想要离开她；他提议把农庄归到她名下，再给她一份宽裕的赡养，可她偏要死死攥住他不放，看起来倒不像是因为对他还有什么情意，而恰恰是因为相反的理由——她的恨意要在眼见他一步步败落之中得到豢养和餍足。仿佛遵从着某种地狱般的力量，她一心要拴住他、以此毁掉他的生涯、他的才华、他的种种可能。而借助那股力量——他有时这般想——她把自己的意志强加于他，因为，尽管他几番打算把这整个可怕的事一刀两断、把这堆残骸抛在身后，却总也不能把决心化作行动。就在几英里外，便是那个火车站，从那儿开出的火车会把他带出这古老的西部王国——在那片土地上，符咒与迷信的信仰像那软绵绵令人懈怠的空气里的草木一样疯长——把他送到城市那干硬的天光底下去。路是敞开的，他却走不上去；某种看不见而强有力、又冷酷而不肯通融的东西，把他拦住了……

===Original===
He had passed no one on his way here, and satisfied now that in the darkness he could proceed without fear of being recognised if a chance wayfarer came from the direction in which he was going, he left the shelter of the hedge, and struck out into the stormy sea of that stupendous gale. Even as a man in the grip of imminent death sees his past life spread itself out in front of him for his final survey before the book is closed, so now, on the brink of the new life from which the deed on which he was determined alone separated him, John Aylsford, as he battled his advance through this great tempest, turned over page after page of his own wretched chronicles, feeling already strangely detached from them; it was as if he read the sordid and enslaved annals of another, wondering at them, half-pitying, half-despising him who had allowed himself to be bound so long in this ruinous noose.

===Chinese===
他这一路上没碰见一个人，便也安下心来：即便前方真来一个偶然的行人，黑暗之中他也尽可放心前行，不愁被认出来。于是他离开了树篱的掩蔽，闯进那场惊天大风所掀起的风暴之海里去。正如一个濒死之人临终前，眼看自己一生的过往在眼前铺展开来供他最后检阅一番、随后书卷便要合上；此刻，站在那崭新的生活的边缘——只除了他铁了心要做的那件事之外，再没有什么把他和那新生活隔开——约翰·艾尔斯福德一面在这场大风暴里挣扎着前行，一面把自家那一卷卷凄惨的编年史一页页翻过去，心里已经觉得怪异地与它们疏离了开来；他仿佛在读另一个人的卑污而受人奴役的纪事，一边诧异着，一边半是怜悯、半是鄙夷那个竟听任自己在这副毁灭性的绞索里被缚了这么久的人。

===Original===
Yes; it had been just that, a noose drawn ever tighter round his neck, while he choked and struggled all unavailingly. But there was another noose which should very soon now be drawn rapidly and finally tight, and the drawing of that in his own strong hands would free him. As he dwelt on that for a moment, his fingers stroked and patted the hank of whipcord that lay white and tough in his pocket. A noose, a knot drawn quickly taut, and he would have paid her back with justice and swifter mercy for the long strangling which he had suffered.

===Chinese===
是的；向来便是这么个东西，一副套在他脖子上越勒越紧的绞索，而他在里头窒息、挣扎，全无用处。可还有另外一副绞索，眼看就要在转眼之间被利落地、一了百了地抽紧，而抽紧它的，正是他自己那双有力的手——那便会叫他得救。他这般思忖着，手指便抚弄起来，轻轻拍着口袋里那一团白色的、坚韧的马鞭绳。一个活结，一个迅速抽紧的绳扣，他便算是秉公而、且更迅捷仁慈地，回报了她这些年加诸他的那场漫长的扼杀。

===Original===
Voluntarily and eagerly at the beginning had he allowed her to slip the noose about him, for Ellen Trenair’s beauty in those days, so long past and so everlastingly regretted, had been enough to ensnare a man. He had been warned at the time, by hint and half-spoken suggestion, that it was ill for a man to mate with a girl of that dark and ill-famed family, or for a woman to wed a boy in whose veins ran the blood of Jonas Trenair, once Methodist preacher, who learned on one All-Hallows’ Eve a darker gospel than he had ever preached before. What had happened to the girls who had married into that dwindling family, now all but extinct? One, before her marriage was a year old, had gone off her head, and now, a withered and ancient crone, mowed and gibbered about the streets of the village, picking garbage from the gutter and munching it in her toothless jaws. Another, Ellen’s own mother, had been found hanging from the banister of her stairs, stark and grim. Then there was young Frank Pencarris, who had wed Ellen’s sister. He had sunk into an awful melancholy, and sat tracing on sheets of paper the visions that beset his eyes, headless shapes, and foaming mouths, and the images of the spawn of hell.﻿ ﻿… John Aylsford, in those early days, had laughed to scorn these old wife tales of spells and sorceries: they belonged to ages long past, whereas fair Ellen Trenair was of the lovely present, and had lit desire in his heart which she alone could assuage. He had no use, in the brightness of her eye, for such shadows and superstitions; her beams dispelled them.

===Chinese===
当初是他自己心甘情愿、甚至迫不及待地让她把绞索套上来的，因为艾伦·特雷纳（Ellen Trenair）在那个早已远去、却永远叫人追悔的年头的貌美，足以把一个男人捕获。那时便有人警告过他，是借了暗示、借了半吞半吐的提点说的：跟那样一个阴沉而恶名昭著的家族里的姑娘成亲，是男人家的祸事；同样，哪个女人嫁了血管里流着乔纳斯·特雷纳（Jonas Trenair）的血的小子，也不得好果——那乔纳斯·特雷纳从前是卫理公会的传教士，后来在某一个万圣节前夜（All-Hallows’ Eve）习得了一门比他从前所传之道更为幽暗的福音。那些嫁进了那个如今已所剩无几、几近绝嗣的衰微之家的姑娘们，落了什么下场呢？有一个，婚不满一年便疯了，如今成了一个干瘪的老婆子，在村子的街上一边做着鬼脸、一边叽里咕噜地从沟里捡垃圾吃，用她那没牙的嘴嚼着。另一个，就是艾伦自己的母亲，被人发现吊在自家楼梯的栏杆上，僵直可怖。还有年轻的弗兰克·彭卡里斯（Frank Pencarris），他娶了艾伦的妹妹。这人沉入了一种可怕的忧郁里，整天坐着把眼前挥之不去的种种幻象描在纸上：无头的身影、口吐白沫的嘴、地狱子孙的形形色色……约翰·艾尔斯福德在那些早年的日子里，对这些关于符咒与巫术的老婆子故事嗤之以鼻：那都是远古年代的事了，而美丽的艾伦·特雷纳却是属于可爱的当下的，她在他的心头点起了唯有她才能平息的欲望。在她明眸的光辉里，这些阴霾与迷信于他全无用处；她的光芒把它们驱散了。

===Original===
Bitter and black as midnight had his enlightenment been, darkening through dubious dusks till the mirk of the pit itself enveloped him. His laughter at the notion that in this twentieth century spells and sorceries could survive, grew silent on his lips. He had seen the cattle of a neighbour who had offended one whom it was wiser not to cross, dwindle and pine, though there were rich pastures for their grazing, till the rib-bones stuck out like the timbers of stranded wrecks. He had seen the spring on another farm run dry at lambing-time because the owner, sceptic like himself, had refused that bounty, which all prudent folk paid to the wizard of Mareuth, who, like Ellen, was of the blood of Jonas Trenair. From scorn and laughter he had wavered to an uneasy wonder, and from wonder his mind had passed to the conviction that there were powers occult and terrible which strove in darkness and prevailed, secrets and spells that could send disease on man and beast, dark incantations, known to few, which could maim and cripple, and of these few his wife was one. His reason revolted, but some conviction, deeper than reason, held its own. To such a view it seemed that the deed he contemplated was no crime, but rather an act of obedience to the ordinance “Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live.” And the sense of detachment was over that, even as over the memories that oozed up in his mind. Somebody﻿—not he﻿—who had planned everything very carefully was in the next hour going to put an end to his bondage.

===Chinese===
他的醒悟来得又苦又黑，如同子夜，穿过一层层暧昧的暮色暗将下去，直到深渊本身的漆黑把他整个裹住。他原本嘲笑说，在这二十世纪居然还会有符咒与巫术留存，这笑声如今在他唇间渐渐沉默下去。他曾亲眼看见一个得罪了某位「顶撞不得」的人物的邻人，家中的牛群明明有丰美的牧草可吃，却日渐消瘦羸弱，直到肋骨一根根支棱出来，像搁浅的破船的龙骨。他又曾看见另一家农庄在产羔的季节泉眼干涸，只因那主人像他一样是个怀疑派，不肯交纳所有谨慎之人都奉给马雷斯（Mareuth）那位巫师的赏钱——那巫师和艾伦一样，也是乔纳斯·特雷纳的血胤。他从嘲讽和大笑动摇到一种不安的惊疑，又从惊疑一转而信定了：确有种种幽暗而可怖的力量在暗中争斗且节节得胜，有种种秘诀和符咒能叫人畜染病，有少数人才懂得的黑暗咒语能致人残废断肢，而他妻子便是这少数人之一。他的理智起而反抗，可某种比理智更深的信念却坚守不动。照这等看法看来，他所盘算的那件事便算不得是罪，倒像是在奉行那句「行邪术的女人，不可容她存活」的训诫。那一种疏离之感也笼罩其上，一如笼罩在那些从他心底渗出来的记忆之上。是另一个人——不是他自己——一个把一切都已仔细筹划好了的人，在接下来这一小时里，就要终结他的奴役了。

===Original===
So the years had passed, he floundering ever deeper in the slough into which he was plunged, out of which while she lived he could never emerge. For the last year, she, wearying of his perpetual presence at the farm, had allowed him to take a lodging in the village. She did not loose her hold over him, for the days were few on which she did not come with demands for a handful of shillings to procure her the raw spirits which alone could slake her thirst. Sometimes as he sat at work there in the north room looking on to the small garden-yard, she would come lurching up the path, with her bloated crimson face set on the withered neck, and tap at his window with fingers shrivelled like bird’s claws. Body and limbs were no more than bones over which the wrinkled skin was stretched, but her face bulged monstrously with layers of fat. He would give her whatever he had about him, and if it was not enough, she would plant herself there, grinning at him and wheedling him, or with screams and curses threatening him with such fate as he had known to overtake those who crossed her will. But usually he gave her enough to satisfy her for that day and perhaps the next, for thus she would the more quickly drink herself to death. Yet death seemed long in coming.﻿ ﻿…

===Chinese===
于是年复一年地过去，他在那他所陷的泥淖里越挣越深，只要她活着一天，他便永无出头之日。这一年来，她在农庄里也腻了他老在眼前，便准他在村中另租一间寓所。她却并不放松对他的钳制，因为她难得有哪一天不来讨一把先令，好给她买那唯能解她渴的烈性子生酒。有时他正坐在朝北那间屋子里面朝着那个小小的花园院子作画，她便摇摇晃晃地从那条小径走来，那张臃肿发红的脸搁在干枯的脖子上，用那皱缩得像鸟爪似的手指敲他的窗。身子和四肢瘦得只剩下骨头包着一层皱皮，可她的脸却可怖地鼓胀着一层层肥肉。他便把身上所有的都给了她，若是不够，她便钉在那里，冲他龇牙咧脸地又哄又骗，不然就是尖叫咒骂，拿他素来所知那些违逆她心意之人的下场来威胁他。可通常他都给她够花的，够她那一天、或许再搭上第二天花，因为这样她便能更快地把自己喝死。可死亡却迟迟不来……

===Original===
He remembered well how first the notion of killing her came into his head, just a little seed, small as that of mustard, which lay long in barrenness. Only the bare idea of it was there, like an abstract proposition. Then imperceptibly in the fruitful darkness of his mind, it must have begun to sprout, for presently a tendril, still soft and white, prodded out into the daylight. He almost pushed it back again, for fear that she, by some divining art, should probe his purpose. But when next she came for supplies, he saw no gleam of surmise in her red-rimmed eyes, and she took her money and went her way, and his purpose put forth another leaf, and the stem of it grew sappy. All autumn through it had flourished, and grown treelike, and fresh ideas, fresh details, fresh precautions, flocked there like building birds and made it gay with singing. He sat under the shadow of it and listened with brightening hopes to their song; never had there been such peerless melody. They knew their tunes now, there was no need for any further rehearsal.

===Chinese===
他清楚地记得，杀她的念头头一回是怎样进到他脑子里来的——一粒小小的种子，小得像芥菜籽，久久地荒在那里。起初只是一桩光秃秃的念头，像一道抽象的命题。后来，在他那肥沃黑暗的心田里，它一定是不知不觉地发了芽，因为不久便有一条藤蔓，还又软又白地探到日光里来了。他几乎要把它按回去，生怕她借了什么占卜的法门，窥破了他的心思。可下一回她来讨钱时，他在她那红了眼眶的眼里看不见一丝猜疑，她拿了她的钱、走了她的路，而他的念头又抽出了一片新叶，那茎也长得水灵起来。整整一个秋天，它茁壮生长，长成了树的模样，新的念头、新的细节、新的防备，像筑巢的鸟儿似的纷纷飞来，把它唱得热闹非凡。他坐在它的阴凉底下，怀着越来越明亮的希望听它们的歌；从未有过这样无双的旋律。它们如今已熟悉了自己的调子，再不必排练了。

===Original===
He began to wonder how soon he would be back on the road again, with face turned from this buffeting wind, and on his way home. His business would not take him long; the central deed of it would be over in a couple of minutes, and he did not anticipate delay about the setting to work on it, for by seven o’clock of the evening, as well he knew, she was usually snoring in the oblivion of complete drunkenness, and even if she was not as far gone as that, she would certainly be incapable of any serious resistance. After that, a quarter of an hour more would finish the job, and he would leave the house secure already from any chance of detection. Night after night during these last ten days he had been up here, peering from the darkness into the lighted room where she sat, then listening for her step on the stairs as she stumbled up to bed, or hearing her snorings as she slept in her chair below. The outhouse, he knew, was well stocked with paraffin; he needed no further apparatus than the whipcord and the matches he carried with him. Then back he would go along the exact route by which he had come, reentering the village again from the eastwards, in which direction he had set out.

===Chinese===
他开始盘算，还要多久自己便能回到路上、背着这阵扑面的风、踏上回家的路。他这趟差事花不了多少时间；其中最关键的那一步，两分钟便能了结，他也不愁会耽搁什么才能动手，因为他深知，一到晚上七点钟，她照例已经在一醉如泥的 oblivion 里打鼾了；即便没醉到那份上，也断然做不出什么像样的反抗。那之后，再过一刻钟便能把事办完，他离开那房子时，便可万无一失、不怕被人发觉了。这最后十天里，他夜夜都到这里来，从黑暗里窥探那间亮着灯的她所坐的屋子，再听着她在楼梯上跌跌撞撞地上床去，或是听见她在楼下椅子里睡着时打的鼾。他知道外屋存了不少煤油；除了随身带的马鞭绳和火柴，他再不需要什么别的器具。然后他便顺着来时那条路一丝不差地回去，从东头——也就是他出发的那个方向——重新进村。

===Original===
This walk of his was now a known and established habit; half the village during the last week or two had seen him every evening set forth along the coast road, for a tramp in the dusk when the light failed for his painting, and had seen him come back again as they hung about and smoked in the warm dusk, a couple of hours later. None knew of his detour to the main road which took him westwards again above the village and so to the stretch of bleak upland along which now he fought his way against the gale. Always round about the hour of eight he had entered the village again from the other side, and had stopped and chatted with the loiterers. Tonight, no later than was usual, he would come up the cobbled road again, and give “good night” to any who lingered there outside the public-house. In this wild wind it was not likely that there would be such, and if so, no matter; he had been seen already setting forth on his usual walk by the coast of the bay, and if none outside saw him return, none could see the true chart of his walk. By eight he should be back to his supper, there would be a soused herring for him, and a cut of cheese, and the kettle would be singing on the hob for his hot whisky-toddy. He would have a keen edge for the enjoyment of them tonight; he would drink long healths to the damned and the dead. Not till tomorrow, probably, would the news of what had happened reach him, for the farmhouse lay lonely and sheltered by the wood of firs. However high might mount the beacon of its blazing, it would scarcely, screened by the tall trees, light up the western sky, and be seen from the village nestling below the steep hill-crest.

===Chinese===
他这趟行走如今已是众人皆知、习以为常的事了；过去这一两周里，半个村子的人每晚都看见他沿着海岸路出发，趁着天色暗得不能作画时出去在暮色里走走，又看见他们在外头闲逛抽烟的暖和暮色里，两小时后，再看见他回来。谁也不知道他绕到了大路上、从村子上方重新折向西、再沿着那片荒凉的高地走——他此刻正是在这高地上顶着风艰难前行。每到八点上下，他便从另一头进了村，停下脚步和那些闲荡的人搭几句话。今夜，他也会在不比平常更晚的时候，再走上那条鹅卵石的街，跟酒馆外头逗留的人道一声「晚安」。这么大的风，怕是没有人会在外头了；若有，也无所谓；已经有人瞧见他照常沿海湾去散步了，若是没人瞧见他回来，那也没有谁能看见他这一趟真实的路线。八点钟他该是回到寓所吃晚饭了，给他预备着一条醋渍鲱鱼、一块奶酪，炉台上水壶正唱着，等他来调一碗热腾腾的威士忌热酒。今夜他胃口会格外好；他要为那些该死的和已死的人干下一杯又一杯。多半要等到明天，那桩事的消息才会传到他耳朵里，因为那农舍孤零零的，又有杉木林挡着。任凭它烧得多高的烽火，被那些高树一遮，怕也难得照亮西边的天、被村子里——那蜷伏在陡峭山顶下头的小村——的人望见。

===Original===
By now John Aylsford had come to the fir wood which bordered the road on the left, and, as he passed into its shelter, cut off from him the violence of the gale. All its branches were astir with the sound of some vexed, overhead sea, and the trunks that upheld them creaked and groaned in the fury of the tempest. Somewhere behind the thick scud of flying cloud the moon must have risen, for the road glimmered more visibly, and the tossing blackness of the branches was clear enough against the grey tumult overhead. Behind the tempest she rode in serene skies, and in the murderous clarity of his mind he likened himself to her. Just for half an hour more he would still grope and scheme and achieve in this hurly-burly, and then, like a balloon released, soar through the clouds and find serenity. A couple of hundred yards now would take him round the corner of the wood; from there the miry lane led from the high-road to the farm.

===Chinese===
到此刻，约翰·艾尔斯福德已到了路边左侧那片杉木林前，他一走进它的掩蔽之下，那风的暴烈便被挡去了。所有的枝桠都搅动着，发出仿佛头顶上一片骚动不安的大海的声响，支撑着它们的树干在狂风的暴怒里咯吱作响、呻吟不已。在飞驰的厚厚乱云后面某处，月亮一定已经升起来了，因为路面亮堂了些，看得更清楚了，而头顶上那灰蒙蒙的翻腾之中，枝桠那翻动的黑色也看得清清楚楚。她在风暴背后的澄明天空里行着，而他在自己那副杀心已定的清明之中，把自己比作了她。再过半个钟头，他便要在这场混乱里摸索、筹谋、得手，然后，像一只放飞的气球，穿过云层，寻得安宁。再走两三百码，便能绕过杉木林的拐角；从那里起，那条泥泞的小巷便从大路通向那座农舍。

===Original===
He hastened rather than retarded his going as he drew near, for the wood, though it roared with the gale, began to whisper to him of memories. Often in that summer before his marriage had he strayed out at dusk into it, certain that before he had gone many paces he would see a shadow flitting towards him through the firs, or hear the crack of dry twigs in the stillness. Here was their tryst; she would come up from the village with the excuse of bringing fish to the farmhouse, after the boats had come in, and deserting the high-road make a shortcut through the wood. Like some distant blink of lightning the memory of those evenings quivered distantly on his mind, and he quickened his step. The years that followed had killed and buried those recollections, but who knew what stirring of corpses and dry bones might not yet come to them if he lingered there? He fingered the whipcord in his pocket, and launched out, beyond the trees, into the full fury of the gale.

===Chinese===
他走近时，反倒把步子加快了些，因为这林子虽在大风中呼啸，却已开始向他低语起一些旧事。婚前那一年夏天，他曾常常在暮色里漫步进这片林子，笃信不出几步便会看见一道影子穿过杉树朝他飘来，或者在寂静里听见枯枝折断的脆响。这里就是他们幽会的所在；船归了港之后，她便借口给农舍送鱼从村里上来，撇开大路，从这林子里抄一条近道。那些黄昏的回忆，像远处一闪一闪的电光，在他心头远远地颤动，他便加快了脚步。后来的那些年已经把这些回忆杀死、埋葬了，可若是他在这里耽搁，谁晓得它们那尸骸和枯骨里还会不会又生出什么动静来？他摸了摸口袋里的马鞭绳，纵身出了树林，闯进了风的全力暴怒之中。

===Original===
The farmhouse was near now and in full view, a black blot against the clouds. A beam of light shone from an uncurtained window on the ground-floor, and the rest was dark. Even thus had he seen it for many nights past, and well knew what sight would greet him as he stole up nearer. And even so it was tonight, for there she sat in the studio he had built, betwixt table and fireplace with the bottle near her, and her withered hands stretched out to the blaze, and the huge bloated face swaying on her shoulders. Beside her tonight were the wrecked remains of a chair, and the first sight that he caught of her was to show her feeding the fire with the broken pieces of it. It had been too troublesome to bring fresh logs from the store of wood; to break up a chair was the easier task.

===Chinese===
农舍近了，望得清清楚楚了，衬着云，是一块黑色的污渍。一楼一扇没挂窗帘的窗里透出一道光，其余一片漆黑。连着许多夜来，他所见的都是这般光景，也清楚自己再悄悄走近些，会看见什么。今夜也是一样：她坐着他亲自盖的那间画室里，在桌子和壁炉之间，酒瓶近在手边，一双枯干的手伸向熊熊的炉火，那张硕大臃肿的脸在她肩膀上摇摇晃晃。今夜她身旁还有一把椅子的残骸，他第一眼看见她时，她正把那椅子的碎块往火里添。从柴房搬新木柴太费事；砸碎一把椅子要省事得多。

===Original===
She stirred and sat more upright, then reached out for the bottle that stood beside her, and drank from the mouth of it. She drank and licked her lips and drank again, and staggered to her feet, tripping on the edge of the hearthrug. For the moment that seemed to anger her, and with clenched teeth and pointing finger she mumbled at it; then once more she drank, and lurching forward, took the lamp from the table. With it in her hand she shuffled to the door, and the room was left to the flickering firelight. A moment afterwards, the bedroom window above sprang into light, an oblong of bright illumination.

===Chinese===
她动了动，坐得更直了些，伸手去够旁边那瓶子，对着瓶口喝起来。她喝了一口，舔舔嘴唇，又喝了一口，踉踉跄跄地站起身，被炉前的地毯边绊了一下。这一时她似乎恼了，咬紧牙关，伸手指着地毯，含含糊糊地咒骂它；接着她又喝了一口，身子往前一歪，从桌上端起了灯。她手里拎着灯，拖着脚步朝门口走，屋里便只剩那摇曳的炉火的光。过了一会儿，楼上的卧室窗户一下子亮了，长方形的一块明亮的灯光。

===Original===
As soon as that appeared he crept round the house to the door. He gently turned the handle of it, and found it unlocked. Inside was a small passage entrance, on the left of which ascended the stairs to the bedroom above the studio. All was silent there, but from where he stood he could see that the door into the bedroom was open, for a shaft of light from the lamp she had carried up with her was shed on to the landing there.﻿ ﻿… Everything was smoothing itself out to render his course most easy. Even the gale was his friend, for it would be bellows for the fire. He slipped off his shoes, leaving them on the mat, and drew the whipcord from his pocket. He made a noose in it, and began to ascend the stairs. They were well-built of seasoned oak, and no creak betrayed his advancing footfall.

===Chinese===
那块光一亮起来，他便绕过屋子，摸到门前。他轻轻转动门把手，发现门没锁。里头是一个小小的门厅，门厅左边便是通往画室上方卧室的楼梯。那儿一片寂静，但从他所站之处能看见卧室的门开着，因为她带上去的那盏灯的一道灯光，正泻在那一片楼梯口上……一切都自行顺遂起来，叫他的事再容易不过。连这场大风也是他的朋友，因为它会给火当风箱。他脱下鞋，把它们留在门垫上，从口袋里抽出那根马鞭绳。他在绳上结了一个活扣，便开始上楼。楼梯是用干透的橡木打造得很结实，没有一声咯吱声出卖他一步步走上去的脚。

===Original===
At the top he paused, listening for any stir of movement within, but there was nothing to be heard but the sound of heavy breathing from the bed that lay to the left of the door and out of sight. She had thrown herself down there, he guessed, without undressing, leaving the lamp to burn itself out. He could see it through the open door already beginning to flicker; on the wall behind it were a couple of watercolours, pictures of his own, one of the little walled garden by the farm, the other of the pinewood of their tryst. Well he remembered painting them: she would sit by him as he worked with prattle and singing. He looked at them now quite detachedly; they seemed to him wonderfully good, and he envied the artist that fresh, clean skill. Perhaps he would take them down presently and carry them away with him.

===Chinese===
到了楼梯顶，他停下来，听里头有没有什么动静，却什么也没听见，只听见门左边那张他看不见的床上传来的沉重的呼吸声。他猜想，她连衣服也没脱便一头栽倒在那里，任由那盏灯自燃至尽。隔着敞开的门他已看得见它开始摇曳起来；它后面的墙上挂着两幅水彩画，都是他自己的作品，一幅画的是农舍旁那座围了墙的小花园，另一幅是他们幽会的那片杉木林。他还清楚地记得画它们时的情景：他作画时，她便坐在他身旁，咿咿呀呀地又说又唱。此刻他看着它们，心里相当疏离；它们在他看来好得出奇，他竟羡慕起那画家这般清新、干净的笔力来。也许待会儿他便要把它们摘下来，带在身边一起带走。

===Original===
Very softly now he advanced into the room, and looking round the corner of the door, he saw her, sprawling and fully dressed on the broad bed. She lay on her back, eyes closed and mouth open, her dull grey hair spread over the pillow. Evidently she had not made the bed that day, for she lay stretched on the crumpled back-turned blankets. A hairbrush was on the floor beside her; it seemed to have fallen from her hand. He moved quickly towards her.

===Chinese===
此刻他极轻地走进房里，从门口转角处一望，便看见她四仰八叉、衣冠未脱地躺在那张宽大的床上。她仰面躺着，闭着眼，张着嘴，她那灰暗无光的头发散在枕头上。这一天她显然没有铺过床，因为她直挺挺地躺在皱巴巴地翻卷着的毯子上。她身旁的地板上有一把梳子；像是从她手里掉下去的。他朝她快步走过去。

===Original===
He put on his shoes again when he came to the foot of the stairs, carrying the lamp with him and the two pictures which he had taken down from the wall, and went into the studio. He set the lamp on the table and drew down the blinds, and his eye fell on the half-empty whisky bottle from which he had seen her drinking. Though his hand was quite steady and his mind composed and tranquil, there was yet at the back of it some impression that was slowly developing, and a good dose of spirits would no doubt expunge that. He drank half a tumbler of it raw and undiluted, and though it seemed no more than water in his mouth, he soon felt that it was doing its work and sponging away from his mind the picture that had been outlining itself there. In a couple of minutes he was quite himself again, and could afford to wonder and laugh at the illusion, for it was no less than that, which had been gaining on him. For though he could distinctly remember drawing the noose tight, and seeing the face grow black, and struggling with the convulsive movements of those withered limbs that soon lay quiet again, there had sprung up in his mind some unaccountable impression that what he had left there huddled on the bed was not just the bundle of withered limbs and strangled neck, but the body of a young girl, smooth of skin and golden of hair, with mouth that smiled drowsily. She had been asleep when he came in, and now was half-awake, and was stirring and stretching herself. In what dim region of his mind that image had formed itself, he had no idea; all he cared about now was that his drink had shattered it again, and he could proceed with order and method to make all secure. Just one drop more first: how lucky it was that this morning he had been liberal with his money when she came to the village, for he would have been sorry to have gone without that fillip to his nerves.

===Chinese===
他回到楼梯脚下才重新穿上鞋，手里拎着那盏灯和从墙上摘下来的两幅画，走进画室。他把灯放在桌上，放下窗帘，眼睛便落到了那半瓶他方才看见她喝过的威士忌上。虽说他的手相当稳，心绪也安宁平静，可这事背后却总有一种慢慢成形的印象，一剂足量的烈酒必能把它抹去。他倒了半杯纯的、不兑水的喝下去，那酒入口虽像白水一般，他却很快便觉出它在起作用了，正在一笔一笔把他脑子里那幅正勾出轮廓的画擦掉。不出两分钟，他又完全恢复了原状，能够去惊异、去嘲笑那一向是他所引起的错觉了——那不折不扣就是个错觉。因为，虽说离婚变黑的脸，虽说他记得自己分明收紧了那个活扣、看着那张脸变黑了、和那一双双枯干的四肢抽搐了一阵很快又静了下来相搏斗过，可他心里却不由自主地冒出一种无从解释的印象：他留在那里蜷在床上的那团东西，并不只是一束枯干的四肢和一条被勒断气的脖子，而是一个年轻姑娘的身体，肌肤光洁，头发金黄，嘴角带着慵懒的微笑。他进门时她在熟睡，此刻半睡半醒，正在翻身、伸展。他全不知道这个影像是在他心里哪个幽暗的角落成形的；他此刻在意的只有：他喝的酒又把它击碎了，他可以有条不紊、按部就班地，把一切安排妥帖了。先再来一口：今早她到村里来时，他多亏手头大方，真是运气——不然，少了这副提神的药剂，他可就要懊恼了。

===Original===
He looked at his watch, and saw to his satisfaction that it was still only a little after seven o’clock. Half an hour’s walking, with this gale to speed his steps, would easily carry him from door to door, round the detour which approached the village from the east, and a quarter of an hour, so he reckoned, would be sufficient to accomplish thoroughly what remained to be done here. He must not hurry and thus overlook some precaution needful for his safety, though, on the other hand, he would be glad to be gone from the house as soon as might be, and he proceeded to set about his work without delay. There was brushwood and fire-kindling to be brought in from the woodshed in the yard, and he made three journeys, returning each time with his arms full, before he had brought in what he judged to be sufficient. Most of this he piled in a loose heap in the studio; with the rest he ascended once more to the bedroom above and made a heap of it there in the middle of the floor. He took the curtains down from the windows, for they would make a fine wick for the paraffin, and stuffed them into the pile. Before he left, he looked once more at what lay on the bed, and marvelled at the illusion which the whisky had dispelled, and as he looked, the sense that he was free mounted and bubbled in his head. The thing seemed scarcely human at all; it was a monster from which he had delivered himself, and now, with the thought of that to warm him, he was no longer eager to get through with his work and be gone, for it was all part of that act of riddance which he had accomplished, and he gloried in it. Soon, when all was ready, he would come back once more and soak the fuel and set light to it, and purge with fire the corruption that lay humped on the bed.

===Chinese===
他看了看表，满意地发现才不过七点刚过一点。走半个小时，有这场大风为他助步，轻轻松松便能从这门到那门，绕过从东边进村的那段弯路；而他盘算着，一刻钟便足以把这里剩下的事办得妥妥帖帖。他不能急、从而疏漏了哪条关乎他安全的防备；可另一方面，他也巴不得尽早离开这屋子，于是便不耽搁，马上动手干起来。得从院子里的柴房搬些细柴和引火的来，他跑了三趟，每趟都抱了满怀，才搬足了他判断够用的分量。这些柴禾他大半在画室里松松地堆成了一堆；剩下的他再上楼到上头的卧室里，在地板正中堆了一堆。他把窗户上的窗帘摘下来——它们给煤油当灯芯再好不过——塞进了那堆里。临走前，他又看了一眼床上躺着的那东西，对那被威士忌驱散了的错觉惊叹不已；他看着看着，一种自己自由了的感觉便涌上来，在他脑子里冒泡。那东西看上去简直不像是人；那是他从其魔掌下解脱出来的一个怪物，如今，一想到这一点身上便暖烘烘的，他反倒不急于把活干完赶紧走了，因为这本来也是他所完成的那场清除的一部分，他为之得意。等一切都齐备了，他还要再回来一趟，把柴禾浇透，点上一把火，用火去净化那蜷在床上的腐朽之物。

===Original===
The fury of the gale had increased with nightfall, and as he went downstairs again he heard the rattle of loosened tiles on the roof, and the crash as they shattered themselves on the cobbles of the yard. At that a sudden misgiving made his breath to catch in his throat, as he pictured to himself some maniac blast falling on the house and crashing in the walls that now trembled and shuddered. Supposing the whole house fell, even if he escaped with his life from the toppling ruin, what would his life be worth? There would be search made in the fallen debris to find the body of her who lay strangled with the whipcord round her neck, and he pictured to himself the slow, relentless march of justice. He had bought whipcord only yesterday at a shop in the village, insisting on its strength and toughness﻿ ﻿… would it be wiser now, this moment, to untie the noose and take it back with him or add it to his brushwood?﻿ ﻿… He paused on the staircase, pondering that; but his flesh quaked at the thought, and master of himself though he had been during those few struggling minutes, he distrusted his power of making himself handle once more that which could struggle no longer. But even as he tried to screw his courage to the point, the violence of the squall passed, and the shuddering house braced itself again. He need not fear that; the gale was his friend that would blow on the flames, not his enemy. The blasts that trumpeted overhead were the voices of the allies who had come to aid him.

===Chinese===
天黑以后，大风的暴烈更甚了，他再下楼时，听见屋顶上松动的瓦片咯啷咯啷地响，听见它们砸在院子鹅卵石上的破碎声。这一来他突然一悸，喉咙里噎住了一口气，因为他想象着某一阵发狂的暴风正落到这房子上，把此刻已在颤抖摇晃的墙壁砸塌。倘若整座房子塌了，就算他保住了性命从倾颓的废墟里逃出来，他这条命又值什么呢？人们会在倒塌的残砾里搜寻，找到那个脖子上还套着马鞭绳被勒死的她的尸体，而他眼前便浮现出正义那缓慢而无情的行进步伐。他昨天才在村里一家铺子里买了这马鞭绳，还特地叮嘱要结实坚韧的那一种……此刻，立刻，把那活扣解开、把它带回去，或是扔进柴堆里，是不是更明智些呢？……他在楼梯上停住脚，盘算着这事；可一想到这里他便浑身打了个冷战，方才那短短几分钟的搏斗里他虽说把持得住自己，此刻却信不过自己还能再去伸手碰一碰那个再也不能挣扎的东西。可就在他鼓着勇气想逼自己动手之际，那一阵疾风过去了，发抖的房子又重新稳住了。他不必怕那个；这场大风是他的朋友，会给火焰鼓风的，不是他的敌人。头顶上号角似的阵阵狂风，都是来助他的盟军的嗓音。

===Original===
All was arranged then upstairs for the pouring of the paraffin and the lighting of the pyre; it remained but to make similar dispositions in the studio. He would stay to feed the flames till they raged beyond all power of extinction; and now he began to plan the line of his retreat. There were two doors in the studio: one by the fireplace which opened on to the little garden; the other gave into the passage entrance from which mounted the stairs and so to the door through which he had come into the house. He decided to use the garden-door for his exit; but when he came to open it, he found that the key was stiff in the rusty lock, and did not yield to his efforts. There was no use in wasting time over that; it made no difference through which door he finally emerged, and he began piling up his heap of wood at that end of the room. The lamp was burning low; but the fire, which only so few minutes ago she had fed with a broken chair, shone brightly, and a flaming ember from it would serve to set light to his conflagration. There was a straw mat in front of it, which would make fine kindling, and with these two fires, one in the bedroom upstairs and the other here, there would be no mistake about the incineration of the house and all that it contained. His own crime, if crime it was, would perish, too, and all evidence thereof, victim and whipcord, and the very walls of the house of sin and hate. It was a great deed and a fine adventure, and as the liquor he had drunk began to circulate more buoyantly through his veins, he gloried at the thought of the approaching consummation. He would slip out of the sordid tragedy of his past life, as from a discarded garment that he threw into the bonfire he would soon kindle.

===Chinese===
那么，楼上的煤油浇泼、火堆点燃的事都已安排好了，剩下的只是在画室里做同样的布置。他要留下来添柴添火，直等到火势大到再也无法扑灭；此刻他开始盘算自己撤退的路线。画室有两扇门：一扇在壁炉旁边，开向那个小花园；另一扇通向门厅，从门厅上楼梯，再通到他进屋的那扇门。他决定从花园那扇门出去；可他过去开门时，发现钥匙在生了锈的锁里涩住了，他怎么使劲也不肯动。在这上头费工夫没有用；反正他最后从哪一扇门出去都一样，他便开始在屋子那一头堆起他的柴堆来。灯快燃尽了；可那炉火——几分钟前她还添了一把破椅子进去——正烧得亮堂，从里头抽出一块烧着的木块便足以点燃他这场大火。炉前有一块草席，是上好的引火物，有了这两处火——一处在楼上的卧室，一处在楼下这里——这房子和屋里的一切要付之一炬，是错不了的。他自己的罪——倘若那是罪的话——也将随之毁灭，连同罪证、受害者和马鞭绳，连同这座罪与恨的屋子的墙壁。这是一桩壮举，一场漂亮的冒险，而他所喝下去的酒开始在血管里越发轻快地流转，他不禁为行将到来的大功告成而志得意满。他将要从他前半生那出肮脏的悲剧里脱身而出，就像从一件他即将扔进篝火里的破旧衣裳里脱身一样。

===Original===
All was ready now for the soaking of the fuel he had piled with the paraffin, and he went out to the shed in the yard where the barrel stood. A big tin ewer stood beside it, which he filled and carried indoors. That would be sufficient for the soaking of the pile upstairs, and fetching the smoky and flickering lamp from the studio, he went up again, and like a careful gardener watering some bed of choice blossoms, he sprinkled and poured till his ewer was empty. He gave but one glance to the bed behind him, where the huddled thing lay so quietly, and as he turned, lamp in hand, to go down again, the draught that came in through the window against which the gale blew, extinguished it. A little blue flame of burning vapour rose in the chimney and went out; so, having no further use for it, he pitched it on to the pile of soaked material. As he left the room he thought he heard some small stir of movement behind him, but he told himself that it was but something slipping in the heap he had built there.

===Chinese===
此刻，他堆好的柴禾只待煤油浇泼了，他便出到院里立着煤油桶的那间棚子里。桶边有一只大锡水壶，他把它灌满，拎进屋里。这分量浇楼上的那堆柴禾尽够了，他从画室里拿了那盏冒烟摇曳的灯，又上了楼，像一个细心的园丁浇灌一畦名贵的花圃那样，淋着、泼着，直泼到壶空了。他只朝身后那张床——那蜷成一团的东西那么静静地躺在那里——瞥了一眼，便转身、手持灯、要再下楼，那一股从正迎着风的窗户里灌进来的穿堂风，便把它吹熄了。烟囱里升起一小朵蓝色火焰、燃着油气，随即灭了；这灯既已再没什么用处，他便把它扔到了那堆浸透了油的东西上。他离开房间时，仿佛听见身后有什么小小的响动，可他告诉自己，那不过是他在那里堆起的那堆里有什么东西滑了一滑。

===Original===
Again he went out into the storm. The clouds that scudded overhead were thinner now, though the gale blew not less fiercely, and the blurred, watery moonlight was brighter. Once for a moment, as he approached the shed, he caught sight of the full orb plunging madly among the streaming vapours; then she was hidden again behind the wrack. Close in front of him were the fir trees of the wood where those sweet trysts had been held, and once again the vision of her as she had been broke into his mind and the queer conviction that it was no withered and bloated hag, who lay on the bed upstairs but the fair, comely limbs and the golden head. It was even more vivid now, and he made haste to get back to the studio, where he would find the trusty medicine that had dispelled that vision before. He would have to make two journeys at least with his tin ewer before he transported enough oil to feed the larger pyre below, and so, to save time, he took the barrel off its stand, and rolled it along the path and into the house. He paused at the foot of the stairs, listening to hear if anything stirred, but all was silent. Whatever had slipped up there was steady again; from outside only came the squeal and bellow of the wind.

===Chinese===
他又出到风暴里去。头顶上飞驰的云薄了些，虽则风并不见得小，那模糊的、水汪汪的月光却更亮了。有一瞬，他走近棚子时，一眼瞥见那轮圆满的月在一缕缕流云之间狂乱地穿行；随即她又隐到乱云后面去了。就在他正前方，便是当年那些甜蜜的幽会举行的那片杉木林，于是她当年的模样又闯进了他的心里，他莫名地信以为：躺在楼上床上的并不是一个枯干臃肿的丑婆子，而是那光洁可爱的肢体、那金黄的头发。这念头此刻分外真切，他便赶忙回到画室里去——在那里他能找到先前驱散这幻象的那服灵丹。他要提着锡壶至少跑两趟，才能把足够喂饱楼下那座更大的火堆的油运齐，于是，为省时计，他把油桶从架子上搬下来，顺着小径一路滚进屋里。他在楼梯脚下停了停，听听上头有没有什么动静，可一片寂静。上头滑了一滑的什么东西此刻又稳住了；外头传来的，只有风的尖啸和怒吼。

===Original===
The studio was brightly but fitfully lit by the flames on the hearth; at one moment a noonday blazed there, the next but the last smoulder of some red sunset. It was easier to decant from the barrel into his ewer than carry the heavy keg and sprinkle from it, and once and once again he filled and emptied it. One more application would be sufficient, and after that he could let what remained trickle out on to the floor. But by some awkward movement he managed to spill a splash of it down the front of his trousers: he must be sure, therefore (how quickly his brain responded with counsels of precautions), to have some accident with his lamp when he came in to his supper, which should account for this little misadventure. Or, probably, the wind through which he would presently be walking would dry it before he reached the village.

===Chinese===
画室被炉床上的火光照得亮堂堂的，只是忽明忽暗；一时像正午当空，一时又像某场红霞满天的日落的最后一缕余烬。从桶里把油灌进壶里，总比拎着重桶四处泼洒来得容易，他便一遍又一遍地灌了又倒空。再淋一道便够了，此后便可由着剩下的油自己淌到地板上。可他不知怎的一个笨拙的动作，把一点油溅到了自己裤子前襟上：因此（他的脑子多么快地便献上了种种小心之策），待会儿他回寓所吃晚饭时，务必要拿那盏灯出点什么意外，好把这点小事故遮掩过去。再不然，他待会儿要走过的这场风，多半会在他进村之前便把它吹干。

===Original===
So, for the last time with matches ready in his hand, he mounted the stairs to set light to the fuel piled in the room above. His second dose of whisky sang in his head, and he said to himself, smiling at the humour of the notion, “She always liked a fire in her bedroom; she shall have it now.” That seemed a very comical idea, and it dwelt in his head as he struck the match which should light it for her. Then, still grinning, he gave one glance to the bed, and the smile died on his face, and the wild cymbals of panic crashed in his brain. The bed was empty; no huddled shape lay there.

===Chinese===
于是，他手里捏着火柴，最后一回上了楼，要去点着堆在上头那间屋里的柴禾。第二剂威士忌在他脑子里唱起歌来，他对这念头的滑稽处微微一笑，自言自语道：「她一向爱在卧室里生一炉火；如今就遂了她这桩心愿罢。」这主意好像十分滑稽，便留在他脑子里，他擦亮了那根要为她点火的火柴。然后，他仍龇着牙笑，朝那张床望了一眼，脸上的笑便僵住了，慌乱的铙钹在他脑子里狂乱地敲响。床是空的；上面没有那一团蜷着的身形。

===Original===
Distraught with terror, he thrust the match into the soaked pile and the flame flared up. Perhaps the body had rolled off the bed. It must, in any case, be here somewhere, and when once the room was alight there would be nothing more to fear. High rose the smoky flame, and banging the door, he leaped down the stairs to set light to the pile below and be gone from the house. Yet, whatever monstrous miracle his eye had assured him of, it could not be that she still lived and had left the place where she lay, for she had ceased to breathe when the noose was tight round her neck, and her fight for life and air had long been stilled. But, if by some hideous witchcraft, she was not dead, it would soon be over now with her in the stupefaction of the smoke and the scorching flames. Let be; the door was shut and she within, for him it remained to be finished with the business, and flee from the house of terror, lest he leave the sanity of his soul behind him.

===Chinese===
他慌得神魂无主，把火柴捅进浇透了油的柴堆，火焰便腾地燃起来。也许是尸体滚下床去了。无论如何，它总该还在这里的什么地方，等屋子一着起来便再没什么好怕的了。冒着烟的火焰高高地蹿起，他砰地一带上门，跳下楼梯，要去点着楼下的那堆柴禾，赶紧离开这屋子。然而，无论他亲眼所见的是怎样一桩荒诞的奇迹，她绝不可能还活着、离开了她躺着的地方，因为活扣一勒紧她便早已断了气，她为命、为气的那场挣扎也早已停歇。可若是借着什么可怖的巫术，她竟未死，那么在这窒息的浓烟和灼人的烈焰里，她也很快就要了账了。随它去罢；门已带上，她在里头，至于他，剩下的事便是把活干完，赶紧逃出这恐怖之屋，免得把自己灵魂的清醒也丢在那里。

===Original===
The red glare from the hearth in the studio lit his steps down the passage from the stairway, and already he could hear from above the dry crack and snap from the fire that prospered there. As he shuffled in, he held his hands to his head, as if pressing the brain back into its cool case, from which it seemed eager to fly out into the welter of storm and fire and hideous imagination. If he could only control himself for a few moments more, all would be done and he would escape from this disordered haunted place into the night and the gale, leaving behind him the blaze that would burn away all perilous stuff. Again the flames broke out in the embers on the hearth, bravely burning, and he took from the heart of the glare a fragment on which the fire was bursting into yellow flowers. He heeded not the scorching of his hand, for it was but for a moment that he held it, and then plunged it into the pile that dripped with the oil he had poured on it. A tower of flame mounted, licking the rafters of the low ceiling, then died away as if suffocated by its own smoke, but crept onwards, nosing its way along till it reached the straw mat, which blazed fiercely. That blaze kindled the courage in him; whatever trick his imagination had played on him just now, he had nothing to fear except his own terror, which now he mastered again, for nothing real could ever escape from the conflagration, and it was only the real that he feared. Spells and witchcrafts and superstitions, such as for the last twenty years had battened on him, were all enclosed in that tight-drawn noose.

===Chinese===
画室炉床里射出的红光照着他穿过楼梯口的那段过道，他已经听得见楼上那烧得正旺的火发出的干裂的噼啪声了。他拖着脚步走进去，双手按住头，仿佛要把脑子按回它那冰凉的脑壳里去——它仿佛急切地要冲出来，扑进这场风雨、烈火和可怖的想象的大混乱里去。只要他再把自己把持住片刻，一切便都了结，他便能逃出这个失了常的、闹鬼似的地方，逃到夜和大风里去，把那场会把一切危险的物事都烧个干净的熊熊烈火留在身后。炉床的余烬里又腾起一片火焰，烧得正旺，他从那火光的核心里抽出一块正爆出一朵朵黄花般火苗的木片。他不顾手上的灼痛，因为他只拿了一瞬，便把它插进了那堆滴着他浇上去的油的柴禾里。一座火焰之塔拔地而起，舔舐着低矮天花板的房梁，随即像是被自己的烟憋住一般矮了下去，却仍一路爬着、嗅着往前摸去，直摸到那块草席前，草席便猛烈地烧了起来。这一片火光点燃了他心头的勇气；方才他的想象力不论跟他耍了什么花招，他所怕的唯有他自己的恐惧而已，而这一点恐惧此刻他又重新制服了，因为任何真实的东西都逃不出这场大火，而他怕的又只是真实的东西。那些二十年来寄生于他身上、把他养肥了的符咒、巫术和迷信，全都收在那副紧紧抽紧的绞索里了。

===Original===
It was time to be gone, for all was safe now, and the room was growing to oven-heat. But as he picked his way across the floor over which runnels of flames from the split barrel were beginning to spread this way and that, he heard from above the sound of a door unlatched, and footsteps light and firm tapped on the stairs. For one second the sheer catalepsy of panic seized him, but he recovered his control, and with hands that groped through the thick smoke he found the door. At that moment the fire shot up in a blaze of blinding flame, and there in the doorway stood Ellen. It was no withered body and bloated face that confronted him, but she with whom he had trysted in the wood, with the bloom of eternal youth upon her, and the smooth soft hand, on which was her wedding-ring, pointed at him.

===Chinese===
是时候走了，因为此刻一切已无虞，屋里热得像烤炉一般了。可正当他小心翼翼穿过那地板——裂开的油桶淌出的细流般的火焰正从那儿往四面八方蔓延——的时候，他听见楼上有一扇门被轻轻拉开了，接着，一阵又轻又稳的脚步声在楼梯上嗒嗒地响起来。一时间他吓得像失了魂似的僵住了，可他随即又把持住了自己，用那在浓烟里摸索的双手找到了门。就在那一刻，火焰猛地蹿起一道耀眼的火光，而门口站着艾伦。他面前的并非一具枯干的身躯和一张臃肿的脸，而是当年在林中与他幽会的那个她，脸上带着永不凋谢的青春的光泽，那光洁柔软的、戴着她的结婚戒指的手，正指着他。

===Original===
It was in vain that he called on himself to rush forward out of that torrid and suffocating air. The front door was open, he had but to pass her and speed forth safe into the night. But no power from his will reached his limbs; his will screamed to him, “Go, go! Push by her: it is but a phantom which you fear!” but muscle and sinew were in mutiny, and step by step he retreated before that pointing finger and the radiant shape that advanced on him. The flames that flickered over the floor had discovered the paraffin he had spilt, and leaped up his leg.

===Chinese===
他竭力叫自己冲出去，逃离那灼热窒息的空气，却是徒劳。前门是开着的，他只需从她身边擦过去，便能安全地冲进夜色之中。可他意志的力量传不到四肢上去；他的意志冲他尖叫：「走啊，走啊！从她身边挤过去：你所怕的不过是一个幻影！」可肌肉和筋腱都哗变了，他在那根指着他的手指、那个向他逼近的发光的身影前，一步一步地往后退。地板上跳跃的火焰找到了他溅洒的煤油，顺着他的裤腿便蹿了上来。

===Original===
Just one spot in his brain retained lucidity from the encompassing terror. Somewhere behind that barrier of fire there was the second door into the garden. He had but cursorily attempted to unlock its rusty wards; now, surely, the knowledge that there alone was escape would give strength to his hand. He leaped backwards through the flames, still with eyes fixed on her who ever advanced in time with his retreat, and turning, wrestled and strove with the key. Something snapped in his hand, and there still in the keyhole was the bare shaft.

===Chinese===
在四面袭来的恐怖之中，他脑子里只有一处还保留着清明。在那道火的屏障背后的某处，是通往花园的第二扇门。他先前不过草草地试着开过它那生了锈的锁；如今，唯有那一处是生路这一个念头，定能给他的手以力量。他倒退着跳过火焰，眼睛仍死死盯着那个随着他步步后退而步步逼近的她，转过身，便和那把钥匙搏斗起来。他手里咔地一响，钥匙孔里只剩下一根光秃秃的轴。

===Original===
Holding his breath, for the heat scorched his throat, he groped towards where he knew was the window through which he had first seen her that night. The flames licked fiercely round it, but there, beneath his hand, was the hasp, and he threw it open. At that the wind poured in as through the nozzle of a plied bellows, and Death rose high and bright around him. Through the flames, as he sank to the floor, a face radiant with revenge smiled on him.

===Chinese===
他屏住呼吸——那高温灼着他的喉咙——摸索着朝他记得的那扇窗爬过去，那一夜他正是从那扇窗里第一次看见了她。火焰猛烈地舔舐着窗子的四周，可就在他手底下，是那个窗搭扣，他一把把它掀开。那一瞬间，风像从一副被人使劲鼓动的风箱的喷嘴里灌了进来，死亡在他身边高高扬起、一片明亮。当他瘫倒在地板上时，透过那熊熊的火焰，一张因复仇而光辉灿烂的脸，正朝着他微笑。

## Between the Lights / 灯与灯之间

===Original===
The day had been one unceasing fall of snow from sunrise until the gradual withdrawal of the vague white light outside indicated that the sun had set again. But as usual at this hospitable and delightful house of Everard Chandler where I often spent Christmas, and was spending it now, there had been no lack of entertainment, and the hours had passed with a rapidity that had surprised us. A short billiard tournament had filled up the time between breakfast and lunch, with badminton and the morning papers for those who were temporarily not engaged, while afterwards, the interval till teatime had been occupied by the majority of the party in a huge game of hide-and-seek all over the house, barring the billiard-room, which was sanctuary for any who desired peace. But few had done that; the enchantment of Christmas, I must suppose, had, like some spell, made children of us again, and it was with palsied terror and trembling misgivings that we had tiptoed up and down the dim passages, from any corner of which some wild screaming form might dart out on us. Then, wearied with exercise and emotion, we had assembled again for tea in the hall, a room of shadows and panels on which the light from the wide open fireplace, where there burned a divine mixture of peat and logs, flickered and grew bright again on the walls. Then, as was proper, ghost-stories, for the narration of which the electric light was put out, so that the listeners might conjecture anything they pleased to be lurking in the corners, succeeded, and we vied with each other in blood, bones, skeletons, armour and shrieks. I had just given my contribution, and was reflecting with some complacency that probably the worst was now known, when Everard, who had not yet administered to the horror of his guests, spoke. He was sitting opposite me in the full blaze of the fire, looking, after the illness he had gone through during the autumn, still rather pale and delicate. All the same he had been among the boldest and best in the exploration of dark places that afternoon, and the look on his face now rather startled me.

===Chinese===
从日出直到外面那一片朦胧的白光渐渐褪去、显示太阳又已落山，这一整天雪下个不停。但在埃弗拉德·钱德勒（Everard Chandler）这好客而又讨人喜欢的宅子里——我常在这儿过圣诞，此刻也正在这儿过——和往常一样，消遣从不少，时辰过得之快，连我们自己也诧异。早饭后到午饭前的一段，由一场简短的台球比赛填满了，暂时轮空的几位则打打羽毛球、翻翻晨报；饭后到喝茶之间，一行人里的大多数又在这幢宅子里里外外玩起了一场盛大的捉迷藏，只有台球室除外——那地方是想要清静者的避难所。可没几个人去躲清静；我想，是圣诞的魔力，像某种符咒一般，又把我们变回了孩子，于是我们踮着脚在那昏暗的走廊里走来走去，心里又是瘫软般的恐惧，又是战战兢兢的疑虑，生怕哪个角落里会冷不丁蹿出一个尖叫着的人影来扑到我们身上。后来，运动和情绪都让我们疲乏了，大家便又聚到大万里喝茶。那是一间光影憧憧、镶着护墙板屋子，敞开的宽大壁炉里烧着一炉泥炭和木柴的绝妙混合物，火光在墙上摇曳，忽明忽暗。接下来，自然便是讲鬼故事了，为此电灯被熄掉，好让听的人尽可以猜想角落里潜伏着什么，于是我们在血污、白骨、骷髅、铠甲和尖叫上头一个比一个下功夫。我刚讲完我那一则，正暗自得意地想，最吓人的大概已经过去了，这时一直还没给客人们的恐怖感添柴加火的埃弗拉德开了口。他坐在我的对面，正对着熊熊的炉火，大病一场——他秋天刚闹过一场病——之后，脸色仍有些苍白单薄。虽说如此，那天下午探查各个暗角的时候，他却数一数二地胆大、数一数二地厉害，此刻他脸上的神情，倒叫我颇吃了一惊。

===Original===
“No, I don’t mind that sort of thing,” he said. “The paraphernalia of ghosts has become somehow rather hackneyed, and when I hear of screams and skeletons I feel I am on familiar ground, and can at least hide my head under the bedclothes.”

“Ah, but the bedclothes were twitched away by my skeleton,” said I, in self-defence.

“I know, but I don’t even mind that. Why, there are seven, eight skeletons in this room now, covered with blood and skin and other horrors. No, the nightmares of one’s childhood were the really frightening things, because they were vague. There was the true atmosphere of horror about them because one didn’t know what one feared. Now if one could recapture that﻿—”

Mrs. Chandler got quickly out of her seat.

“Oh, Everard,” she said, “surely you don’t wish to recapture it again. I should have thought once was enough.”

===Chinese===
「不，我倒不怕那种东西，」他说，「鬼魂的那一套行头，不知怎的，已经变得相当老套了，我一听见尖叫啦骷髅啦，就觉得是在熟门熟路的地界，至少还能把头缩进被窝里去。」

「哎，可我的骷髅是把被褥一把抽走的呀，」我自辩道。

「我知道，可我连那也不在乎。嗳，此刻这屋里就有七八具骷髅，盖着血、皮和其他种种可怖的玩意儿。不，真正吓人的，是小时候的那些噩梦，因为它们是模糊的。它们身上才有真正的恐怖气氛，因为你不知道自己怕的是什么。要是人能把那种感觉再抓回来——」

钱德勒太太（Mrs. Chandler）很快从座位上站了起来。

「哦，埃弗拉德，」她说，「你总不至于想把它再抓回来吧。我还以为一次就够了。」

===Original===
This was enchanting. A chorus of invitation asked him to proceed: the real true ghost-story firsthand, which was what seemed to be indicated, was too precious a thing to lose.

Everard laughed. “No, dear, I don’t want to recapture it again at all,” he said to his wife. Then to us: “But really the﻿—well, the nightmare perhaps, to which I was referring, is of the vaguest and most unsatisfactory kind. It has no apparatus about it at all. You will probably all say that it was nothing, and wonder why I was frightened. But I was; it frightened me out of my wits. And I only just saw something, without being able to swear what it was, and heard something which might have been a falling stone.”

“Anyhow tell us about the falling stone,” said I.

===Chinese===
这话可太勾人了。众人齐声催他讲下去：看来他所指的，是第一手的、货真价实的鬼故事，这东西太宝贵，万不能错过。

埃弗拉德笑了。「不，亲爱的，我一点也不想把它再抓回来，」他对妻子说。又转向我们：「不过，我说的那个——嗯，也许该叫噩梦吧——实在是再模糊不过、最不让人过瘾的那一种。它身上根本没有什么排场。你们多半都会说那什么也不是，并纳罕我何以会害怕。可我确实怕了；它把我吓得魂飞魄散。我只不过是瞥见了什么东西，却不敢起誓那究竟是什么，又听见了点什么声响，那声响也许不过是一块落下的石头。」

「不管怎样，给我们讲讲那块落下的石头吧。」我说。

===Original===
There was a stir of movement about the circle round the fire, and the movement was not of purely physical order. It was as if﻿—this is only what I personally felt﻿—it was as if the childish gaiety of the hours we had passed that day was suddenly withdrawn; we had jested on certain subjects, we had played hide-and-seek with all the power of earnestness that was in us. But now﻿—so it seemed to me﻿—there was going to be real hide-and-seek, real terrors were going to lurk in dark corners, or if not real terrors, terrors so convincing as to assume the garb of reality, were going to pounce on us. And Mrs. Chandler’s exclamation as she sat down again, “Oh, Everard, won’t it excite you?” tended in any case to excite us. The room still remained in dubious darkness except for the sudden lights disclosed on the walls by the leaping flames on the hearth, and there was wide field for conjecture as to what might lurk in the dim corners. Everard, moreover, who had been sitting in bright light before, was banished by the extinction of some flaming log into the shadows. A voice alone spoke to us, as he sat back in his low chair, a voice rather slow but very distinct.

“Last year,” he said, “on the twenty-fourth of December, we were down here, as usual, Amy and I, for Christmas. Several of you who are here now were here then. Three or four of you at least.”

I was one of these, but like the others kept silence, for the identification, so it seemed to me, was not asked for. And he went on again without a pause.

“Those of you who were here then,” he said, “and are here now, will remember how very warm it was this day year. You will remember, too, that we played croquet that day on the lawn. It was perhaps a little cold for croquet, and we played it rather in order to be able to say﻿—with sound evidence to back the statement﻿—that we had done so.”

===Chinese===
围着火炉的这一圈人里起了一阵骚动，而这骚动并不仅仅是身体上的。仿佛——这只是我个人的感觉——仿佛我们这一天里度过的那几个小时的孩子气的欢乐，忽然被收走了；我们曾经拿某些题目打趣，曾经拿出全身的认真劲儿来玩捉迷藏。可现在——我是这么觉得——真正的捉迷藏要开始了，真正的恐怖要在暗角里潜伏，或者即便不是真正的恐怖，也是逼真得以至于披上了真实外衣的恐怖，要向我们扑过来了。况且钱德勒太太重新坐下时那一句「哦，埃弗拉德，这不会刺激到你吧？」无论如何总算是把我们刺激了一下。屋里依旧是一片暧昧的黑暗，只有壁炉里跳动的火焰在墙上不时照出一块块骤亮的光，至于那昏暗的角落里可能潜伏着什么，便大有猜测的余地。再者，方才还坐在亮处的埃弗拉德，被一段烧塌的木柴一掩，也退进了阴影里。只剩一个声音朝我们说着话，他向后靠在那张低低的椅子里，那声音颇慢，却非常清晰。

「去年，」他说，「十二月二十四日，我和艾米（Amy）照例下来这儿过圣诞。现在在座的各位，有几位当时也在。至少有三四位。」

我也是其中之一，但和别人一样没有作声，因为照我看，他并不是要人来认领。他顿也不顿地接着讲了下去。

「当时在这里、现在也在这里的各位，」他说，「会记得去年的今天有多暖和。你们也会记得，那天我们在草坪上打了槌球。打槌球也许还略冷了些，我们打它，倒多半是为了能说上一句——而且有十足的佐证来撑这一句话——我们确实打过。」

===Original===
Then he turned and addressed the whole little circle.

“We played ties of half-games,” he said, “just as we have played billiards today, and it was certainly as warm on the lawn then as it was in the billiard-room this morning directly after breakfast, while today I should not wonder if there was three feet of snow outside. More, probably; listen.”

A sudden draught fluted in the chimney, and the fire flared up as the current of air caught it. The wind also drove the snow against the windows, and as he said “Listen,” we heard a soft scurry of the falling flakes against the panes, like the soft tread of many little people who stepped lightly, but with the persistence of multitudes who were flocking to some rendezvous. Hundreds of little feet seemed to be gathering outside; only the glass kept them out. And of the eight skeletons present four or five anyhow turned and looked at the windows. These were small-paned, with leaden bars. On the leaden bars little heaps of snow had accumulated, but there was nothing else to be seen.

“Yes, last Christmas Eve was very warm and sunny,” went on Everard. “We had had no frost that autumn, and a temerarious dahlia was still in flower. I have always thought that it must have been mad.”

He paused a moment.

“And I wonder if I were not mad too,” he added.

===Chinese===
然后他转过身，对这一小圈人全体说：

「我们打的是半局半局的淘汰赛，」他说，「就跟今天打台球一样，那时草坪上的暖和劲儿，确实和今早一吃过早饭那台球室里一模一样，而今天呢，外头若有三英尺厚的雪，我都不会惊奇。多半还不止；你们听。」

一阵穿堂风在烟囱里呜呜作响，气流一扑，炉火便窜了起来。风又把雪直往窗子上推，他一说「你们听」，我们便听见落下的雪絮扑在窗玻璃上发出一阵细碎的窸窣声，恍如许多小人儿轻手轻脚地踩着步子，却带着成群结队涌向某个约会地点的那股执拗劲儿。外头仿佛聚拢来了成百只小脚；只隔着一层玻璃，没让它们进来。在座的八具骷髅里，少说也有四五具回过头去，朝窗子望了望。那是些小格子的窗，镶着铅条。铅条上积着一小堆一小堆的雪，别的便什么也看不见了。

「是的，去年平安夜又暖又晴，」埃弗拉德接着说，「那年秋天没上过冻，一株不知天高地厚的大丽花（dahlia）竟还开着。我一直觉得它一定是疯了。」

他停了一下。

「我也纳罕，我自己是不是也疯了。」他补了一句。

===Original===
No one interrupted him; there was something arresting, I must suppose, in what he was saying; it chimed in anyhow with the hide-and-seek, with the suggestions of the lonely snow. Mrs. Chandler had sat down again, but I heard her stir in her chair. But never was there a gay party so reduced as we had been in the last five minutes. Instead of laughing at ourselves for playing silly games, we were all taking a serious game seriously.

“Anyhow I was sitting out,” he said to me, “while you and my wife played your half-game of croquet. Then it struck me that it was not so warm as I had supposed, because quite suddenly I shivered. And shivering I looked up. But I did not see you and her playing croquet at all. I saw something which had no relation to you and her﻿—at least I hope not.”

Now the angler lands his fish, the stalker kills his stag, and the speaker holds his audience. And as the fish is gaffed, and as the stag is shot, so were we held. There was no getting away till he had finished with us.

===Chinese===
没有人打断他；他的话里，我想，必有某种叫人非听下去不可的东西；它 anyhow 与那场捉迷藏、与那孤零零的雪意彼此应和。钱德勒太太又坐下了，可我听见她在椅子里不安地动了一下。可也从来没有一场快活的聚会，像我们这最后一五分钟里这样败了兴。我们不再笑自己玩那些傻游戏了，我们都把一场严肃的游戏当真起来。

「总之，我当时坐在场外，」他对我说，「你和我妻子在打你们那半局槌球。这时我忽然觉得并不像我原先以为的那么暖和，因为我猛地打了一个寒噤。我一边打着寒噤，一边抬起头来。可我根本没有看见你和她打槌球。我看见的是一件和你和她毫不相干的事——至少我希望不相干。」

钓鱼的人起鱼，猎鹿的人射鹿，说话的人攫住听众。我们便如被钩住的鱼、被射中的鹿一般，被他攫住了。他要不放过我们，谁也走不掉。

===Original===
“You all know the croquet lawn,” he said, “and how it is bounded all round by a flower border with a brick wall behind it, through which, you will remember, there is only one gate. Well, I looked up and saw that the lawn﻿—I could for one moment see it was still a lawn﻿—was shrinking, and the walls closing in upon it. As they closed in too, they grew higher, and simultaneously the light began to fade and be sucked from the sky, till it grew quite dark overhead and only a glimmer of light came in through the gate.

“There was, as I told you, a dahlia in flower that day, and as this dreadful darkness and bewilderment came over me, I remember that my eyes sought it in a kind of despair, holding on, as it were, to any familiar object. But it was no longer a dahlia, and for the red of its petals I saw only the red of some feeble firelight. And at that moment the hallucination was complete. I was no longer sitting on the lawn watching croquet, but I was in a low-roofed room, something like a cattle-shed, but round. Close above my head, though I was sitting down, ran rafters from wall to wall. It was nearly dark, but a little light came in from the door opposite to me, which seemed to lead into a passage that communicated with the exterior of the place. Little, however, of the wholesome air came into this dreadful den; the atmosphere was oppressive and foul beyond all telling, it was as if for years it had been the place of some human menagerie, and for those years had been uncleaned and unsweetened by the winds of heaven. Yet that oppressiveness was nothing to the awful horror of the place from the view of the spirit. Some dreadful atmosphere of crime and abomination dwelt heavy in it, its denizens, whoever they were, were scarce human, so it seemed to me, and though men and women, were akin more to the beasts of the field. And in addition there was present to me some sense of the weight of years; I had been taken and thrust down into some epoch of dim antiquity.”

===Chinese===
「你们都知道那片槌球草坪，」他说，「也都知道它四周围着花坛，花坛后面是一道砖墙，你们该记得，墙上只有一道门。嗳，我抬起头，看见那草坪——有那么一刻我还看得出它是一片草坪——正在缩拢，而四壁正朝它逼拢过来。它们一边逼拢，一边越长越高，与此同时，光线开始消退，被从天上抽走，直到头顶上完全黑了下来，只剩一线微光从那道门里透进来。

「那一天，正如我告诉过你们的，有一株大丽花开着，当这可怖的黑暗和迷乱朝我压下来的时候，我记得自己是用一种绝望的心情把目光去寻找它，仿佛要攀住任何一件熟悉的东西。可它已不再是一株大丽花，它花瓣的红色，我看到的只是一点微弱火光的红色。就在那一刻，幻觉完整了。我不再坐在草坪上看槌球了，而是置身于一间低矮屋顶的屋子里，有点像牛棚，却是圆的。我明明坐着，头顶上却紧挨着一根根从这墙横到那墙的椽子。屋里几乎全黑，只有从我对面那扇门里透进来一点光，那门似乎通向一条过道，与这地方的外头相连。然而几乎没有什么新鲜空气进到这可怖的窟穴里来；那气氛窒闷、恶臭得无法言说，仿佛多年来这里一直是关着某种人形兽类的笼子，那些年里也从未被天上的风吹扫过、清新过。可那窒闷，比起这地方在精神上的可怖来，根本算不得什么。某种罪恶与污秽的可怖气氛沉沉地笼罩着它，住在里面的，不论是什么东西，几乎都算不得是人——在我感觉如此——他们虽是男人和女人，却更近于田野里的走兽。除此之外，我还隐隐觉出一种岁月的重压；我被擒住，被掷进了某个幽暗古远的时代。」

===Original===
He paused a moment, and the fire on the hearth leaped up for a second and then died down again. But in that gleam I saw that all faces were turned to Everard, and that all wore some look of dreadful expectancy. Certainly I felt it myself, and waited in a sort of shrinking horror for what was coming.

“As I told you,” he continued, “where there had been that unseasonable dahlia, there now burned a dim firelight, and my eyes were drawn there. Shapes were gathered round it; what they were I could not at first see. Then perhaps my eyes got more accustomed to the dusk, or the fire burned better, for I perceived that they were of human form, but very small, for when one rose, with a horrible chattering, to his feet, his head was still some inches off the low roof. He was dressed in a sort of shirt that came to his knees, but his arms were bare and covered with hair. Then the gesticulation and chattering increased, and I knew that they were talking about me, for they kept pointing in my direction. At that my horror suddenly deepened, for I became aware that I was powerless and could not move hand or foot; a helpless, nightmare impotence had possession of me. I could not lift a finger or turn my head. And in the paralysis of that fear I tried to scream, but not a sound could I utter.

“All this I suppose took place with the instantaneousness of a dream, for at once, and without transition, the whole thing had vanished, and I was back on the lawn again, while the stroke for which my wife was aiming was still unplayed. But my face was dripping with perspiration, and I was trembling all over.

“Now you may all say that I had fallen asleep, and had a sudden nightmare. That may be so; but I was conscious of no sense of sleepiness before, and I was conscious of none afterwards. It was as if someone had held a book before me, whisked the pages open for a second and closed them again.”

===Chinese===
他停了一下，壁炉里的火窜起一瞬，又低下去。可就在那一闪的光里，我看见所有的脸都转向了埃弗拉德，每一张脸上都带着某种可怖的期待。我自己也确有此感，便在一种瑟缩的恐惧里等着下文。

「我刚才说过，」他接着讲，「原先那株不合时令的大丽花所在的地方，此刻燃着一团昏暗的火光，我的目光被它吸了过去。火光四周聚着几个人影；起初我看不清它们是什么。后来也许是我的眼睛更适应了昏暗，也许是火烧得更好了，我看出它们是人形，却非常矮小，因为当其中一个带着可怖的嘁嘁喳喳声站到脚上时，他的头离那低矮的屋顶还差着几英寸。他穿着一种长及膝盖的衬衫似的东西，可两条胳膊是光的，上面盖着毛。接着那指手画脚和嘁嘁喳喳愈演愈烈，我明白他们谈论的正是我，因为他们一直朝我这个方向指指点点。这一来我的恐怖骤然加深了，因为我发觉自己使不上力气，手脚都动弹不得；一种噩梦般的、无助的瘫痪攫住了我。我连一根手指都抬不起来，连头都转不了。在那种恐惧的麻痹里我想要尖叫，可一个音都发不出来。

「这一切，我想，都是像梦境一般瞬间发生的，因为整件事一下子、毫无过渡地便消失了，我又回到了草坪上，而我妻子正要打的那一杆球仍未打出。可我满脸淌着冷汗，浑身都在发抖。

「现在你们可能都会说，我是睡着了，骤然做了一个噩梦。也许是这样；可这之前我并不觉得有半点困意，这之后也不觉得有。那情形，就仿佛有人把一本书举到我面前，哗地把书页翻开了一秒，又合上了。」

===Original===
Somebody, I don’t know who, got up from his chair with a sudden movement that made me start, and turned on the electric light. I do not mind confessing that I was rather glad of this.

Everard laughed.

“Really I feel like Hamlet in the play-scene,” he said, “and as if there was a guilty uncle present. Shall I go on?”

I don’t think anyone replied, and he went on:

“Well, let us say for the moment that it was not a dream exactly, but a hallucination. Whichever it was, in any case it haunted me; for months, I think, it was never quite out of my mind, but lingered somewhere in the dusk of consciousness, sometimes sleeping quietly, so to speak, but sometimes stirring in its sleep. It was no good my telling myself that I was disquieting myself in vain, for it was as if something had actually entered into my very soul, as if some seed of horror had been planted there. And as the weeks went on the seed began to sprout, so that I could no longer even tell myself that that vision had been a moment’s disorderment only. I can’t say that it actually affected my health. I did not, as far as I know, sleep or eat insufficiently, but morning after morning I used to wake, not gradually and through pleasant dozings into full consciousness, but with absolute suddenness, and find myself plunged in an abyss of despair. Often too, eating or drinking, I used to pause and wonder if it was worth while.

“Eventually I told two people about my trouble, hoping that perhaps the mere communication would help matters, hoping also, but very distantly, that though I could not believe at present that digestion or the obscurities of the nervous system were at fault, a doctor by some simple dose might convince me of it. In other words I told my wife, who laughed at me, and my doctor who laughed also, and assured me that my health was quite unnecessarily robust. At the same time he suggested that change of air and scene does wonders for the delusions that exist merely in the imagination. He also told me, in answer to a direct question, that he would stake his reputation on the certainty that I was not going mad.

===Chinese===
不知是谁——我不知道是谁——猛地从椅子上站了起来，把我吓了一跳，又啪地把电灯打开了。我不妨承认，我对此倒颇觉庆幸。

埃弗拉德笑了。

「我真觉得自己像戏中戏那一幕里的哈姆雷特，」他说，「仿佛在场有一位心怀鬼胎的叔父。我还要讲下去吗？」

我想没人答话，他便接着讲：

「好吧，咱们暂且就说它不是一场纯粹的梦，而是一场幻觉。不论它是哪一种，总之它从此缠上了我；我想有好几个月，它从未真正离开过我的脑子，而是在意识的昏暗处徘徊着，有时——这么说吧——安静地睡着，有时却又在睡梦里翻动。我再怎么对自己说这是庸人自扰也无济于事，因为那感觉就像是有什么东西真的钻进了我的灵魂里，像是有什么恐怖的种子被种在了那里。随着一周周过去，那种子开始发芽，我便连对自己说『那景象不过是一时的神志错乱』也说不出口了。我说不上它真的影响了我的健康。据我所知，我并没有睡得不够、吃得不够，可是一天又一天，每天早晨我醒来，都不是渐渐地、经由惬意的半梦半醒进入完全的清醒，而是绝对地骤然醒来，发觉自己已坠入了一处绝望的深渊。常常地，吃着饭、喝着东西的时候，我也会停下来，纳罕这一切是否还值得。

「到末了我把我的苦恼告诉了两个人，盼着也许单是倾诉一番便能有所助益，也盼着——不过这盼望很渺茫——虽然我眼下不信是消化或是神经系统的什么疑难出了岔子，但愿一位医生凭某一剂简单的药就能叫我信服。换言之，我把这事告诉了我的妻子，她笑了我；又告诉了我的医生，他也笑了，并向我保证，以我这副出奇强健的身子，那些担心纯属多余。与此同时他建议说，换换空气、换换环境，对那些仅仅存在于想象中的妄想，是有奇效的。他还回答了我一个直截了当的问题：他愿意拿自己的名声打赌，担保我绝不会发疯。

===Original===
“Well, we went up to London as usual for the season, and though nothing whatever occurred to remind me in any way of that single moment on Christmas Eve, the reminding was seen to all right, the moment itself took care of that, for instead of fading as is the way of sleeping or waking dreams, it grew every day more vivid, and ate, so to speak, like some corrosive acid into my mind, etching itself there. And to London succeeded Scotland.
