“I took last year for the first time a small forest up in Sutherland, called Glen Callan, very remote and wild, but affording excellent stalking. It was not far from the sea, and the gillies used always to warn me to carry a compass on the hill, because sea-mists were liable to come up with frightful rapidity, and there was always a danger of being caught by one, and of having perhaps to wait hours till it cleared again. This at first I always used to do, but, as everyone knows, any precaution that one takes which continues to be unjustified gets gradually relaxed, and at the end of a few weeks, since the weather had been uniformly clear, it was natural that, as often as not, my compass remained at home.

“One day the stalk took me on to a part of my ground that I had seldom been on before, a very high tableland on the limit of my forest, which went down very steeply on one side to a loch that lay below it, and on the other, by gentler gradations, to the river that came from the loch, six miles below which stood the lodge. The wind had necessitated our climbing up﻿—or so my stalker had insisted﻿—not by the easier way, but up the crags from the loch. I had argued the point with him, for it seemed to me that it was impossible that the deer could get our scent if we went by the more natural path, but he still held to his opinion, and therefore, since after all this was his part of the job, I yielded. A dreadful climb we had of it, over big boulders with deep holes in between, masked by clumps of heather, so that a wary eye and a prodding stick were necessary for each step if one wished to avoid broken bones. Adders also literally swarmed in the heather; we must have seen a dozen at least on our way up, and adders are a beast for which I have no manner of use. But a couple of hours saw us to the top, only to find that the stalker had been utterly at fault, and that the deer must quite infallibly have got wind of us, if they had remained in the place where we last saw them. That, when we could spy the ground again, we saw had happened; in any case they had gone. The man insisted the wind had changed, a palpably stupid excuse, and I wondered at that moment what other reason he had﻿—for reason I felt sure there must be﻿—for not wishing to take what would clearly now have been a better route. But this piece of bad management did not spoil our luck, for within an hour we had spied more deer, and about two o’clock I got a shot, killing a heavy stag. Then sitting on the heather I ate lunch, and enjoyed a well-earned bask and smoke in the sun. The pony meantime had been saddled with the stag, and was plodding homewards.

===Chinese===
「嗳，社交季节开始后，我们照例上了伦敦，虽说没有任何事情来让我想起圣诞前夕那一刹那，那提醒却自有办法，那一刹那本身便料理了这事——因为它并不像睡梦或是白日梦那样日渐褪色，反而一天比一天鲜明，可以说像某种腐蚀性的酸一般咬进了我的脑子，把自己蚀刻在了上头。伦敦之后，便到了苏格兰。

「去年我第一次在萨瑟兰郡（Sutherland）租下了一小片林地，叫格伦卡伦（Glen Callan），极是偏僻荒凉，却是个猎鹿的上佳去处。那地方离海不远，猎手们（gillies）总提醒我上山要带上罗盘，因为海上起雾来得极快，叫人猝不及防，总有被一场雾困住、也许要等上好几个钟头才能再放晴的危险。起初我一向照办，可人人都知道，凡是一种一再被证明是多余的防备，总会渐渐松懈下去；过了几个礼拜，天气又是一律地晴好，我的罗盘十有八九留在家里，也就很自然了。

「有一天，那一猎把我带上了我那片林地里很少去的一处——一块极高、位于林地边界的高原台地，它的一侧极陡地直落到下方的一个湖泊（loch），另一侧则以较为和缓的坡度降到从湖里流出来的那条河，顺河往下六英里便是我们的住屋。风向使我们——或者按猎手（stalker）的说法，是他坚持——非得从更难走的那条路、即从湖边攀上岩壁上来不可。我与他争过这一点，因为在我看来，我们若走那条更合常理的路，鹿是断然闻不到我们气味的，可他仍固执己见，于是，既然这终究是他分内的事，我也就依了他。那可真是一次可怕的攀登，脚下尽是巨石，石间是深深的窟窿，又一簇簇石楠花掩着，因而每走一步都得瞪大眼睛、用手杖探路，否则便难免摔断骨头。蝰蛇在石楠丛里简直多得成群；我们一路上来少说也看见了十几条，而蝰蛇这东西，我是最派不上用场的。可两个钟头后我们还是上到了顶，结果发觉那猎手完全错了，鹿若还留在我们最后一次看见它们的地方，就一定闻到了我们的气味。等我们再能看清地形，果然发现事情正是如此；不管怎样，它们是走了。那人坚持说是风向变了，这借口蠢得明明白白，那一刻我纳罕他究竟另有何缘故——我确信他必有缘故——不愿走眼下明明更好走的那条路。但这一通瞎指挥并未糟蹋我们的运气，因为不出一个钟头我们又觅到了更多的鹿，两点光景我开了枪，打到了一头沉甸甸的雄鹿。随后我坐在石楠上吃午饭，享受着这来之不易的、晒太阳抽烟的一份惬意。这其间，那匹小马已驮上了那头鹿，正一步一颠地往家走。

===Original===
“The morning had been extraordinarily warm, with a little wind blowing off the sea, which lay a few miles off sparkling beneath a blue haze, and all morning in spite of our abominable climb I had had an extreme sense of peace, so much so that several times I had probed my mind, so to speak, to find if the horror still lingered there. But I could scarcely get any response from it. Never since Christmas had I been so free of fear, and it was with a great sense of repose, both physical and spiritual, that I lay looking up into the blue sky, watching my smoke-whorls curl slowly away into nothingness. But I was not allowed to take my ease long, for Sandy came and begged that I would move. The weather had changed, he said, the wind had shifted again, and he wanted me to be off this high ground and on the path again as soon as possible, because it looked to him as if a sea-mist would presently come up.

“ ‘And yon’s a bad place to get down in the mist,’ he added, nodding towards the crags we had come up.

“I looked at the man in amazement, for to our right lay a gentle slope down on to the river, and there was now no possible reason for again tackling those hideous rocks up which we had climbed this morning. More than ever I was sure he had some secret reason for not wishing to go the obvious way. But about one thing he was certainly right, the mist was coming up from the sea, and I felt in my pocket for the compass, and found I had forgotten to bring it.

===Chinese===
「那天上午异乎寻常地暖和，海在几英里外，在一层蓝色的薄霭下闪闪发光，从海上吹来一丝微风。整个上午，尽管我们爬了那段要命的坡，我心里却有一种极大的安宁，以致有好几回我都在心里——这么说吧——探查自己，看看那桩恐怖是不是还盘踞在心里。可我几乎探不出什么回响。自圣诞以来，我从未这般无所畏惧，我便怀着一种身心两方面的极大安恬，躺着仰望碧蓝的天，看我自己吐出的一圈圈烟缓缓地卷散成无。可这份清闲没让我享受多久，因为桑迪（Sandy）过来求我动身。天气变了，他说，风向又转了，他要我尽快离开这块高地、回到路上去，因为照他看，海上很快就要起雾了。

「『那一带在雾里下来可不是好玩的，』他补了一句，朝我们上来的那片岩壁点了点头。

我惊奇地看着这个人，因为在我们右边就有一道缓坡通到河边，眼下再没有任何理由去重新对付今早爬上来的那一片可憎的岩石了。我比任何时候都更确信，他之不愿走那条显而易见的路，必有某种隐秘的缘故。但有一件事他肯定说对了，雾正从海上涌起来，我便伸手到口袋里去摸罗盘，发觉自己忘了带。

===Original===
“Then there followed a curious scene which lost us time that we could really ill afford to waste, I insisting on going down by the way that common sense directed, he imploring me to take his word for it that the crags were the better way. Eventually, I marched off to the easier descent, and told him not to argue any more but follow. What annoyed me about him was that he would only give the most senseless reasons for preferring the crags. There were mossy places, he said, on the way I wished to go, a thing patently false, since the summer had been one spell of unbroken weather; or it was longer, also obviously untrue; or there were so many vipers about. But seeing that none of these arguments produced any effect, at last he desisted, and came after me in silence.

“We were not yet half down when the mist was upon us, shooting up from the valley like the broken water of a wave, and in three minutes we were enveloped in a cloud of fog so thick that we could barely see a dozen yards in front of us. It was therefore another cause for self-congratulation that we were not now, as we should otherwise have been, precariously clambering on the face of those crags up which we had come with such difficulty in the morning, and as I rather prided myself on my powers of generalship in the matter of direction, I continued leading, feeling sure that before long we should strike the track by the river. More than all, the absolute freedom from fear elated me; since Christmas I had not known the instinctive joy of that; I felt like a schoolboy home for the holidays. But the mist grew thicker and thicker, and whether it was that real rain-clouds had formed above it, or that it was of an extraordinary density itself, I got wetter in the next hour than I have ever been before or since. The wet seemed to penetrate the skin, and chill the very bones. And still there was no sign of the track for which I was making. Behind me, muttering to himself, followed the stalker, but his arguments and protestations were dumb, and it seemed as if he kept close to me, as if afraid.

===Chinese===
「接下来便发生了一幕古怪的情景，耽误了我们实在耽搁不起的工夫：我执意要按常识所指的路下去，他则恳求我相信他的话，说走那片岩壁才是更好的路。到末了，我径自朝那条好走的下坡路走去，叫他别再争了，跟着就是。叫我恼火的是，他偏要给些最无道理的理由来坚持走岩壁。他说我想走的那条路上有青苔——这分明是假话，因为整个夏天都是一连串的好天；又说那条路更长——也显然不实；再说那一带蝰蛇太多。可眼见这些理由一概无效，他终于作罢，默默地跟了上来。

「我们还没下到一半，雾便追上了我们，从山谷里腾起来，像一道浪头碎裂的水花，不出三分钟，我们便被裹进了一团浓得化不开的雾里，前面十二码开外都看不清。这倒又是一件值得自庆的事：幸亏我们没有——否则便要——在那片今早好不容易才爬上来的岩壁上岌岌可危地攀着；而我又颇以自己辨别方向的统帅之才自诩，便继续领着路，深信不久便会撞上河边的那条小径。更叫我快活的是，那种全然无所畏惧的心境；自圣诞以来，我还从未尝过这一份本能的喜悦；我觉得自己像个放假回家的学童。可雾越来越浓，也不知是真有雨云在上头结成了，还是这雾本身稠得出奇，接下来一个钟头里，我淋得比这辈子哪一次都透。那湿气仿佛能钻透皮、寒透骨。可我朝之赶去的那条小径仍不见踪影。身后那猎手一面嘟囔着一面跟着，但他那套道理和抗议都不作声了，倒像是紧紧挨着我，仿佛害怕。

===Original===
“Now there are many unpleasant companions in this world; I would not for instance care to be on the hill with a drunkard or a maniac, but worse than either, I think, is a frightened man, because his trouble is infectious, and, insensibly, I began to be afraid of being frightened too. From that it is but a short step to fear. Other perplexities too beset us. At one time we seemed to be walking on flat ground, at another I felt sure we were climbing again, whereas all the time we ought to have been descending, unless we had missed the way very badly indeed. Also, for the month was October, it was beginning to get dark, and it was with a sense of relief that I remembered that the full moon would rise soon after sunset. But it had grown very much colder, and soon, instead of rain, we found we were walking through a steady fall of snow.

“Things were pretty bad, but then for the moment they seemed to mend, for, far away to the left, I suddenly heard the brawling of the river. It should, it is true, have been straight in front of me and we were perhaps a mile out of our way, but this was better than the blind wandering of the last hour, and turning to the left, I walked towards it. But before I had gone a hundred yards, I heard a sudden choked cry behind me, and just saw Sandy’s form flying as if in terror of pursuit, into the mists. I called to him but got no reply, and heard only the spurned stones of his running. What had frightened him I had no idea, but certainly with his disappearance, the infection of his fear disappeared also, and I went on, I may almost say, with gaiety. On the moment, however, I saw a sudden well-defined blackness in front of me, and before I knew what I was doing I was half stumbling, half walking up a very steep grass slope.

===Chinese===
「这世上有许多叫人不快的同行者；比方说，我不愿和一个醉汉或疯子同在山上，可我觉得比这两者更糟的，是一个受了惊的人，因为他的毛病是会传染的，于是不知不觉间，我也开始怕自己会被吓着。由此到害怕，不过一步之遥。还有别的困惑来扰。一会儿我们像是在平地上走着，一会儿我又确信我们在往上爬，而按理我们应当一直在往下走，除非我们迷路迷得一塌糊涂。再者，时令既是十月，天开始黑了，我想起满月在日落后不久就要升起，不觉松了一口气。可天又冷了许多，不久，落下来的便不是雨，而是我们一路踩着的一场稳稳的雪。

「情形已经够糟了，可这一时又好像有了转机，因为在远远的左方，我忽然听见了那条河的潺潺声。说实话，它本该就在我正前方，我们也许偏离了路线足有一英里，可比过去一个钟头里那种瞎摸乱转强多了，我便朝左转，朝它走去。可还没走出一百码，我便听见身后一声哽住的喊叫，只见桑迪的身影仿佛被什么东西追着似的，惊惶地一头钻进了雾里。我喊他，没有回音，只听见他脚下踢飞的石子。什么东西吓着了他，我毫无头绪，但可以肯定的是，他这一消失，他那恐惧的传染也随之消失了，我往前走，几乎可以说是带着轻快的心情。然而就在那一刻，我看见前面陡然现出一团清晰的黑暗，还没回过神来，我已经半跌半走地爬上了一道极陡的草坡。

===Original===
“During the last few minutes the wind had got up, and the driving snow was peculiarly uncomfortable, but there had been a certain consolation in thinking that the wind would soon disperse these mists, and I had nothing more than a moonlight walk home. But as I paused on this slope, I became aware of two things, one, that the blackness in front of me was very close, the other that, whatever it was, it sheltered me from the snow. So I climbed on a dozen yards into its friendly shelter, for it seemed to me to be friendly.

“A wall some twelve feet high crowned the slope, and exactly where I struck it there was a hole in it, or door rather, through which a little light appeared. Wondering at this I pushed on, bending down, for the passage was very low, and in a dozen yards came out on the other side. Just as I did this the sky suddenly grew lighter, the wind, I suppose, having dispersed the mists, and the moon, though not yet visible through the flying skirts of cloud, made sufficient illumination.

“I was in a circular enclosure, and above me there projected from the walls some four feet from the ground, broken stones which must have been intended to support a floor. Then simultaneously two things occurred.

“The whole of my nine months’ terror came back to me, for I saw that the vision in the garden was fulfilled, and at the same moment I saw stealing towards me a little figure as of a man, but only about three foot six in height. That my eyes told me; my ears told me that he stumbled on a stone; my nostrils told me that the air I breathed was of an overpowering foulness, and my soul told me that it was sick unto death. I think I tried to scream, but could not, I know I tried to move and could not. And it crept closer.

“Then I suppose the terror which held me spellbound so spurred me that I must move, for next moment I heard a cry break from my lips, and was stumbling through the passage. I made one leap of it down the grass slope, and ran as I hope never to have to run again. What direction I took I did not pause to consider, so long as I put distance between me and that place. Luck, however, favoured me, and before long I struck the track by the river, and an hour afterwards reached the lodge.

“Next day I developed a chill, and as you know pneumonia laid me on my back for six weeks.

“Well, that is my story, and there are many explanations. You may say that I fell asleep on the lawn, and was reminded of that by finding myself, under discouraging circumstances, in an old Picts’ castle, where a sheep or a goat that, like myself, had taken shelter from the storm, was moving about. Yes, there are hundreds of ways in which you may explain it. But the coincidence was an odd one, and those who believe in second sight might find an instance of their hobby in it.”

“And that is all?” I asked.

“Yes, it was nearly too much for me. I think the dressing-bell has sounded.”

===Chinese===
「最后那几分钟里风大了起来，扑面打来的雪花叫人格外难受，不过心里还有一种安慰：这风很快便会把这雾吹散，我剩下的不过是一场月光下的散步回家罢了。可我在坡上停住时，便察觉了两件事：一，前面那团黑离我极近；二，不论它是什么，它替我挡住了雪。于是我又往上爬了十几码，钻进它那仿佛友善的遮蔽里——因为在我看来它是友善的。

「一道约莫十二英尺高的墙立在坡顶，恰好在我撞到它的地方有一个洞，或者不如说一扇门，从里头透出一点光。我纳罕着，弯下腰继续往前挤，因为那过道极矮，十几码后便从另一头钻了出来。就在我钻出来的那一刻，天忽然亮了一些，我想是风把雾吹散了，月亮虽还被乱云的飞裙遮着、看不见，却已洒下了足够的光。

「我置身于一个圆形的围垣之中，在我头顶上方约莫四英尺高的地方，从墙壁上突出一些断裂的石头，想必当年是用来承托一层地板的。接着，有两件事同时发生。

「我这九个月来的全部恐怖，一齐回到我身上，因为我看见，花园里那场幻象应验了；与此同时，我看见一个小小的人影正朝我偷偷摸来，似是一个男人，却只有三英尺六英寸高。这是我的眼睛告诉我的；我的耳朵告诉我，他在一块石头上绊了一下；我的鼻孔告诉我，我呼吸着的空气有一股压倒一切的恶臭；而我的灵魂告诉我，它已病入膏肓。我想我是想叫的，却叫不出来；我知道我想动，却动不了。它越爬越近。

「后来我想，那把我钉住的恐惧反倒这样鞭策了我，叫我非动不可，因为下一刻我听见一声叫喊从自己唇间迸出，便踉跄着钻过了那条过道。我顺着草坡一纵便跳了下去，随即拼命地跑，我但愿这辈子永远不必再那样跑一回。我朝哪个方向跑的，根本没停下来想过，只要把自己和那地方拉开距离就行。可运气是帮我的，不久我便撞上了河边的那条小径，一个钟头后便到了住屋。

「第二天我着了凉，你们是知道的，肺炎把我按倒在床上足足六个星期。

「嗳，这就是我的故事，解释可以有很多。你们大可说我是自己在草坪上睡着了，后来又在不妙的境地里发觉自己置身于一座古皮克特人（Picts）的城堡中，里头一只羊或一只山羊——和我一样进来避风雪的——正走来走去，这才让我想起了草坪上的那一幕。是的，要解释它可以有上百种说法。但那巧合未免太奇了些，信第二视觉（second sight）那套的人，也许倒能从中为他们的癖好寻到一个例证。」

「就这些？」我问。

「是的，这对我几乎已经太多了。我想，换装的铃已经响过了。」

## Caterpillars / 毛虫

===Original===
I saw a month or two ago in an Italian paper that the Villa Cascana, in which I once stayed, had been pulled down, and that a manufactory of some sort was in process of erection on its site. There is therefore no longer any reason for refraining from writing of those things which I myself saw (or imagined I saw) in a certain room and on a certain landing of the villa in question, nor from mentioning the circumstances which followed, which may or may not (according to the opinion of the reader) throw some light on or be somehow connected with this experience.

The Villa Cascana was in all ways but one a perfectly delightful house, yet, if it were standing now, nothing in the world﻿—I use the phrase in its literal sense﻿—would induce me to set foot in it again, for I believe it to have been haunted in a very terrible and practical manner. Most ghosts, when all is said and done, do not do much harm; they may perhaps terrify, but the person whom they visit usually gets over their visitation. They may on the other hand be entirely friendly and beneficent. But the appearances in the Villa Cascana were not beneficent, and had they made their “visit” in a very slightly different manner, I do not suppose I should have got over it any more than Arthur Inglis did.

===Chinese===
一两个月前，我在一份意大利报纸上看到，我曾住过的那座卡斯卡纳别墅（Villa Cascana）已被拆毁，原址上正在兴建某种工厂。既然如此，我也就再没有理由不去写下我亲见（或者自以为亲见）于那座别墅里某一个房间、某一段楼梯平台上的种种情形，也没有理由不去记述此后发生的那些事情——这些事情，或可（也或不可，全凭读者如何看）对这一段经历有所阐明，又或者与之有着某种关联。

那座卡斯卡纳别墅，除却一桩之外，样样都称得上是一处极令人心悦的宅子。然而，倘若它今日还矗立着，世上无论什么——我这话是字字当真的——都不能再诱我踏进它一步，因为我相信，它曾以一种极其可怖而又切实的方式闹过鬼。说到底，大多数鬼魂并不为害太甚；它们也许叫人惊惧，但受其造访的人，通常总能从那造访中缓过劲来。在另一种情形下，它们也完全可以是友善的、施惠的。然而卡斯卡纳别墅里显现的那些，并非施惠之物；倘若它们的「造访」再稍稍换个样子，我想，我恐怕也未必能比阿瑟·英格利斯（Arthur Inglis）更好地从中脱身。

===Original===
The house stood on an ilex-clad hill not far from Sestri di Levante on the Italian Riviera, looking out over the iridescent blues of that enchanted sea, while behind it rose the pale green chestnut woods that climb up the hillsides till they give place to the pines that, black in contrast with them, crown the slopes. All round it the garden in the luxuriance of mid-spring bloomed and was fragrant, and the scent of magnolia and rose, borne on the salt freshness of the winds from the sea, flowed like a stream through the cool vaulted rooms.

On the ground floor a broad pillared loggia ran round three sides of the house, the top of which formed a balcony for certain rooms of the first floor. The main staircase, broad and of grey marble steps, led up from the hall to the landing outside these rooms, which were three in number, namely two big sitting-rooms and a bedroom arranged en suite. The latter was unoccupied, the sitting-rooms were in use. From these the main staircase was continued to the second floor, where were situated certain bedrooms, one of which I occupied, while from the other side of the first-floor landing some half-dozen steps led to another suite of rooms, where, at the time I am speaking of, Arthur Inglis, the artist, had his bedroom and studio. Thus the landing outside my bedroom at the top of the house, commanded both the landing of the first floor, and also the steps that led to Inglis’ rooms. Jim Stanley and his wife, finally (whose guest I was), occupied rooms in another wing of the house, where also were the servants’ quarters.

I arrived just in time for lunch on a brilliant noon of mid-May. The garden was shouting with colour and fragrance, and not less delightful after my broiling walk up from the marina, should have been the coming from the reverberating heat and blaze of the day into the marble coolness of the villa. Only (the reader has my bare word for this, and nothing more), the moment I set foot in the house I felt that something was wrong. This feeling, I may say, was quite vague, though very strong, and I remember that when I saw letters waiting for me on the table in the hall I felt certain that the explanation was here: I was convinced that there was bad news of some sort for me. Yet when I opened them I found no such explanation of my premonition: my correspondents all reeked of prosperity. Yet this clear miscarriage of a presentiment did not dissipate my uneasiness. In that cool fragrant house there was something wrong.

I am at pains to mention this because to the general view it may explain that though I am as a rule so excellent a sleeper that the extinction of my light on getting into bed is apparently contemporaneous with being called on the following morning, I slept very badly on my first night in the Villa Cascana. It may also explain the fact that when I did sleep (if it was indeed in sleep that I saw what I thought I saw) I dreamed in a very vivid and original manner, original, that is to say, in the sense that something that, as far as I knew, had never previously entered into my consciousness, usurped it then. But since, in addition to this evil premonition, certain words and events occurring during the rest of the day, might have suggested something of what I thought happened that night, it will be well to relate them.

After lunch, then, I went round the house with Mrs. Stanley, and during our tour she referred, it is true, to the unoccupied bedroom on the first floor, which opened out of the room where we had lunched.

“We left that unoccupied,” she said, “because Jim and I have a charming bedroom and dressing-room, as you saw, in the wing, and if we used it ourselves we should have to turn the dining-room into a dressing-room and have our meals downstairs. As it is, however, we have our little flat there, Arthur Inglis has his little flat in the other passage; and I remembered (aren’t I extraordinary?) that you once said that the higher up you were in a house the better you were pleased. So I put you at the top of the house, instead of giving you that room.”

It is true, that a doubt, vague as my uneasy premonition, crossed my mind at this. I did not see why Mrs. Stanley should have explained all this, if there had not been more to explain. I allow, therefore, that the thought that there was something to explain about the unoccupied bedroom was momentarily present to my mind.

The second thing that may have borne on my dream was this.

At dinner the conversation turned for a moment on ghosts. Inglis, with the certainty of conviction, expressed his belief that anybody who could possibly believe in the existence of supernatural phenomena was unworthy of the name of an ass. The subject instantly dropped. As far as I can recollect, nothing else occurred or was said that could bear on what follows.

We all went to bed rather early, and personally I yawned my way upstairs, feeling hideously sleepy. My room was rather hot, and I threw all the windows wide, and from without poured in the white light of the moon, and the love-song of many nightingales. I undressed quickly, and got into bed, but though I had felt so sleepy before, I now felt extremely wide-awake. But I was quite content to be awake: I did not toss or turn, I felt perfectly happy listening to the song and seeing the light. Then, it is possible, I may have gone to sleep, and what follows may have been a dream. I thought anyhow that after a time the nightingales ceased singing and the moon sank. I thought also that if, for some unexplained reason, I was going to lie awake all night, I might as well read, and I remembered that I had left a book in which I was interested in the dining-room on the first floor. So I got out of bed, lit a candle, and went downstairs. I went into the room, saw on a side-table the book I had come to look for, and then, simultaneously, saw that the door into the unoccupied bedroom was open. A curious grey light, not of dawn nor of moonshine, came out of it, and I looked in. The bed stood just opposite the door, a big four-poster, hung with tapestry at the head. Then I saw that the greyish light of the bedroom came from the bed, or rather from what was on the bed. For it was covered with great caterpillars, a foot or more in length, which crawled over it. They were faintly luminous, and it was the light from them that showed me the room. Instead of the sucker-feet of ordinary caterpillars they had rows of pincers like crabs, and they moved by grasping what they lay on with their pincers, and then sliding their bodies forward. In colour these dreadful insects were yellowish-grey, and they were covered with irregular lumps and swellings. There must have been hundreds of them, for they formed a sort of writhing, crawling pyramid on the bed. Occasionally one fell off on to the floor, with a soft fleshy thud, and though the floor was of hard concrete, it yielded to the pincer-feet as if it had been putty, and, crawling back, the caterpillar would mount on to the bed again, to rejoin its fearful companions. They appeared to have no faces, so to speak, but at one end of them there was a mouth that opened sideways in respiration.

Then, as I looked, it seemed to me as if they all suddenly became conscious of my presence. All the mouths at any rate were turned in my direction, and next moment they began dropping off the bed with those soft fleshy thuds on to the floor, and wriggling towards me. For one second a paralysis as of a dream was on me, but the next I was running upstairs again to my room, and I remember feeling the cold of the marble steps on my bare feet. I rushed into my bedroom, and slammed the door behind me, and then﻿—I was certainly wide awake now﻿—I found myself standing by my bed with the sweat of terror pouring from me. The noise of the banged door still rang in my ears. But, as would have been more usual, if this had been mere nightmare, the terror that had been mine when I saw those foul beasts crawling about the bed or dropping softly on to the floor did not cease then. Awake now, if dreaming before, I did not at all recover from the horror of dream: it did not seem to me that I had dreamed. And until dawn, I sat or stood, not daring to lie down, thinking that every rustle or movement that I heard was the approach of the caterpillars. To them and the claws that bit into the cement the wood of the door was child’s play: steel would not keep them out.

But with the sweet and noble return of day the horror vanished: the whisper of wind became benignant again: the nameless fear, whatever it was, was smoothed out and terrified me no longer. Dawn broke, hueless at first; then it grew dove-coloured, then the flaming pageant of light spread over the sky.

===Chinese===
那宅子矗立在一座覆满冬青的山丘上，离意大利里维埃拉的塞斯特里·莱万泰（Sestri di Levante）不远，眺望着那片如幻海面波光粼粼的层层蔚蓝；它的身后，浅绿的栗树林沿着山坡攀援而上，到了高处便让位给松树，与栗树的浅绿相衬之下黑压压的，覆盖着山脊。宅子四周的花园正值仲春的葳蕤，花开四散、芳香扑鼻；木兰与玫瑰的香气，乘着海上吹来的带咸味的清风，宛如一道溪流，淌过那些凉爽的、拱顶的房间。

底楼有一条宽阔的柱廊，环绕着宅子的三面，其顶便成了二楼几间房间的露台。正中的楼梯宽阔，踏着灰白大理石的级，从门厅直通到这几间房外的平台。这几间房共有三间，即两间大起居室和一间与之成套的卧室。后者空着不用，两间起居室则在使用之中。正楼梯从这两间起居室再往上，通往三楼，那里有几间卧室，其中一间便是我所住的；而由二楼平台的另一边，再上六七级台阶，便又通向另一套房间——在我所说的那段日子里，画家阿瑟·英格利斯便把他的卧室和画室设在那里。于是，我在宅子顶层那间卧室外的平台，既可俯瞰二楼的平台，也可俯瞰通往英格利斯房间的台阶。至于吉姆·斯坦利（Jim Stanley）夫妇——我是他们的客人——则住在宅子的另一翼，仆人的住处也在那一带。

我恰好在午饭时分赶到，那是五月中旬一个灿烂的正午。花园里色彩与芬芳几乎要呐喊出来；我从码头一路顶着烈日走来，从外头白晃晃、烫人的酷热里走进别墅大理石般的清凉，这本该是再惬意不过的事。只是（这一点读者除了我空口一言之外，再无别证），我一踏进这宅子，便觉得有哪里不对劲。这感觉，我得说，十分模糊，却又异常强烈。我记得，当看见门厅桌上摆着等我的几封信时，我便认定谜底就在这里：我深信其中有某种坏消息在等着我。然而拆开一看，却全然不见对我那预感的任何解释：给我写信的人，字里行间无不是一派顺遂兴旺。然而，这一回分明落了空的预感，却并未驱散我的不安。那座凉爽、芳香的宅子里，有哪里不对劲。

我之所以特意记下这一笔，是因为在旁观者看来，这或许便能解释：为何我向来是个极佳的睡眠者——熄灯上床与次日早晨被叫醒，在外人看来几乎是同一瞬间的事——却在卡斯卡纳别墅的头一夜睡得极糟。这或许也能解释：当真睡着时（倘若我所见的，确是在睡梦中所见），我何以会做得那样鲜明、那样别致的梦——所谓别致，是说我平生从未进入过我意识之中的某种东西，在那梦里篡夺了我的全部心神。然而，除了这一层不祥的预感之外，当天余下的时光里所说的几句话、所发生的几件事，也许同样暗示了那夜我所认为发生之事的某些由头；那么，把它们一并记述下来，也是相宜的。

午饭之后，我便随斯坦利太太（Mrs. Stanley）在宅子里各处走了一圈，途中她确曾提到过二楼那间空着的卧室——它就从我们方才用午餐的那间房里开门进去。

「我们把那间空着，」她说，「是因为吉姆和我有一间很可爱的卧室和更衣室，你也见着了，就在那一翼里；我们自己若用那间，就得把餐室改成更衣室，到楼下吃饭了。如今这样呢，我们在那头有一小套自己的住处，阿瑟·英格利斯在另一条过道里也有他一小套；我又记起来（我可真有本事，是不是？），你曾说过，人在宅子里住得越高便越称心。所以我就把你安在宅子顶上，没给你那间。」

的确，听到这话时，一个疑念——和我那不安的预感一般模糊——掠过了我的心头。我看不出斯坦利太太何须把这许多都解释一番，倘若不是还有更多要解释的话。所以我也承认，关于那间空着的卧室、其中或有某种待解之事的念头，曾在我心头一闪而过。

第二件可能与我的梦有关的事是这样的。

晚餐时，话题一度转到了鬼魂上。英格利斯以一种确信无疑的口气断言：凡是有可能相信超自然现象存在的人，都连「驴子」这名字都不配。话题当即就揭过了。据我所能追忆，再没有发生、再没有说出什么与下文相关的话来。

我们大家早早便都上了楼，就我个人而言，是一路打着哈欠上楼的，困得厉害。我的房间相当热，我便把所有窗子都敞开，外面涌进了白色的月光，和许多夜莺求偶的歌。我匆匆脱衣上了床，可方才还困得要命，此刻却清醒异常。但我倒也乐得醒着：我不翻来覆去，听那歌声、看那月色，只觉得十分快活。随后，我也许睡着了，而下文也许只是一场梦。无论如何，我以为过了一阵，夜莺不再唱了，月亮也沉了下去。我又想，倘若不知何故我竟要整夜醒着，倒不如读读书，于是我想起有一本我正读得有趣的书，落在了二楼的餐室里。我便下了床，点起一支蜡烛，走下楼去。我走进那间房，看见一张边桌上摆着我来找的那本书，与此同时，也看见通往那间空卧室的门是开着的。一道奇异的灰光——既非晨曦，也非月色——从里面透出来，我便朝里张望。床正对着门，是一张大四柱床，床头挂着花毯。随即我便看见，那卧室里的灰光，是从床上发出来的，更确切地说，是从床上的那些东西上发出来的。因为床上爬满了硕大的毛虫，每一只足有一英尺多长。它们微微发着光，正是它们的光，照亮了整个房间。它们没有寻常毛虫那种吸盘似的脚，取而代之的是一行行蟹螯般的钳子；它们靠着用钳子钳住身下之物、再把身体向前滑动来行进。这些可怖的昆虫颜色黄灰，身上布满了大小不一的疙瘩与肿胀。它们少说也有几百只，在床上堆成了一座蠕动的、爬行着的金字塔。偶尔有一只啪嗒一声掉到地上——那是软肉的闷响——而地板虽是坚硬的水泥，在它们的钳脚下却软如油灰；于是那毛虫爬回床边，重又攀上床去，与它那些可怖的同伴会合。它们可谓没有脸，但在身体的一端有一张嘴，随着呼吸一开一合，张向侧旁。

接着，就在我凝视之际，我仿佛觉得它们忽然全都察觉到了我的存在。无论如何，所有的嘴都转到了我这一边，下一刻它们便开始一只只啪嗒一声掉到地上，朝我蜿蜒而来。有一秒钟，我如同梦中那般僵住了，可下一秒我已奔回楼上自己的房间，我记得赤脚踩在大理石台阶上冰凉冰凉的。我冲进卧室，砰地关上身后的门，随后——这下我无疑是彻底清醒了——我发现自己正站在床边，冷汗如注。那砰的一声关门声还在我耳边回荡。然而，倘若这只是一场噩梦，情形通常不该是这样：当我看见那些污秽的兽在床上四处爬行、或软软地掉到地上时我所感到的那份恐惧，并没有就此止息。此刻我已清醒——倘若方才是梦——我却丝毫没有从那梦的恐怖中复原：我并不觉得自己方才是在做梦。直到天明，我坐着、或站着，不敢躺下，听见每一阵窸窣、每一丝动静，都以为是毛虫逼近了。对它们、对那些能咬进水泥的利爪而言，那扇木门不过是儿戏：便是钢铁也挡不住它们。

然而随着白日那美好而高贵地归来，恐怖消散了：风的低语重新变得和善：那无以名之的恐惧，不管它究竟是什么，也被抚平，再不能令我惊惧。天破了晓，起初淡得几乎无色；继而转为鸽灰；再继而，那辉煌的光之盛装漫天铺开。

===Original===
The admirable rule of the house was that everybody had breakfast where and when he pleased, and in consequence it was not till lunchtime that I met any of the other members of our party, since I had breakfast on my balcony, and wrote letters and other things till lunch. In fact, I got down to that meal rather late, after the other three had begun. Between my knife and fork there was a small pillbox of cardboard, and as I sat down Inglis spoke.

“Do look at that,” he said, “since you are interested in natural history. I found it crawling on my counterpane last night, and I don’t know what it is.”

I think that before I opened the pillbox I expected something of the sort which I found in it. Inside it, anyhow, was a small caterpillar, greyish-yellow in colour, with curious bumps and excrescences on its rings. It was extremely active, and hurried round the box, this way and that. Its feet were unlike the feet of any caterpillar I ever saw: they were like the pincers of a crab. I looked, and shut the lid down again.

“No, I don’t know it,” I said, “but it looks rather unwholesome. What are you going to do with it?”

“Oh, I shall keep it,” said Inglis. “It has begun to spin: I want to see what sort of a moth it turns into.”

I opened the box again, and saw that these hurrying movements were indeed the beginning of the spinning of the web of its cocoon. Then Inglis spoke again.

“It has got funny feet, too,” he said. “They are like crabs’ pincers. What’s the Latin for crab? Oh, yes, *Cancer*. So in case it is unique, let’s christen it: ‘*Cancer Inglisensis*. ’ ”

Then something happened in my brain, some momentary piecing together of all that I had seen or dreamed. Something in his words seemed to me to throw light on it all, and my own intense horror at the experience of the night before linked itself on to what he had just said. In effect, I took the box and threw it, caterpillar and all, out of the window. There was a gravel path just outside, and beyond it, a fountain playing into a basin. The box fell on to the middle of this.

Inglis laughed.

“So the students of the occult don’t like solid facts,” he said. “My poor caterpillar!”

The talk went off again at once on to other subjects, and I have only given in detail, as they happened, these trivialities in order to be sure myself that I have recorded everything that could have borne on occult subjects or on the subject of caterpillars. But at the moment when I threw the pillbox into the fountain, I lost my head: my only excuse is that, as is probably plain, the tenant of it was, in miniature, exactly what I had seen crowded on to the bed in the unoccupied room. And though this translation of those phantoms into flesh and blood﻿—or whatever it is that caterpillars are made of﻿—ought perhaps to have relieved the horror of the night, as a matter of fact it did nothing of the kind. It only made the crawling pyramid that covered the bed in the unoccupied room more hideously real.

===Chinese===
这宅子有一条可赞的规矩：每个人愿在何处、何时用早餐，悉听尊便。于是乎，直到午饭时分我才见到我们一行人中的任何一位，因为我在自己露台上用了早餐，又写信、做这做那，一直忙到午饭。事实上，我下楼吃饭时已相当晚了，其余三人已经动上了餐。在我的刀叉之间，摆着一只小小的硬纸板药盒，我刚一落座，英格利斯便开了口。

「你瞧瞧这个，」他说，「你不是对博物学有兴趣嘛。昨夜我发现它在我的罩被上爬，我也说不出它是什么。」

我想，在打开那只药盒之前，我已隐隐料到盒里会是某种什么东西。无论如何，盒里是一只小小的毛虫，色黄灰，环节上长着古怪的疙瘩与赘疣。它极其活跃，在盒子里这边那边地匆匆乱转。它的脚，与我平生所见任何毛虫的脚都不同：像是蟹的螯钳。我看了一眼，又把盖子按了下去。

「不，我不认得它，」我说，「不过它瞧着不太对头。你打算拿它怎么办？」

「嗳，我要留着它，」英格利斯说，「它已经开始吐丝了：我想看看它会变成什么样的一只蛾。」

我又打开盒子，看见它那些匆匆忙忙的动作，确实是在开始结它的茧丝。这时英格利斯又开口了。

「它的脚也挺逗，」他说，「像蟹的螯钳。蟹的拉丁文怎么说来着？哦，对了，*Cancer*（癌）。那么，万一是独一无二的新种，就给它命名吧：『*Cancer Inglisensis*（英格利斯氏癌虫）。』」

随即，我的脑子里发生了一点什么，一种瞬间将我所见、所梦的一切串联起来的灵光。他的话里似乎有什么，把这一切都照亮了；而我前夜那段经历所唤起的强烈恐惧，又与他方才所说的话衔接在了一起。结果，我拿起那只盒子，连虫带盒，一把从窗口扔了出去。窗外不远处有一条碎石路，路的那边有一座喷泉，正喷着水落入一个石盆。盒子正好落进了盆中央。

英格利斯笑了起来。

「原来研究玄学的人不喜欢确凿的事实，」他说，「我可怜的毛虫！」

话头当即又转到了别的题目上去。我之所以把这些琐事一一详记下来，无非是为了让自己确信：但凡可能与玄学题目、或与毛虫题目相关的一切，我都已录下。可是，在我把药盒扔进喷泉的那一刻，我是失了态的：我唯一的辩解是——想必也已不言自明——那盒里的住客，恰是我曾见挤满在那间空房床上的东西的微缩版。而尽管这一回，那些幻影化作了血肉——或者化作了毛虫究竟是何物所成的那种东西——按理也许本该减轻那夜的恐怖，事实上却毫无此效。它只不过让那覆盖着空房床铺的、蠕动的金字塔，变得更加狰狞地真实罢了。

===Original===
After lunch we spent a lazy hour or two strolling about the garden or sitting in the loggia, and it must have been about four o’clock when Stanley and I started off to bathe, down the path that led by the fountain into which I had thrown the pillbox. The water was shallow and clear, and at the bottom of it I saw its white remains. The water had disintegrated the cardboard, and it had become no more than a few strips and shreds of sodden paper. The centre of the fountain was a marble Italian Cupid which squirted the water out of a wineskin held under its arm. And crawling up its leg was the caterpillar. Strange and scarcely credible as it seemed, it must have survived the falling-to-bits of its prison, and made its way to shore, and there it was, out of arm’s reach, weaving and waving this way and that as it evolved its cocoon.

Then, as I looked at it, it seemed to me again that, like the caterpillar I had seen last night, it saw me, and breaking out of the threads that surrounded it, it crawled down the marble leg of the Cupid and began swimming like a snake across the water of the fountain towards me. It came with extraordinary speed (the fact of a caterpillar being able to swim was new to me), and in another moment was crawling up the marble lip of the basin. Just then Inglis joined us.

“Why, if it isn’t old *Cancer Inglisensis* again,” he said, catching sight of the beast. “What a tearing hurry it is in.”

We were standing side by side on the path, and when the caterpillar had advanced to within about a yard of us, it stopped, and began waving again, as if in doubt as to the direction in which it should go. Then it appeared to make up its mind, and crawled on to Inglis’ shoe.

“It likes me best,” he said, “but I don’t really know that I like it. And as it won’t drown I think perhaps﻿—”

He shook it off his shoe on to the gravel path and trod on it.

===Chinese===
午饭之后，我们懒洋洋地散了一两个钟头的步，或在花园里、或坐在柱廊下，大约四点光景，斯坦利和我动身去洗海水浴，沿的小径正经过我扔下药盒的那座喷泉。水又浅又清，我在水底看见了那只盒子白色的残骸。水已把硬纸板泡散了，它如今不过是几条湿烂的纸条与碎片。喷泉中央是一尊意大利式的大理石丘比特，腋下夹着一只酒囊，水便从那囊里喷出来。而正爬上它小腿的，是那只毛虫。尽管这事看来古怪、几乎难以置信，它想必是从那只支离破碎的囚笼里逃过了一劫，又游上了岸；此刻它就在那里，我伸手够它不着，一边这边那边地摇摆着，一边结它的茧。

接着，就在我凝视它之际，我再次觉得，它一如昨夜我所见的那只毛虫，看见了我；它挣脱了围在身周的丝线，沿着丘比特那条大理石的小腿爬了下来，像蛇一般划着水，穿过喷泉的水面，朝我游来。它的速度奇快（毛虫居然能游泳，这于我是闻所未闻），转眼之间便爬上了石盆那大理石的盆沿。就在这时，英格利斯走了过来。

「哎呀，这不是咱们的老朋友 *Cancer Inglisensis* 嘛，」他一眼瞥见那东西，说道，「它可真够急的。」

我们俩并肩站在小径上，那毛虫行进到离我们大约一码远的地方时，停了下来，又开始左右摇摆，似乎拿不定主意该往哪一边去。随后它像是下定了决心，爬上了英格利斯的鞋。

「它跟我最亲，」他说，「可我说不准自己是不是真喜欢它。既然淹不死它，我想也许——」

他把它从鞋上甩到了碎石路上，一脚踩了下去。

===Original===
All afternoon the air got heavier and heavier with the Sirocco that was without doubt coming up from the south, and that night again I went up to bed feeling very sleepy; but below my drowsiness, so to speak, there was the consciousness, stronger than before, that there was something wrong in the house, that something dangerous was close at hand. But I fell asleep at once, and﻿—how long after I do not know﻿—either woke or dreamed I awoke, feeling that I must get up at once, *or I should be too late*. Then (dreaming or awake) I lay and fought this fear, telling myself that I was but the prey of my own nerves disordered by Sirocco or whatnot, and at the same time quite clearly knowing in another part of my mind, so to speak, that every moment’s delay added to the danger. At last this second feeling became irresistible, and I put on coat and trousers and went out of my room on to the landing. And then I saw that I had already delayed too long, and that I was now too late.

The whole of the landing of the first floor below was invisible under the swarm of caterpillars that crawled there. The folding doors into the sitting-room from which opened the bedroom where I had seen them last night, were shut, but they were squeezing through the cracks of it, and dropping one by one through the keyhole, elongating themselves into mere string as they passed, and growing fat and lumpy again on emerging. Some, as if exploring, were nosing about the steps into the passage at the end of which were Inglis’ rooms, others were crawling on the lowest steps of the staircase that led up to where I stood. The landing, however, was completely covered with them: I was cut off. And of the frozen horror that seized me when I saw that, I can give no idea in words.

===Chinese===
整个下午，那无疑正从南方涌来的西罗科风（Sirocco），使空气越来越沉。那天夜里，我又一次上楼就寝时困得要命；可在我的困倦之下，不妨这样说，有一层意识，比前夜更强，告诉我宅子里有什么不对劲，有某种危险已迫在眉睫。然而我立刻便睡着了，过了多久我不知道——我或者真的醒了，或者梦见自己醒来——只觉自己必须立刻起身，*否则就太迟了*。随后（无论睡着还是醒着）我躺着与这股恐惧搏斗，对自己说，我不过是受了西罗科风之类的搅扰，神经错乱所致的猎物；可与此同时，在心头的另一处，不妨这样说，我又清清楚楚地知道：每多耽搁一刻，便多添一分危险。终于，这第二种感觉变得不可抗拒，我套上外衣和长裤，走出房间，到了平台上。这时我才看见，我已经耽搁得太久，已经来不及了。

下面二楼整个平台，密密麻麻爬满了毛虫，已全然看不见地面。通往起居室的那两扇折门——正是从那起居室里，开着我昨夜见到它们的卧室——是关着的，可它们正从门缝里挤出来，又一只接一只地从钥匙孔里掉下来，挤过去时把自己拉成了一根细线，钻出来后又重新变得臃肿疙疸。有几只仿佛在探路，正沿着通往英格利斯房间那条过道的台阶嗅来嗅去；另几只则已爬上了通向我脚下那段楼梯最底下的几级。然而整个平台已被它们盖得严严实实：我被截断了。当我看见这一幕时，那将我攫住的、彻骨的恐怖，我实在无法以言辞传达。

===Original===
Then at last a general movement began to take place, and they grew thicker on the steps that led to Inglis’ room. Gradually, like some hideous tide of flesh, they advanced along the passage, and I saw the foremost, visible by the pale grey luminousness that came from them, reach his door. Again and again I tried to shout and warn him, in terror all the time that they would turn at the sound of my voice and mount my stair instead, but for all my efforts I felt that no sound came from my throat. They crawled along the hinge-crack of his door, passing through as they had done before, and still I stood there making impotent efforts to shout to him, to bid him escape while there was time.

===Chinese===
终于，一种普遍的移动开始了，通向英格利斯房间那段台阶上的毛虫越聚越厚。渐渐地，宛如一股腥肉的骇人潮水，它们沿着过道推进，我看见打头的那些——凭着它们自身发出的淡灰微光依稀可辨——已经到了他的门前。我一次又一次地想大喊着警告他，心里却始终恐惧着：它们一听见我的声音便会掉头，转而涌上我的楼梯。然而任凭我如何使劲，我觉得自己的喉咙里发不出一丝声响。它们沿着门轴的缝隙爬行，一如方才那样钻了进去；而我仍站在那里，徒劳地想喊他，想趁着还有时间叫他逃命。

===Original===
At last the passage was completely empty: they had all gone, and at that moment I was conscious for the first time of the cold of the marble landing on which I stood barefooted. The dawn was just beginning to break in the eastern sky.

===Chinese===
终于，那条过道整个地空了：它们全都走了。就在那一刻，我才头一回觉出，我赤脚所站的那块大理石平台冰冷冰冷的。东边的天空，正要破晓。

===Original===
Six months later I met Mrs. Stanley in a country house in England. We talked on many subjects and at last she said:

“I don’t think I have seen you since I got that dreadful news about Arthur Inglis a month ago.”

“I haven’t heard,” said I.

“No? He has got cancer. They don’t even advise an operation, for there is no hope of a cure: he is riddled with it, the doctors say.”

Now during all these six months I do not think a day had passed on which I had not had in my mind the dreams (or whatever you like to call them) which I had seen in the Villa Cascana.

“It is awful, is it not?” she continued, “and I feel, I can’t help feeling, that he may have﻿—”

“Caught it at the villa?” I asked.

She looked at me in blank surprise.

“Why did you say that?” she asked. “How did you know?”

Then she told me. In the unoccupied bedroom a year before there had been a fatal case of cancer. She had, of course, taken the best advice and had been told that the utmost dictates of prudence would be obeyed so long as she did not put anybody to sleep in the room, which had also been thoroughly disinfected and newly whitewashed and painted. But﻿—

===Chinese===
半年之后，我在英国一处乡间宅邸里遇见了斯坦利太太。我们谈了许多话题，末了她说道：

「我想，自从一个月前我得到那个可怕的消息——关于阿瑟·英格利斯——以后，就再没见过你。」

「我没听说，」我说。

「没听说吗？他得了癌。医生甚至连手术都不主张做了，因为已无治愈的希望：他浑身上下都是，医生们说。」

在这整整半年里，我想没有哪一天，我的脑子里不曾浮现我在卡斯卡纳别墅所见的那场梦（或随你怎么称呼它）。

「太可怕了，是不是？」她接着说，「而我不由得觉得，他也许——」

「是在那别墅里染上的？」我问。

她茫然惊讶地望着我。

「你怎么这样说？」她问，「你怎么知道的？」

于是她告诉了我。一年之前，那间空着的卧室里，曾有过一例致死的癌症。她自然已请教过最好的医生，得到的意见是：只要她不让任何人在那间房里过夜，便算遵从了审慎的最高准则；那间房也已经过彻底消毒、重新粉刷油漆。然而——

## Gavon’s Eve / 加文之夜

===Original===
It is only the largest kind of ordnance map that records the existence of the village of Gavon, in the shire of Sutherland, and it is perhaps surprising that any map on whatever scale should mark so small and huddled a group of huts, set on a bare, bleak headland between moor and sea, and, so one would have thought, of no import at all to any who did not happen to live there. But the river Gavon, on the right bank of which stand this half-dozen of chimneyless and windswept habitations, is a geographical fact of far greater interest to outsiders, for the salmon there are heavy fish, the mouth of the river is clear of nets, and all the way up to Gavon Loch, some six miles inland, the coffee-coloured water lies in pool after deep pool, which verge, if the river is in order and the angler moderately sanguine, on a fishing probability amounting almost to a certainty. In any case during the first fortnight of September last I had no blank day on those delectable waters, and up till the fifteenth of that month there was no day on which someone at the lodge in which I was stopping did not land a fish out of the famous Picts’ pool. But after the fifteenth that pool was not fished again. The reason why is here set forward.

===Chinese===
只有那种最大比例尺的军用地图，才会标出萨瑟兰郡（Sutherland）境内加文（Gavon）这个村子的存在；无论何种比例尺的地图都肯标出这样一小簇挤作一团的茅屋，倒也实在令人称奇——它们坐落在荒原与大海之间一片光秃秃、萧瑟的岬地上，照理说，对任何并非恰好住在那里的人而言，都毫无意义可言。然而，这五六幢没有烟囱、终年承受风灌的住处所依附的加文河，对局外人来说却是一个有意思得多的地理事实：河里的鲑鱼都是肥大的鱼，河口没有拦网，从河口一路上行到内陆约六英里处的加文湖（Gavon Loch），那咖啡色的河水一段接一段地汇成一个又一个深潭；只要河水水位合适、垂钓者又不过分悲观，这些深潭几乎可以说是十拿九稳的好钓场。总之，去年九月头两个礼拜，我在那一片乐也融融的水面上没有哪天空手而归；到那个月十五号为止，没有哪一天，我下榻的那间钓屋里没有人从著名的皮克特人潭（Picts' pool）里钓起一条鱼来。可十五号一过，那口潭就再没人去钓过。个中缘由，便记在下面。

===Original===
The river at this point, after some hundred yards of rapid, makes a sudden turn round a rocky angle, and plunges madly into the pool itself. Very deep water lies at the head of it, but deeper still further down on the east side, where a portion of the stream flicks back again in a swift dark backwater towards the top of the pool again. It is fishable only from the western bank, for to the east, above this backwater, a great wall of black and basaltic rock, heaved up no doubt by some fault in strata, rises sheer from the river to the height of some sixty feet. It is in fact nearly precipitous on both sides, heavily serrated at the top, and of so curious a thinness, that at about the middle of it where a fissure breaks its topmost edge, and some twenty feet from the top, there exists a long hole, a sort of lancet window, one would say, right through the rock, so that a slit of daylight can be seen through it. Since, therefore, no one would care to cast his line standing perched on that razor-edged eminence, the pool must needs be fished from the western bank. A decent fly, however, will cover it all.

===Chinese===
河流到了这一段，先是经过百余码的急流，紧接着在一处嶙峋的河角猛地一拐，便疯了似的扎进这口潭里。潭头一带水极深，而东岸再往下些则更深，那里有一股水流又迅速地回旋成一道幽暗的回水，反向朝着潭头涌去。这潭只能从西岸下钩，因为东岸、在这道回水上方，一道巍然的黑色玄武岩峭壁——无疑是由某处地层错动所拱起——从河边笔直地拔起到六十英尺上下。它两面其实都近乎峭立，顶部锯齿嶙峋，而又薄得颇为奇特：在大约正中处，一道裂缝截断了它的顶缘，距顶部约二十英尺的地方，赫然有一个长长的孔洞，直直地贯穿岩壁，形如一扇柳叶窗，一线天光可以从中透过来。因此，既然没有人愿意站在那剃刀般锋利的脊上甩竿，这潭自然就只能从西岸来钓了。不过，一枚像样的飞蝇，足以把整潭都罩住。

===Original===
It is on the western bank that there stand the remains of that which gave its title to the pool, namely, the ruins of a Pict castle, built out of rough and scarcely hewn masonry, unmortared but on a certain large and impressive scale, and in a very well-preserved condition considering its extreme antiquity. It is circular in shape and measures some twenty yards of diameter in its internal span. A staircase of large blocks with a rise of at least a foot leads up to the main gate, and opposite this on the side towards the river is another smaller postern through which down a rather hazardously steep slope a scrambling path, where progress demands both caution and activity, conducts to the head of the pool which lies immediately beneath it. A gate-chamber still roofed over exists in the solid wall: inside there are foundation indications of three rooms, and in the centre of all a very deep hole, probably a well. Finally, just outside the postern leading to the river is a small artificially levelled platform, some twenty feet across, as if made to support some superincumbent edifice. Certain stone slabs and blocks are dispersed over it.

===Chinese===
正是在西岸，矗立着那给此潭冠名的遗迹——一座皮克特人城堡（Pict castle）的废墟；它以粗凿、近乎未加工的石块垒成，并不抹灰浆，但规模颇为可观、令人肃然，且就其年代之古远而言，保存得相当完好。它呈圆形，内径约二十码。一道以大石块砌成、每级足有一英尺高的阶梯通向正门；与正门相对、靠河一侧，另有一扇较小的边门，门外一条坡度险陡、攀爬时需手脚并用的乱径，顺势而下，直通到就在其下方的潭头。厚实的城墙里还嵌着一间至今仍有顶盖的门房；城内有三间屋子的地基痕迹，正中央有一个很深的洞，大约是口井。最后，在通往河边的边门外，有一小块人工整平的台地，约二十英尺见方，仿佛是为了承托其上某座建筑而设。几块石板和石块散落其上。

===Original===
Brora, the post-town of Gavon, lies some six miles to the southwest, and from it a track over the moor leads to the rapids immediately above the Picts’ pool, across which by somewhat extravagant striding from boulder to boulder a man can pass dry-foot when the river is low, and make his way up a steep path to the north of the basaltic rock, and so to the village. But this transit demands a steady head, and at the best is a somewhat giddy passage. Otherwise the road between it and Brora lies in a long detour higher up the moor, passing by the gates of Gavon Lodge, where I was stopping. For some vague and ill-defined reason the pool itself and the Picts’ Castle had an uneasy reputation on the country side, and several times trudging back from a day’s fishing I have known my gillie take a longish circuit, though heavy with fish, rather than make this shortcut in the dusk by the castle. On the first occasion when Sandy, a strapping yellow-bearded viking of twenty-five, did this he gave as a reason that the ground round about the castle was “mossy,” though as a God-fearing man, he must have known he lied. But on another occasion he was more frank, and said that the Picts’ pool was “no canny” after sunset. I am now inclined to agree with him, though, when he lied about it, I think it was because as a God-fearing man he feared the devil also.

===Chinese===
加文的邮政镇布罗拉（Brora），坐落在西南方约六英里外，从那里有一条穿过荒原的小径通到皮克特人潭正上方的急流；水浅时，只要大步从一块巨石跨到另一块巨石上，人便可干着脚过河，再沿玄武岩北面的一条陡径上行，便能到村子里。但这一段路需要稳得住的头脑，往好里说也是一段有些叫人发晕的险途。除此之外，布罗拉与村子之间的通路，就得绕一大圈、走荒原更高处的远路，经过我下榻的加文钓屋（Gavon Lodge）的大门。出于某种说不清道不明的缘故，这口潭和皮克特人城堡在乡里名声不靖；有几次钓了一整天鱼扛着满筐渔获往回走，我的钓仆宁可绕上一大段远路，也不肯在暮色里从城堡边上抄这条近道。头一回这么做时，身材魁伟、黄须飘飘、二十五岁的维金人般的桑迪（Sandy）推说城堡四周的地面「长满了苔」，可他一个敬畏神的人，心里必明白自己说的是谎话。但另一次他便坦率得多，说皮克特人潭日落后「邪门」。如今我倒倾向于附和他的看法，至于当初他扯谎，我想，正因为他是个敬畏神的人，所以他也怕魔鬼。

===Original===
It was on the evening of September 14 that I was walking back with my host, Hugh Graham, from the forest beyond the lodge. It had been a day unseasonably hot for the time of year, and the hills were blanketed with soft, furry clouds. Sandy, the gillie of whom I have spoken, was behind with the ponies, and, idly enough, I told Hugh about his strange distaste for the Picts’ pool after sunset. He listened, frowning a little.

===Chinese===
九月十四日傍晚，我正和我的主人休·格雷厄姆（Hugh Graham）从钓屋那头更深处的林子往回走。那天的热，对这个时节来说反常得很，群山被一层柔软、毛茸茸的云毯盖着。我说过的那位钓仆桑迪，牵着小马跟在后面；我百无聊赖，便把桑迪对日落后皮克特人潭那种古怪的嫌恶讲给休听。他听着，微微皱起了眉。

===Original===
“That’s curious,” he said. “I know there is some dim local superstition about the place, but last year certainly Sandy used to laugh at it. I remember asking him what ailed the place, and he said he thought nothing about the rubbish folk talked. But this year you say he avoids it.”

===Chinese===
「这倒怪了，」他说，「我知道那地方有某种含糊的当地迷信，可去年桑迪分明还拿它当笑话。我记得问过他那地方到底有什么不对劲，他说那些闲话全是胡扯，他才不放在心上。可今年你说他却避之不及了。」

===Original===
“On several occasions with me he has done so.”

===Chinese===
「跟我一道的时候，他好几次都这么绕道。」

===Original===
Hugh smoked a while in silence, striding noiselessly over the dusky fragrant heather.

===Chinese===
休沉默地抽了一会儿烟，在那昏暗、芬芳的石楠花丛中悄然迈着大步。

===Original===
“Poor chap,” he said. “I don’t know what to do about him. He’s becoming useless.”

===Chinese===
「可怜的家伙，」他说，「我都不知道拿他怎么办。他越来越不顶用了。」

===Original===
“Drink?” I asked.

===Chinese===
「酗酒？」我问。

===Original===
“Yes, drink in a secondary manner. But trouble led to drink, and trouble, I am afraid, is leading him to worse than drink.”

===Chinese===
「是的，酗酒，不过是次要的。是愁把他逼到了酒上，而我怕这愁正把他引向比酒更糟的东西。」

===Original===
“The only thing worse than drink is the devil,” I remarked.

===Chinese===
「比酒更糟的，可就只有魔鬼了。」我说。

===Original===
“Precisely. That’s where he is going. He goes there often.”

===Chinese===
「一点不错。他正是往那条路上走。而且常常去。」

===Original===
“What on earth do you mean?” I asked.

===Chinese===
「你这话到底什么意思？」我问。

===Original===
“Well, it’s rather curious,” said Hugh. “You know I dabble a bit in folklore and local superstition, and I believe I am on the track of something odder than odd. Just wait a moment.”

===Chinese===
「嗳，这事儿挺蹊跷，」休说，「你知道我对民俗和乡野迷信稍稍有那么一点涉猎，我相信我正循着一条比蹊跷更蹊跷的踪迹。先等一下。」

===Original===
We stood there in the gathering dusk till the ponies laboured up the hillside to us, Sandy with his six feet of lithe strength strolling easily beside them up the steep brae, as if his long day’s trudging had but served to half awaken his dormant powers of limb.

===Chinese===
我们便在那渐浓的暮色里站定，直到小马吭哧吭哧地爬上山坡来到我们跟前；六英尺身量、筋骨柔韧有力的桑迪，毫不费力地随着它们走上陡坡，仿佛那一整天的长途跋涉，只不过把他蛰伏着的肢体之力唤醒了一半。

===Original===
“Going to see Mistress Macpherson again tonight?” asked Hugh.

===Chinese===
「今儿晚上还要去看麦克弗森太太吗？」休问。

===Original===
“Aye, puir body,” said Sandy. “She’s auld, and she’s lone.”

===Chinese===
「嗯哪，可怜的人儿，」桑迪说，「她又老，又是一个人。」

===Original===
“Very kind of you, Sandy,” said Hugh, and we walked on.

===Chinese===
「你真够意思，桑迪，」休说，我们便继续往前走。

===Original===
“What then?” I asked when the ponies had fallen behind again.

===Chinese===
「然后呢？」等小马又落到后头时，我问道。

===Original===
“Why, superstition lingers here,” said Hugh, “and it’s supposed she’s a witch. To be quite candid with you, the thing interests me a good deal. Supposing you asked me, on oath, whether I believed in witches, I should say ‘No.’ But if you asked me again, on oath, whether I suspected I believed in them, I should, I think, say ‘Yes.’ And the fifteenth of this month﻿—tomorrow﻿—is Gavon’s Eve.”

===Chinese===
「哦，这里的迷信还没散尽，」休说，「人家都说她是个女巫。跟你掏心窝子讲，这事儿挺叫我感兴趣。倘若你叫我起誓，问我是不是信女巫，我会说『不信』。可你要是再叫我起一次誓，问我是否怀疑自己其实信这一套，我想我会说『信』。而本月十五号——也就是明天——便是加文之夜。」

===Original===
“And what in Heaven’s name is that?” I asked. “And who is Gavon? And what’s the trouble?”

===Chinese===
「那这到底是个什么名堂，看在老天的份上？」我问，「加文又是谁？到底有什么愁？」

===Original===
“Well, Gavon is the person, I suppose, not saint, who is what we should call the eponymous hero of this district. And the trouble is Sandy’s trouble. Rather a long story. But there’s a long mile in front of us yet, if you care to be told.”

===Chinese===
「嗯，我想加文大概就是这么个人——不是圣徒——是这一带的名祖，也就是这一片地方因他而得名的那位主人公。至于那愁，是桑迪的愁。说来话长。不过我们前面还有长长一英里的路，你愿意听的话，我就讲给你。」

===Original===
During that mile I heard. Sandy had been engaged a year ago to a girl of Gavon who was in service at Inverness. In March last he had gone, without giving notice, to see her, and as he walked up the street in which her mistress’ house stood, had met her suddenly face to face, in company with a man whose clipped speech betrayed him English, whose manner a kind of gentleman. He had a flourish of his hat for Sandy, pleasure to see him, and scarcely any need of explanation as to how he came to be walking with Catrine. It was the most natural thing possible, for a city like Inverness boasted its innocent urbanities, and a girl could stroll with a man. And for the time, since also Catrine was so frankly pleased to see him, Sandy was satisfied. But after his return to Gavon, suspicion, fungus-like, grew rank in his mind, with the result that a month ago he had, with infinite pains and blottings, written a letter to Catrine, urging her return and immediate marriage. Thereafter it was known that she had left Inverness; it was known that she had arrived by train at Brora. From Brora she had started to walk across the moor by the path leading just above the Picts’ Castle, crossing the rapids to Gavon, leaving her box to be sent by the carrier. But at Gavon she had never arrived. Also it was said that, though it was a hot afternoon, she wore a big cloak.

===Chinese===
那一英里路上，我把事情听了个全。桑迪一年前与本村一个在因弗内斯（Inverness）帮佣的姑娘订了婚。今年三月，他没打招呼便跑去看她；正走上她女东家所在的那条街，迎面便撞见她，身边还伴着个男人——那人咬字利落，一听便是英格兰口音，举手投足间有几分绅士派头。他朝桑迪扬了扬帽子致意，像是见了面很高兴，对于自己为何正与卡特琳（Catrine）走在一起，几乎无须任何解释。这再自然不过，因弗内斯这样的城里自有它无伤大雅的都市客套，姑娘家与男子同走一段路也不稀奇。况且卡特琳见了他也是那样坦率地欢喜，所以一时之间桑迪也就心满意足了。可回到加文之后，疑心像真菌一般在他心里疯长起来，结果是：一个月前，他费了九牛二虎之力、写写涂涂，给卡特琳去了一封信，催她回来立即成婚。此后有消息说她离开了因弗内斯；又有人知她是乘火车到了布罗拉。从布罗拉，她便动身徒步穿过荒原，走的正是从皮克特人城堡上方经过、跨过急流到加文的那条小径，行李则留给搬运工后送。可她始终没到加文。还有人说，那天下午明明天热，她却披着一件大斗篷。

===Original===
By this time we had come to the lodge, the lights of which showed dim and blurred through the thick hill-mists that had streamed sullenly down from the higher ground.

===Chinese===
这时我们已走到钓屋跟前，它的灯火透过从高处山坡沉郁地漫流而下的浓重山雾，显得朦胧而模糊。

===Original===
“And the rest,” said Hugh, “which is as fantastic as this is sober fact, I will tell you later.”

===Chinese===
「剩下的事，」休说，「和这段同样离奇，却也同样句句属实，回头我再告诉你。」

===Original===
Now, a fruit-bearing determination to go to bed is, to my mind, as difficult to ripen as a fruit-bearing determination to get up, and in spite of our long day, I was glad when Hugh (the rest of the men having yawned themselves out of the smoking-room) came back from the hospitable dispensing of bedroom candlesticks with a briskness that denoted that, as far as he was concerned, the distressing determination was not imminent.

===Chinese===
在我看来，那种真能结出果子来的「该睡觉了」的决心，和「该起床了」的决心一样难成熟；尽管我们走了长长一天，我还是很高兴地看到，休（其余的人都打着哈欠陆续退出了吸烟室）从殷勤分发的寝烛那头折回来时步履轻快——这表明，就他而言，那桩叫人犯难的决心一时半会儿还下不了。

===Original===
“As regards Sandy,” I suggested.

===Chinese===
「说说桑迪吧。」我提议。

===Original===
“Ah, I also was thinking of that,” he said. “Well, Catrine Gordon left Brora, and never arrived here. That is fact. Now for what remains. Have you any remembrance of a woman always alone walking about the moor by the loch? I think I once called your attention to her.”

===Chinese===
「哦，我也正想着这桩，」他说，「嗯，卡特琳·戈登（Catrine Gordon）离开了布罗拉，却始终没到这里。这是事实。下面说剩下的。你还记不记得，有个女人，总是一个人在湖边的荒原上走来走去？我想我曾叫你留意过她。」

===Original===
“Yes, I remember,” I said. “Not Catrine, surely; a very old woman, awful to look at. Moustache, whiskers, and muttering to herself. Always looking at the ground, too.”

===Chinese===
「记得，我记得，」我说，「不是卡特琳吧；那是个很老的老太太，模样可怖。长着髭，有连鬓胡子，嘴里还自言自语。眼睛也总是盯着地面。」

===Original===
“Yes, that is she﻿—not Catrine. Catrine! My word, a May morning! But the other﻿—it is Mrs. Macpherson, reputed witch. Well, Sandy trudges there, a mile and more away, every night to see her. You know Sandy: Adonis of the north. Now, can you account by any natural explanation for that fact? That he goes off after a long day to see an old hag in the hills?”

===Chinese===
「是的，就是她——不是卡特琳。卡特琳！哎哟，那可是五月清晨般的人物！可另一位——就是麦克弗森太太（Mrs. Macpherson），传说里的女巫。桑迪呢，却每天夜里跋涉一英里多路去看她。桑迪你是知道的：北地的阿多尼（Adonis）。那么，这件事你能用任何合乎情理的解释来圆过去吗？一个大白天走了一整天的人，竟还要跑去看山里的一个老妖婆？」

===Original===
“It would seem unlikely,” said I.

===Chinese===
「看来不大说得通。」我说。

===Original===
“Unlikely! Well, yes, unlikely.”

===Chinese===
「说不通！嗯，是的，说不通。」

===Original===
Hugh got up from his chair and crossed the room to where a bookcase of rather fusty-looking volumes stood between windows. He took a small morocco-backed book from a top shelf.

===Chinese===
休从椅子上起身，穿过房间，走到两窗之间那只堆着些看着就霉味扑鼻的旧书的书架前。他从顶层取下一本小开本、摩洛哥皮脊的书。

===Original===
“Superstitions of Sutherlandshire,” he said, as he handed it to me. “Turn to page 128, and read.”

===Chinese===
「《萨瑟兰郡迷信志》（Superstitions of Sutherlandshire），」他一面说一面递给我，「翻到第128页，念。」

===Original===
I obeyed, and read.

===Chinese===
我遵命翻到那一页，念了起来。

===Original===
“September 15 appears to have been the date of what we may call this devil festival. On the night of that day the powers of darkness held preeminent dominion, and overrode for any who were abroad that night and invoked their aid, the protective Providence of Almighty God. Witches, therefore, above all, were peculiarly potent. On this night any witch could entice to herself the heart and the love of any young man who consulted her on matters of philtre or love charm, with the result that on any night in succeeding years of the same date, he, though he was lawfully affianced and wedded, would for that night be hers. If, however, he should call on the name of God through any sudden grace of the Spirit, her charm would be of no avail. On this night, too, all witches had the power by certain dreadful incantations and indescribable profanities, to raise from the dead those who had committed suicide.”

===Chinese===
「九月十五日，似乎便是这个我们不妨称之为魔鬼节庆的日子。这一夜的掌权者是黑暗的诸势力，它们盖过了一切当夜在外、并祈求它们襄助之人头上那全能上帝护佑的旨意。因此，女巫们在这一夜尤为法力无边。任何一个少年，凡在这一夜就春药或媚惑之事向女巫请益，她便能勾得他的心与爱，结果是：在往后年份的同月同夜，纵使他已经名正言顺地订亲、成婚，那一夜他也将归她所有。然而，倘若他因圣灵一时赐下的恩典而呼求了神的名，她的法术便全然失效。也正是在这一夜，所有的女巫都能借着某些可怖的咒语和不可言说的亵渎，把那些自戕而死的人从死里招出来。」

===Original===
“Top of the next page,” said Hugh. “Leave out this next paragraph; it does not bear on this last.”

===Chinese===
「下一页开头，」休说，「中间这一段跳过，跟这段无关。」

===Original===
“Near a small village in this country,” I read, “called Gavon, the moon at midnight is said to shine through a certain gap or fissure in a wall of rock close beside the river on to the ruins of a Pict castle, so that the light of its beams falls on to a large flat stone erected there near the gate, and supposed by some to be an ancient and pagan altar. At that moment, so the superstition still lingers in the country side, the evil and malignant spirits which hold sway on Gavon’s Eve, are at the zenith of their powers, and those who invoke their aid at this moment and in this place, will, though with infinite peril to their immortal souls, get all that they desire of them.”

===Chinese===
「在本郡一个叫加文的小村子附近，」我念道，「据说子夜时分，月亮会透过河畔一道岩壁上的某个豁口或裂缝照进来，照到一座皮克特人城堡的废墟上，使月光落在城门附近立着的一块大平石上——有些人猜测那是一处古老的异教祭坛。乡间至今还流传着这样的说法：正是在那一刻，加文之夜当权的那些凶邪恶毒的精灵法力最盛，凡在这一刻、在此地祈求它们襄助的人，虽然要拿自己灵魂的永福去冒无尽的凶险，却能从它们那里得到所求的一切。」

===Original===
The paragraph on the subject ended here, and I shut the book.

===Chinese===
关于这件事的这段文字到此为止，我合上了书。

===Original===
“Well?” I asked.

===Chinese===
「怎么样？」我问。

===Original===
“Under favourable circumstances two and two make four,” said Hugh.

===Chinese===
「凑齐了条件，二加二就等于四。」休说。

===Original===
“And four means﻿—”

===Chinese===
「四的意思是——」

===Original===
“This. Sandy is certainly in consultation with a woman who is supposed to be a witch, whose path no crofter will cross after nightfall. He wants to learn, at whatever cost, poor devil, what happened to Catrine. Thus I think it more than possible that tomorrow, at midnight, there will be folk by the Picts’ pool. There is another curious thing. I was fishing there yesterday, and just opposite the river gate of the castle, someone has set up a great flat stone, which has been dragged (for I noticed the crushed grass) from the debris at the bottom of the slope.”

===Chinese===
「是这个。桑迪无疑正与一个被认作女巫的女人往来——这个女人的踪迹，日落后没有哪个佃农肯去踩。他想不惜一切代价，可怜虫，弄清楚卡特琳到底出了什么事。所以我认为，明儿个半夜，皮克特人潭边，多半会有人。还有一桩蹊跷事。我昨儿在那儿钓鱼，只见正对城堡河门的地方，有人竖起了一块巨大的平石，那石头是从坡底的碎石堆里拖来的（因为我注意到了被碾倒的草）。」

===Original===
“You mean that the old hag is going to try to raise the body of Catrine, if she is dead?”

===Chinese===
「你是说，那老妖婆打算把卡特琳的尸首招出来——如果她已经死了的话？」

===Original===
“Yes, and I mean to see myself what happens. Come too.”

===Chinese===
「对，而且我打算亲眼看一看会出什么事。你也来。」

===Original===
The next day Hugh and I fished down the river from the lodge, taking with us not Sandy, but another gillie, and ate our lunch on the slope of the Picts’ Castle after landing a couple of fish there. Even as Hugh had said, a great flat slab of stone had been dragged on to the platform outside the river gate of the castle, where it rested on certain rude supports, which, now that it was in place, seemed certainly designed to receive it. It was also exactly opposite that lancet window in the basaltic rock across the pool, so that if the moon at midnight did shine through it, the light would fall on the stone. This then was the almost certain scene of the incantations.

===Chinese===
第二天，我和休从钓屋沿河一路往下钓，带去的不是桑迪，而是另一个钓仆；在城堡边钓上两条鱼后，我们便在皮克特人城堡的坡上吃了午饭。果然如休所说，城堡河门外的那块台地上，已被拖来一块巨大的平石板，搁在几根粗陋的支架上——这些支架一旦让石板就位，便显然正是为承托它而设的。它又恰与潭对面玄武岩上那扇柳叶窗遥遥相对，所以子夜的月亮若真的透过那孔洞照进来，月光便会正好落在石上。那么，这里几乎可以断定就是那场咒仪的现场。

===Original===
Below the platform, as I have said, the ground fell rapidly away to the level of the pool, which owing to rain on the hills was running very high, and, streaked with lines of greyish bubbles, poured down in amazing and ear-filling volume. But directly underneath the steep escarpment of rock on the far side of the pool it lay foamless and black, a still backwater of great depth. Above the altar-like erection again the ground rose up seven rough-hewn steps to the gate itself, on each side of which, to the height of about four feet, ran the circular wall of the castle. Inside again were the remains of partition walls between the three chambers, and it was in the one nearest to the river gate that we determined to conceal ourselves that night. From there, should the witch and Sandy keep tryst at the altar, any sound of movement would reach us, and through the aperture of the gate itself we could see, concealed in the shadow of the wall, whatever took place at the altar or down below at the pool. The lodge, finally, was but a short ten minutes away, if one went in the direct line, so that by starting at a quarter to twelve that night, we could enter the Picts’ Castle by the gate away from the river, thus not betraying our presence to those who might be waiting for the moment when the moon should shine through the lancet window in the wall of rock on to the altar in front of the river gate.

===Chinese===
台地下方，正如我所说，地面迅速下沉到与潭面齐平；因山上落雨，潭水涨得很满，挟着一道道灰色气泡奔泻而下，水势惊人，涛声盈耳。但就在潭对岸那道陡峭岩壁的正下方，水面却不起一点泡沫，黑沉沉的，是一道极深的静水回湾。在那座祭坛般的构筑物上方，地面又顺着七级粗凿的石阶升到城门跟前；门两侧，圆形的城墙各延伸约四英尺高。再往里，便是三间屋子之间隔墙的残迹，我们决定当夜就藏身在最靠河门的那一间里。在那里，倘若女巫与桑迪当真到祭坛赴会，任何响动都逃不过我们的耳朵；而通过城门的孔洞，我们隐在墙影里，便能看清祭坛上、或下面潭边所发生的一切。最后，钓屋若抄直路走，不过短短十分钟路程，所以那夜十一点三刻动身，我们便可从远离河岸的那道城门进入皮克特人城堡，从而不致惊动那些也许正等候月光穿过岩壁柳叶窗、照在河门前祭坛上那一刻的人。

===Original===
Night fell very still and windless, and when not long before midnight we let ourselves silently out of the lodge, though to the east the sky was clear, a black continent of cloud was creeping up from the west, and had now nearly reached the zenith. Out of the remote fringes of it occasional lightning winked, and the growl of very distant thunder sounded drowsily at long intervals after. But it seemed to me as if another storm hung over our heads, ready every moment to burst, for the oppression in the air was of a far heavier quality than so distant a disturbance could have accounted for. To the east, however, the sky was still luminously clear; the curiously hard edges of the western cloud were star-embroidered, and by the dove-coloured light in the east it was evident that the moonrise over the moor was imminent. And though I did not in my heart believe that our expedition would end in anything but yawns, I was conscious of an extreme tension and rawness of nerves, which I set down to the thunder-charged air.

===Chinese===
夜色降临得极其静谧、无风。子夜前不多时，我们悄然溜出钓屋：东边天色虽清，西边却有一片乌云如黑色大陆般压上来，此刻已将近天顶。云的远缘偶有闪电眨眼，间隔良久，才传来远处闷雷那昏沉的隆隆声。可我觉得头顶上空似乎另有一场雷暴蓄势待发，随时都会砸下来，因为空气里那种压迫感，远不是远处那场扰动所能解释的。然而东边的天空仍清亮通透；西边乌云那出奇硬朗的边缘上绣着点点繁星，而东天那一片鸽灰色微光分明在说，荒原上的月升已迫在眉睫。我心底里并不相信我们这趟出行会落得个什么下场，除了打哈欠；可我还是感到一种极度的紧绷与神经的刺痛，我把它归咎于这雷雨欲来的空气。

===Original===
For noiselessness of footstep we had both put on india-rubber soled shoes, and all the way down to the pool we heard nothing but the distant thunder and our own padded tread. Very silently and cautiously we ascended the steps of the gate away from the river, and keeping close to the wall inside, sidled round to the river gate and peered out. For the first moment I could see nothing, so black lay the shadow of the rock-wall opposite across the pool, but by degrees I made out the lumps and line of the glimmering foam which streaked the water. High as the river was running this morning it was infinitely more voluminous and turbulent now, and the sound of it filled and bewildered the ear with its sonorous roaring. Only under the very base of the rock opposite it ran quite black and unflecked by foam: there lay the deep still surface of the backwater. Then suddenly I saw something black move in the dimness in front of me, and against the grey foam rose up first the head, then the shoulders, and finally the whole figure of a woman coming towards us up the bank. Behind her walked another, a man, and the two came to where the altar of stone had been newly erected and stood there side by side silhouetted against the churned white of the stream. Hugh had seen too, and touched me on the arm to call my attention. So far then he was right: there was no mistaking the stalwart proportions of Sandy.

===Chinese===
为了脚步无声，我们俩都换上了橡胶底的鞋；一路下到潭边，除了远处的雷声和我们自己踩地的闷响，什么也没听见。我们悄无声息、小心翼翼地登上远离河岸那道城门的石阶，贴着里头的城墙挪到河门，向外张望。头一眼我什么也看不见，潭对面那道岩壁投下的阴影黑压压地盖了一片；渐渐地，我才辨认出水中一道道泡沫那影影绰绰的轮廓与线条。今晨河水虽已涨得厉害，此刻的水量与湍急更不知要猛烈多少倍，那轰然的涛声灌满双耳，叫人耳鸣目眩。唯独在对岸岩壁的正下方，水色漆黑、不沾一点泡沫：那里便是那道极深、极静的回水湾。突然，我看见眼前昏暗中有个黑色的东西在动；在灰白泡沫的衬托下，先是一颗头、再是双肩、继而是整个身形——一个女人——朝我们这边、从岸边爬上来。她身后还跟着另一个人，是个男人；两人走到那座新竖的石头祭坛前，并肩而立，背后是被搅成白沫的激流。休也看见了，伸手在我胳膊上一拍，叫我留意。那么，到目前为止，他是对的：那副魁梧的身板，错不了，正是桑迪。

===Original===
Suddenly across the gloom shot a tiny spear of light, and momentarily as we watched, it grew larger and longer, till a tall beam, as from some window cut in the rock opposite, was shed on the bank below us. It moved slowly, imperceptibly to the left till it struck full between the two black figures standing there, and shone with a curious bluish gleam on the flat stone in front of them. Then the roar of the river was suddenly overscored by a dreadful screaming voice, the voice of a woman, and from her side her arms shot up and out as if in invocation of some power. At first I could catch none of the words, but soon from repetition they began to convey an intelligible message to my brain, and I was listening as in the paralytic horror of nightmare to a bellowing of the most hideous and unnameable profanity. What I heard I cannot bring myself to record; suffice it to say that Satan was invoked by every adoring and reverent name, that cursing and unspeakable malediction was poured forth on Him whom we hold most holy. Then the yelling voice ceased as suddenly as it had begun, and for a moment there was silence again, but for the reverberating river.

===Chinese===
猛然间，一道细小的光矛划破黑暗射过来；我们眼看着它一寸寸地变粗、变长，直到一道高高的光柱——仿佛从对面岩壁上凿出的某扇窗子里泻出——落在我们下方的岸上。它缓缓地、几乎察觉不到地向左移动，直到正正地打在并肩而立的那两个黑色身影之间，并带着一种奇异的蓝幽幽的光泽，照在他们面前那块平石上。紧接着，河水的轰鸣突然被一个尖利可怕的嘶喊声盖过——那是女人的声音——她双臂从身侧猛地向上、向外甩出，仿佛在召唤某种力量。起初我一个字也听不清，但很快，反复的吟诵开始在我脑中拼出可解的词句，我就像在梦魇那种瘫软的惊恐中一样，听着那最丑恶、最不堪言说的亵渎在咆哮。我所听到的，实在无法落笔复述；只消说：撒但被以种种敬爱、虔敬的名号呼唤着；而我们奉为至圣的那一位，则被咒诅，被泼上不可言说的咒骂。随后，那嘶喊戛然而止，和它响起时一样突兀；片刻间又归于沉寂——只剩下回响不绝的河水。

===Original===
Then once more that horror of sound was uplifted.

===Chinese===
接着，那一声骇人的嘶喊又扬了起来。

===Original===
“So, Catrine Gordon,” it cried, “I bid ye in the name of my master and your’s to rise from where ye lie. Up with ye﻿—up!”

===Chinese===
「那么，卡特琳·戈登，」它喊道，「我奉我主、你主的名，吩咐你从你躺着的地方起来。起来呀——起来！」

===Original===
Once more there was silence; then I heard Hugh at my elbow draw a quick sobbing breath, and his finger pointed unsteadily to the dead black water below the rock. And I too looked and saw.

===Chinese===
又是一阵静寂；随后我听见身边的休急促地吸了一口抽噎似的气，他的手指颤颤地指向岩壁下方那死黑的水面。我也看过去，看见了。

===Original===
Right under the rock there appeared a pale subaqueous light, which waved and quivered in the stream. At first it was very small and dim, but as we looked it seemed to swim upwards from remote depths and grew larger till I suppose the space of some square yard was illuminated by it. Then the surface of the water was broken, and a head, the head of a girl, dead-white and with long, flowing hair, appeared above the stream. Her eyes were shut, the corners of her mouth drooped as in sleep, and the moving water stood in a frill round her neck. Higher and higher rose the figure out of the tide, till at last it stood, luminous in itself, so it appeared, up to the middle. The head was bent down over the breast, and the hands clasped together. As it emerged from the water it seemed to get nearer, and was by now halfway across the pool, moving quietly and steadily against the great flood of the hurrying river.

===Chinese===
就在岩壁正下方，水底泛起一团苍白的微光，在水流中摇曳颤动。起初它又小又暗，可我们盯着看时，它仿佛从极深远处浮游上来，越变越大，直到——我估摸——有一平方码的水面被它照亮。随后水面破开，一颗头颅——一个姑娘的头——死人般苍白、披散着长长秀发的，浮现在水流之上。她双眼紧闭，嘴角像睡着那样耷拉着，流动的水在她颈边立成一道花边。那身形越涨越高地浮出潮面，到末了，半身已立在水上，仿佛自身便是发光的。她的头低垂到胸前，双手交握。随着她浮出水面，那身形似乎越来越近，此刻已到了潭的半途，正迎着奔腾巨流，安静而稳当地逆水而来。

===Original===
Then I heard a man’s voice crying out in a sort of strangled agony.

===Chinese===
这时我听见一个男人的声音，带着一种扼住喉咙般的痛苦嘶喊出来。

===Original===
“Catrine!” it cried; “Catrine! In God’s name; in God’s name!”

===Chinese===
「卡特琳！」它喊，「卡特琳！看在上帝份上；看在上帝份上！」

===Original===
In two strides Sandy had rushed down the steep bank, and hurled himself out into that mad swirl of waters. For one moment I saw his arms flung up into the sky, the next he had altogether gone. And on the utterance of that name the unholy vision had vanished too, while simultaneously there burst in front of us a light so blinding, followed by a crack of thunder so appalling to the senses, that I know I just hid my face in my hands. At once, as if the floodgates of the sky had been opened, the deluge was on us, not like rain, but like one sheet of solid water, so that we cowered under it. Any hope or attempt to rescue Sandy was out of the question; to dive into that whirlpool of mad water meant instant death, and even had it been possible for any swimmer to live there, in the blackness of the night there was absolutely no chance of finding him. Besides, even if it had been possible to save him, I doubt whether I was sufficiently master of my flesh and blood as to endure to plunge where that apparition had risen.

===Chinese===
桑迪两步冲下陡岸，纵身扑进那片疯狂的漩涡。我只看见他的双臂有一瞬朝天空张开，下一刻他便整个儿没了踪影。而在那一声名唤出口之际，那不洁的异象也一同消失了；与此同时，我们面前陡地炸开一道令人目眩的强光，紧随其后是一声惊心动魄的炸雷，我只知道自己当即把脸埋进了双手。霎时间，仿佛天闸大开，暴雨倾盆而至——那不像雨，倒像整整一面墙的实水劈头盖脸砸下，逼得我们缩成一团。任何营救桑迪的念头或尝试都无从谈起：一头扎进那疯水的漩涡，就意味着立刻送命；即便真有什么游泳好手能在那儿活下来，漆黑的夜里也绝对找不着他。况且，即便还能救他，我也怀疑自己管不住这副血肉之躯，能忍受得了纵身跳进那异象升起的地方。

===Original===
Then, as we lay there, another horror filled and possessed my mind. Somewhere close to us in the darkness was that woman whose yelling voice just now had made my blood run ice-cold, while it brought the streaming sweat to my forehead. At that moment I turned to Hugh.

===Chinese===
这时，正当我们伏在那里，另一种恐惧又灌满、攫住了我的心。在黑暗中、就在我们身边不远的地方，还有那个女人——她刚才那声嘶喊令我血液冰凉，却又叫冷汗如注地涌上额头。我转向休。

===Original===
“I cannot stop here,” I said. “I must run, run right away. Where is she?”

===Chinese===
「我待不下去了，」我说，「我得跑，跑得远远的。她在哪儿？」

===Original===
“Did you not see?” he asked.

===Chinese===
「你没看见吗？」他问。

===Original===
“No. What happened?”

===Chinese===
「没有。怎么啦？」

===Original===
“The lightning struck the stone within a few inches of where she was standing. We﻿—we must go and look for her.”

===Chinese===
「闪电劈在那块石头上，离她站的地方不过几英寸。我们——我们得去找找她。」

===Original===
I followed him down the slope, shaking as if I had the palsy, and groping with my hands on the ground in front of me, in deadly terror of encountering something human. The thunderclouds had in the last few minutes spread over the moon, so that no ray from the window in the rock guided our search. But up and down the bank from the stone that lay shattered there to the edge of the pool we groped and stumbled, but found nothing. At length we gave it up: it seemed morally certain that she, too, had rolled down the bank after the lightning stroke, and lay somewhere deep in the pool from which she had called the dead.

===Chinese===
我跟着他下坡，抖得像个中了风的人，双手在面前的地上摸索着，生怕撞见什么属于人的东西。方才几分钟里，雷雨云已漫过月亮，岩壁窗孔里再没有一线光指引我们搜寻。但我们仍从那块已碎成几爿的石头处起，沿着岸上上下下地摸、跌跌撞撞地找，却一无所获。终于我们放弃了：看来几乎可以断定，她也在那一记雷击之后滚下了岸，正躺在她招魂的那口潭的某个深处。

===Original===
None fished the pool next day, but men with dragnets came from Brora. Right under the rock in the backwater lay two bodies, close together, Sandy and the dead girl. Of the other they found nothing.

===Chinese===
第二天，没人去那潭下钓，布罗拉来了几个拖着拖网的人。就在岩壁下那道回水湾里，紧紧挨着躺着两具尸体——桑迪和那死去的姑娘。另一个，他们什么也没找到。

===Original===
It would seem, then, that Catrine Gordon, in answer to Sandy’s letter, left Inverness in heavy trouble. What happened afterwards can only be conjectured, but it seems likely she took the shortcut to Gavon, meaning to cross the river on the boulders above the Picts’ pool. But whether she slipped accidentally in her passage, and so was drawn down by the hungry water, or whether, unable to face the future, she had thrown herself into the pool, we can only guess. In any case they sleep together now in the bleak, windswept graveyard at Brora, in obedience to the inscrutable designs of God.

===Chinese===
这么说来，卡特琳·戈登应是接到桑迪的信后，满心愁苦地离开了因弗内斯。其后发生了什么，只能揣测；但她很可能抄近路赶往加文，打算从皮克特人潭上方的乱石上过河。至于她究竟是过河时失足滑倒、被贪婪的河水卷了下去，还是因不堪面对将来、自己纵身跳进了潭里，我们只能各凭猜测。无论如何，此刻他们都一同长眠在布罗拉那片萧瑟、风声呼啸的墓地里——顺服于上帝那不可测度的旨意。

## How Fear Departed from the Long Gallery / 恐惧如何从长廊离去

===Original===
Church-Peveril is a house so beset and frequented by spectres, both visible and audible, that none of the family which it shelters under its acre and a half of green copper roofs takes psychical phenomena with any seriousness. For to the Peverils the appearance of a ghost is a matter of hardly greater significance than is the appearance of the post to those who live in more ordinary houses. It arrives, that is to say, practically every day, it knocks (or makes other noises), it is observed coming up the drive (or in other places). I myself, when staying there have seen the present Mrs. Peveril, who is rather shortsighted, peer into the dusk, while we were taking our coffee on the terrace after dinner, and say to her daughter:
“My dear, was not that the Blue Lady who has just gone into the shrubbery. I hope she won’t frighten Flo. Whistle for Flo, dear.”
(Flo, it may be remarked, is the youngest and most precious of many dachshunds).
Blanche Peveril gave a cursory whistle, and crunched the sugar left unmelted at the bottom of her coffee-cup between her very white teeth.
“Oh, darling, Flo isn’t so silly as to mind,” she said. “Poor blue Aunt Barbara is such a bore! Whenever I meet her she always looks as if she wanted to speak to me, but when I say, ‘What is it, Aunt Barbara?’ she never utters, but only points somewhere towards the house, which is so vague. I believe there was something she wanted to confess about two hundred years ago, but she has forgotten what it is.”
Here Flo gave two or three short pleased barks, and came out of the shrubbery wagging her tail, and capering round what appeared to me to be a perfectly empty space on the lawn.
“There! Flo has made friends with her,” said Mrs. Peveril. “I wonder why she dresses in that very stupid shade of blue.”

===Chinese===
查奇-佩弗里尔（Church-Peveril）这座宅子，被形形色色或可见、或可闻的鬼魂如此频繁地叨扰与光顾，以至于在它那一英亩半的绿铜屋顶庇护之下的一家人，对种种灵异现象全不放在心上。因为在佩弗里尔（Peveril）一家看来，鬼魂的现身，与寻常人家眼里邮差上门相差无几。也就是说，它几乎是天天到的，敲门（或弄出别的响动），被人瞧见沿着车道走来（或在别处出没）。我自己住在那儿时，便亲眼见过如今这位佩弗里尔太太（Mrs. Peveril）——她眼神不大好——晚饭后我们一道在露台上喝咖啡时，眯眼朝暮色里张望，对她女儿说：
「亲爱的，刚进灌木丛去的那位，不就是蓝衣夫人（the Blue Lady）么。但愿她别吓着弗洛（Flo）。亲爱的，吹个口哨叫叫弗洛吧。」
（顺便说一句，弗洛是这家里众多腊肠犬（dachshund）中最年幼、也最宝贝的一只。）
布兰奇·佩弗里尔（Blanche Peveril）随口吹了一声口哨，又用她那雪白的牙齿，把咖啡杯底没化开的糖块咬得咯吱作响。
「哦，亲爱的，弗洛才不会那么傻，犯不上介意，」她说，「可怜的蓝衣巴巴拉姑奶奶（Aunt Barbara）就是这么个叫人腻烦的人！我每回撞见她，她总像是有话要对我说，可我一开口『怎么了，巴巴拉姑奶奶？』她便一言不发，只朝着宅子那一边指指点点，模模糊糊的，真叫人摸不着头脑。我估摸着约莫两百年前，她原是有桩什么事想要忏悔的，可如今她已经把那是什么给忘啦。」
正说着，弗洛欢喜地短吠了两三声，从灌木丛里跑了出来，摇着尾巴，围着我眼中分明空空如也的一片草坪蹦跳着。
「瞧！弗洛已经跟她交上朋友了，」佩弗里尔太太说，「我就纳闷，她干嘛要穿那么一种蠢透了的蓝色。」

===Original===
From this it may be gathered that even with regard to psychical phenomena there is some truth in the proverb that speaks of familiarity. But the Peverils do not exactly treat their ghosts with contempt, since most of that delightful family never despised anybody except such people as avowedly did not care for hunting or shooting, or golf or skating. And as all of their ghosts are of their family, it seems reasonable to suppose that they all, even the poor Blue Lady, excelled at one time in field-sports. So far then they harbour no unkindness or contempt, but only pity. Of one Peveril, indeed, who broke his neck in vainly attempting to ride up the main staircase on a thoroughbred mare after some monstrous and violent deed in the back-garden, they are very fond, and Blanche comes downstairs in the morning with an eye unusually bright when she can announce that Master Anthony was “very loud” last night. He (apart from the fact of his having been so foul a ruffian) was a tremendous fellow across country, and they like these indications of the continuance of his superb vitality. In fact, it is supposed to be a compliment, when you go to stay at Church-Peveril, to be assigned a bedroom which is frequented by defunct members of the family. It means that you are worthy to look on the august and villainous dead, and you will find yourself shown into some vaulted or tapestried chamber, without benefit of electric light, and are told that great-great-grandmamma Bridget occasionally has vague business by the fireplace, but it is better not to talk to her, and that you will hear Master Anthony “awfully well” if he attempts the front staircase any time before morning. There you are left for your night’s repose, and, having quakingly undressed, begin reluctantly to put out your candles. It is draughty in these great chambers, and the solemn tapestry swings and bellows and subsides, and the firelight dances on the forms of huntsmen and warriors and stern pursuits. Then you climb into your bed, a bed so huge that you feel as if the desert of Sahara was spread for you, and pray, like the mariners who sailed with St. Paul, for day. And, all the time, you are aware that Freddy and Harry and Blanche and possibly even Mrs. Peveril are quite capable of dressing up and making disquieting tappings outside your door, so that when you open it some inconjecturable horror fronts you. For myself, I stick steadily to the assertion that I have an obscure valvular disease of the heart, and so sleep undisturbed in the new wing of the house where Aunt Barbara, and great-great-grandmamma Bridget and Master Anthony never penetrate. I forget the details of great-great-grandmamma Bridget, but she certainly cut the throat of some distant relation before she disembowelled herself with the axe that had been used at Agincourt. Before that she had led a very sultry life, crammed with amazing incident.

===Chinese===
由此可见，即便是论及灵异现象，所谓「见多不怪」那句老话也颇有几分道理。不过佩弗里尔一家人倒也不算瞧不起他们的鬼魂，因为这一家可爱的人儿，向来只鄙视一种人——明明白白表示不爱打猎、不爱射击、不爱打高尔夫也不爱滑冰的那种人。而既然宅子里出没的鬼魂都出自他们自家，那么想当然耳，他们——就连那可怜的蓝衣夫人也一样——当年个个都是野外运动的好手。故而对他们，家里头怀的不是恶意或鄙夷，而只是怜悯。有一位佩弗里尔——他是在后花园里干下一桩骇人暴行之后，骑着纯种牝马妄想冲上主楼梯，结果摔断了脖子的——一家人对他着实疼爱得很；清早布兰奇下楼来，要是能报告一声安东尼少爷（Master Anthony）昨夜「闹得很凶」，她的眼睛便会格外地亮。他（撇开他那副恶棍行径不谈）原是一位越野骑马的好手，他们乐见这种迹象，可见他那旺盛的生命力犹自不息。事实上，你到查奇-佩弗里尔做客，被分到一间有家族亡魂常来常往的卧室，是被视为一种礼遇的。那意思是说，你够资格一瞻这些威严而作恶多端的亡者，于是你便被引进某间拱顶或挂满花毡的屋子——里头不通电灯——有人告诉你，曾曾外祖母布丽吉特（great-great-grandmamma Bridget）偶尔会在壁炉旁有桩不明不白的差事，不过最好别搭理她；又告诉你，若是安东尼少爷在天亮前的什么时候去攀前楼梯，你准会把他听得「清清楚楚」。随后便只剩你一人在那儿过夜，你战战兢兢地脱了衣，又老大不情愿地去熄烛。这种大屋子里穿堂风飕飕的，肃穆的花毡猎猎鼓动又颓然贴回墙上，炉火的光在猎人、武士和紧张追猎的身影上跳荡。然后你爬上床——那床大得叫你觉得自己仿佛被铺在了撒哈拉沙漠上——便像与圣保罗（St. Paul）同舟的水手那样，求着天赶紧亮。而这一夜里，你心里又始终清楚：弗雷迪（Freddy）、哈里（Harry）、布兰奇，甚至可能连佩弗里尔太太，都完全可能乔装打扮一番，在你门外敲出令人不安的响动，好叫你一开门便迎面撞上某种不可揣度的可怖玩意。至于我呢，我始终死死咬定自己患有一种说不清道不的心脏瓣膜病，于是便在新厢房里安睡无扰——蓝衣姑奶奶、曾曾外祖母布丽吉特和安东尼少爷是从不踏进那里一步的。曾曾外祖母布丽吉特的种种详情我已记不大清，但她确实是在用那把曾在阿金库尔（Agincourt）战场上用过的斧头开膛破肚之前，先割断过某位远亲的喉咙。在那之前，她过的也是一种相当炽烈的人生，里面塞满了种种惊人的变故。

===Original===
But there is one ghost at Church-Peveril at which the family never laugh, in which they feel no friendly and amused interest, and of which they only speak just as much as is necessary for the safety of their guests. More properly it should be described as two ghosts, for the “haunt” in question is that of two very young children, who were twins. These, not without reason, the family take very seriously indeed. The story of them, as told me by Mrs. Peveril, is as follows:
In the year 1602, the same being the last of Queen Elizabeth’s reign, a certain Dick Peveril was greatly in favour at Court. He was brother to Master Joseph Peveril, then owner of the family house and lands, who two years previously, at the respectable age of seventy-four, became father of twin boys, firstborn of his progeny. It is known that the royal and ancient virgin had said to handsome Dick, who was nearly forty years his brother’s junior, “’Tis pity that you are not master of Church Peveril,” and these words probably suggested to him a sinister design.
