Be that as it may, handsome Dick, who very adequately sustained the family reputation for wickedness, set off to ride down to Yorkshire, and found that, very conveniently, his brother Joseph had just been seized with an apoplexy, which appeared to be the result of a continued spell of hot weather combined with the necessity of quenching his thirst with an augmented amount of sack, and had actually died while handsome Dick, with God knows what thoughts in his mind, was journeying northwards. Thus it came about that he arrived at Church-Peveril just in time for his brother’s funeral. It was with great propriety that he attended the obsequies, and returned to spend a sympathetic day or two of mourning with his widowed sister-in-law, who was but a fainthearted dame, little fit to be mated with such hawks as these. On the second night of his stay, he did that which the Peverils regret to this day. He entered the room where the twins slept with their nurse, and quietly strangled the latter as she slept. Then he took the twins and put them into the fire which warms the long gallery. The weather, which up to the day of Joseph’s death had been so hot, had changed suddenly to bitter cold, and the fire was heaped high with burning logs and was exultant with flame. In the core of this conflagration he struck out a cremation-chamber, and into that he threw the two children, stamping them down with his riding-boots. They could just walk, but they could not walk out of that ardent place. It is said that he laughed as he added more logs. Thus he became master of Church Peveril.

===Chinese===
然而，查奇-佩弗里尔有一桩鬼，是一家人绝不肯拿它打趣的；他们对它既无情谊，也不觉有几分有趣的看头，至于谈到它，也只是把为客人安全所必需的那几句话说出来便罢。更确切地说，它该被称作两桩鬼，因为这里所说的「闹鬼」，是两个极幼的孩子——一对双胞胎。对这两个，一家人——也并非没有缘故——着实看得极其郑重。佩弗里尔太太讲给我听的那段来历，是这样的：
1602 年，也就是伊丽莎白女王（Queen Elizabeth）在位的最后一年，有位迪克·佩弗里尔（Dick Peveril）在朝廷里极得圣眷。他是当时家宅与田产的主人约瑟夫·佩弗里尔少爷（Master Joseph Peveril）的兄弟；两年前，约瑟夫以七十四岁可观的年纪，得了两个孪生的男孩，那是他膝下的头胎。众所周知，那位尊贵而高龄的童贞女王，曾对这位比他哥哥小了近四十岁的俊俏的迪克（handsome Dick）说过：「可惜你不是查奇-佩弗里尔的主人。」这话大约便在他心中勾起了一桩阴险的图谋。不管究竟如何，俊俏的迪克——他颇有家风，作恶的本事一点不让人——动身骑马南下约克郡（Yorkshire），却发现十分凑巧，他哥哥约瑟夫刚中了风，似乎是因为连日酷暑，再加上不得不加大剂量以葡萄酒（sack）来解渴所致，而且竟在俊俏的迪克一路北上的途中——天知道他肚子里转的是什么念头——便已断了气。于是他便恰好赶在哥哥的葬礼之前到了查奇-佩弗里尔。他以十足的得体出席了葬礼，又回来陪他那守寡的嫂子——不过是个软弱的妇人，与这一窝鹰隼实非良配——度过一两天同情的丧居之日。在他留住的第二夜，他干下了佩弗里尔一家至今痛悔的事。他摸进那对双胞胎与乳母同睡的房间，乘那乳母睡着，悄悄把她掐死了。然后他抱起双胞胎，把他们扔进了为长廊供暖的那炉火里。原来约瑟夫死前天气一直酷热，那一日却陡然转了苦寒，炉膛里高高地堆着熊熊的木柴，火舌正欢腾。他在那团烈火中央扒出一个焚尸的膛口，便把两个孩子丢进去，用马靴把他们踩实。他们刚刚会走，却走不出那片炽烈。据说他一边添柴，一边笑。他便这样做了查奇-佩弗里尔的主人。

===Original===
The crime was never brought home to him, but he lived no longer than a year in the enjoyment of his bloodstained inheritance. When he lay a-dying he made his confession to the priest who attended him, but his spirit struggled forth from its fleshly coil before Absolution could be given him. On that very night there began in Church-Peveril the haunting which to this day is but seldom spoken of by the family, and then only in low tones and with serious mien. For, only an hour or two after handsome Dick’s death, one of the servants passing the door of the long gallery heard from within peals of the loud laughter so jovial and yet so sinister, which he had thought would never be heard in the house again. In a moment of that cold courage, which is so nearly akin to mortal terror, he opened the door and entered, expecting to see he knew not what manifestation of him who lay dead in the room below. Instead he saw two little white-robed figures toddling towards him hand in hand across the moonlit floor.
The watchers in the room below ran upstairs startled by the crash of his fallen body, and found him lying in the grip of some dread convulsion. Just before morning he regained consciousness and told his tale. Then pointing with trembling and ash-grey finger towards the door, he screamed aloud, and so fell back dead.

===Chinese===
这桩罪行始终未曾归罪到他头上，可他坐享那血腥的遗产，也不过一年光景。临终之时，他向守在床畔的神父作了告解，然而他的灵魂在尚未领得赦罪之前，便已挣扎着挣脱了肉躯的羁绊。正是那一夜，查奇-佩弗里尔开始了那种闹鬼，一家人至今很少谈起，谈起来也只是压低声音、神色凝重。原来俊俏的迪克死后才一两个钟头，一个仆人从长廊门口经过，听见里头传出一阵洪亮的笑声——那么欢快，又那么阴森——他本以为这声音再不会在这宅子里响起了。借着那一股冷的勇气（它简直与致命的恐惧相差无几），他推开门走了进去，正预备看见楼下那个死人现出何种形貌，他自己也说不清。结果他看见的，是两个一袭白衣的小小身影，手牵着手，正摇摇晃晃地穿过月光铺地的地板，朝他走来。
楼下守灵的人被那仆人倒地的巨响惊起，跑上楼来，只见他正被某种可怖的痉挛紧紧攫住。快到清晨时他才醒了过来，把所见之事说了一遍。然后，他用颤抖的、灰如死灰的手指朝那扇门一指，发出一声尖叫，便向后一仰，死去。

===Original===
During the next fifty years this strange and terrible legend of the twin-babies became fixed and consolidated. Their appearance, luckily for those who inhabit the house, was exceedingly rare, and during these years they seem to have been seen four or five times only. On each occasion they appeared at night, between sunset and sunrise, always in the same long gallery, and always as two toddling children scarcely able to walk. And on each occasion the luckless individual who saw them died either speedily or terribly, or with both speed and terror, after the accursed vision had appeared to him. Sometimes he might live for a few months: he was lucky if he died, as did the servant who first saw them, in a few hours. Vastly more awful was the fate of a certain Mrs. Canning, who had the ill-luck to see them in the middle of the next century, or to be quite accurate, in the year 1760. By this time the hours and the place of their appearance were well-known, and, as up till a year ago, visitors were warned not to go between sunset and sunrise into the long gallery.
But Mrs. Canning, a brilliantly clever and beautiful woman, admirer also and friend of the notorious sceptic M. Voltaire, wilfully went and sat night after night, in spite of all protestations, in the haunted place. For four evenings she saw nothing, but on the fifth she had her will, for the door in the middle of the gallery opened, and there came toddling towards her the ill-omened innocent little pair. It seemed that even then she was not frightened, but she thought good, poor wretch, to mock at them, telling them it was time for them to get back into the fire. They gave no word in answer, but turned away from her crying and sobbing. Immediately after they disappeared from her vision and she rustled downstairs to where the family and guests in the house were waiting for her, with the triumphant announcement that she had seen them both, and must needs write to M. Voltaire, saying that she had spoken to spirits made manifest. It would make him laugh. But when some months later the whole news reached him he did not laugh at all.

===Chinese===
在接下来的五十年里，这对孪生婴孩那古怪而骇人的传说便如此固定下来、凝固下来。所幸对住在宅中的人来说，他们的现身极罕见，这些年间仿佛只被瞧见过四五次。每一回，他们都在夜间、在日落与日出之间现身，总在那同一道长廊里，总作两个刚刚会走、走也走不稳的小儿模样。而每一回，那倒霉的目击者在瞧见这可咒的幻影之后，不是死得飞快，便是死得极惨，要么又快又惨。有时他还能拖上几个月：若像头一个看见他们的那个仆人那样，几个钟头便死了，那已是侥幸。远比这更可怖的，是某位坎宁太太（Mrs. Canning）的下场——她倒霉，在下一个世纪的中叶，确切说是 1760 年，看见了他们。到了这个时候，他们现身的时辰与地点已尽人皆知，而直到一年前为止，访客都会被郑重告诫：日落与日出之间，万不可踏入那道长廊。
可坎宁太太是个极聪明又极貌美的女子，也是声名狼藉的怀疑论者伏尔泰先生（M. Voltaire）的仰慕者与友人，她偏不顾一切劝阻，一夜一夜地执意坐到那闹鬼的地方去。头四个晚上她什么也没瞧见，到第五个晚上，她终于如愿——长廊中间那扇门开了，那对不祥而无辜的小小身影朝她摇晃着走了过来。即便到了那一刻，她似乎也不害怕，反倒觉得戏弄他们一番甚为妥当，这可怜虫，竟讥笑他们，说他们该回炉子里去了。他们一言不发，只是转身离开了她，一路啼哭抽噎。他们才从她眼前消失，她便窸窸窣窣地下楼，回到宅中正等着她的家人和客人那里，得意洋洋地宣布她已把那两个都看见了，非要立马写信给伏尔泰先生，说她已同显灵的鬼魂说过话不可。这准会叫他发笑。然而几个月后，全部的消息传到他耳中，他却一点也笑不出来。

===Original===
Mrs. Canning was one of the great beauties of her day, and in the year 1760 she was at the height and zenith of her blossoming. The chief beauty, if it is possible to single out one point where all was so exquisite, lay in the dazzling colour and incomparable brilliance of her complexion. She was now just thirty years of age, but, in spite of the excesses of her life, retained the snow and roses of girlhood, and she courted the bright light of day which other women shunned, for it but showed to greater advantage the splendour of her skin. In consequence she was very considerably dismayed one morning, about a fortnight after her strange experience in the long gallery, to observe on her left cheek an inch or two below her turquoise-coloured eyes, a little greyish patch of skin, about as big as a threepenny piece. It was in vain that she applied her accustomed washes and ungents: vain, too, were the arts of her *gardeuse* and of her medical adviser. For a week she kept herself secluded, martyring herself with solitude and unaccustomed physics, and for result at the end of the week she had no amelioration to comfort herself with: instead this woeful grey patch had doubled itself in size. Thereafter the nameless disease, whatever it was, developed in new and terrible ways. From the centre of the discoloured place there sprouted forth little lichen-like tendrils of greenish-grey, and another patch appeared on her lower lip. This, too, soon vegetated, and one morning on opening her eyes to the horror of a new day, she found that her vision was strangely blurred. She sprang to her looking-glass, and what she saw caused her to shriek aloud with horror. From under her upper eyelid a fresh growth had sprung up, mushroom-like, in the night, and its filaments extended downwards, screening the pupil of her eye. Soon after her tongue and throat were attacked: the air passages became obstructed, and death by suffocation was merciful after such suffering.
More terrible yet was the case of a certain Colonel Blantyre who fired at the children with his revolver. What he went through is not to be recorded here.

===Chinese===
坎宁太太是她那个时代的大美人之一，1760 年正值她盛放的鼎盛与巅峰。倘若处处皆如此精致，竟要单挑一处出来说，那她首要的姿色，便在那种令人目眩的色彩与无与伦比的光泽的肤色上。她这一年刚满三十，然而尽管一生纵恣，却仍保留着少女的雪肤红颜，而且偏爱别个女人所躲避的那明亮的天光，因为那光只会把她肌肤的华彩衬得更加鲜明。因此，在长廊那番奇遇之后约莫两个星期，某一天清晨，她发觉自己左颊上、在那双绿松石色的眼睛下方一两英寸处，冒出一小块灰扑扑的斑、约莫一个三便士硬币那么大——她着实大为沮丧。她照常用惯的洗液和膏子去涂，全是枉然；她的美容侍媪（gardeuse）和她的医生那一身本事，也是枉然。她闭门独处了一个星期，以孤独和种种不惯服的药剂折磨自己，结果到周末，却连一丝好转都无从聊以自慰：反倒那块可忧的灰斑扩大了一倍。此后那无名之症——管它究竟是什么——便以新的、可怖的方式蔓延开来。从那块变色的皮肤中央，冒出了几缕灰绿色的、苔藓般的触须；接着她下唇又出现了另一块斑。这一块也很快滋长起来，一天清晨，她睁开眼迎接又一天可怖的现实，发觉自己的视线古怪地模糊了。她一跃扑到镜前，所见之物叫她吓得大声尖叫。一夜之间，从她的上眼睑底下又冒出一处新的增生物，蘑菇似的，它的丝缕向下延伸，遮住了她的瞳孔。不久，她的舌头和喉咙也被侵染：气道阻塞了，受尽这番折磨之后，窒息而死已是上天的仁慈。
比这更可怖的，是某位布兰泰尔上校（Colonel Blantyre）的下场——他竟拿左轮手枪朝那两个孩子开枪。他所经历的种种，此处不载。

===Original===
It is this haunting, then, that the Peverils take quite seriously, and every guest on his arrival in the house is told that the long gallery must not be entered after nightfall on any pretext whatever. By day, however, it is a delightful room and intrinsically merits description, apart from the fact that the due understanding of its geography is necessary for the account that here follows. It is full eighty feet in length, and is lit by a row of six tall windows looking over the gardens at the back of the house. A door communicates with the landing at the top of the main staircase, and about halfway down the gallery in the wall facing the windows is another door communicating with the back staircase and servants’ quarters, and thus the gallery forms a constant place of passage for them in going to the rooms on the first landing. It was through this door that the baby-figures came when they appeared to Mrs. Canning, and on several other occasions they have been known to make their entry here, for the room out of which handsome Dick took them lies just beyond at the top of the back stairs. Further on again in the gallery is the fireplace into which he thrust them, and at the far end a large bow-window looks straight down the avenue. Above this fireplace there hangs with grim significance a portrait of handsome Dick, in the insolent beauty of early manhood, attributed to Holbein, and a dozen other portraits of great merit face the windows. During the day this is the most frequented sitting-room in the house, for its other visitors never appear there then, nor does it then ever resound with the harsh jovial laugh of handsome Dick, which sometimes, after dark has fallen, is heard by passersby on the landing outside. But Blanche does not grow bright-eyed when she hears it: she shuts her ears and hastens to put a greater distance between her and the sound of that atrocious mirth.
But during the day the long gallery is frequented by many occupants, and much laughter in no wise sinister or saturnine resounds there. When summer lies hot over the land, those occupants lounge in the deep window seats, and when winter spreads his icy fingers and blows shrilly between his frozen palms, congregate round the fireplace at the far end, and perch, in companies of cheerful chatterers, upon sofa and chair, and chair-back and floor. Often have I sat there on long August evenings up till dressing-time, but never have I been there when anyone has seemed disposed to linger over-late without hearing the warning: “It is close on sunset: shall we go?” Later on in the shorter autumn days they often have tea laid there, and sometimes it has happened that, even while merriment was most uproarious, Mrs. Peveril has suddenly looked out of the window and said, “My dears, it is getting so late: let us finish our nonsense downstairs in the hall.” And then for a moment a curious hush always falls on loquacious family and guests alike, and as if some bad news had just been known, we all make our silent way out of the place. But the spirits of the Peverils (of the living ones, that is to say) are the most mercurial imaginable, and the blight which the thought of handsome Dick and his doings casts over them passes away again with amazing rapidity.

===Chinese===
佩弗里尔一家人郑重其事的，便是这桩闹鬼；每逢客人到宅，必被告知：入夜之后，无论以任何借口，都不得踏入那道长廊。不过白日里，那却是一间叫人舒心的屋子，单就其本身也值得一描，何况要听懂下文这段叙述，原也得先把它的格局弄清楚。它足有八十多英尺长，由一排六扇高大的窗子采光，窗外望出去便是宅子后花园。一道门通到主楼梯顶的楼梯口，而顺着长廊走约莫一半，在对着那排窗子的墙上，另有一道门通向后楼梯和仆人住处，于是这道长廊便成了他们前往一层楼梯口各房间的常经之路。坎宁太太瞧见时，那两个婴孩的身影便是从这道门里出来的；另有几回，他们也被人知道是从这里现身的，因为当年俊俏的迪克把他们抱出来的那间屋子，便在后楼梯顶再过去一点。再往前去，便是他把他们扔进去的那座壁炉；长廊的最尽头，则有一扇大弓形窗，正对着宅前那条林荫道直望出去。这座壁炉的上方，意味深长地挂着一幅俊俏的迪克的画像，画的是他早年那份骄横的美貌，相传出自霍尔拜因（Holbein）之手；面窗那一边，还另有十二幅极具功力的画像。白日里，这是宅中最热闹的起居室，因为它那些另类的访客此时绝不出没，俊俏的迪克那粗哑而欢快的笑声，也绝不在此时回荡——那笑声，有时天黑之后，会被外头楼梯口上经过的人听见。可布兰奇听见时，眼睛不会发亮：她堵上耳朵，匆匆走开，恨不得把自己与那可怖的笑声隔得越远越好。
然而白日里，长廊里有许许多多的人出没，那回荡在其中的笑声，毫无阴鸷或阴郁之气。夏日酷暑笼罩大地时，那些人便懒洋洋地倚在深深的窗座上；冬日伸出他冰冷的手指，在冻僵的掌心间尖声吹气时，他们便聚到最尽头那座壁炉周围，三五成群、叽叽喳喳地欢笑着，或栖于沙发，或栖于椅子，或栖于椅背，或干脆栖于地板。八月的漫长傍晚，我常在那里坐到该更衣的时候，却从未见过有谁似乎打算多留片刻而不听见这一句提醒：「快日落了：咱们走吧？」再后来，在白昼更短的秋日里，他们常把茶点摆在这里；有时甚至会出现这样的情形：正当欢笑声最为鼎沸之时，佩弗里尔太太会忽然朝窗外一望，说道：「亲爱的们，天色太晚了：咱们到楼下大厅里去把这点疯闹收尾吧。」于是一时之间，话多的一家人和客人们总会奇异地静下来，仿佛刚听到了什么噩耗似的，我们一个一个默默无言地走出那地方。不过佩弗里尔一家（这是说，活着的那些）的性情又是想象得到的最易变，一念及俊俏的迪克及其所作所为而罩在他们心头的那片阴翳，转眼之间又以惊人的速度散去了。

===Original===
A typical party, large, young, and peculiarly cheerful, was staying at Church-Peveril shortly after Christmas last year, and as usual on December 31, Mrs. Peveril was giving her annual New Year’s Eve ball. The house was quite full, and she had commandeered as well the greater part of the Peveril Arms to provide sleeping-quarters for the overflow from the house. For some days past a black and windless frost had stopped all hunting, but it is an ill windlessness that blows no good (if so mixed a metaphor may be forgiven), and the lake below the house had for the last day or two been covered with an adequate and admirable sheet of ice. Everyone in the house had been occupied all the morning of that day in performing swift and violent manoeuvres on the elusive surface, and as soon as lunch was over we all, with one exception, hurried out again. This one exception was Madge Dalrymple who had had the misfortune to fall rather badly earlier in the day, but hoped, by resting her injured knee, instead of joining the skaters again, to be able to dance that evening. The hope, it is true, was of the most sanguine sort, for she could but hobble ignobly back to the house, but with the breezy optimism which characterises the Peverils (she is Blanche’s first cousin), she remarked that it would be but tepid enjoyment that she could, in her present state, derive from further skating, and thus she sacrificed little, but might gain much.
Accordingly after a rapid cup of coffee which was served in the long gallery, we left Madge comfortably reclined on the big sofa at right-angles to the fireplace, with an attractive book to beguile the tedium till tea. Being of the family, she knew all about handsome Dick and the babies, and the fate of Mrs. Canning and Colonel Blantyre, but as we went out I heard Blanche say to her, “Don’t run it too fine, dear,” and Madge had replied, “No; I’ll go away well before sunset.” And so we left her alone in the long gallery.

===Chinese===
去年圣诞节刚过不久，查奇-佩弗里尔正住着一群人——这是一次颇典型的聚会：人多、年轻，又格外地快活；按照 12 月 31 日的惯例，佩弗里尔太太正举办她一年一度的除夕舞会。宅子里住得满满当当，她连「佩弗里尔纹章客栈」（the Peveril Arms）的大部分也都征用了，好给宅子里住不下的人安排歇宿之处。连日来，一场无风的严霜把一切狩猎都停了下来；不过，无风未必无福（这比喻混杂，还望见谅），宅子下方的那片湖，这一两日已结起了一层够厚、够漂亮的冰。那天一上午，宅子里的人都在那滑不留足的冰面上做着迅疾而剧烈的腾挪；午饭一过，我们一行人——只除了一位——又一齐赶了出去。这唯一例外的是玛奇·达尔林普尔（Madge Dalrymple），她这天早些时候倒霉，摔了重重的一跤，但盼着把伤了的膝盖歇一歇，不再跟众人一道去滑，晚上便能跳舞。这份指望，自然，是最最乐观的那种，因为她当时只能狼狈地一瘸一拐走回宅子；可凭着佩弗里尔一家那种天塌下来也不当回事的乐天（她是布兰奇的亲表妹），她说道：以她眼下这情形再去滑冰，能得到的也不过是温吞吞的乐趣，于是她牺牲的少，却可能得着的多。
于是在长廊里匆匆喝过一杯咖啡之后，我们便把玛奇舒舒服服地安顿在壁炉边、与炉子成直角摆放的那张宽大沙发上，又给她一本引人入胜的书，好打发喝茶之前这段无聊时光。既是自家人，俊俏的迪克和那两个婴孩、坎宁太太和布兰泰尔上校的下场，她全知道；可我们出去时，我听见布兰奇对她说：「亲爱的，可别把时间掐得太死。」玛奇答道：「不会；日落前我老早就走。」于是我们便把她一个人留在了长廊里。

===Original===
Madge read her attractive book for some minutes, but failing to get absorbed in it, put it down and limped across to the window. Though it was still but little after two, it was but a dim and uncertain light that entered, for the crystalline brightness of the morning had given place to a veiled obscurity produced by flocks of thick clouds which were coming sluggishly up from the northeast. Already the whole sky was overcast with them, and occasionally a few snowflakes fluttered waveringly down past the long windows. From the darkness and bitter cold of the afternoon, it seemed to her that there was like to be a heavy snowfall before long, and these outward signs were echoed inwardly in her by that muffled drowsiness of the brain, which to those who are sensitive to the pressures and lightnesses of weather portends storm. Madge was peculiarly the prey of such external influences: to her a brisk morning gave an ineffable brightness and briskness of spirit, and correspondingly the approach of heavy weather produced a somnolence in sensation that both drowsed and depressed her.
It was in such mood as this that she limped back again to the sofa beside the log-fire. The whole house was comfortably heated by water-pipes, and though the fire of logs and peat, an adorable mixture, had been allowed to burn low, the room was very warm. Idly she watched the dwindling flames, not opening her book again, but lying on the sofa with face towards the fireplace, intending drowsily and not immediately to go to her own room and spend the hours, until the return of the skaters made gaiety in the house again, in writing one or two neglected letters. Still drowsily she began thinking over what she had to communicate: one letter several days overdue should go to her mother, who was immensely interested in the psychical affairs of the family. She would tell her how Master Anthony had been prodigiously active on the staircase a night or two ago, and how the Blue Lady, regardless of the severity of the weather, had been seen by Mrs. Peveril that morning, strolling about. It was rather interesting: the Blue Lady had gone down the laurel walk and had been seen by her to enter the stables, where, at the moment, Freddy Peveril was inspecting the frost-bound hunters. Identically then, a sudden panic had spread through the stables, and the horses had whinnied and kicked, and shied, and sweated. Of the fatal twins nothing had been seen for many years past, but, as her mother knew, the Peverils never used the long gallery after dark.

===Chinese===
玛奇把那本引人入胜的书翻了几分钟，却怎么也看不进去，便把它搁下，一瘸一拐地走到窗前。虽说才刚过两点不久，照进来的光却已十分昏暗不定，因为上午那水晶般的明丽已被一层蒙蒙的晦冥所取代——那是有大团大团厚云从东北方懒洋洋地涌上来所致。整片天空已被它们盖满，间或几片雪花悠悠晃晃地，从那一长排窗前飘落下去。看这天色的阴沉、这下午苦寒的劲儿，她心想怕是不久就要下一场大雪了；这些外在的征候，也在她内里激起了那一种闷闷的困倦——凡是对气压与天色的轻重敏感的人，都有这种困倦来预告风暴。玛奇尤其受这种种外因所左右：一个清朗的早晨能给她带来难以言说的明亮与轻快的心境；相应地，坏天气的逼近，也在她感觉中唤起一种昏沉，既叫她困，又叫她闷。
正是在这种心境下，她又一瘸一拐地回到了木柴炉旁的沙发上。整座宅子由热水管舒舒服服地供暖着，虽说那炉里烧的木柴与泥炭——一种可爱的混合——已被任由烧得低了些，屋子里仍十分暖和。她慵懒地看着那越来越小的火苗，没有再翻开书，只面朝壁炉侧躺在沙发上，迷迷糊糊地、并不急着想回自己屋里去——打算趁着滑冰的人回来之前宅中重新热闹起来的这几个钟头，写两封拖欠已久的信。依旧迷迷糊糊地，她开始盘算要写些什么：有一封已耽搁了好几天的信，是要写给她母亲的——她母亲对这一家的灵异之事兴致极浓。她要告诉她，安东尼少爷一两个晚上之前是如何在楼梯上闹得格外凶；蓝衣夫人又如何不顾天气严寒，被佩弗里尔太太当天早晨撞见在外头溜达。这事颇有趣：蓝衣夫人沿着月桂小径走下去，被佩弗里尔太太瞧见进了马厩——当时弗雷迪·佩弗里尔正在那里查看那些被霜冻住了的猎马。同一瞬间，一阵突如其来的惊恐传遍了马厩，马儿们又是嘶鸣，又是踢腾，又是惊退，又是冒汗。至于那一对要命的双胞胎，多年以来倒是谁也没再瞧见过，不过，她母亲是知道的，佩弗里尔一家人入夜之后是从不踏进长廊的。

===Original===
Then for a moment she sat up, remembering that she was in the long gallery now. But it was still but a little after half-past two, and if she went to her room in half an hour, she would have ample time to write this and another letter before tea. Till then she would read her book. But she found she had left it on the windowsill, and it seemed scarcely worth while to get it. She felt exceedingly drowsy.
The sofa where she lay had been lately re-covered, in a greyish green shade of velvet, somewhat the colour of lichen. It was of very thick soft texture, and she luxuriously stretched her arms out, one on each side of her body, and pressed her fingers into the nap. How horrible that story of Mrs. Canning was: the growth on her face was of the colour of lichen. And then without further transition or blurring of thought Madge fell asleep.

===Chinese===
一念及此，她忽地坐直了身子，才想起自己眼下便在这长廊里。可这才刚过两点半不久，要是她半个钟头之后再回房，喝茶之前还有的是工夫写这封和另外一封。在那之前，她要看她的书。可她发觉自己把书搁在了窗台上，又似乎犯不上再去取了。她困得厉害。
她躺的这张沙发不久前刚刚换过面，是一种灰绿色的天鹅绒，颜色倒有些像苔藓。那绒面又厚又软，她舒舒服服地把两条胳膊朝身子两边伸开，把手指按进绒毛里去。坎宁太太那桩事真是骇人：她脸上长出的那东西，就是苔藓的颜色。紧接着，思绪再无别的转折，也再无任何模糊，玛奇便睡着了。

===Original===
She dreamed. She dreamed that she awoke and found herself exactly where she had gone to sleep, and in exactly the same attitude. The flames from the logs had burned up again, and leaped on the walls, fitfully illuminating the picture of handsome Dick above the fireplace. In her dream she knew exactly what she had done today, and for what reason she was lying here now instead of being out with the rest of the skaters. She remembered also (still dreaming), that she was going to write a letter or two before tea, and prepared to get up in order to go to her room. As she half-rose she caught sight of her own arms lying out on each side of her on the grey velvet sofa. But she could not see where her hands ended, and where the grey velvet began: her fingers seemed to have melted into the stuff. She could see her wrists quite clearly, and a blue vein on the backs of her hands, and here and there a knuckle. Then, in her dream she remembered, the last thought which had been in her mind before she fell asleep, namely the growth of the lichen-coloured vegetation on the face and the eyes and the throat of Mrs. Canning. At that thought the strangling terror of real nightmare began: she knew that she was being transformed into this grey stuff, and she was absolutely unable to move. Soon the grey would spread up her arms, and over her feet; when they came in from skating they would find here nothing but a huge misshapen cushion of lichen-coloured velvet, and that would be she. The horror grew more acute, and then by a violent effort she shook herself free of the clutches of this very evil dream, and she awoke.
For a minute or two she lay there, conscious only of the tremendous relief at finding herself awake. She felt again with her fingers the pleasant touch of the velvet, and drew them backwards and forwards, assuring herself that she was not, as her dream had suggested, melting into greyness and softness. But she was still, in spite of the violence of her awakening, very sleepy, and lay there till, looking down, she was aware that she could not see her hands at all. It was very nearly dark.

===Chinese===
她做了一个梦。她梦见自己醒了过来，发觉自己仍睡在原先入睡之处，姿势也一模一样。木柴的火苗又烧旺了，在墙上跳动着，一阵一阵地照亮壁炉上方俊俏的迪克那幅画像。在梦里，她清楚地知道自己今天都做了些什么，又是为了什么缘故此刻躺在这里，而没有跟其余的滑冰者一道在外头。她也记起（仍在梦里）自己原打算喝茶之前写一两封信，便准备起身回屋。半起身时，她瞥见自己两条胳膊摊在灰天鹅绒沙发的两边。可她看不清自己的手到哪里为止、灰色的天鹅绒又从哪里开始：她的手指仿佛已经融进了那料子。手腕她却看得清清楚楚，手背上的一根青筋也看得见，这儿那儿，还能看见一个指节。继而，在梦里她记起了入睡前脑海中最后的那一个念头，那就是坎宁太太脸上、眼睛上、喉咙上长出的那一片苔藓色的东西。这一想，真正梦魇的那种扼喉的恐怖便开始了：她知道自己正在被变成这种灰色的东西，而她丝毫动弹不得。很快这灰色就会爬上她的胳膊，爬过她的双脚；等他们滑完冰回来，会在这里看见的，不过是一只巨大的、畸形的苔藓色天鹅绒垫子，而那便是她。恐怖愈来愈尖锐，接着，她猛地一使劲，把自己从这极其凶险的梦境魔掌中挣了出来，醒了。
有一两分钟，她躺在那里，所感到的唯有发现自己醒了的那种极大的如释重负。她又用手指去感受那天鹅绒惬意的触感，把它们来回摩挲，向自己证实她并不像梦中所提示的那样，正在融化成灰色与柔软。可她虽然醒得很猛，此刻却仍困倦得很，便那么躺着，直到她低头一看，才发觉自己的双手竟一点也看不见了。屋里已几乎漆黑。

===Original===
At that moment a sudden flicker of flame came from the dying fire, and a flare of burning gas from the peat flooded the room. The portrait of handsome Dick looked evilly down on her, and her hands were visible again. And then a panic worse than the panic of her dreams seized her. Daylight had altogether faded, and she knew that she was alone in the dark in the terrible gallery. This panic was of the nature of nightmare, for she felt unable to move for terror. But it was worse than nightmare because she knew she was awake. And then the full cause of this frozen fear dawned on her; she knew with the certainty of absolute conviction that she was about to see the twin-babies.

===Chinese===
正在那一刻，将熄的炉火忽地一闪，泥炭里一团燃烧的气体噗地一亮，照亮了整间屋子。俊俏的迪克的画像阴鸷地俯视着她，她的双手又看得见了。紧接着，一阵比梦中的恐慌更甚的恐慌攫住了她。天光已全然褪尽，她知道，自己正独自在这可怕的长廊里，独处于黑暗之中。这恐慌是梦魇那一类的，因为她觉得自己因恐惧而动弹不得。可比梦魇更糟的，是她知道自己醒着。继而，她明白了自己这浑身冰冷的恐惧的全部缘由；她以一种绝对的、不容置疑的确信知道：她就要看见那对孪生婴孩了。

===Original===
She felt a sudden moisture break out on her face, and within her mouth her tongue and throat went suddenly dry, and she felt her tongue grate along the inner surface of her teeth. All power of movement had slipped from her limbs, leaving them dead and inert, and she stared with wide eyes into the blackness. The spurt of flame from the peat had burned itself out again, and darkness encompassed her.
Then on the wall opposite her, facing the windows, there grew a faint light of dusky crimson. For a moment she thought it but heralded the approach of the awful vision, then hope revived in her heart, and she remembered that thick clouds had overcast the sky before she went to sleep, and guessed that this light came from the sun not yet quite sunk and set. This sudden revival of hope gave her the necessary stimulus, and she sprang off the sofa where she lay. She looked out of the window and saw the dull glow on the horizon. But before she could take a step forward it was obscured again. A tiny sparkle of light came from the hearth which did no more than illuminate the tiles of the fireplace, and snow falling heavily tapped at the window panes. There was neither light nor sound except these.
But the courage that had come to her, giving her the power of movement, had not quite deserted her, and she began feeling her way down the gallery. And then she found that she was lost. She stumbled against a chair, and, recovering herself, stumbled against another. Then a table barred her way, and, turning swiftly aside, she found herself up against the back of a sofa. Once more she turned and saw the dim gleam of the firelight on the side opposite to that on which she expected it. In her blind gropings she must have reversed her direction. But which way was she to go now? She seemed blocked in by furniture. And all the time insistent and imminent was the fact that the two innocent terrible ghosts were about to appear to her.

===Chinese===
她只觉脸上忽然沁出一层湿意，嘴里头的舌头和喉咙却一下子干透了，她感到自己的舌头擦过牙齿的内侧。一切行动之力都已从她四肢中溜走，把它们留在那儿，死了似的、毫无生气，她睁大了眼，瞪着那一片漆黑。泥炭的那一簇火苗已经燃尽，黑暗又把她团团围住。
接着，在她对面、朝着窗子的那面墙上，渐渐亮起了一抹昏暗的殷红。一时之间，她以为那不过是可怖的幻影将至的前奏；继而她心中又生出了希望，记起自己入睡前厚云已遮满了天空，便猜这光是那尚未尽沉、未尽西坠的太阳所发。这突如其来的希望的复苏给了她必要的刺激，她一跃从所躺的沙发上翻身下地。她朝窗外一望，看见了地平线上那一抹暗红的光。可她还没来得及迈出一步，那光又被遮蔽了。炉床那边透出一点微弱的火花，至多只照得见壁炉的瓷砖；纷纷扬扬的大雪敲打着窗玻璃。除了这些，既无光，也无声。
可方才那一点给了她行动之力的勇气，并未完全抛下她，她便摸索着顺着长廊走下去。可随即她发觉自己迷了路。她绊在一张椅子上，刚稳住，又绊在另一张上。接着一张桌子挡住了她的去路，她急忙一转身，又撞在了一张沙发的背上。她再一转身，看见炉火那一线微光出现在了她所以为的反方向。在那样瞎摸一气之中，她一定是把方向走反了。可眼下她该往哪一边走呢？她像是被家具团团围住了。而与此同时，那一桩事实一刻比一刻更迫切、更迫近：那两个无辜而可怖的鬼魂就要出现在她面前了。

===Original===
Then she began to pray, “Lighten our darkness, O Lord,” she said to herself. But she could not remember how the prayer continued, and she had sore need of it. There was something about the perils of the night. All this time she felt about her with groping, fluttering hands. The fire-glimmer which should have been on her left was on her right again; therefore she must turn herself round again. “Lighten our darkness,” she whispered, and then aloud she repeated, “Lighten our darkness.”
She stumbled up against a screen, and could not remember the existence of any such screen. Hastily she felt beside it with blind hands, and touched something soft and velvety. Was it the sofa on which she had lain? If so, where was the head of it. It had a head and a back and feet—it was like a person, all covered with grey lichen. Then she lost her head completely. All that remained to her was to pray; she was lost, lost in this awful place, where no one came in the dark except the babies that cried. And she heard her voice rising from whisper to speech, and speech to scream. She shrieked out the holy words, she yelled them as if blaspheming as she groped among tables and chairs and the pleasant things of ordinary life which had become so terrible.

===Chinese===
于是她开始祷告：「主啊，求你照亮我们的黑暗，」她在心里默念。可她记不起底下该接什么，而她又是何等需要这祷告。下面似乎有一句是关于黑夜的种种险恶的。这一路她始终用那双摸索的、抖动的手在身前身后探着。本该在她左边的炉火微光，这会儿又到了她右边；可见她还得再把自己转上一转。「求你照亮我们的黑暗，」她低语道，接着又出声重复了一遍：「求你照亮我们的黑暗。」
她绊到了一架屏风上，而她根本记不起有这么一架屏风。她慌忙地用一双看不见的手在它旁边摸索，触到了一样又软、又像天鹅绒的东西。莫非就是她方才躺过的那张沙发？若是，那它的扶手又在哪儿呢？它有头、有靠背、有脚——它像是一个人，浑身上下披满了灰色的苔藓。于是她彻底慌了神。她所能做的只剩下祷告；她迷了路，迷失在这可怖的地方——这里，入夜之后除了啼哭的婴孩，谁也不会来。她听见自己的声音从低语到说话，从说话到尖叫。她把那些圣洁的词句尖叫出来，她像亵渎神明一般嘶喊出来，一面在那些桌子和椅子、那些已经变得如此可怖的寻常而惬意的什物之间摸索。

===Original===
Then came a sudden and an awful answer to her screamed prayer. Once more a pocket of inflammable gas in the peat on the hearth was reached by the smouldering embers, and the room started into light. She saw the evil eyes of handsome Dick, she saw the little ghostly snowflakes falling thickly outside. And she saw where she was, just opposite the door through which the terrible twins made their entrance. Then the flame went out again, and left her in blackness once more. But she had gained something, for she had her geography now. The centre of the room was bare of furniture, and one swift dart would take her to the door of the landing above the main staircase and into safety. In that gleam she had been able to see the handle of the door, bright-brassed, luminous like a star. She would go straight for it; it was but a matter of a few seconds now.
She took a long breath, partly of relief, partly to satisfy the demands of her galloping heart. But the breath was only half-taken when she was stricken once more into the immobility of nightmare.

===Chinese===
于是，对她那声嘶力竭的祷告，忽地来了一个突如其来、可怖的回答。炉床泥炭里又一团可燃气体，被那将熄的余烬引燃，整间屋子陡然一亮。她看见了俊俏的迪克那双阴鸷的眼，她看见外面大片大片幽灵似的雪花纷纷落下。她也看清了自己身在何处——正对着那两个可怖双胞胎现身的那扇门。随即火光又熄了，把她重新留在了漆黑里。可她已经得到了一点东西，因为她已弄清了自己所处的方位。屋子中央没有家具，只要一个箭步，她便能冲到主楼梯顶楼梯口的那扇门前，逃入安全之地。在那一线闪光里，她已能看见那扇门的把手——擦得锃亮的黄铜，像一颗星似的发光。她要径直朝它冲过去；如今不过是几秒钟的事了。
她深深地吸了一口气，一半是出于如释重负，一半是为了安抚她那狂奔的心。可这口气才吸到一半，她便又一下子被击入了梦魇般的不能动弹。

===Original===
There came a little whisper, it was no more than that, from the door opposite which she stood, and through which the twin-babies entered. It was not quite dark outside it, for she could see that the door was opening. And there stood in the opening two little white figures, side by side. They came towards her slowly, shufflingly. She could not see face or form at all distinctly, but the two little white figures were advancing. She knew them to be the ghosts of terror, innocent of the awful doom they were bound to bring, even as she was innocent. With the inconceivable rapidity of thought, she made up her mind what to do. She had not hurt them or laughed at them, and they, they were but babies when the wicked and bloody deed had sent them to their burning death. Surely the spirits of these children would not be inaccessible to the cry of one who was of the same blood as they, who had committed no fault that merited the doom they brought. If she entreated them they might have mercy, they might forebear to bring the curse on her, they might allow her to pass out of the place without blight, without the sentence of death, or the shadow of things worse than death upon her.
It was but for the space of a moment that she hesitated, then she sank down on to her knees, and stretched out her hands towards them.
“Oh, my dears,” she said, “I only fell asleep. I have done no more wrong than that—”

===Chinese===
从她对面的那扇门——那两个孪生婴孩进来的那扇门——传来一声低语，仅仅是一声低语罢了。门外并非全黑，因为她能看见那扇门正在打开。门口站着两个白色的小小身影，并肩而立。他们慢慢地、拖着脚朝她走来。他们的脸和身形她一点也看不清，可那两个白色的小小身影确确实实在朝她逼近。她知道他们便是恐惧的鬼魂，对他们必带来的可怖厄运一无所知，正如她自己一样无辜。她以心思之快那种不可思议的速度，拿定了主意要怎么做。她不曾伤害过他们，也不曾嗤笑过他们；而他们，当那桩恶毒血腥的罪行把他们送去那场炽烈的死时，他们不过是婴孩。这两个孩子的亡灵，总不至于对一个与他们血脉相同、又未犯任何该当他们所带来的厄运之罪的人的呼告充耳不闻吧。倘若她恳求他们，他们或许会大发慈悲；或许会忍住不把那诅咒加在她身上；或许会容她从这地方安然离去，不沾灾殃，不受死判，也不致罩上比死更可怕之事的阴影。
她只犹豫了那么一刹那，便双膝跪倒，朝他们伸出双手。
「哦，我的小可怜们，」她说，「我不过是睡着了。我做的错事，不过如此——」

===Original===
She paused a moment, and her tender girl’s heart thought no more of herself, but only of them, those little innocent spirits on whom so awful a doom was laid, that they should bring death where other children bring laughter, and doom for delight. But all those who had seen them before had dreaded and feared them, or had mocked at them.
Then, as the enlightenment of pity dawned on her, her fear fell from her like the wrinkled sheath that holds the sweet folded buds of Spring.
“Dears, I am so sorry for you,” she said. “It is not your fault that you must bring me what you must bring, but I am not afraid any longer. I am only sorry for you. God bless you, you poor darlings.”
She raised her head and looked at them. Though it was so dark, she could now see their faces, though all was dim and wavering, like the light of pale flames shaken by a draught. But the faces were not miserable or fierce—they smiled at her with shy little baby smiles. And as she looked they grew faint, fading slowly away like wreaths of vapour in frosty air.

===Chinese===
她顿了一顿，她那温柔的少女之心便不再想到自己，只想到他们——想到那两个无辜的小小亡灵，他们背负着如此可怖的一桩厄运：别的孩子到哪儿，便把欢笑带到哪儿，他们却要把死亡带去，把厄运当作欢愉。然而在他们之前，凡瞧见过他们的人，无不恐惧惊惶，或是对他们嗤笑嘲弄。
继而，当怜悯的觉悟在她心里升起，她的恐惧便从她身上褪落了，犹如包着春日芬芳含苞的、皱缩的苞衣从枝头褪落一般。
「小可怜们，我真为你们难过，」她说，「你们不得不带给我的东西，那不是你们的错，可我已不再害怕了。我只是为你们难过。愿上帝保佑你们，你们这两个可怜的小宝贝。」
她抬起头来看着他们。尽管天色那么黑，她如今却能看见他们的脸了——虽然一切都是朦胧而摇曳的，仿佛一阵穿堂风吹得那苍白的火苗摇曳不定。然而那两张脸既不愁苦，也不凶恶——他们朝她微笑着，怯生生地、像婴孩那样地笑。她望着望着，他们便渐渐淡去，像霜天里的几缕水汽，慢慢地消散了。

===Original===
Madge did not at once move when they had vanished, for instead of fear there was wrapped round her a wonderful sense of peace, so happy and serene that she would not willingly stir, and so perhaps disturb it. But before long she got up, and feeling her way, but without any sense of nightmare pressing her on, or frenzy of fear to spur her, she went out of the long gallery, to find Blanche just coming upstairs whistling and swinging her skates.
“How’s the leg, dear,” she asked. “You’re not limping any more.”
Till that moment Madge had not thought of it.
“I think it must be all right,” she said, “I had forgotten it anyhow. Blanche, dear, you won’t be frightened for me, will you, but—but I have seen the twins.”
For a moment Blanche’s face whitened with terror.
“What?” she said in a whisper.
“Yes, I saw them just now. But they were kind, they smiled at me, and I was so sorry for them. And somehow I am sure I have nothing to fear.”

===Chinese===
那两个身影消失之后，玛奇并没有马上动弹，因为此时裹住她的，不再是恐惧，而是一股奇异的安宁之感——那般幸福，那般恬静，她竟不愿轻易挪动，生怕扰动了它。可没过多久，她还是站起身来，摸索着走出去——既没有梦魇在身后催逼，也没有恐惧的狂乱在鞭策——她出了长廊，便迎面看见布兰奇正吹着口哨、把冰鞋甩得晃晃悠悠地上楼来。
「腿怎么样啦，亲爱的？」她问，「你不瘸了。」
直到那一刻，玛奇才头一回想起这条腿来。
「我想一定是不碍事了，」她说，「我反正已经把它忘了。布兰奇，亲爱的，你不会为我害怕的，是吗？不过——不过我已经看见那对双胞胎了。」
一时之间，布兰奇的脸唰地白了。
「什么？」她低声说。
「是的，我刚才看见了他们。可他们很和善，他们对我笑，我也为他们难过极了。而且不知怎的，我确信我没什么好怕的。」

===Original===
It seems that Madge was right, for nothing untoward has come to her. Something, her attitude to them, we must suppose, her pity, her sympathy, touched and dissolved and annihilated the curse. Indeed, I was at Church Peveril only last week, arriving there after dark. Just as I passed the gallery door, Blanche came out.
“Ah, there you are,” she said, “I’ve just been seeing the twins. They looked too sweet and stopped nearly ten minutes. Let us have tea at once.”

===Chinese===
看来玛奇是对的，因为并没有任何不祥之事降临到她头上。必是有什么东西——我们只能推测，是她待他们的态度，是她的怜悯，她的同情——触动、消释、并且彻底瓦解了那道诅咒。事实上，我不过上星期才到过查奇-佩弗里尔，到时天已经黑了。我正打长廊门口经过，布兰奇恰好从里头出来。
「啊，你来了，」她说，「我刚才一直在看那对双胞胎。他们看着太惹人爱了，停了差不多有十分钟呢。咱们这就喝茶去吧。」

## In the Tube / 在地铁隧道中

===Original===
“It’s a convention,” said Anthony Carling cheerfully, “and not a very convincing one. Time, indeed! There’s no such thing as Time really; it has no actual existence. Time is nothing more than an infinitesimal point in eternity, just as space is an infinitesimal point in infinity. At the most, Time is a sort of tunnel through which we are accustomed to believe that we are travelling. There’s a roar in our ears and a darkness in our eyes which makes it seem real to us. But before we came into the tunnel we existed forever in an infinite sunlight, and after we have got through it we shall exist in an infinite sunlight again. So why should we bother ourselves about the confusion and noise and darkness which only encompass us for a moment?”

For a firm-rooted believer in such immeasurable ideas as these, which he punctuated with brisk application of the poker to the brave sparkle and glow of the fire, Anthony has a very pleasant appreciation of the measurable and the finite, and nobody with whom I have acquaintance has so keen a zest for life and its enjoyments as he. He had given us this evening an admirable dinner, had passed round a port beyond praise, and had illuminated the jolly hours with the light of his infectious optimism. Now the small company had melted away, and I was left with him over the fire in his study. Outside the tattoo of wind-driven sleet was audible on the windowpanes, over-scoring now and again the flap of the flames on the open hearth, and the thought of the chilly blasts and the snow-covered pavement in Brompton Square, across which, to skidding taxicabs, the last of his other guests had scurried, made my position, resident here till tomorrow morning, the more delicately delightful. Above all there was this stimulating and suggestive companion, who, whether he talked of the great abstractions which were so intensely real and practical to him, or of the very remarkable experiences which he had encountered among these conventions of time and space, was equally fascinating to the listener.

===Chinese===
「这是一种约定俗成，」安东尼·卡林（Anthony Carling）轻快地说道，「而且不很有说服力。时间，哼！时间这东西其实根本不存在，它没有任何真实的存在。时间无非是永恒之中一个无穷小的点，正如空间无非是无穷之中一个无穷小的点罢了。至多，时间是一条隧道，我们习惯相信自己正穿行其间。耳畔那一阵轰鸣、眼前那一片黑暗，让它在我们感觉中显得真实。可在我们进入这条隧道之前，我们曾永远存在于一片无尽的日光里；待我们穿过它，我们又将再度存在于一片无尽的日光之中。既然如此，那仅在片刻间包围着我们的纷乱、喧嚣与黑暗，我们又何必为它自寻烦恼？」

对于这般不可度量的念头——他一边说着，一边利落地用拨火棍敲打着炉中那片明亮欢腾的火光——安东尼可谓是一个根深蒂固的信徒；可与此同时，他对那可度量、有穷尽的事物，又有着极令人愉快的高雅鉴赏，而且在我所认识的人里，再没有谁像他那样对生命与生之乐趣怀有如此热烈的兴味。这天傍晚，他招待了我们一顿无可挑剔的晚餐，传了一圈无可赞誉的波特酒，又以他那极富感染力的乐观之光，照亮了这一段快活的时光。眼下这一小群人已四散而去，只余下我和他对着他书房里的炉火而坐。窗外，风卷着雨夹雪敲击玻璃的笃笃声清晰可闻，时不时盖过敞开的炉床上火舌拍打的声响；布朗普顿广场（Brompton Square）上寒风凛冽、人行道积满白雪——他其余的客人最后便是在那片雪地上，跌跌滑滑地奔向出租车的——这么一想，我在此借宿至明晨的境遇，便更添了一层精微的惬意。更何况还有这样一位引人入胜、发人深思的同伴；无论他是谈论那些在他心中异常真切而切实的宏大抽象，还是讲述他在这时间与空间的种种俗约之中所遭遇的种种非凡经历，对听者而言都同样迷人。

===Original===
“I adore life,” he said. “I find it the most entrancing plaything. It’s a delightful game, and, as you know very well, the only conceivable way to play a game is to treat it extremely seriously. If you say to yourself, ‘It’s only a game,’ you cease to take the slightest interest in it. You have to know that it’s only a game, and behave as if it was the one object of existence. I should like it to go on for many years yet. But all the time one has to be living on the true plane as well, which is eternity and infinity. If you come to think of it, the one thing which the human mind cannot grasp is the finite, not the infinite, the temporary, not the eternal.”

“That sounds rather paradoxical,” said I.

“Only because you’ve made a habit of thinking about things that seem bounded and limited. Look it in the face for a minute. Try to imagine finite Time and Space, and you find you can’t. Go back a million years, and multiply that million of years by another million, and you find that you can’t conceive of a beginning. What happened before that beginning? Another beginning and another beginning? And before that? Look at it like that, and you find that the only solution comprehensible to you is the existence of an eternity, something that never began and will never end. It’s the same about space. Project yourself to the farthest star, and what comes beyond that? Emptiness? Go on through the emptiness, and you can’t imagine it being finite and having an end. It must needs go on forever: that’s the only thing you can understand. There’s no such thing as before or after, or beginning or end, and what a comfort that is! I should fidget myself to death if there wasn’t the huge soft cushion of eternity to lean one’s head against. Some people say—I believe I’ve heard you say it yourself—that the idea of eternity is so tiring; you feel that you want to stop. But that’s because you are thinking of eternity in terms of Time, and mumbling in your brain, ‘And after that, and after that?’ Don’t you grasp the idea that in eternity there isn’t any ‘after,’ any more than there is any ‘before’? It’s all one. Eternity isn’t a quantity: it’s a quality.”

===Chinese===
「我热爱生命，」他说，「我觉得它是最迷人的玩物。它是一场令人愉悦的游戏，而你也十分清楚，要玩一场游戏，唯一可以想见的玩法，就是极其认真地对待它。你若对自己说，『不过是一场游戏罢了』，便再也不会对它有丝毫兴致。你既要明白它不过是一场游戏，又要行事如同它是生存的唯一目的。我倒愿意它再延续许多年。可与此同时，人还要活在真正的层面上，那便是永恒与无穷。你仔细想想便会发现，人心所无法把握的，恰恰是有穷，而非无穷；是短暂，而非永恒。」

「这话听起来未免自相矛盾。」我说。

「那只不过是因为你已养成了思考那些看似有界有限之物的习惯。你且正眼瞧它片刻。试着去想象有穷的时间与空间，你会发现你做不到。往回推一百万年，再把这一百万年再乘上一百万，你会发现你仍构想不出一个开端。在那个开端之前又发生了什么？又一个开端、又一个开端？在那之前呢？这么一看，你就会发现，你能理解的唯一答案，便是永恒的存在——某种从未开始、也永远不会终结的东西。空间也是一样。你把自己投射到最远的星辰，那之外又是什么？空无？你穿过那片空无继续走下去，却无法想象它是有穷的、有个尽头。它非得永远延续下去不可：这是你唯一能理解的事。根本就没有所谓的前与后，也没有所谓的始与终，这是何等的慰藉！倘若没有永恒这巨大柔软的靠垫供我把头倚靠，我一定会坐立不安至死。有些人说——我相信我曾亲耳听你说过——永恒这个念头叫人疲惫不堪；你会觉得自己想要停下。可那是因为你是在用时间来衡量永恒，在脑子里咕哝着『然后呢，然后呢？』。你难道不明白，在永恒里压根儿就没有什么『然后』，正如没有什么『之前』？一切都是一。永恒不是一个量：它是一种质。」

===Original===
Sometimes, when Anthony talks in this manner, I seem to get a glimpse of that which to his mind is so transparently clear and solidly real, at other times (not having a brain that readily envisages abstractions) I feel as though he was pushing me over a precipice, and my intellectual faculties grasp wildly at anything tangible or comprehensible. This was the case now, and I hastily interrupted.

“But there is a ‘before’ and ‘after,’” I said. “A few hours ago you gave us an admirable dinner, and after that—yes, after—we played bridge. And now you are going to explain things a little more clearly to me, and after that I shall go to bed—”

He laughed.

“You shall do exactly as you like,” he said, “and you shan’t be a slave to Time either tonight or tomorrow morning. We won’t even mention an hour for breakfast, but you shall have it in eternity whenever you awake. And as I see it is not midnight yet, we’ll slip the bonds of Time, and talk quite infinitely. I will stop the clock, if that will assist you in getting rid of your illusion, and then I’ll tell you a story, which to my mind, shows how unreal so-called realities are; or, at any rate, how fallacious are our senses as judges of what is real and what is not.”

“Something occult, something spookish?” I asked, pricking up my ears, for Anthony has the strangest clairvoyances and visions of things unseen by the normal eye.

“I suppose you might call some of it occult,” he said, “though there’s a certain amount of rather grim reality mixed up in it.”

“Go on; excellent mixture,” said I.

He threw a fresh log on the fire.

===Chinese===
安东尼这般侃侃而谈时，我有时似乎能隐约窥见一点那在他心中如此澄澈明晰、如此坚实真切的东西；可另一些时候（我的脑子并不擅长观想抽象之物），我又觉得他仿佛在把我往悬崖下推，我的理智拼命去抓任何具体可感、可以理解的东西。此刻正是后一种情形，于是我心急地打断了他。

「可毕竟是有『之前』和『之后』的，」我说，「几小时前你还招待了我们一顿无可挑剔的晚餐，之后——是的，之后——我们打了桥牌。眼下你正要给我把事情解释得更清楚一些，再之后我就要上床睡觉——」

他笑了起来。

「你想怎样就怎样，」他说，「今夜也好，明早也好，你都大可不做时间的奴隶。我们连早餐的钟点都不必提，你什么时候醒来，就在永恒里什么时候用早餐。依我看，此刻还不到午夜，我们索性挣脱时间的桎梏，无拘无束地谈谈。我把那座钟停了，若这能助你摆脱你的幻觉的话；然后我给你讲个故事——在我看来，它正好说明所谓现实之物是多么不真实；至少，也说明了我们的感官在判断何者为真、何者为假时是多么靠不住。」

「是什么玄秘的事，什么灵异的事吗？」我竖起耳朵问，因为安东尼对常人目所不见之物，有着最离奇的灵视与异象。

「我想你不妨把其中一部分称作玄秘，」他说，「尽管里头也夹杂着一定分量的、颇为严峻的现实。」

「讲下去；这搭配妙极了。」我说。

他往火里又添了一根新柴。

===Original===
“It’s a longish story,” he said. “You may stop me as soon as you’ve had enough. But there will come a point for which I claim your consideration. You, who cling to your ‘before’ and ‘after,’ has it ever occurred to you how difficult it is to say *when* an incident takes place? Say that a man commits some crime of violence, can we not, with a good deal of truth, say that he really commits that crime when he definitely plans and determines upon it, dwelling on it with gusto? The actual commission of it, I think we can reasonably argue, is the mere material sequel of his resolve: he is guilty of it when he makes that determination. When, therefore, in the term of ‘before’ and ‘after,’ does the crime truly take place? There is also in my story a further point for your consideration. For it seems certain that the spirit of a man, after the death of his body, is obliged to reenact such a crime, with a view, I suppose we may guess, to his remorse and his eventual redemption. Those who have second sight have seen such reenactments. Perhaps he may have done his deed blindly in this life; but then his spirit recommits it with its spiritual eyes open, and able to comprehend its enormity. So, shall we view the man’s original determination and the material commission of his crime only as preludes to the real commission of it, when with eyes unsealed he does it and repents of it?… That all sounds very obscure when I speak in the abstract, but I think you will see what I mean, if you follow my tale. Comfortable? Got everything you want? Here goes, then.”

He leaned back in his chair, concentrating his mind, and then spoke:

===Chinese===
「这是桩不算短的故事，」他说，「你听够了，随时可以打断我。不过其中有这么一处，我要请你留意。你这个紧抱着『之前』和『之后』不放的人，可曾想过，要说出一件事情究竟发生在何时，是多么困难？比方说一个人犯下了某种暴力的罪行，我们难道不可以相当有道理地说：当他明确地谋划、决意去做这件事，并且津津有味地反复盘算它的时候，他其实就已经真正犯下了那罪行？那罪行的实际施行，我们大可以如此论证，不过是他的决意所带来的物质后果罢了：当他下定那个决心之时，他便已经有罪了。既然如此，在所谓『之前』与『之后』的序列里，这桩罪行究竟真正发生于何时？我的故事里还有另一处，也要请你留意。因为似乎可以确定的是：一个人的灵魂在他肉身死后，不得不重新演绎这样一桩罪行——我们不妨猜测，其用意在于促其悔恨、并最终得到救赎。生有第二视力的人，曾目睹过这样的重演。也许他在这一世里是盲盲目目地做下了那件事；可他的灵魂再次犯下它时，灵眼却是睁开的，能够看清其罪孽之深重。那么，我们是否该把这个人最初的决心、以及他在物质层面上犯下的罪行，仅仅视作真正犯下它的前奏——要等到他睁着眼睛去做它、并为之忏悔之时，那真正的犯行才算完成？……我这样抽象地说出来，听上去都很晦涩，可我想，你若跟着我的故事听下去，便会明白我的意思。舒服吗？要的都齐了吗？那我就讲起来了。」

他把身子往椅背上一靠，凝神片刻，随即开了口：

===Original===
“The story that I am about to tell you,” he said, “had its beginning a month ago, when you were away in Switzerland. It reached its conclusion, so I imagine, last night. I do not, at any rate, expect to experience any more of it. Well, a month ago I was returning late on a very wet night from dining out. There was not a taxi to be had, and I hurried through the pouring rain to the tube-station at Piccadilly Circus, and thought myself very lucky to catch the last train in this direction. The carriage into which I stepped was quite empty except for one other passenger, who sat next the door immediately opposite to me. I had never, to my knowledge, seen him before, but I found my attention vividly fixed on him, as if he somehow concerned me. He was a man of middle age, in dress-clothes, and his face wore an expression of intense thought, as if in his mind he was pondering some very significant matter, and his hand which was resting on his knee clenched and unclenched itself. Suddenly he looked up and stared me in the face, and I saw there suspicion and fear, as if I had surprised him in some secret deed.

“At that moment we stopped at Dover Street, and the conductor threw open the doors, announced the station and added, ‘Change here for Hyde Park Corner and Gloucester Road.’ That was all right for me since it meant that the train would stop at Brompton Road, which was my destination. It was all right apparently, too, for my companion, for he certainly did not get out, and after a moment’s stop, during which no one else got in, we went on. I saw him, I must insist, after the doors were closed and the train had started. But when I looked again, as we rattled on, I saw that there was no one there. I was quite alone in the carriage.

“Now you may think that I had had one of those swift momentary dreams which flash in and out of the mind in the space of a second, but I did not believe it was so myself, for I felt that I had experienced some sort of premonition or clairvoyant vision. A man, the semblance of whom, astral body or whatever you may choose to call it, I had just seen, would sometime sit in that seat opposite to me, pondering and planning.”

===Chinese===
「我接下来要给你讲的这个故事，」他说，「始于一个月前，也就是你去瑞士那阵子。而它——我这么猜想——是在昨夜画上了句点。至少，我不指望还会再经历它的任何后续。呃，一个月前，有一个雨夜，我外出赴宴，归来时已经很晚。一辆出租车也叫不到，我便冒着瓢泼大雨一路赶到皮卡迪利广场（Piccadilly Circus）的地铁站，心里还觉得自己运气真好，竟赶上了这个方向上的末班车。我踏进的那节车厢空空荡荡，除了另有一名乘客，正坐在我正对面紧挨车门的位置。据我所知，我从没见过他，可我发觉自己的注意力竟活生生地落在他身上，仿佛他不知怎地与我有关。他是个中年人，穿着礼服，脸上神情凝重深思，仿佛脑子里正盘算着某件极要紧的事，搁在膝盖上的那只手不住地握紧又松开。突然间他抬起头，直直地盯着我的脸，我在他眼中看到了疑虑与惧色，仿佛我撞破了他什么隐秘的勾当。

「就在那一刻，车在多佛街（Dover Street）停下，列车员把车门一齐拉开，报了站名，又补了一句：『在此换乘海德公园角（Hyde Park Corner）与格洛斯特路（Gloucester Road）。』这于我正合适，因为这就意味着车会在布朗普顿路（Brompton Road）停——那正是我要去的地方。这显然对我的同伴也合适，因为他确实没有下车；停车片刻之间并无他人上来，于是车又开了。我必须强调：在车门关上、列车启动之后，我仍看见他在那里。可是，当列车咯咯前行、我再度望去时，却看见那里已空无一人。整节车厢里只剩我一个。

「你也许会觉得，我只不过是做了那种倏忽来去的梦——一秒之内便在脑中一闪而过；可我自己并不以为然，因为我感到自己所经历的，是某种预兆，或说是某种天眼的灵视。一个男子——我方才所见的那个，其形相，无论你称之为星质体（astral body）还是别的什么——总有一天会真真切切地坐在我对面那个位子上，凝神盘算着什么。」

===Original===
“But why?” I asked. “Why should it have been the astral body of a living man which you thought you had seen? Why not the ghost of a dead one?”

“Because of my own sensations. The sight of the spirit of someone dead, which has occurred to me two or three times in my life, has always been accompanied by a physical shrinking and fear, and by the sensation of cold and of loneliness. I believed, at any rate, that I had seen a phantom of the living, and that impression was confirmed, I might say proved, the next day. For I met the man himself. And the next night, as you shall hear, I met the phantom again. We will take them in order.

“I was lunching, then, the next day with my neighbour Mrs. Stanley: there was a small party, and when I arrived we waited but for the final guest. He entered while I was talking to some friend, and presently at my elbow I heard Mrs. Stanley’s voice—

“‘Let me introduce you to Sir Henry Payle,’ she said.

“I turned and saw my vis-à-vis of the night before. It was quite unmistakably he, and as we shook hands he looked at me I thought with vague and puzzled recognition.

“‘Haven’t we met before, Mr. Carling?’ he said. ‘I seem to recollect—’

“For the moment I forgot the strange manner of his disappearance from the carriage, and thought that it had been the man himself whom I had seen last night.

“‘Surely, and not so long ago,’ I said. ‘For we sat opposite each other in the last tube-train from Piccadilly Circus yesterday night.’

“He still looked at me, frowning, puzzled, and shook his head.

“‘That can hardly be,’ he said. ‘I only came up from the country this morning.’

“Now this interested me profoundly, for the astral body, we are told, abides in some half-conscious region of the mind or spirit, and has recollections of what has happened to it, which it can convey only very vaguely and dimly to the conscious mind. All lunchtime I could see his eyes again and again directed to me with the same puzzled and perplexed air, and as I was taking my departure he came up to me.

“‘I shall recollect some day,’ he said, ‘where we met before, and I hope we may meet again. Was it not—?’—and he stopped. ‘No: it has gone from me,’ he added.”

===Chinese===
「可为什么呢？」我问，「你所见的，为什么一定是生者的星质体，而不是死者的鬼魂呢？」

「凭我自己的感觉。我一生中有过两三次看见死者亡魂的经历，每一次都伴随着身体的瑟缩与恐惧，伴随着一种寒冷与孤寂之感。而我至少相信，自己所见到的是一个生者的幻影；这个印象在第二天便得到了证实——我甚至可以说是得到了证明。因为我遇见了他本人。而第二夜，你接着便会听见，我又遇见了那幻影。我们一件一件按顺序说。

「那么，第二天我是在邻人斯坦利夫人（Mrs. Stanley）家吃午饭：那是个小小的聚会，我到时只等最后一位客人。他进门时我正和某位朋友说着话，不一会儿，我耳畔便响起了斯坦利夫人的声音——

「『让我给您介绍一下亨利·佩尔爵士（Sir Henry Payle），』她说。

「我一转身，便看见了昨夜坐在对面的人。千真万确就是他，我们握手时，我觉得他望着我的目光里，带着一种模糊而困惑的相认之色。

「『我们从前是不是见过，卡林先生？』他说，『我似乎记得——』

「我一时忘了他在车厢中消失得何等古怪，还以为昨夜我所见的便是他本人。

「『当然见过，而且还不算太久之前，』我说，『因为昨晚从皮卡迪利广场搭末班地铁时，我们俩正坐对面。』

「他仍旧望着我，皱着眉，一脸困惑，摇了摇头。

「『那不大可能，』他说，『我今天早上才从乡下上来。』

「这话叫我大感兴趣，因为我们听说，星质体栖息于心智或灵魂中某个半明半昧的区域，对发生在自己身上的事存有记忆，却只能极模糊、极隐约地传达给自觉的意识。整个午餐期间，我都不时看见他一次又一次地以同样困惑、迷惘的神情望向我；待我要告辞时，他走了过来。

「『总有一天我会记起来的，』他说，『我们从前在哪儿见过，我也希望我们能再见。是不是在——？』——他顿住了。『不：我想不起来了，』他又道。」

===Original===
The log that Anthony had thrown on the fire was burning bravely now, and its high-flickering flame lit up his face.

“Now, I don’t know whether you believe in coincidences as chance things,” he said, “but if you do, get rid of the notion. Or if you can’t at once, call it a coincidence that that very night I again caught the last train on the tube going westwards. This time, so far from my being a solitary passenger, there was a considerable crowd waiting at Dover Street, where I entered, and just as the noise of the approaching train began to reverberate in the tunnel I caught sight of Sir Henry Payle standing near the opening from which the train would presently emerge, apart from the rest of the crowd. And I thought to myself how odd it was that I should have seen the phantom of him at this very hour last night and the man himself now, and I began walking towards him with the idea of saying, ‘Anyhow, it is in the tube that we meet tonight.’… And then a terrible and awful thing happened. Just as the train emerged from the tunnel he jumped down on to the line in front of it, and the train swept along over him up the platform.

“For a moment I was stricken with horror at the sight, and I remember covering my eyes against the dreadful tragedy. But then I perceived that, though it had taken place in full sight of those who were waiting, no one seemed to have seen it except myself. The driver, looking out from his window, had not applied his brakes, there was no jolt from the advancing train, no scream, no cry, and the rest of the passengers began boarding the train with perfect nonchalance. I must have staggered, for I felt sick and faint with what I had seen, and some kindly soul put his arm round me and supported me into the train. He was a doctor, he told me, and asked if I was in pain, or what ailed me. I told him what I thought I had seen, and he assured me that no such accident had taken place.

“It was clear then to my own mind that I had seen the second act, so to speak, in this psychical drama, and I pondered next morning over the problem as to what I should do. Already I had glanced at the morning paper, which, as I knew would be the case, contained no mention whatever of what I had seen. The thing had certainly not happened, but I knew in myself that it would happen. The flimsy veil of Time had been withdrawn from my eyes, and I had seen into what you would call the future. In terms of Time of course it was the future, but from my point of view the thing was just as much in the past as it was in the future. It existed, and waited only for its material fulfilment. The more I thought about it, the more I saw that I could do nothing.”

===Chinese===
安东尼方才扔进炉里的那根柴，此刻已烧得旺了，高高跳动的火焰照亮了他的脸。

「这么说吧，我不知道你信不信巧合是出于偶然，」他说，「可你若信，就丢掉这个念头吧。或者，你若不能立刻丢掉，那就姑且算作一桩巧合：就在那天夜里，我又一次赶上了西行的末班地铁。这一回，我非但不是孤身一人，多佛街——也就是我上车那站——站台上还等着一大群人；而就在驶来的列车在隧道中激起的轰鸣刚刚回荡起来之时，我瞥见亨利·佩尔爵士正站在列车即将驶出的那个洞口附近，与人群隔着一段距离。我心里不禁觉得多么古怪——昨夜此时我看见了他的幻影，此刻又看见了他本人；我便朝他走去，心里想着说一句：『不管怎么说，今晚我们是在地铁里相见了。』……紧接着便发生了一桩可怖而骇人的事。列车刚刚驶出隧道，他便跳了下去，落到它前方的铁轨上，列车便呼啸着从他身上碾过，一路开上站台。

「霎时间，我被那景象吓住了，我记得自己捂住了眼睛，不忍看那可怖的惨剧。可随即我便发觉：虽然这事是在所有候车者众目睽睽之下发生的，除了我之外，却似乎再没有人看见。司机从车窗探出头来看，并未踩下刹车；前进的列车没有一丝颠簸，没有尖叫，也没有呼喊；其余的乘客全若无其事地开始上车。我一定是踉跄了一下，因为我所见的叫我又恶心又发晕，有个好心人伸出胳膊揽住我，把我扶进了车厢。他说他是个医生，问我是哪儿疼，还是怎么了。我把自以为看见的事告诉了他，他向我保证，根本不曾发生过这样的事故。

「于是我心中便清楚了：我所见的，可以说是这出灵异戏剧的第二幕。第二天一早，我苦苦思索着自己该怎么做。我已经瞄了一眼晨报，不出我所料，上面对我所见之事只字未提。那件事确实没有发生，可我心中明白它必将发生。时间那层薄薄的帷幕已从我眼前揭开，我窥见了你所称的未来。用时间的说法，它当然是未来；可在我看来，它既在未来，也同样在过去。它已存在，只待一个物质层面的成全罢了。我越想，越发觉自己无能为力。」

===Original===
I interrupted his narrative.

“You did nothing?” I exclaimed. “Surely you might have taken some step in order to try to avert the tragedy.”

He shook his head.

“What step precisely?” he said. “Was I to go to Sir Henry and tell him that once more I had seen him in the tube in the act of committing suicide? Look at it like this. Either what I had seen was pure illusion, pure imagination, in which case it had no existence or significance at all, or it was actual and real, and essentially it had happened. Or take it, though not very logically, somewhere between the two. Say that the idea of suicide, for some cause of which I knew nothing, had occurred to him or would occur. Should I not, if that was the case, be doing a very dangerous thing, by making such a suggestion to him? Might not the fact of my telling him what I had seen put the idea into his mind, or, if it was already there, confirm it and strengthen it? ‘It’s a ticklish matter to play with souls,’ as Browning says.”

“But it seems so inhuman not to interfere in any way,” said I, “not to make any attempt.”

“What interference?” asked he. “What attempt?”

The human instinct in me still seemed to cry aloud at the thought of doing nothing to avert such a tragedy, but it seemed to be beating itself against something austere and inexorable. And cudgel my brain as I would, I could not combat the sense of what he had said. I had no answer for him, and he went on.

“You must recollect, too,” he said, “that I believed then and believe now that the thing had happened. The cause of it, whatever that was, had begun to work, and the effect, in this material sphere, was inevitable. That is what I alluded to when, at the beginning of my story, I asked you to consider how difficult it was to say when an action took place. You still hold that this particular action, this suicide of Sir Henry, had not yet taken place, because he had not yet thrown himself under the advancing train. To me that seems a materialistic view. I hold that in all but the endorsement of it, so to speak, it had taken place. I fancy that Sir Henry, for instance, now free from the material dusks, knows that himself.”

===Chinese===
我打断了他的讲述。

「你竟什么也没做？」我失声道，「你总该可以采取点措施，设法避免这场惨剧吧。」

他摇了摇头。

「究竟采取什么措施呢？」他说，「难道要我去找亨利爵士，告诉他我又一次看见他在地铁里自杀吗？你且这么想：要么我所见的是纯粹的幻觉、纯粹的想象，既然如此，它就全无存在、全无意义可言；要么它是确有其事、真实不虚的，那么本质上它已经发生了。或者，虽不甚合逻辑，姑且取两者之间的某一点来说：自杀的念头，出于某种我所不知道的缘由，已经在他心头浮现，或将要浮现。若当真如此，我去向他这般提一句，岂不是在做一桩极其危险的事？我把我所见告诉了他，会不会反倒把这个念头植入了他的心里，或者，那念头若已存在，反倒坐实了它、加固了它？『玩弄灵魂，是桩棘手的事，』正如勃朗宁（Browning）所言。」

「可完全不加干预，不作任何尝试，似乎太不近人情了。」我说。

「怎么个干预法？」他问，「什么尝试？」

我身上的人性本能仍似乎在大声呼喊着：对这样一桩惨剧袖手旁观，岂有此理；可这呼声却仿佛撞在某种严峻而不容通融的东西上。我绞尽脑汁，也无法驳倒他那番话中的道理。我无言以对，他便继续说了下去。

「你还得记得，」他说，「那时我相信，如今也仍相信，那件事已经发生了。它的成因，无论是什么，已经起了作用，而其在这个物质层面上的后果，是不可避免的。这正是我在故事开头，请你留意的那一点——要说出一个行为究竟发生于何时，是多么困难。你仍旧认为，这桩特定的行为，即亨利爵士的自杀，尚未发生，因为他尚未扑到驶来的列车之下。在我看来，这是一种唯物之见。我则认为，除了——可以这么说——它的盖印确认之外，它已经发生了。我甚至想，亨利爵士本人，如今既已摆脱了物质上的种种阴翳，自己也是明白这一点的。」

===Original===
Exactly as he spoke there swept through the warm lit room a current of ice-cold air, ruffling my hair as it passed me, and making the wood flames on the hearth to dwindle and flare. I looked round to see if the door at my back had opened, but nothing stirred there, and over the closed window the curtains were fully drawn. As it reached Anthony, he sat up quickly in his chair and directed his glance this way and that about the room.

“Did you feel that?” he asked.

“Yes: a sudden draught,” I said. “Ice-cold.”

“Anything else?” he asked. “Any other sensation?”

I paused before I answered, for at the moment there occurred to me Anthony’s differentiation of the effects produced on the beholder by a phantasm of the living and the apparition of the dead. It was the latter which accurately described my sensations now, a certain physical shrinking, a fear, a feeling of desolation. But yet I had seen nothing. “I felt rather creepy,” I said.

As I spoke I drew my chair rather closer to the fire, and sent a swift and, I confess, a somewhat apprehensive scrutiny round the walls of the brightly lit room. I noticed at the same time that Anthony was peering across to the chimneypiece, on which, just below a sconce holding two electric lights, stood the clock which at the beginning of our talk he had offered to stop. The hands I noticed pointed to twenty-five minutes to one.

“But you saw nothing?” he asked.

“Nothing whatever,” I said. “Why should I? What was there to see? Or did you—”

“I don’t think so,” he said.

Somehow this answer got on my nerves, for the queer feeling which had accompanied that cold current of air had not left me. If anything it had become more acute.

“But surely you know whether you saw anything or not?” I said.

“One can’t always be certain,” said he. “I say that I don’t think I saw anything. But I’m not sure, either, whether the story I am telling you was quite concluded last night. I think there may be a further incident. If you prefer it, I will leave the rest of it, as far as I know it, unfinished till tomorrow morning, and you can go off to bed now.”

His complete calmness and tranquillity reassured me.

“But why should I do that?” I asked.

Again he looked round on the bright walls.

“Well, I think something entered the room just now,” he said, “and it may develop. If you don’t like the notion, you had better go. Of course there’s nothing to be alarmed at; whatever it is, it can’t hurt us. But it is close on the hour when on two successive nights I saw what I have already told you, and an apparition usually occurs at the same time. Why that is so, I cannot say, but certainly it looks as if a spirit that is earthbound is still subject to certain conventions, the conventions of time for instance. I think that personally I shall see something before long, but most likely you won’t. You’re not such a sufferer as I from these—these delusions—”

I was frightened and knew it, but I was also intensely interested, and some perverse pride wriggled within me at his last words. Why, so I asked myself, shouldn’t I see whatever was to be seen?…

===Chinese===
恰在他说话的当儿，一股冰冷刺骨的气流掠过了这间温暖明亮的房间，从我身边经过时拂乱了我的头发，又使炉中的柴火一时缩小、一时猛燃。我回头看看身后的门是否开了，那里却纹丝不动；而紧闭的窗上窗帘已严严地拉拢。气流到了安东尼跟前时，他猛地在椅子上坐直了身子，目光朝房间四处扫视。

「你感觉到了吗？」他问。

「感觉到了：一阵突如其来的穿堂风，」我说，「冰冷冰冷的。」

「还有别的吗？」他问，「还有别的感觉吗？」

我答话前犹豫了一下，因为此时我想起了安东尼所作的那个区分——生者的幻影与死者的亡魂，在目击者身上所引起的效果各不相同。此刻我所感到的，正是后者那一种：某种身体的瑟缩、一种恐惧、一种凄凉孤寂之感。可我又分明什么也没看见。「我觉得有点发毛。」我说。

说着我把椅子往炉边挪了挪，同时飞快地、我承认也带着几分惴惴不安地，把那间灯光明亮的房间的四壁扫视了一遍。与此同时我留意到，安东尼正凝目望向壁炉台——台上，在一对壁灯的正下方，摆着那座在我们谈话之初他曾提议要停掉的钟。我看见它的指针正指着差二十五分一点。

「可你什么也没看见？」他问。

「什么也没有，」我说，「我又怎么会看见？有什么可看的？还是说，你——」

「我想没有。」他说。

不知怎的，这个回答叫我心神不宁，因为伴随那股冷气流而来的古怪感觉并未离我而去。非但如此，反倒愈发尖锐了。

「可你自己到底看见没看见，你总该清楚吧？」我说。

「人并不总能确定，」他说，「我只是说我大概什么也没看见。但我也说不准，我讲给你听的这个故事，是不是昨晚便已完全收尾。我想可能还有一桩后续。你若愿意，我可以把其余我所知道的部分，留到明天早上再讲完，你现在就可以去睡。」

他那份彻底的平静与安详叫我安下了心。

「我为什么要那样做？」我问。

他又朝那明亮的四壁扫视了一眼。

「呃，我想方才有什么东西进了这间房，」他说，「而且它或许还会滋蔓。你若不喜欢这个念头，最好就走。当然，没有什么可惊慌的；无论它是什么，都伤不了我们。可眼下已快到我连续两夜看见那些我已告诉你的东西的时辰了，而亡魂的显形通常都发生在同一时刻。为何如此，我说不上来，不过看上去，一个滞留尘世的亡灵似乎仍受制于某些俗约——比方说，时间的俗约。我想，用不了多久，我自己就会看见点什么，但多半你不会。你在这类——这类错觉上——可没我受的罪多——」

我心里害怕，自己也知道；可我又同时兴致极浓，他最后那几句话在我心里勾起了一股别扭的好胜之心。为什么不呢——我暗自问自己——凡是能被看见的，我凭什么就不能也看见？……

===Original===
“I don’t want to go in the least,” I said. “I want to hear the rest of your story.”

“Where was I, then? Ah, yes: you were wondering why I didn’t do something after I saw the train move up to the platform, and I said that there was nothing to be done. If you think it over, I fancy you will agree with me.… A couple of days passed, and on the third morning I saw in the paper that there had come fulfilment to my vision. Sir Henry Payle, who had been waiting on the platform of Dover Street Station for the last train to South Kensington, had thrown himself in front of it as it came into the station. The train had been pulled up in a couple of yards, but a wheel had passed over his chest, crushing it in and instantly killing him.

“An inquest was held, and there emerged at it one of those dark stories which, on occasions like these, sometimes fall like a midnight shadow across a life that the world perhaps had thought prosperous. He had long been on bad terms with his wife, from whom he had lived apart, and it appeared that not long before this he had fallen desperately in love with another woman. The night before his suicide he had appeared very late at his wife’s house, and had a long and angry scene with her in which he entreated her to divorce him, threatening otherwise to make her life a hell to her. She refused, and in an ungovernable fit of passion he attempted to strangle her. There was a struggle, and the noise of it caused her manservant to come up, who succeeded in overmastering him. Lady Payle threatened to proceed against him for assault with the intention to murder her. With this hanging over his head, the next night, as I have already told you, he committed suicide.”

He glanced at the clock again, and I saw that the hands now pointed to ten minutes to one. The fire was beginning to burn low and the room surely was growing strangely cold.

“That’s not quite all,” said Anthony, again looking round. “Are you sure you wouldn’t prefer to hear it tomorrow?”

The mixture of shame and pride and curiosity again prevailed.

“No: tell me the rest of it at once,” I said.

Before speaking, he peered suddenly at some point behind my chair, shading his eyes. I followed his glance, and knew what he meant by saying that sometimes one could not be sure whether one saw something or not. But was that an outlined shadow that intervened between me and the wall? It was difficult to focus; I did not know whether it was near the wall or near my chair. It seemed to clear away, anyhow, as I looked more closely at it.

“You see nothing?” asked Anthony.

“No: I don’t think so,” said I. “And you?”

“I think I do,” he said, and his eyes followed something which was invisible to mine. They came to rest between him and the chimneypiece. Looking steadily there, he spoke again.

===Chinese===
「我一点儿也不想走，」我说，「我想听完你故事的其余部分。」

「那我说到哪儿了？啊，对了：你方才在纳闷，我看见列车开上站台之后为何什么也没做，而我说我什么也做不了。你若仔细想想，我想你会同意我的。……两三天过去了，第三天早上，我在报上看见，我的灵视应验了。亨利·佩尔爵士在多佛街车站站台上等候开往南肯辛顿（South Kensington）的末班车，列车进站时，他扑到了它前面。列车在两三码之内便刹住了，可一只车轮已从他胸口碾过，把胸膛压瘪了，当场便要了他的命。

「随后开了死因研讯，其间浮出了一桩黑暗的内情——这类事在这样的时候，有时会如午夜的阴影一般，投到一段世人也许向来以为是顺遂的人生之上。他与妻子早已不睦，分居已久；而据查，就在此事前不久，他死心塌地地爱上了另一个女人。自杀前夜，他深夜来到妻子的住所，与她发生了一场持久而激烈的争执，恳求她与他离婚，否则便威胁要让她的日子变成人间地狱。她拒绝了，他在一股无法遏制的暴怒之下，竟企图掐死她。两人扭打起来，闹出的动静引得她的男仆上楼，终于将他制服。佩尔夫人（Lady Payle）扬言要以意图谋杀的人身侵害罪名起诉他。此事悬在头顶，第二夜——如我方才所言——他便自杀了。」

他又看了一眼钟，我看见此刻指针已指向差十分一点。炉火渐渐低落下去，而房间里——的确——正古怪地变得愈发冷了。

「这还没完，」安东尼说着，又环顾四下，「你果真不愿意留到明天再听吗？」

羞耻、好胜，加上好奇，三者掺在一起，又一次占了上风。

「不：现在就把它讲完。」我说。

开口之前，他突然把眼睛眯起来望着椅子后方的某处，拿手搭在眼上遮着光。我顺着他的目光望去，这才明白他所谓有时人说不清自己到底看见没有，是什么意思。可那是横在我与墙壁之间的一团影子的轮廓吗？很难聚焦；我分辨不清它是在墙根处，还是在我椅子边。反正，我盯着它仔细看时，它似乎便散去了。

「你什么也没看见？」安东尼问。

「没有：我想没有。」我说，「你呢？」

「我想我看见了，」他说着，两眼追随某个我所看不见的东西。那目光最终停在他与壁炉台之间的某处。他凝望着那里，又开了口：

===Original===
“All this happened some weeks ago,” he said, “when you were out in Switzerland, and since then, up till last night, I saw nothing further. But all the time I was expecting something further. I felt that, as far as I was concerned, it was not all over yet, and last night, with the intention of assisting any communication to come through to me from—from beyond, I went into the Dover Street tube-station at a few minutes before one o’clock, the hour at which both the assault and the suicide had taken place. The platform when I arrived on it was absolutely empty, or appeared to be so, but presently, just as I began to hear the roar of the approaching train, I saw there was the figure of a man standing some twenty yards from me, looking into the tunnel. He had not come down with me in the lift, and the moment before he had not been there. He began moving towards me, and then I saw who it was, and I felt a stir of wind icy-cold coming towards me as he approached. It was not the draught that heralds the approach of a train, for it came from the opposite direction. He came close up to me, and I saw there was recognition in his eyes. He raised his face towards me and I saw his lips move, but, perhaps in the increasing noise from the tunnel, I heard nothing come from them. He put out his hand, as if entreating me to do something, and with a cowardice from which I cannot forgive myself, I shrank from him, for I knew, by the sign that I have told you, that this was one from the dead, and my flesh quaked before him, drowning for the moment all pity and all desire to help him, if that was possible. Certainly he had something which he wanted of me, but I recoiled from him. And by now the train was emerging from the tunnel, and next moment, with a dreadful gesture of despair, he threw himself in front of it.”

As he finished speaking he got up quickly from his chair, still looking fixedly in front of him. I saw his pupils dilate, and his mouth worked.

“It is coming,” he said. “I am to be given a chance of atoning for my cowardice. There is nothing to be afraid of: I must remember that myself.…”

As he spoke there came from the panelling above the chimneypiece one loud shattering crack, and the cold wind again circled about my head. I found myself shrinking back in my chair with my hands held in front of me as instinctively I screened myself against something which I knew was there but which I could not see. Every sense told me that there was a presence in the room other than mine and Anthony’s, and the horror of it was that I could not see it. Any vision, however terrible, would, I felt, be more tolerable than this clear certain knowledge that close to me was this invisible thing. And yet what horror might not be disclosed of the face of the dead and the crushed chest.… But all I could see, as I shuddered in this cold wind, was the familiar walls of the room, and Anthony standing in front of me stiff and firm, making, as I knew, a call on his courage. His eyes were focused on something quite close to him, and some semblance of a smile quivered on his mouth. And then he spoke again.

“Yes, I know you,” he said. “And you want something of me. Tell me, then, what it is.”

There was absolute silence, but what was silence to my ears could not have been so to his, for once or twice he nodded, and once he said, “Yes: I see. I will do it.” And with the knowledge that, even as there was someone here whom I could not see, so there was speech going on which I could not hear, this terror of the dead and of the unknown rose in me with the sense of powerlessness to move that accompanies nightmare. I could not stir, I could not speak. I could only strain my ears for the inaudible and my eyes for the unseen, while the cold wind from the very valley of the shadow of death streamed over me. It was not that the presence of death itself was terrible; it was that from its tranquillity and serene keeping there had been driven some unquiet soul unable to rest in peace for whatever ultimate awakening rouses the countless generations of those who have passed away, driven, no less, from whatever activities are theirs, back into the material world from which it should have been delivered. Never, until the gulf between the living and the dead was thus bridged, had it seemed so immense and so unnatural. It is possible that the dead may have communication with the living, and it was not that exactly that so terrified me, for such communication, as we know it, comes voluntarily from them. But here was something icy-cold and crime-laden, that was chased back from the peace that would not pacify it.

And then, most horrible of all, there came a change in these unseen conditions. Anthony was silent now, and from looking straight and fixedly in front of him, he began to glance sideways to where I sat and back again, and with that I felt that the unseen presence had turned its attention from him to me. And now, too, gradually and by awful degrees I began to see.…

===Chinese===
「这一切都发生在几周之前，」他说，「也就是你在瑞士那阵子；从那时起，直到昨夜为止，我再未见任何后续。可我心里始终在等着某种后续。我觉得，就我而言，事情还没有完。昨夜，为了便于让某种来自——来自彼岸的——信息传达给我，我在差几分一点的时候走进了多佛街地铁站——那个时辰，正是那场施暴与那场自杀所发生的钟点。我走上站台时，那里空空荡荡，或者看上去是如此；可没过多久，就在我刚开始听见驶来的列车轰鸣声之时，我看见了一个男人的身影，站在距我约莫二十码的地方，朝着隧道里张望。他并非和我一道乘电梯下来的；方才那一瞬间，他还不在那里。他开始朝我走来，我这才看清他是谁，并感到一阵冰冷的寒风随着他的逼近向我袭来。那不是预告列车将至的穿堂风，因为它是从相反的方向吹来的。他走到我跟前，我看见他眼中带着相认之色。他仰起脸对着我，我看见他嘴唇翕动，可也许是被隧道里越来越响的轰鸣所淹没，我没听见它们吐出任何声音。他伸出手来，仿佛恳求我为他做点什么；而我竟怀着一种至今无法宽恕自己的怯懦，从他面前瑟缩了开去——因为凭我所告诉你的那个征兆，我认出这是一个亡者的鬼魂，我的血肉在他面前战栗不已，一时淹没了所有的怜悯，以及一切想要帮助他的意愿——倘若那还可能的话。他分明是有求于我的，可我却从他面前退开了。而此刻列车正驶出隧道，下一刻，他做了一个绝望已极的姿态，纵身扑到了它的前面。」

他讲完这番话，便飞快地从椅子上站了起来，仍目不转睛地凝视着前方。我看见他的瞳孔放大了，嘴也在抽动。

「它来了，」他说，「我要得到一个弥补我那怯懦的机会了。没有什么可怕的：这一点我自己也须牢记。」

他说着，壁炉台上方的护墙镶板里发出一声震耳的爆裂，那股冷风又在我的头顶盘旋起来。我发觉自己正缩回椅子里，双手举在身前，本能地抵挡着某个我明知在那儿、却又看不见的东西。每一种感官都告诉我，房间里除了我和安东尼之外，还有一个别的存在；而最可怕的是，我竟看不见它。我感到，无论多么骇人的形象，都比这份清清楚楚、确凿无疑地知道有个看不见的东西近在咫尺，要更可忍受。然而，那死者的脸、那被压瘪的胸膛，一旦显形，又将泄露何等可怖的景象。……可我在这股冷风中战栗时所看见的，无非是房间里那几面熟悉的墙壁，以及 Antony——安东尼——僵硬而坚定地立在我面前，我知道，他正在向自己的勇气发出召唤。他的目光聚焦在离他很近的某处，嘴角颤动着一丝似有若无的笑意。随后他又开了口。

「是的，我认得你，」他说，「你有求于我。那么，告诉我，是什么事。」

一片绝对的寂静，可在我耳中为寂静的，于他却并非如此，因为他有一两次点了点头，还有一次说道：「是，我明白。我会去办的。」而一意识到——这里正有一个我所看不见的人，同样也正有一段我所听不见的对话在进行——这种对亡者、对未知的恐惧便伴着噩梦般无法动弹的无力感在我心头升起。我动弹不得，也做声不得。我只能竖起耳朵去捕捉那听不见的声音，瞪大双眼去寻觅那看不见的事物，而那股来自死亡阴影之谷的冷风正不断从我身上掠过。可怕的不是死亡本身的降临；而是从那宁静、安详的归宿之中，被驱出了某个不安息的灵魂——它因某种终将唤醒那无数代逝者的终极觉醒而不能安息，也同样从亡者所拥有的种种活动之中被逐出，被赶回到它本应已从中获得解脱的物质世界里来。直到生者与死者之间的鸿沟这样被架起桥梁之前，它从未显得如此辽阔、如此悖逆常理。死者也许确实能与生者相通，而叫我如此恐惧的，确切地说，并非这一点，因为据我们所知，那种相通是出诸他们自愿的。可眼前这东西冰冷彻骨、罪孽深重，是从那不肯将它安抚的安宁之中被撵了回来的。

紧接着，最最可怕的事发生了——这些看不见的情形起了变化。安东尼此刻沉默了，他的目光从笔直坚定地凝视前方，变成朝我所坐的方向斜瞟过来、又瞟回去；随着这一变化，我感到那个看不见的存在已把注意从他身上转向了我。于是，也就在这时，一点一点地，经过可怖的层层递进，我开始看见了……

===Original===
There came an outline of shadow across the chimneypiece and the panels above it. It took shape: it fashioned itself into the outline of a man. Within the shape of the shadow details began to form themselves, and I saw wavering in the air, like something concealed by haze, the semblance of a face, stricken and tragic, and burdened with such a weight of woe as no human face had ever worn. Next, the shoulders outlined themselves, and a stain livid and red spread out below them, and suddenly the vision leaped into clearness. There he stood, the chest crushed in and drowned in the red stain, from which broken ribs, like the bones of a wrecked ship, protruded. The mournful, terrible eyes were fixed on me, and it was from them, so I knew, that the bitter wind proceeded.…

Then, quick as the switching off of a lamp, the spectre vanished, and the bitter wind was still, and opposite to me stood Anthony, in a quiet, bright-lit room. There was no sense of an unseen presence any more; he and I were then alone, with an interrupted conversation still dangling between us in the warm air. I came round to that, as one comes round after an anaesthetic. It all swam into sight again, unreal at first, and gradually assuming the texture of actuality.

“You were talking to somebody, not to me,” I said. “Who was it? What was it?”

He passed the back of his hand over his forehead, which glistened in the light.

“A soul in hell,” he said.

Now it is hard ever to recall mere physical sensations, when they have passed. If you have been cold and are warmed, it is difficult to remember what cold was like: if you have been hot and have got cool, it is difficult to realise what the oppression of heat really meant. Just so, with the passing of that presence, I found myself unable to recapture the sense of the terror with which, a few moments ago only, it had invaded and inspired me.

“A soul in hell?” I said. “What are you talking about?”

He moved about the room for a minute or so, and then came and sat on the arm of my chair.

“I don’t know what you saw,” he said, “or what you felt, but there has never in all my life happened to me anything more real than what these last few minutes have brought. I have talked to a soul in the hell of remorse, which is the only possible hell. He knew, from what happened last night, that he could perhaps establish communication through me with the world he had quitted, and he sought me and found me. I am charged with a mission to a woman I have never seen, a message from the contrite.… You can guess who it is.…”

He got up with a sudden briskness.

“Let’s verify it anyhow,” he said. “He gave me the street and the number. Ah, there’s the telephone book! Would it be a coincidence merely if I found that at No. 20 in Chasemore Street, South Kensington, there lived a Lady Payle?”

He turned over the leaves of the bulky volume.

“Yes, that’s right,” he said.

===Chinese===
壁炉台及其上方的护墙镶板上掠过了一团影子的轮廓。它渐渐成形：把自己塑成了一个男人的轮廓。在这影子的形状之内，细节开始一一浮现，我看见半空中浮动着——仿佛被薄雾遮掩一般——一张脸的形相，那张脸悲苦而凄惨，负载着人间任何一张脸都不曾承受过的、那样沉重的哀痛。紧接着，双肩也勾勒了出来，肩下一片青紫发红的污渍洇散开来，骤然间，那幻象跃入了清晰。他就立在那里，胸膛被压瘪、浸没在那片红斑之中，从里面凸出几根折断的肋骨，一如沉船的骸骨。那双哀戚而可怕的眼睛直勾勾地盯着我，而我所感到的那股阴冷彻骨的风，正是从它们之中吹出来的。

随即，快如一盏灯被掐灭，那鬼影消散了，阴冷的风也止息了；我面前立着安东尼，置身于一间安静、灯火明亮的房间里。再也没有那种看不见的存在的预感了；此刻只剩他和我，之间还悬着一段被打断的话头，在温暖的空气里荡漾。我这才恍然回到这件事上来，就像一个人从麻醉中悠悠醒转。这一切又重新游进了视野，起初显得虚幻，渐渐地才披上了真实的质感。

「你在跟什么人说话，不是在跟我，」我说，「那是谁？那是什么？」

他用手背抹了一下额头，额头在灯光下闪闪发亮。

「一个地狱里的灵魂。」他说。

要重新唤起纯粹的肉体感觉，在它们过去之后，向来是困难的。你若曾经寒冷、如今已暖和，便很难记起寒冷是何滋味：你若曾经燥热、如今已凉爽，便很难真正体会燥热的憋闷是什么意思。同样地，随着那个存在的离去，我发觉自己再也无法重新捕捉到——仅仅片刻之前——它所侵入并灌输给我的那种恐惧之感了。

「一个地狱里的灵魂？」我说，「你在说什么呀？」

他在房间里来回走动了一分钟左右，然后走过来坐在我椅子的扶手上。

「我不知道你看见了什么，」他说，「也不知道你感觉到了什么，可我这辈子，还从未有过比刚刚这几分钟里所发生的更真切的事。我跟一个处在悔恨地狱里的灵魂交谈过——而悔恨，是唯一可能存在的地狱。他从昨夜发生的事上知道，他也许能借着我，与他所离开的那个世界建立起沟通，于是他寻到了我，也找到了我。我受了一个委托，要带一个口信给一位我素未谋面的女子——一个来自忏悔者的口信。……你猜得到她是谁。」

他突然利落地站起身来。

「无论如何，我们来验证一下，」他说，「他把街名和门牌号给了我。啊，电话簿在那儿！倘若我查到南肯辛顿的查斯莫街（Chasemore Street）20 号住着一位佩尔夫人（Lady Payle），那该不会只是巧合吧？」

他翻动起那本厚厚的卷册。

「是的，没错。」他说。

## Inscrutable Decrees / 难解的天命

===Original===
I had found nothing momentous in the more august pages of the *Times* that morning, and so, just because I was lazy and unwilling to embark on a host of businesses that were waiting for me, I turned to the first page and, beginning with the seventh column, pondered profoundly over “Situations Vacant,” and hoped that the “Gentlewoman fond of games,” who desired the position of governess, would find the very thing to suit her. I glanced at the notices of lectures to be delivered under the auspices of various learned societies, and was thankful that I had not got to give or to listen to any of them. I debated over “Business Opportunities”; I vainly tried to conjecture clues to mysterious “Personal” paragraphs, and, still pursuing my sideways, crab-fashion course, came to “Deaths Continued.”

There, with a shock of arrest, I saw that Sybil Rorke, widow of the late Sir Ernest Rorke, had died at Torquay, suddenly, at the age of thirty-two. It seemed strange that there should be only this bare announcement concerning a woman who at one time had been so well-known and dazzling a figure; and turning to the obituary notices, I found that my inattentive skimming had overlooked a paragraph there of appreciation and regret. She had died during her sleep, and it was announced that an inquest would be held. My laziness then had been of some use, for Archie Rorke, distant cousin but successor to Sir Ernest’s estates and title, was arriving that evening to spend a few country days with me, and I was glad to have known this before he came. How it would affect him, or whether, indeed, it would affect him at all, I had no idea.

What a mysterious affair it had been! No one, I supposed, knew the history of it except he, now that Lady Rorke was dead. If anyone knew, it should have been myself, and yet Archie, my oldest friend, whose best man I was to have been, had never opened his lips to a syllable of explanation. I knew, in fact, no whit more than the whole world knew, namely, that a year after Sir Ernest Rorke’s death the engagement of his widow to the new baronet, Sir Archibald Rorke, was made public, and that within a fortnight of the date fixed for the wedding it was laconically announced that the marriage would not take place. When, on seeing that, I rang Archie up on the telephone, I was told that he had already left London, and he wrote to me a few days later from Lincote﻿—the place in Hampshire, which he had inherited from his cousin﻿—saying that he had nothing to tell me about the breaking off of his engagement beyond the fact that it was true. The whole﻿—he had written a word and carefully erased it﻿—episode was now an excised leaf from his life.
