「任何一种波，不论其为谁，都会留下它的印痕，不是吗？你要是对这一切全然不信，我可不可以给你一间房，就安排在那位可怜的、无辜被杀的夜行者所经过的路线上？」
我站起身来。
「多谢，我待在原处就很舒服了。」我说。

## Roderick’s Story / 罗德里克的故事

===Original===
My powers of persuasion at first seemed quite ineffectual; I could not induce my friend Roderick Cardew to strike his melancholy tent in Chelsea, and (leaving it struck) steal away like the Arabs and spend this month of spring with me at my newly acquired house at Tilling to observe the spell of April’s wand making magic in the country. I seemed to have brought out all the arguments of which I was master; he had been very ill, and his doctor recommended a clearer air with as mild a climate as he could conveniently attain; he loved the great stretches of drained marshland which lay spread like a pool of verdure round the little town; he had not seen my new home which made a breach in the functions of hospitality, and he really could not be expected to object to his host, who, after all, was one of his oldest friends. Besides (to leave no stone unturned) as he regained his strength he could begin to play golf again, and it entailed, as he well remembered, a very mild exertion for him to keep me in my proper position in such a pursuit.

===Chinese===
我起初的那些劝说起先似乎全然不见效用；我说不动我的朋友罗德里克·卡杜（Roderick Cardew），让他把搭在切尔西（Chelsea）的那顶忧郁帐篷收起来，并（既已收起，便由它收着）像阿拉伯人那样悄悄溜走，与我同到我在蒂灵（Tilling）新置的宅子里度过这一个月的春光，看看四月的魔杖如何在乡间施展它的法术。我似乎已把一切我所能想到的道理都摆了出来：他大病了一场，医生嘱咐他寻一处空气更清、气候尽可能温和的地方；他素来喜爱那片排水过后一望无际的沼泽地——它像一汪翠绿的水泊似地铺展在这座小城四周；他还没有看过我的新居，这在待客之道上原是一桩缺憾；再者，他也实在挑不出东家的不是，毕竟东家是他最老的朋友之一。何况（为了不留一条路没走到）待他力气回复，他又可以重新打高尔夫了，而在这等营生里要把我压在我本该呆的下风位置，他记得清清楚楚，于他不过是极轻微的一桩操劳。

===Original===
At last there was some sign of yielding.

“Yes. I should like to see the marsh and the big sky once more,” he said.

A rather sinister interpretation of his words “once more,” made a sudden flashed signal of alarm in my mind. It was utterly fanciful, no doubt, but that had better be extinguished first.

“Once more?” I asked. “What does that mean?”

“I always say ‘once more,’ ” he said. “It’s greedy to ask for too much.”

The very fact that he fenced so ingeniously deepened my suspicion.

“That won’t do,” I said. “Tell me, Roddie.”

===Chinese===
终于，他有了几分松动的迹象。

「好吧。我倒想再去看一眼那片沼泽和那片辽阔的天空。」他说。

他这「再」字，在我心里倏地闪起了一道不祥的警号。这无疑是毫无来由的胡思乱想，可总得先把它摁下去才行。

「再？」我问，「这是什么意思？」

「我总说『再』的，」他说，「贪得无厌地要得太多，是要不得的。」

他这般巧妙地闪躲，反倒加深了我的疑心。

「这可不行，」我说，「告诉我吧，罗迪（Roddie）。」

===Original===
He was silent a moment.

“I didn’t intend to,” he said, “for there can be no use in it. But if you insist, as apparently you mean to do, I may as well give in. It’s what you think; ‘once more’ will very likely be the most. But you mustn’t fuss about it; I’m not going to. No proper person fusses about death; that’s a train which we are all sure to catch. It always waits for you.”

I have noticed that when one learns tidings of that sort, one feels, almost immediately, that one has known them a long time. I felt so now.

“Go on,” I said.

“Well, that’s about all there is. I’ve had sentence of death passed upon me, and it will probably be carried out, I’m delighted to say, in the French fashion. In France, you know, they don’t tell you when you are to be executed till a few minutes before. It is likely that I shall have even less than that, so my doctor informs me. A second or two will be all I shall get. Congratulate me, please.”

===Chinese===
他沉默了一阵。

「我原本不打算说的，」他说，「因为说出来也没什么用。可你既执意如此——看样子你也确要如此——我不如就招了吧。事情正如你所想；我这『再』，多半就是『最』了。可你千万不要为此大惊小怪；我自己是不会的。没有一个体面的人会为死亡大惊小怪；那是一班我们谁都必然赶得上的火车。它总是候着你的。」

我曾注意到，人一旦得知了那一类的消息，几乎当下便会觉得，自己其实早已知道许久。此刻我也正是这般感觉。

「往下说吧。」我说。

「嗯，事情大约就是这些。我已被判了死刑，而这判决，我很高兴地说，多半将以法国方式执行。你知道，在法国，他们不到行刑前几分钟是不会告诉你何时处决的。据我的医生相告，我大概连这点工夫都不到，只有一两秒钟的预告。那么，请向我道贺吧。」

===Original===
I thought it over for a moment.

“Yes, heartily,” I said. “I want to know a little more though.”

“Well, my heart’s all wrong, quite unmendably so. Heart disease! Doesn’t it sound romantic? In mid-Victorian romance, heroes and heroines alone die of heart disease. But that’s by the way. The fact is that I may die at any time without a moment’s warning. I shall give a couple of gasps, so he told me when I insisted on knowing details, and that’ll be all. Now, perhaps, you understand why I was unwilling to come and stay with you. I don’t want to die in your house; I think it’s dreadfully bad manners to die in other people’s houses. I long to see Tilling again, but I think I shall go to an hotel. Hotels are fair game, for the management overcharges those who live there to compensate themselves for those who die there. But it would be rude of me to die in your house; it might entail a lot of bother for you, and I couldn’t apologize﻿—”

“But I don’t mind your dying in my house,” I said. “At least you see what I mean﻿—”

He laughed.

“I do, indeed,” he said. “And you couldn’t give a warmer assurance of friendship. But I couldn’t come and stay with you in my present plight without telling you what it was, and yet I didn’t mean to tell you. But there we are now. Think again; reconsider your decision.”

“I don’t,” I said. “Come and die in my house by all means, if you’ve got to. I would much sooner you lived there: your dying will, in any case, annoy me immensely. But it would annoy me even more to know that you had done it in some beastly hotel among plush and looking-glasses. You shall have any bedroom you like. And I want you dreadfully to see my house, which is adorable.﻿ ﻿… O Roddie, what a bore it all is!”

===Chinese===
我把这事琢磨了一会儿。

「好，真心实意地向你道贺，」我说，「不过我还想再多知道一点。」

「嗯，我这颗心脏全然坏了，坏到了无可修补的地步。心脏病！听上去岂不浪漫？在维多利亚中期的言情小说里，唯有男女主人公才会死于心脏病。不过这是闲话。要紧的是，我随时可能在毫无先兆的情形下死去。我会倒抽两口气——这是我非追着问详情时他告诉我的——然后便一切完结。如今你或许明白我为何不愿来与你同住了。我不想死在你家里；我觉得，死在别人家里是极其失礼的事。我渴望再看蒂灵一眼，可我想我还是住旅馆为宜。旅馆倒是公道的猎物，因为旅馆的东家向住客多收钱，正是为了补偿死在他们那儿的人所造成的亏空。可我若死在你家，未免失礼；那也许要给你添好些麻烦，而我那时又无从致歉——」

「可我并不介意你死在我家。」我说，「至少，你明白我的意思——」

他笑了。

「我的确明白，」他说，「这便是友情最热切的保证了。可我如今这副光景，若不把真相告诉你，便不能来与你同住，而我原本又不打算告诉你。可事到如今，我们已说到这里了。你再想想；重新拿个主意吧。」

「我不重新拿。」我说，「你尽可以到我家来死，如果你非死不可。我倒宁可你住在那里：无论如何，你的死会叫我大为恼火。可要是知道你在某家塞满长毛绒和镜子的糟糕旅馆里了结了，我只会更恼火。你爱挑哪间卧房就挑哪间。还有，我极其盼着你能看看我的宅子，它可爱极了。……唉，罗迪，这一切真叫人厌烦！」

===Original===
It was impossible to speak or to think differently. I knew well how trivial a matter death was to my friend, and I was not sure that at heart I did not agree with him. We were quite at one, too, in that we had so often gossiped about death with cheerful conjecture and interested surmise based on the steady assurance that something of new and delightful import was to follow, since neither of us happened to be of that melancholy cast of mind that can envisage annihilation. I had promised, in case I was the first to embark on the great adventure, to do my best to “get through,” and give him some irrefutable proof of the continuance of my existence, just by way of endorsement of our belief, and he had given a similar pledge, for it appeared to us both, that, whatever the conditions of the future might turn out to be, it would be impossible when lately translated there, not to be still greatly concerned with what the present world still held for us in ties of love and affection. I laughed now to remember how he had once imagined himself begging to be excused for a few minutes, directly after death, and saying to St. Peter: “May I keep your Holiness waiting for a minute before you finally lock me into Heaven or Hell with those beautiful keys? I won’t be a minute, but I do want so much to be a ghost, and appear to a friend of mine who is on the lookout for such a visit. If I find I can’t make myself visible I will come back at once.﻿ ﻿… Oh, *thank* you, your Holiness.”

===Chinese===
说别样的话、作别样的想，都已是不可能的了。我深知死亡在我这位朋友原是何等微不足道的一件事，而我在心底里，也未尝不与他同此心思。在另一桩上我们也全然相投：我们曾无数次以欢快的揣测、以兴致勃勃的推敲谈论过死亡，所本的，乃是一份笃定的信心——信那其后必有某种崭新而可喜的境地随之而来——因为我们俩碰巧都不属于那种能够设想自身归于虚无的阴郁性情。我曾答应过他，万一我先一步踏上那场大冒险，必尽我所能「穿过去」，给他某种不容辩驳的证据，证明我的存在仍在延续，作为对我们这份信念的一点印鉴；他也作过同样的承诺。因为在我们俩看来，无论那未来的境况最终如何，一旦新近迁居彼岸，便断不可能不再深深地牵挂现世以爱与情谊的纽带为我们保留着的一切。此刻我想起他曾怎样设想自己一死之下，便立即告假几分钟，对圣彼得（St. Peter）说道：「可否请阁下在最终用您那串漂亮的钥匙把我锁进天堂或地狱之前，稍候我片刻？我只要一分钟，可我实在太想去做一回鬼，显形给我那位正盼着这种造访的朋友看一看。要是我发现自己显不了形，我马上就回来。……啊，多谢阁下了。」

===Original===
So we agreed that I should run the risk of his dying in my house, and promised not to make any reproaches posthumously (as far as he was concerned) in case he did so. He on his side promised not to die if he could possibly help it, and next week or so he would come down to me in the heart of the country that he loved, and see April at work.

“And I haven’t told you anything about my house yet,” I said. “It’s right at the top of the hill, square and Georgian and red-bricked. A panelled hall, dining-room and panelled sitting-room downstairs, and more panelled rooms upstairs. And there’s a garden with a lawn, and a high brick wall round it, and there is a big garden room, full of books, with a bow-window looking down the cobbled street. Which bedroom will you have? Do you like looking on to the garden or on to the street? You may even have my room if you like.”

He looked at me a moment with eager attention. “I’ll have the square panelled bedroom that looks out on to the garden, please,” he said. “It’s the second door on the right when you stand at the top of the stairs.”

“But how do you know?” I asked.

“Because I’ve been in the house before, once only, three years ago,” he said. “Margaret Alton took it furnished and lived there for a year or so. She died there, and I was with her. And if I had known that this was your house, I should never have dreamed of hesitating whether I should accept your invitation. I should have thrown my good manners about not dying in other people’s houses to the winds. But the moment you began to describe the garden and garden-room I knew what house it was. I have always longed to go there again. When may I come, please? Next week is too far ahead. You’re off there this afternoon, aren’t you?”

===Chinese===
于是我们议定，由我来承担他死在我家的风险，并答应（就他这一面而言）万一果真如此，绝不作任何身后的责难。他那一面则答应，但凡还能不作数，便不死；大约下周，他便要下到我那深处于他所钟爱的乡野之中的居所，看一看四月在那里如何劳作。

「我还没跟你讲过我的宅子呢，」我说，「它就在山顶上，方方正正，乔治王朝式样，红砖砌成。楼下是一间镶着护壁板的门厅、一间餐室和一间镶护壁板的起居室，楼上还有几间同样镶着护壁板的房间。还有一座带草坪的花园，四周围着一道高高的砖墙；另有一间宽敞的花园书房，里头满满都是书，一扇凸窗俯瞰着那条卵石铺的街道。你要哪间卧房？你爱朝花园的，还是朝街的？你若喜欢，就睡我那间也成。」

他以热切而专注的目光望了我一会儿。「劳驾，我要那间朝花园的、镶护壁板的方形卧房，」他说，「就在你站到楼梯顶上时右手第二扇门。」

「可你怎么知道？」我问。

「因为我从前进过这宅子，只有一回，是三年前，」他说，「当年是玛格丽特·奥尔顿（Margaret Alton）连家具一道租下的，在那儿住了一年光景。她就是在这宅子里去世的，那时我在她身边。当初我若知道这是你的宅子，做梦也不会为接不接受你的邀请而犹豫。我早就把那份『不可死在别人家里』的体面抛到九霄云外去了。可你一开始描摹那花园和那花园书房，我便知道这是哪一座宅子了。我一直盼着能再到那儿去一次。请问，我什么时候能来？下周太迟了。你今天下午就要动身过去，不是么？」

===Original===
I rose: the clock warned me that it was time for me to go to the station.

“Yes. Come this afternoon,” I suggested. “Come with me.”

“I wish I could, but I take that to mean that it will suit you if I come tomorrow. For I certainly will. Good Lord! To think of your having got just that house! It ought to be a wonderfully happy one, for I saw﻿—But I’ll tell you about that perhaps when I’m there. But don’t ask me to: I’ll tell you if and when I can, as the lawyers say. Are you really off?”

I was really off, for I had no time to spare, but before I got to the door he spoke again.

“Of course, the room I have chosen was *the* room,” he said, and there was no need for me to ask what he meant by *the* room.

---

===Chinese===
我站起身：时钟提醒我，该去火车站了。

「好。今天下午就来吧，」我提议，「跟我一道走。」

「我巴不得能如此，不过我且把这当作：我明日来也合你的意。因为我是一定要来的。老天！想想你竟偏偏得了这一座宅子！这本该是一栋格外幸福的宅子，因为我曾看见——不过这件事，等我到了那里，也许会告诉你。可你别逼我说：我会按律师们爱讲的那句话——『只要我能够、并且时机成熟』——便告诉你。你当真要走吗？」

我当真要走了，因为我已没有多余的时间，可我还没走到门口，他又开了口。

「自然，我选的那间，就是『那间』屋子。」他说。而我无需再问他所谓『那间』屋子是什么意思。

---

===Original===
I knew no more than the barest and most public outline of that affair, distant now by the space of many years, but, so I conceived, ever green in Roderick’s heart, and, as my train threaded its way through the gleams of this translucent spring evening, I retraced this outline as far as I knew it. It was the one thing of which Roderick never spoke (even now he was not sure that he could manage to tell me the end of it), and I had to rummage in my memory for the reconstruction of the half-obliterated lines.

Margaret﻿—her maiden-name would not be conjured back into memory﻿—had been an extremely beautiful girl when Roderick first met her, and, not without encouragement, he had fallen head over ears in love with her. All seemed to be going well with his wooing, he had the air of a happy lover, when there appeared on the scene that handsome and outrageous fellow, Richard Alton. He was the heir to his uncle’s barony and his really vast estates, and the girl, when he proceeded to lay siege, very soon capitulated. She may have fallen in love with him, for he was an attractive scamp, but the verdict at the time was that it was her ambition, not her heart, that she indulged. In any case, there was the end of Roderick’s wooing, and before the year was out she had married the other.

===Chinese===
那桩往事如今已隔着许多个年头，我只知它最粗略、最广为人知的一个轮廓，但我想它在罗德里克心里却始终鲜绿如初。当我的火车在这澄澈春夜的点点微光里穿行向前，我便就我所知把那轮廓重新追想了一遍。这是罗德里克唯一从不提起的事（即便此刻，他也没有把握能不能把它的结局告诉我），我只得在自己的记忆里翻寻，重新拼凑那些半已磨灭的线条。

玛格丽特——她的娘家姓已无从记忆里招回——罗德里克初识她时，还是个极其美貌的少女；而他既非没有受到她的鼓励，便一头深深地爱上了她。他的求爱原似一帆风顺，他也摆出一副幸福情人的神气，偏在此时，那个英俊而放肆的家伙——理查德·奥尔顿（Richard Alton）——登场了。他是他叔父男爵爵位以及那一笔着实庞大的产业的继承人；那姑娘一旦被他围攻，很快便投降了。她也许真是爱上了他，因为这个无赖倒颇有几分动人之处，但当时的定论却是，她纵容的是自己的野心，而不是她的心。无论怎样，罗德里克的求爱便就此了结；不出年底，她已嫁给了另一个人。

===Original===
I remembered seeing her once or twice in London about this time, splendid and brilliant, of a beauty that dazzled, with the world very much at her feet. She bore him two sons; she succeeded to a great position; and then with the granting of her heart’s desire, the leanness withal followed. Her husband’s infidelities were numerous and notorious; he treated her with a subtle cruelty that just kept on the right side of the law, and, finally, seeking his freedom, he deserted her, and openly lived with another woman. Whether it was pride that kept her from divorcing him, or whether she still loved him (if she had ever done so) and was ready to take him back, or whether it was out of revenge that she refused to have done with him legally, was an affair of which I knew nothing. Calamity followed on calamity; first one and then the other of her sons was killed in the European War, and I remembered having heard that she was the victim of some malignant and disfiguring disease, which caused her to lead a hermit life, seeing nobody. It was now three years or so since she had died.

Such, with the addition that she had died in my house, and that Roderick had been with her, was the sum of my meagre knowledge, which might or might not, so he had intimated, be supplemented by him. He arrived next day, having motored down from London for the avoidance of fatigue, and certainly as we sat after dinner that night in the garden-room, he had avoided it very successfully, for never had I seen him more animated.

===Chinese===
我记得那阵子曾在伦敦见过她一两回，光华照人，明艳不可方物，那一份美令人目眩，而整个世界几乎都匍匐在她脚下。她为他生了两个儿子；她登上了一桩显赫的地位；继而，心愿既偿，荒年也随之而来。她丈夫的外遇既多又尽人皆知；他以一种精微的残忍待她，恰巧卡在法律的容许之内；终于，为了求得自身的自由，他抛弃了她，公然与另一个女人同居。究竟是自尊使她不肯与他离婚，还是她仍爱着他（如果她曾经爱过）并愿意重新接纳他，抑或出于报复她才拒绝在法律上与他一刀两断，这件事我便一无所知了。灾祸接踵而至；她的两个儿子，先是一个、再是另一个，在欧洲大战中阵亡；我又记得曾听说她患了一种恶性而毁容的病症，因此过着隐士般的日子，不见外客。她去世至今，已有三年光景。

这便是我那点贫乏的全部所知——再加上她是在我家去世的，而罗德里克当时在她身边——至于这点所知会不会由他再作补充，他方才已暗示过，未可知。他第二天便到了，是从伦敦乘汽车下来以免劳顿；而那一夜饭后我们在花园书房里对坐时，他的确把那劳顿躲避得极其成功，因为我从没见他比那时更为精神焕发。

===Original===
“Oh, I have been so right to come here,” he said, “for I feel steeped in tranquillity and content. There’s such a tremendous sense of Margaret’s presence here, and I never knew how much I wanted it. Perhaps that is purely subjective, but what does that matter so long as I feel it? How a scene soaks into the place where it has been enacted; my room, which you know was her room, is alive with her. I want nothing better than to be here, prowling and purring over the memory of the last time, which was the only one, that I was here. Yes, just that; and I know how odd you must think it. But it’s true, it was here that I saw her die, and instead of shunning the place, I bathe myself in it. For it was one of the happiest hours of my life.”

“Because﻿—” I began.

“No; not because it gave her release, if that’s in your mind,” he said. “It’s because I saw﻿—”

He broke off, and remembering his stipulation that I should ask him nothing, but that he would tell me “if and when” he could, I put no question to him. His eyes were dancing with the sparkle of fire that burned on the hearth, for though April was here, the evenings were still chilly, and it was not the fire that gave them their light, but a joyousness that was as bright as glee, and as deep as happiness.

===Chinese===
「啊，我到这里来真是太对了，」他说，「因为我觉得自己浸润在一种宁静与满足之中。此间玛格丽特的存在感强烈极了，而我从前竟不知自己多么需要它。这也许是纯粹主观的，可只要我感觉得到，又有什么要紧？一幕情景竟能这般渗入它演出过的所在；我这间屋子——你也知道，原是她的屋子——处处都活脱脱地是她。我别无他求，只想留在这里，像猫一般踱着、咕噜着，反复咀嚼我上一次——也是唯一一次——在此处的那些记忆。是的，就是这样；我也知道你必定觉得这有多古怪。可这是真的：我正是在这里看着她死去的，而我没有躲避此地，反倒把自己浸溺其中。因为那是我一生中最幸福的几个钟头之一。」

「因为——」我开口道。

「不；不是因为它让她得了解脱，如果你心里想的是这个的话，」他说，「是因为我看见了——」

他打住了话头，而我记起他先前所定的那条规矩——我什么也不问他，他『只要能够、并且时机成熟』便会告诉我——便没有开口追问。他的双目正随着壁炉里那簇火光的跳跃而舞动——四月虽已到来，夜里却仍有寒意——可照亮它们的并不是炉火，而是一种欢欣，明亮如雀跃，深沉如幸福。

===Original===
“No, I’m not going on with that now,” he said, “though I expect I shall before my days are out. At present I shall leave you wondering why a place that should hold such mournful memories for me, is such a wellspring. And as I am not for telling you about me, let me enquire about you. Bring yourself up to date; what have you been doing, and much more important, what have you been thinking about?”

“My doings have chiefly been confined to settling into this house,” I said. “I’ve been pulling and pushing furniture into places where it wouldn’t go, and cursing it.”

He looked round the room.

“It doesn’t seem to bear you any grudge,” he said. “It looks contented. And what else?”

“In the intervals, when I couldn’t push and curse any more,” I said, “I’ve been writing a few spook stories. All about the borderland, which I love as much as you do.”

He laughed outright.

“Do you, indeed?” he said. “Then it’s no use my saying that it is quite impossible. But I should like to know your views on the borderland.”

===Chinese===
「不，眼下我不往下讲了，」他说，「不过我料想在我这些日子走到头之前，总会讲的。此刻我且让你去纳闷：一个本该为我藏着这样伤感记忆的地方，竟会是这样一口快乐的活泉。至于我呢，既不打算讲我自己，就让我来问问你吧。把你近况说给我听：你都做了些什么？更要紧的是，你想了些什么？」

「我做的事，多半不出安顿进这宅子这一桩，」我说，「我把家具拖来推去，硬塞到它不肯去的地方，一边对它们破口大骂。」

他环视了一下屋子。

「它仿佛并不记你的仇，」他说，「瞧着挺知足。还有呢？」

「闲下来的时候——实在推不动也骂不动了——」我说，「我便写了几篇鬼故事。都写的是那片边境之地（borderland），那地方我与你一样钟爱。」

他爽声大笑起来。

「当真么？」他说，「那我再说『全然不是那么回事』也没用了。不过我倒愿意听听你对那片边境之地的看法。」

===Original===
I pointed to a sheaf of typewritten stuff that littered my table.

“Them’s my sentiments,” I said, “and quite at your service.”

“Good; then I’ll take them to bed with me when I go, if you’ll allow me. I’ve always thought that you had a pretty notion of the creepy, but the mistake that you make is to imagine that creepiness is characteristic of the borderland. No doubt there are creepy things there, but so there are everywhere, and a thunderstorm is far more terrifying than an apparition. And when you get really close to the borderland, you see how enchanting it is, and how vastly more enchanting the other side must be. I got right on to the borderland once, here in this house, as I shall probably tell you, and I never saw so happy and kindly a place. And without doubt I shall soon be careering across it in my own person. That’ll be, as we’ve often determined, wildly interesting, and it will have the solemnity of a first night at a new play about it. There’ll be the curtain close in front of you, and presently it will be raised, and you will see something you never saw before. How well, on the whole, the secret has been kept, though from time to time little bits of information, little scraps of dialogue, little descriptions of scenery have leaked out. Enthrallingly interesting; one wonders how they will come into the great new drama.”

“You don’t mean the sort of thing that mediums tell us?” I asked.

===Chinese===
我指了指摊满我桌子的那一沓打字稿。

「这便是我的见解，」我说，「尽可供你赏鉴。」

「好；那么等我一会儿去睡时，你若允许，我便带它们上床。我一向以为，你对那种叫人汗毛直竖的东西颇有几分天赋，可你所犯的一个错误是，你以为阴森可怖正是那片边境之地的本色。那里头固然有阴森可怖之物，但到处都有；一场雷暴远比一个鬼影更为骇人。而当你真走到那片边境之地的近旁，你便看见它何等迷人，而它的彼岸，必又何等更加迷人。我曾有一次径直踏上了那片边境之地——就在这宅子里——这件事我大概会讲给你听——而我从未见过那样一处欢快、那样一处和善的地方。毫无疑问，不久我自己就要亲身驰骋过那片地方了。那将如我们常常断言的那样，是一件极其有趣的事，并且要带着一种新戏首演之夜般的庄严意味。你面前先是垂着一道幕，过一会儿，幕升起来，你便看见你从未见过的东西。整个看来，这秘密守得多么好啊，尽管时不时也有那么一点点的消息、一两句台词、几笔景物描写泄露出来。迷人极了；人不禁要琢磨，它们将怎样汇入那出新的大戏里。」

「你指的不是灵媒们对我们说的那一套吧？」我问。

===Original===
“Of course I don’t. I hate the sloshy﻿—really there’s no other word for it, and why should there be, since that word fits so admirably﻿—the sloshy utterances of the ordinary high-class, beyond-suspicion medium at half a guinea a sitting, who asks if there’s anybody present who once knew a Charles, or if not Charles, Thomas or William. Naturally somebody has known a Charles, Thomas or William who has passed over, and is the son, brother, father or cousin of a lady in black. So when she claims Thomas, he tells her that he is very busy and happy, helping people.﻿ ﻿… O Lord, what rot! I went to one such séance a month ago, just before I was taken ill, and the medium said that Margaret wanted to get into touch with somebody. Two of us claimed Margaret, but Margaret chose me and said she was the spirit of my wife. Wife, you know! You must allow that this was a very unfortunate shot. When I said that I was unmarried, Margaret said that she was my mother, whose name was Charlotte. Oh dear, oh dear! Well, I shall go to bed with joy, bringing your spooks with me.﻿ ﻿…”

“Sheaves,” said I.

“Yes, but aren’t they the sheaves? Isn’t one’s gleaning of sheaves in this world what they call spooks? That is, the knowledge of what one takes across?”

“I don’t understand one word,” said I.

“But you must understand. All the knowledge﻿—worth anything﻿—which you or I have collected here, is the beginning of the other life. We toil and moil, and make our gleanings and our harvestings, and all our decent efforts help us to realize what the real harvest is. Surely we shall take with us exactly that which we have reaped.﻿ ﻿…”

===Chinese===
「当然不是。我恨那种稀烂的——实在没有别的词可形容，又何须别的词，既然这一个词已贴切到了极点——我恨半几尼一场、上流出身、『无可怀疑』的寻常灵媒所吐出来的那种稀烂的言辞，她们总爱问，在座有没有谁，曾经认识一位查尔斯，要不是查尔斯，便是托马斯或威廉。自然总有谁认识一位已经过了身的查尔斯、托马斯或威廉，而且他正是某位一身黑衣的女士的儿子、兄弟、父亲或表亲。于是当她认下这位托马斯，他便告诉她，他非常忙，也非常快乐，正忙着帮助别人。……主啊，多好的胡扯！一个月前，就在我病倒之前，我去参加过这样一场降神会（séance），那灵媒说，玛格丽特想要与某位在座者取得联络。我们当中有两位都声称认识玛格丽特，可玛格丽特挑中了我，说她是我的妻子的亡灵。妻子，你想！你得承认，这一箭射得未免太离谱。等我说我并未婚娶，玛格丽特又改口说，她是我母亲，母亲名叫夏洛特（Charlotte）。老天，老天！好了，我要怀着喜悦去睡了，把你的这些鬼故事也一并带上。……」

「是『一沓』。」我说。

「是，可这些不也正是『禾捆』么？人在此世所拾取的禾捆，难道不正是他们所谓的鬼魂么？也就是，人所携往彼岸的那种知识？」

「我一个字也听不懂。」我说。

「可你必须听懂。你我在此地所汇集起来的一切——但凡有几分价值的——知识，便是彼岸生命的开端。我们劳苦，我们奔波，我们做我们的拾穗、我们的收割；我们一切尚算体面的努力，都在帮我们认清真正的收成究竟是什么。我们将带走的，必正是我们所收割的那一切。……

===Original===
After he had gone up to bed I sat trying to correct the errors of a typist, but still between me and the pages there dwelt that haunting sense of all that we did here being only the grist for what was to come. Our achievements were rewarded, so he seemed to say, by a glimpse. And those glimpses﻿—so I tried to follow him﻿—were the hints that had leaked out of the drama for which the curtain was twitching. Was that it?

Roderick came down to breakfast next morning, superlatively frank and happy.

“I didn’t read a single line of your stories,” he said. “When I got into my bedroom I was so immeasurably content that I couldn’t risk getting interested in anything else. I lay awake a long time, pinching myself in order to prolong my sheer happiness, but the flesh was weak, and at last, from sheer happiness, I slept and probably snored. Did you hear me? I hope not. And then sheer happiness dictated my dreams, though I don’t know what they were, and the moment I was called I got up, because﻿… because I didn’t want to miss anything. Now, to be practical again, what are you doing this morning?”

“I was intending to play golf,” I said, “unless﻿—”

“There isn’t an ‘unless,’ if you mean *me*. My plan made itself for me, and I intend﻿—this is my plan﻿—to drive out with you, and sit in the hollow by the fourth tee, and read your stories there. There’s a great southwesterly wind, like a celestial housemaid, scouring the skies, and I shall be completely sheltered there, and in the intervals of my reading, I shall pleasantly observe the unsuccessful efforts of the golfers to carry the big bunker. I can’t personally play golf any more, but I shall enjoy seeing other people attempting to do it.”

“And no prowling or purring?” I asked.

“Not this morning. That’s all right: it’s there. It’s so much all right that I want to be active in other directions. Sitting in a windless hollow is about the range of my activities. I say that for fear that you should.”

===Chinese===
他上楼去睡之后，我还坐着，想替一位打字员改一改稿子上的错；可在我与那几页纸之间，仍盘旋着一种挥之不去的感觉——感到我们在此世所做的一切，不过是供给那将至之事的谷物。我们的种种成就，他仿佛在说，所换得的，不过是一瞥。而那些一瞥——我尽力跟上他的思路——便是那出幕布正微微掀动、即将开启的戏里，泄漏出来的暗示。是那样的么？

次日清晨，罗德里克下来用早餐，神情分外坦荡、分外快乐。

「你的故事，我一个字也没读，」他说，「我一走进卧房，便感到一种无可衡量的满足，不敢拿别的任何事来冒险分心。我醒着躺了好一会儿，掐着自己，想借此延长那一份纯粹的快乐，无奈肉体毕竟是软弱的，到末了，出于纯粹的快乐，我便睡着了，多半还打了鼾。你听见我了吗？但愿没有。其后，纯粹的快乐又支配了我的梦——虽然我不知道自己梦见了什么——等人一叫我，我便一跃而起，因为……因为我不想错过任何东西。好了，再谈实际的：今天上午你打算做什么？」

「我打算去打高尔夫，」我说，「除非——」

「没有『除非』，如果你指的是我的话。我的计划是自己为我生出来的，我打算——这就是我的计划——跟你一道坐车出去，然后坐在第四个发球台旁边那个洼地里，在那里读你的故事。这会儿正刮着一场大西南风，像一位天上的女佣，在打扫这一片天空；而在那个洼地里我可以完全避风，读到间歇的时候，我便好整以暇地欣赏那些打球人怎样白费气力、想越过那一座大沙坑。我自己是再不能打高尔夫了，可见别人试着打，我倒会看得津津有味。」

「就不踱着、不咕噜了吗？」我问。

「今天上午不。放心好了：它在那儿呢。它太在那儿了，以致我倒想在别的方向上活泼一些。坐在一处无风的洼地里，这大概就是我的活动范围了。我先把它说了，免得你来说。」

===Original===
I found a match when we arrived at the clubhouse, and Roderick strolled away to the goal of his observations. Half an hour afterwards I found him watching with criminally ecstatic joy the soaring drives that, in the teeth of the great wind, were arrested and blown back into the unholiest bunker in all the world or the low clever balls that never rose to the height of the shored-up cliff of sand. The couple in front of my partner and me were sarcastic dogs, and bade us wait only till they had delved themselves over the ridge, and then we might follow as soon as we chose. After violent deeds in the bunker they climbed over the big dune, thirty yards beyond which lay the green on which they would now be putting.

As soon as they had disappeared, Roderick snatched my driver from my hand.

“I can’t bear it,” he said. “I must hit a ball again. Tee it low, caddie.﻿ ﻿… No, no tee at all.”

He hit a superb shot, just high enough to carry the ridge, and not so high that it caught the opposing wind and was stopped towards the end of its flight. He gave a loud croak of laughter.

“That’ll teach them not to insult my friend,” he said. “It must have been pitched right among their careful puttings. And now I shall read his ghost-stories.”

===Chinese===
我们到了俱乐部会所，我寻到了一位对手，罗德里克便踱开去，到他要观察的目标那里。半小时之后，我见他正以一种近乎犯罪的狂喜，看着那些高高飞起的开球——它们迎着大风，被截住、被吹回全世界最不像样的大沙坑里——又看着那些贴地低飞、巧妙之至的球，它们压根儿升不到那座垒起的沙崖的高度。排在我和我的搭子前面的那两位，是两个嘴尖舌快的家伙，他们叫我们只管等他们自己挖过那道沙脊便罢，之后我们爱多快跟上就多快跟上。在沙坑里大干了一通之后，他们翻过了那座大沙丘，沙丘过去三十码开外，便是那一片他们这会儿正在推球的果岭。

他们一消失，罗德里克便从我手里一把抢过我的开球杆。

「我受不了了，」他说，「我必须再打一球。球架低些，球童。……不，干脆不要球架。」

他打出了漂亮之至的一杆，刚好高过那道沙脊，又不至于高到在飞行的末段被迎面的风截住。他发出一声沙哑的大笑。

「这便能教会他们别再小瞧我的朋友，」他说，「那球准是正好落在他们正细心推球的果岭之中。现在，我来读他的鬼故事了。」

===Original===
I have recorded this athletic incident because better than any analysis of his attitude towards life and death it conveys just what that attitude was. He knew perfectly well that any swift exertion might be fatal to him, but he wanted to hit a golf ball again as sweetly and as hard as it could be hit. He had done it: he had scored off death. And as I went on my way I felt perfectly confident that if, with that brisk free effort, he had fallen dead on the tee, he would have thought it well worth while, provided only that he had made that irreproachable shot. While alive, he proposed to partake in the pleasures of life, amongst which he had always reckoned that of hitting golf balls, not caring, though he liked to be alive, whether the immediate consequence was death, just because he did not in the least object to being dead. The choice was of such little consequence.﻿ ﻿… The history of that I was to know that evening.

The stories which Roderick had taken to read were designed to be of an uncomfortable type: one concerned a vampire, one an elemental, the third the reincarnation of a certain execrable personage, and as we sat in the garden-room after tea, he with these pages on his knees, I had the pleasure of seeing him give hasty glances round, as he read, as if to assure himself that there was nothing unusual in the dimmer corners of the room.﻿ ﻿… I liked that; he was doing as I intended that a reader should.

Before long he came to the last page.

“And are you intending to make a book of them?” he asked. “What are the other stories like?”

“Worse,” said I, with the complacency of the horror-monger.

===Chinese===
我记下这段运动场上的小插曲，是因为它比任何对他生死观的剖析，都更真切地传达了那态度究竟是什么。他清楚得很，任何一阵急促的用力都可能要了他的命，可他偏要再把一只高尔夫球，打得像所能打出的那样漂亮、那样远。他做到了：他在死亡跟前赢了一分。而我接着走自己的路时，心里十分笃定：倘若他凭着那一记干脆利落的挥杆，竟倒在发球台上猝然死去，他也会觉得这再划算不过——只要那一杆打得无可指摘。只要活着一天，他便打算照常参与生之乐事——其中他一向把打高尔夫之乐也算上一桩——他并不在乎直接的后果是不是死，尽管他乐于活着，原因无他，只因为他一点也不反对死去。这一拣择，其轻重竟是这样微不足道。……这件事的始末，我到那天傍晚便会知晓。

罗德里克带去读的那几个故事，我刻意写得属于那种叫人不自在的类型：一篇讲吸血鬼，一篇讲元素精灵（elemental），第三篇讲某位可憎人物的转世。午后我们在花园书房里坐着，他把那几页摊在膝上读，我则颇为得意地看见，他读着读着，不时飞快地四下里瞟上一眼，仿佛要确认屋里那些幽暗的角落里并没有什么异样。……我高兴的就是这个；他正照着我所希望的读者会做的那样去做。

不久他便读到了最后一页。

「你打算把它们凑成一本书么？」他问，「其他几篇又是什么样子？」

「更糟。」我说，带着一个贩卖恐怖者的自得。

===Original===
“Then﻿—did you ask for criticism? I shall give it in any case﻿—you will make a book that not only is inartistic, all shadows and no light, but a false book. Fiction can be false, you know, inherently false. You play godfather to your stories, you see: you tell them in the first person, those at least that I have read, and that, though it need not be supposed that those experiences were actually yours, yet gives a sort of guarantee that you believe the borderland of which you write to be entirely terrible. But it isn’t: there are probably terrors there﻿—I think for instance that I believe in elemental spirits, of some ghastly kind﻿—but I am sure that I believe that the borderland, for the most part, is almost inconceivably delightful. I’ve got the best of reasons for believing that.”

“I’m willing to be convinced,” said I.

Again, as he looked at the fire, his eye sparkled, not with the reflected flame, but with the brightness of some interior vision.

“Well, there’s an hour yet before dinner,” he said, “and my story won’t take half of that. It’s about my previous experience of this house; what I saw, in fact, in the room which I now occupy. It was because of that, naturally, that I wanted the same room again. Here goes, then.

===Chinese===
「那么——你征求批评么？无论如何我都要说——你做出来的，将不仅是一本不艺术的、只有阴影没有光的书，而且是一本失真的书。你知道，小说是可能失真的，骨子里失真。你给你这些故事当教父，你看：你用第一人称来讲——至少我读过的这几篇是如此——这一点，纵然不必假定那些经历当真出自你身，却也等于在某种程度上担保了：你相信你所写的那片边境之地，是彻头彻尾可怖的。可它不是的：那里头或许也有恐怖——比方说，我想我是相信确有某种可怖的元素精灵的——但我可以肯定地相信，那片边境之地，就其大半而言，几乎是美得难以想象。我有最十足的理由这样相信。」

「我愿意被你说服。」我说。

他又像方才那样望着炉火，眼里闪烁起来——那不是反射的火光，而是某种内在视象的光辉。

「好，离晚饭还有一个钟头，」他说，「而我的故事用不了半个钟头。它讲的是我上一次在这宅子里的经历；说穿了，就是我在我此刻住着的这间屋子里看见了什么。自然，正是因为那件事，我才又要了同一间屋子。这就开讲吧。

===Original===
“For the twenty years of Margaret’s married life,” he said, “I never saw her except quite accidentally and casually. Casually, like that, I had seen her at theatres and whatnot with her two boys whom thus I knew by sight. But I had never spoken to either of them, nor, after her marriage, to their mother. I knew, as all the world knew, that she had a terrible life, but circumstances being what they were, I could not bring myself to her notice, the more so because she made no sign or gesture of wanting me. But I am sure that no day passed on which I did not long to be able to show her that my love and sympathy were hers. Only, so I thought, I had to know that she wanted them.

“I heard, of course, of the death of her sons. They were both killed in France within a few days of each other; one was eighteen, the other nineteen. I wrote to her then formally, so long had we been strangers, and she answered formally. After that, she took this house, where she lived alone. A year later, I was told that she had now for some months been suffering from a malignant and disfiguring disease.

“I was in London, strolling down Piccadilly when my companion mentioned it, and I at once became aware that I must go to see her, not tomorrow or soon, but now. It is difficult to describe the quality of that conviction, or tell you how instinctive and overmastering it was. There are some things which you can’t help doing, not exactly because you desire to do them, but because they must be done. If, for instance, you are in the middle of the road, and see a motor coming towards you at top-speed, you have to step to the side of the road, unless you deliberately choose to commit suicide. It was just like that; unless I intended to commit a sort of spiritual suicide there was no choice.

===Chinese===
「玛格丽特婚后那二十年里，」他说，「我只在完全偶然、极其随便的情形下才见过她。就这样随随便便地，我在戏院里之类的地方见过她，身边带着她的两个男孩，我因此才认得那两个孩子的模样。可我从未与他们当中任何一个说过话；自她婚后，也未曾与他们的母亲说过话。我跟世人一样，知道她过的是可怕的日子，可在那样的情形下，我无法强自走到她跟前，更何况她没有半点想要我出现的表示。但我确信，没有哪一天，我不渴望能让她知道，我的爱与同情都是向着她那一边的。只是——我那时想——我总得先知道，她是想要它们的。

「她儿子阵亡的事，我自然听说了。他们两个是在法国前后没几天相继阵亡的；一个十八岁，一个十九岁。那时我给她写了一封信，措辞是客套的——我们做陌生人已有这样久了——她的回信也是客套的。那之后，她便租下了这座宅子，独自住着。又过了一年，我听说她患了一种恶性而毁容的病，已有几个月之久。

「当时我在伦敦，正沿着皮卡迪利（Piccadilly）大街散步，我那位同伴提起了这件事，我当下便意识到：我必须去看她，不是明天，也不是哪天，而是现在。那种确信是怎样的性质，要描述出来很难；要告诉你它何等出乎本能、何等不可抗拒，也很难。世上有些事你是不能不做的，并不完全因为你想要做，而是因为它们非做不可。譬如，你若站在马路正中，看见一辆汽车正全速朝你驶来，你就不得不走到路边——除非你有意要寻死。这件事正如这般；除非我打算犯下一种精神上的自杀，否则我别无选择。

===Original===
“A few hours later I was at your door here, asked to see her, and was told that she was desperately ill and could see nobody. But I got her maid to take the message that I was here, and presently her nurse came down to tell me that she would see me. I should find Margaret, she said, wearing a veil so as to conceal from me the dreadful ravages which the disease had inflicted on her face, and the scars of the two operations which she had undergone. Very likely she would not speak to me, for she had great difficulty in speaking at all, and in any case I was not to stay for more than a few minutes. Probably she could not live many hours: I had only just come in time. And at that moment I wished I had done anything rather than come here, for though instinct had driven me here, yet instinct now recoiled with unspeakable horror. The flesh wars against the spirit, you know, and under its stress I now suggested that it was better perhaps that I should not see her.﻿ ﻿… But the nurse merely said again that Margaret wished to see me, and guessing perhaps the cause of my unwillingness, ‘Her face will be quite invisible,’ she added. ‘There will be nothing to shock you.’

“I went in alone: Margaret was propped up in bed with pillows, so that she sat nearly upright, and over her head was a dark veil through which I could see nothing whatever. Her right hand lay on the coverlet, and as I seated myself by her bedside, where the nurse had put a chair for me, Margaret advanced her hand towards me, shyly, hesitatingly, as if not sure that I would take it. But it was a sign, a gesture.”

He paused, his face beaming and radiant with the light of that memory.

===Chinese===
「几个小时之后，我便到了你这道门前，求见她，得到的回话却是：她病势沉重，不能见任何人。但我请她的侍女把口信送上去，说我到了；不多时，她的看护下楼来告诉我，她愿意见我。她说，我见到的玛格丽特将戴着一层面纱，为的是不让我看见病魔在她脸上造成的可怖毁损，以及她两次手术留下的疤痕。她很可能不会跟我说话，因为她开口说话已是极其困难；而无论怎样，我待在那儿不能超过几分钟。多半她也活不过几个钟头了：我来得正是时候，刚刚赶上。而就在那一刻，我宁愿自己做了任何别的事，也不愿来到这里；因为虽然本能把我驱到了这里，可本能此刻又怀着无法言说的恐惧向后退缩。你知道，肉体与灵性相争；在它的压迫下，我此刻便提议，也许我不见她为好。……可看护只是又说了一遍，玛格丽特愿意见我；她大概猜到了我不情愿的缘故，便又添了一句：『她的脸您是看不见的。没有什么会吓着您。』

「我一个人走了进去：玛格丽特被枕头垫高在床上，几乎直直地坐着，她头上罩着一层深色的面纱，我隔着面纱什么也看不见。她的右手搁在被面上，待我在床边坐下——看护已替我在那里放了一把椅子——玛格丽特便把手朝我伸过来，怯怯地、犹犹豫豫地，仿佛不确定我会不会接。但这终归是一个表示，一个姿态。」

他停了一下，那张脸因那段记忆的光辉而焕发着、明亮着。

===Original===
“I am speaking of things unspeakable,” he said. “I can no more convey to you all that meant than by a mere enumeration of colours can I steep your soul in the feeling of a sunset.﻿ ﻿… So there I sat, with her hand covered and clasped in mine. I had been told that very likely she would not speak, and for myself there was no word in the world which would not be dross in the gold of that silence.

“And then from behind her veil there came a whisper.

“ ‘I couldn’t die without seeing you,’ she said. ‘I was sure you would come. I’ve one thing to say to you. I loved you, and I tried to choke my love. And for years, my dear, I have been reaping the harvest of what I did. I tried to kill love, but it was so much stronger than I. And now the harvest is gathered. I have suffered cruelly, you know, but I bless every pang of it. I needed it all.﻿ ﻿…’

“Only a few minutes before, I had quaked at the thought of seeing her. But now I could not suffer that the veil should cover her face.

“ ‘Put up your veil, darling,’ I said. ‘I must see you.’

“ ‘No, no,’ she whispered. ‘I should horrify you. I am terrible.’

“ ‘You can’t be terrible to me,’ I said. ‘I am going to lift it.’

===Chinese===
「我说的，是不可言说之事，」他说，「要我把它当时一切的含义都传达给你，恰如单凭罗列一堆颜色，便能把你灵魂浸入一场日落的感受一般，是不可能的。……于是我便那样坐着，她的手被我合在掌中、紧紧握着。别人曾告诉我，她很可能不会开口；而就我自己而言，世上没有任何一句话，不会在那金子一般的沉默里沦为渣滓。

「接着，从她那层面纱背后，传来了一声低语。

「『我非得再见你一面才能死，』她说，『我笃定你会来的。我有一句话要对你说。我曾爱过你，而我曾试图扼杀我的爱。而这些年来，亲爱的，我便一直在收获我当日所作所为的果实。我要杀的是爱，可爱远比我强大得多。如今，庄稼已收割完毕。你知道，我受了酷烈的苦，可我感激其中每一阵剧痛。这一切苦，我全都需要的。……』

「就在几分钟之前，我一想到要见她，还心惊胆战。可此刻，我却再也受不了那层面纱还罩着她的脸。

「『把面纱掀起来，亲爱的，』我说，『我一定要看看你。』

「『不，不，』她低语道，『我会吓着你的。我可怕极了。』

「『你对我而言不可能可怕，』我说，『我要把它揭起来了。』

===Original===
“I raised her veil. And what did I see? I might have known, I think: I might have guessed that at this moment, supreme and perfect, I should see with vision.

“There was no scar or ravage of disease or disfigurement there. She was far lovelier than she had ever been, and on her face there shone the dawn of the everlasting day. She had shed all that was perishable and subject to decay, and her immortal spirit was manifested to me, purged and punished if you will, but humble and holy. There was granted to my frail mortal sight the power of seeing truly; it was permitted to me to be with her beyond the bounds of mortality.﻿ ﻿…

“And then, even as I was lost in an amazement of love and wonder, I saw we were not alone in the room. Two boys, whom I recognized, were standing at the other side of the bed, looking at her. It seemed utterly natural that they should be there.

“ ‘We’ve been allowed to come for you, mother darling,’ said one. ‘Get up.’

“She turned her face to them.

“ ‘Ah, my dears,’ she said. ‘How lovely of you. But just one moment.’

“She bent over towards me and kissed me.

“ ‘Thank you for coming, Roderick,’ she said. ‘Goodbye, just for a little while.’

“At that my power of sight﻿—my power of true sight﻿—failed. Her head fell back on the pillows and turned over on one side. For one second, before I let the veil drop over it again, I had a glimpse of her face, marred and cruelly mutilated. I saw that, I say, but never then nor afterwards could I remember it. It was like a terrible dream, which utterly fades on the awaking. Then her hand, which had been clasping mine, in that moment of her farewell slackened its hold, and dropped on to the bed. She had just moved away, somewhere out of sight, with her two boys to look after her.”

He paused.

“That’s all,” he said. “And do you wonder that I chose that room? How I hope that she will come for me.”

===Chinese===
「我揭起了她的面纱。我看见了什么呢？我想，我本该如何道的：我本可以猜到，在这至高至美的一刻，我将以灵目去看。

「那张脸上，没有半点疤痕，没有半点病魔的毁损、半点残缺。她比她平生任何时候都更为可爱得多，她的脸上，正辉耀着那永恒之日的晨光。凡属会朽坏、会衰败的一切，她都已卸下；她那不朽的灵魂显现于我眼前——你尽可以说它是已经涤炼、已经受过罚的——却是谦卑而圣洁的。我这一副孱弱的凡胎肉眼，被赋予了真正看清的能力；我被允许，在凡界的界限之外，与她同在。……

「接着，正当我沉浸在那爱与惊异交织的恍惚里时，我看见屋里除了我们，还有别人。两个男孩——我认得他们——正站在床的另一边，望着她。他们在那里，仿佛再自然不过。

「『我们获准来接你了，妈妈亲爱的，』其中一个说道，『起来吧。』

「她把脸转向他们。

「『啊，我的宝贝们，』她说，『你们真好。可是稍等片刻。』

「她向我俯下身来，吻了我。

「『谢谢你来了，罗德里克，』她说，『再会，不过是很短一阵子的再会。』

「就在那一刻，我那看得见的能力——我那以灵目看清的能力——失灵了。她的头倒回枕上，朝一侧歪了过去。在我重新放下面纱遮住它之前的那一秒，我瞥见了她的脸——毁损了、被残忍地割裂了。我说我看见了，可无论是当时还是事后，我都再想不起它的样子来。它就像一场可怖的梦，在醒来的一刻便褪得干干净净。接着，她那只一直紧握着我的手，在那声道别的瞬间松开了劲，落到了床上。她不过是刚刚迁居到了别处，某个看不见的地方，由她那两个男孩照看着她罢了。」

他停了下来。

「就是这个，」他说，「那么，你可会奇怪我为何偏要挑那间屋子？我多么盼着她也会来接我。」

===Original===
My room was next to Roderick’s, the head of his bed being just opposite the head of mine on the other side of the wall. That night I had undressed, lain down, and had just put out my light, when I heard a sharp tap just above me. I thought it was some fortuitous noise, as of a picture swinging in a draught, but the moment after it was repeated, and it struck me that it was perhaps a summons from Roderick who wanted something. Still quite unalarmed, I got out of bed, and, candle in hand, went to his door. I knocked, but receiving no answer, opened it an inch or two.

“Did you want anything?” I asked, and, again receiving no answer, I went in.

His lights were burning, and he was sitting up in bed. He did not appear to see me or be conscious of my presence, and his eyes were fixed on some point a few feet away in front of him. His mouth smiled, and in his eyes was just such a joy as I had seen there when he told me his story. Then, leaning on his arm, he moved as if to rise.

“Oh, Margaret, my dear.﻿ ﻿…” he cried.

He drew a couple of short breaths, and fell back.

===Chinese===
我的卧房就在罗德里克隔壁，我的床头正隔着墙，对着他的床头。那天夜里，我已脱衣躺下，刚把灯熄了，便听见头顶「嗒」的一声轻响。我起先当那是某种偶然的声响，比方说一幅画在穿堂风里晃了一下；可紧接着它又响了一声，我便想到，这或许是罗德里克有什么事，在叫我。我依旧全无惊慌，下了床，端着一支蜡烛，走到他门前。我敲了敲门，不见应声，便把门推开了两三寸。

「你要什么吗？」我问，仍是不见应声，我便走了进去。

他屋里灯都亮着，他正坐卧在床上。他似乎没看见我，也不觉有我在场；他的双眼直直地望着身前几英尺外的某一点。他嘴角含笑，眼里正是我听他讲故事时所见过的那同一种喜悦。接着，他撑着一条胳膊，做出要起身的模样。

「啊，玛格丽特，亲爱的。……」他喊道。

他急促地喘了两口气，便倒了回去。

## The Bus-Conductor / 售票员

===Original===
My friend, Hugh Grainger, and I had just returned from a two days’ visit in the country, where we had been staying in a house of sinister repute which was supposed to be haunted by ghosts of a peculiarly fearsome and truculent sort. The house itself was all that such a house should be, Jacobean and oak-panelled, with long dark passages and high vaulted rooms. It stood, also, very remote, and was encompassed by a wood of sombre pines that muttered and whispered in the dark, and all the time that we were there a southwesterly gale with torrents of scolding rain had prevailed, so that by day and night weird voices moaned and fluted in the chimneys, a company of uneasy spirits held colloquy among the trees, and sudden tattoes and tappings beckoned from the windowpanes. But in spite of these surroundings, which were sufficient in themselves, one would almost say, to spontaneously generate occult phenomena, nothing of any description had occurred. I am bound to add, also, that my own state of mind was peculiarly well adapted to receive or even to invent the sights and sounds we had gone to seek, for I was, I confess, during the whole time that we were there, in a state of abject apprehension, and lay awake both nights through hours of terrified unrest, afraid of the dark, yet more afraid of what a lighted candle might show me.

===Chinese===
我的朋友休·格兰杰（Hugh Grainger）和我刚从乡间两日的盘桓中归来。我们借宿的那所宅子名声可怖，据说常有格外狰狞凶戾的鬼魂出没。宅子本身倒也正合这样一所宅子该有的模样：詹姆斯一世时代的样式，镶着橡木护墙板，有又长又暗的走廊、高高的拱顶房间。它还坐落在极偏僻处，被一片阴森的松林环绕，那些松树在黑暗里喁喁低语、簌簌作响。我们在那儿的整段时日，一场西南大风夹着倾盆责骂似的骤雨肆虐不休，于是无论昼夜，烟囱里都有奇异的声息呻吟着、如笛般长吟着，一群不安的鬼魂在树间窃窃私议，窗玻璃上忽而响起一阵笃笃的叩击声，像是在召唤什么。然而，尽管这些周遭的氛围本身——人们几乎要说——已足以自行催生出玄秘的现象来，可那里面什么事也没有发生。我也不得不补上一句：当时我的心境，又最是适宜去接收、乃至去虚构我们专程去寻觅的种种声与影的；因为我不妨承认，在那儿的全部时间里，我一直处于一种可怖的惶恐之中，两夜都彻夜难眠，在惊惧的不安里熬过几个钟头——我怕黑暗，可更怕一支点亮的蜡烛会照给我看什么。

===Original===
Hugh Grainger, on the evening after our return to town, had dined with me, and after dinner our conversation, as was natural, soon came back to these entrancing topics.

“But why you go ghost-seeking I cannot imagine,” he said, “because your teeth were chattering and your eyes starting out of your head all the time you were there, from sheer fright. Or do you like being frightened?”

Hugh, though generally intelligent, is dense in certain ways; this is one of them.

“Why, of course, I like being frightened,” I said. “I want to be made to creep and creep and creep. Fear is the most absorbing and luxurious of emotions. One forgets all else if one is afraid.”

“Well, the fact that neither of us saw anything,” he said, “confirms what I have always believed.”

“And what have you always believed?”

“That these phenomena are purely objective, not subjective, and that one’s state of mind has nothing to do with the perception that perceives them, nor have circumstances or surroundings anything to do with them either. Look at Osburton. It has had the reputation of being a haunted house for years, and it certainly has all the accessories of one. Look at yourself, too, with all your nerves on edge, afraid to look round or light a candle for fear of seeing something! Surely there was the right man in the right place then, if ghosts are subjective.”

===Chinese===
回到城里那天的傍晚，休·格兰杰在我家用了餐，饭后我们的谈话——也属自然——很快又回到这些迷人的题目上来。

「我真想不通你为什么要去找鬼，」他说，「因为你待在那儿的时候，吓得牙齿直打颤，眼珠子都要从脑袋里瞪出来了。还是说，你喜欢被吓？」

休这人虽然大体聪明，某些方面却挺迟钝；这便是其中之一。

「哎呀，我当然喜欢被吓，」我说，「我就要被吓得汗毛直竖、汗毛直竖、汗毛直竖。恐惧是最最教人全神贯注、最最奢华的一种情感。人一害怕，便把别的什么都忘了。」

「那么，咱俩谁也没瞧见什么，」他说，「这倒印证了我一向的信念。」

「你一向相信什么？」

「我相信这些现象纯属客观，并非主观，人的心境和感知它们的那副感官毫无干系，境遇、周遭也和它们毫无干系。瞧瞧奥斯伯顿（Osburton）吧。它挂了这么多年闹鬼宅子的名声，自然也齐全了一切闹鬼宅子该有的摆设。再瞧瞧你自己，神经绷得紧紧的，连回头看一看、点一支蜡烛都不敢，生怕瞧见什么！倘若鬼魂当真是主观的，那会儿可真是人对了、地方也对了。」

===Original===
He got up and lit a cigarette, and looking at him—Hugh is about six feet high, and as broad as he is long—I felt a retort on my lips, for I could not help my mind going back to a certain period in his life, when, from some cause which, as far as I knew, he had never told anybody, he had become a mere quivering mass of disordered nerves. Oddly enough, at the same moment and for the first time, he began, to speak of it himself.

“You may reply that it was not worth my while to go either,” he said, “because I was so clearly the wrong man in the wrong place. But I wasn’t. You for all your apprehensions and expectancy have never seen a ghost. But I have, though I am the last person in the world you would have thought likely to do so, and, though my nerves are steady enough again now, it knocked me all to bits.”

He sat down again in his chair.

“No doubt you remember my going to bits,” he said, “and since I believe that I am sound again now, I should rather like to tell you about it. But before I couldn’t; I couldn’t speak of it at all to anybody. Yet there ought to have been nothing frightening about it; what I saw was certainly a most useful and friendly ghost. But it came from the shaded side of things; it looked suddenly out of the night and the mystery with which life is surrounded.

===Chinese===
他起身点了一支烟。我望着他——休身高约莫六英尺，前后左右一般宽厚——一句反驳已到了嘴边，因为我禁不住想起他生平中有一段日子：不知为了什么缘故（据我所知，他从未告诉过任何人），他整个人变成了一团颤抖的、乱了套的神经。奇怪的是，就在同一时刻，他竟破天荒地主动提起这事来。

「你也许会回敬我说，那我也不该去，」他说，「因为我显然更是不对的人、放在了不对的地方。可我并不是。你呢，尽管那样惶恐、那样满怀期待，却从未见过鬼。我却见过，虽说在全天下的人里头，你最想不到能见鬼的便是我；而如今我的神经虽然又稳住了，那一次可把我整个人击得粉碎。」

他又在椅子上坐下了。

「我那回崩溃，你无疑还记得，」他说，「如今我相信自己已经复原了，倒挺想跟你讲讲。可从前我讲不出口；我根本没法跟任何人提起。况且，那事按说没有什么可怕之处；我所见到的，分明是个最最有用、最最和善的鬼。可它是从事物的阴面里来的；它猝然从黑夜之中、从生命所笼罩的那重神秘之中探出脸来。

===Original===
“I want first to tell you quite shortly my theory about ghost-seeing,” he continued, “and I can explain it best by a simile, an image. Imagine then that you and I and everybody in the world are like people whose eye is directly opposite a little tiny hole in a sheet of cardboard which is continually shifting and revolving and moving about. Back to back with that sheet of cardboard is another, which also, by laws of its own, is in perpetual but independent motion. In it too there is another hole, and when, fortuitously it would seem, these two holes, the one through which we are always looking, and the other in the spiritual plane, come opposite one another, we see through, and then only do the sights and sounds of the spiritual world become visible or audible to us. With most people these holes never come opposite each other during their life. But at the hour of death they do, and then they remain stationary. That, I fancy, is how we ‘pass over.’

“Now, in some natures, these holes are comparatively large, and are constantly coming into opposition. Clairvoyants, mediums are like that. But, as far as I knew, I had no clairvoyant or mediumistic powers at all. I therefore am the sort of person who long ago made up his mind that he never would see a ghost. It was, so to speak, an incalculable chance that my minute spyhole should come into opposition with the other. But it did: and it knocked me out of time.”

===Chinese===
「我先简单跟你讲讲我关于见鬼（ghost-seeing）的理论，」他接着说，「这层道理，我最好用一个比喻、一个意象来阐明。那么，请你设想：你、我和这世上所有的人，都像是一些把眼睛紧贴在一小块硬纸板上一个小小孔洞的人，而那块纸板一刻不停地挪动着、旋转着、移来移去。和这块纸板背靠着背的，还有另一块，它也依着自己的一套法则，永不停息地、却又彼此独立地运动着。那上头也有一个孔洞，而当这两个孔洞——一个是我们始终借以窥视的那个，另一个是灵界（the spiritual plane）上的那个——偶然地、似乎是出于巧合地，彼此正对着的时候，我们便望穿了过去，唯有在那一刹那，灵界的种种声与影，才对我们成为可见、可闻。对世上大多数人而言，这两个孔洞终其一生也不会正对到一处。可到了临终的那一刻，它们正对了，然后就停住不动了。我猜想，我们便是这样『渡过去（pass over）』的。

「再者，在有些天性里，这两个孔洞相当之大，而且时时彼此相对。那些开天眼的、那些灵媒（clairvoyants, mediums）便是如此。可就我所知，我全无半点开天眼或通灵的本事。于是，我正是那种早早便拿定了主意、认定自己绝见不着鬼的人。可以说，我那个细微的窥孔（spyhole）要和另一个窥孔彼此正对，乃是一件无法估量其几率的偶然。可它偏偏正对了：于是我便被击出了时间之外。」

===Original===
I had heard some such theory before, and though Hugh put it rather picturesquely, there was nothing in the least convincing or practical about it. It might be so, or again it might not.

“I hope your ghost was more original than your theory,” said I, in order to bring him to the point.

“Yes, I think it was. You shall judge.”

I put on more coal and poked up the fire. Hugh has got, so I have always considered, a great talent for telling stories, and that sense of drama which is so necessary for the narrator. Indeed before now, I have suggested to him that he should take this up as a profession, sit by the fountain in Piccadilly Circus, when times are, as usual, bad, and tell stories to the passersby in the street, Arabian fashion, for reward. The most part of mankind, I am aware, do not like long stories, but to the few, among whom I number myself, who really like to listen to lengthy accounts of experiences, Hugh is an ideal narrator. I do not care for his theories, or for his similes, but when it comes to facts, to things that happened, I like him to be lengthy.

===Chinese===
这一类的理论，从前我也听过一些；休这番话虽说讲得颇为生动，却丝毫谈不上有什么说服力，或有什么实在之处。事情也许是这样的，可也许并不是。

「但愿你的鬼比你的理论更新奇些，」我说，为的是好把他引到正题上。

「是，我想是的。你自己来评判吧。」

我添了些煤，把火拨旺。休这人——我一向这么觉得——极有讲故事的天赋，也具备一个叙述者所必不可少的戏剧感。说真的，从前我还曾怂恿他以此为止生之道：赶上世道一如往常地艰难时，便去皮卡迪利广场（Piccadilly Circus）的喷泉旁边坐下，仿着阿拉伯人的式样，向过路的人讲故事讨赏钱。我知道，世人多半不爱听长故事；可对那少数几个——我把自己也算在里面——当真爱听冗长经历的人而言，休是个再理想不过的叙述者。我不在乎他那些理论，也不在乎他那些比喻，可一旦落到事实、落到真发生过的事情上，我倒巴不得他讲得长些。

===Original===
“Go on, please, and slowly,” I said. “Brevity may be the soul of wit, but it is the ruin of storytelling. I want to hear when and where and how it all was, and what you had for lunch and where you had dined and what—”

Hugh began:

“It was the 24th of June, just eighteen months ago,” he said. “I had let my flat, you may remember, and came up from the country to stay with you for a week. We had dined alone here—”

I could not help interrupting.

“Did you see the ghost here?” I asked. “In this square little box of a house in a modern street?”

“I was in the house when I saw it.”

I hugged myself in silence.

===Chinese===
「请讲下去，讲慢一点，」我说，「简洁或许是机智的灵魂，却是讲故事的死穴。我要听的是：何时、何地、来龙去脉，你午饭吃了什么，在哪儿用的晚餐，还有——」

休开了口：

「那是6月24日，整整十八个月以前，」他说，「你可能还记得，我把自己的公寓租了出去，从乡下进城来在你这儿住一星期。就咱俩在这儿用的晚餐——」

我忍不住打断了他。

「你是在这儿见到那鬼的？」我问，「就在这条现代街道上、这方方正正小盒子似的房子里？」

「我见到它的时候，是在这所房子里。」

我在心里暗自得意。

===Original===
“We had dined alone here in Graeme Street,” he said, “and after dinner I went out to some party, and you stopped at home. At dinner your man did not wait, and when I asked where he was, you told me he was ill, and, I thought, changed the subject rather abruptly. You gave me your latchkey when I went out, and on coming back, I found you had gone to bed. There were, however, several letters for me, which required answers. I wrote them there and then, and posted them at the pillar-box opposite. So I suppose it was rather late when I went upstairs.

“You had put me in the front room, on the third floor, overlooking the street, a room which I thought you generally occupied yourself. It was a very hot night, and though there had been a moon when I started to my party, on my return the whole sky was cloud-covered, and it both looked and felt as if we might have a thunderstorm before morning. I was feeling very sleepy and heavy, and it was not till after I had got into bed that I noticed by the shadows of the window-frames on the blind that only one of the windows was open. But it did not seem worth while to get out of bed in order to open it, though I felt rather airless and uncomfortable, and I went to sleep.

===Chinese===
「那天晚上，就咱俩在格雷姆街（Graeme Street）这儿用了晚餐，」他说，「饭后我出门去参加一个聚会，你留在家里。吃饭时你那男仆没有上来伺候，我问起他在哪儿，你告诉我他病了，我还觉得——你相当生硬地把话头岔开了。我出门时，你把你家的门钥匙给了我；等我回来，发现你已经睡下了。不过我有好几封信要回，便当即在那里写了，投到对面那只圆柱形邮筒里。所以我想，我上楼的时候大概已不算早了。

「你把我安置在三楼朝着街的那间前房里，我以为这间房平日是你自己住的。那一夜天气极热，我去赴会时还有月亮，可等我回来，整个天空已盖满了云，看样子、也感觉起来，都像是天亮之前要来一场雷雨。我困得厉害，身子也沉得很，直到上了床，我才借着窗帘上映着的窗框的影子看出来，两扇窗只开了一扇。可我也懒得爬起来去开另一扇了，虽说我觉得有点气闷、有点不舒服，也就这么睡了。

===Original===
“What time it was when I awoke I do not know, but it was certainly not yet dawn, and I never remember being conscious of such an extraordinary stillness as prevailed. There was no sound either of foot-passengers or wheeled traffic; the music of life appeared to be absolutely mute. But now instead of being sleepy and heavy, I felt, though I must have slept an hour or two at most, since it was not yet dawn, perfectly fresh and wide-awake, and the effort which had seemed not worth making before, that of getting out of bed and opening the other window, was quite easy now, and I pulled up the blind, threw it wide open, and leaned out, for somehow I parched and pined for air. Even outside the oppression was very noticeable, and though, as you know, I am not easily given to feel the mental effects of climate, I was aware of an awful creepiness coming over me. I tried to analyse it away, but without success; the past day had been pleasant, I looked forward to another pleasant day tomorrow, and yet I was full of some nameless apprehension. I felt, too, dreadfully lonely in this stillness before the dawn.

“Then I heard suddenly and not very far away the sound of some approaching vehicle; I could distinguish the tread of two horses walking at a slow foot’s pace. They were, though yet invisible, coming up the street, and yet this indication of life did not abate that dreadful sense of loneliness which I have spoken of. Also in some dim unformulated way that which was coming seemed to me to have something to do with the cause of my oppression.

===Chinese===
「我醒来时是什么时辰，我不知道，可天肯定还没亮，而我也不记得自己何时曾意识到过这般异乎寻常的死寂。既没有行人的脚步声，也没有车轮的辚辚声；生命的乐章仿佛被按成了绝对的静音。可这一回，我非但不困不沉，反倒觉得——虽说至多只睡了一两个钟头，因为天还没亮——神清气爽、毫无睡意。先前觉得不值当做的事——下床去把另一扇窗打开——如今轻而易举，我便拉起窗帘，把窗扇大大推开，探身出去，因为不知怎的，我口干舌燥，渴盼着一口空气。便是在窗外，那份郁结的沉闷也十分明显，虽说你也知道，我素来不轻易受气候在心神上的影响，这会儿却感到一阵可怖的寒意爬遍全身。我试图把它分析掉，却没有成功；头一天过得很愉快，我期待着第二天也是个愉快的日子，可我心中仍充满某种叫不出名目的忧虑。再者，在这黎明前的死寂里，我还觉得说不出的孤寂。

「接着，我忽然听见不远处有车驶来的声响；我辨得出那是两匹马迈着慢步轻缓地走。它们——虽还看不见——正顺着街上来，可这一点生命的迹象，丝毫没有减轻我方才所说的那种可怖的孤寂之感。况且，在某种朦胧而难以言宣的层面上，我觉得那正逼近过来的东西，似乎和我这份郁结的沉闷有什么干系。

===Original===
“Then the vehicle came into sight. At first I could not distinguish what it was. Then I saw that the horses were black and had long tails, and that what they dragged was made of glass, but had a black frame. It was a hearse. Empty.

“It was moving up this side of the street. It stopped at your door.

“Then the obvious solution struck me. You had said at dinner that your man was ill, and you were, I thought, unwilling to speak more about his illness. No doubt, so I imagined now, he was dead, and for some reason, perhaps because you did not want me to know anything about it, you were having the body removed at night. This, I must tell you, passed through my mind quite instantaneously, and it did not occur to me how unlikely it really was, before the next thing happened.

===Chinese===
「随后那辆车驶入了视线。起初我辨不清是什么。接着我看见那两匹马是黑色的，尾巴长长的，而它们所拉的东西是玻璃做的，镶着一副黑色的框子。是一辆灵车。空的。

「它顺着街的这一边驶上来。它在你家门口停下了。

「紧接着，那显而易见的解释掠过了我的心头。你吃饭时说过你那仆人病了，而我觉得，你不大愿意再多谈他的病。于是这会儿我便设想：毫无疑问，他已经死了，而出于某种缘故——也许是因为你不愿让我知道一点风声——你便趁着夜色把尸首运走。我得告诉你，这一切在我心头只是一闪而过，我还没来得及想一想这事其实多么不可能，下一件事便发生了。

===Original===
“I was still leaning out of the window, and I remember also wondering, yet only momentarily, how odd it was that I saw things—or rather the one thing I was looking at—so very distinctly. Of course, there was a moon behind the clouds, but it was curious how every detail of the hearse and the horses was visible. There was only one man, the driver, with it, and the street was otherwise absolutely empty. It was at him I was looking now. I could see every detail of his clothes, but from where I was, so high above him, I could not see his face. He had on grey trousers, brown boots, a black coat buttoned all the way up, and a straw hat. Over his shoulder there was a strap, which seemed to support some sort of little bag. He looked exactly like—well, from my description what did he look exactly like?”

“Why—a bus-conductor,” I said instantly.

“So I thought, and even while I was thinking this, he looked up at me. He had a rather long thin face, and on his left cheek there was a mole with a growth of dark hair on it. All this was as distinct as if it had been noonday, and as if I was within a yard of him. But—so instantaneous was all that takes so long in the telling—I had not time to think it strange that the driver of a hearse should be so unfunereally dressed.

===Chinese===
「我还探身倚在窗台上，我也还记得，自己当时只在一瞬间纳闷过：真怪，我竟看得这样清楚——或者不如说，我所盯着看的那唯一一样东西，我竟看得这样清楚。当然，云后头是有月亮的，可也真奇了，那灵车、那两匹马身上的每一个细节，竟全都看得见。车上只有一个人，便是那车夫，此外街上空无一人。我此刻盯着看的正是他。他衣裳的每一处细节我都看得一清二楚，可从我所站的位置——那么高高在上地俯瞰着他——我瞧不见他的脸。他穿着灰裤子、棕色的靴子，一件黑外衣，扣子一路扣到了顶上，头上戴一顶草帽。他肩头搭着一根带子，似乎吊着一只什么小袋子。他这一身打扮活脱儿像是——嗯，凭我这番描述，他活脱儿像是什么？」

「怎么——像一位公共汽车售票员（bus-conductor），」我立刻说道。

「我也是这么想的，而就在我想到这一点的当儿，他抬眼朝我望过来。他的脸略显狭长瘦削，左颊上有一颗痣，上头长着一撮黑毛。这一切都看得清清楚楚，仿佛时值正午，仿佛我离他不过一码远。然而——这讲来费时、其实不过是一瞬的事——我竟来不及去想：一辆灵车的车夫竟穿得这样毫无服丧之意，岂非古怪。

===Original===
“Then he touched his hat to me, and jerked his thumb over his shoulder.

“‘Just room for one inside, sir,’ he said.

“There was something so odious, so coarse, so unfeeling about this that I instantly drew my head in, pulled the blind down again, and then, for what reason I do not know, turned on the electric light in order to see what time it was. The hands of my watch pointed to half-past eleven.

“It was then for the first time, I think, that a doubt crossed my mind as to the nature of what I had just seen. But I put out the light again, got into bed, and began to think. We had dined; I had gone to a party, I had come back and written letters, had gone to bed and had slept. So how could it be half-past eleven?… Or—*what* half-past eleven was it?

“Then another easy solution struck me; my watch must have stopped. But it had not; I could hear it ticking.

===Chinese===
「随后，他抬手碰了碰帽檐向我致意，又把大拇指朝肩后一挑。

「『里头刚好还有一个空位，先生。』他说。

「这话里头有某种叫人厌恶的、粗鄙的、无情的东西，我立刻便把脑袋缩了回来，把窗帘重新拉下，接着——不知为了什么缘故——拧开了电灯，好看看是什么时辰。我那只表的指针正指在十一点半。

「我想，便是在那一刻，我心里头头一回对我刚所见之物的性质生出一丝疑窦。可我又把灯关了，上了床，开始琢磨。我们吃过晚饭；我去参加了一个聚会，回来写了信，上了床，又睡了一觉。那怎么可能还是十一点半？……再者——那究竟是哪一个十一点半？

「紧接着，又一个现成的解释掠过我心头：准是我的表停了。可它没有；我还听得见它在滴答作响。

===Original===
“There was stillness and silence again. I expected every moment to hear muffled footsteps on the stairs, footsteps moving slowly and smally under the weight of a heavy burden, but from inside the house there was no sound whatever. Outside, too, there was the same dead silence, while the hearse waited at the door. And the minutes ticked on and ticked on, and at length I began to see a difference in the light in the room, and knew that the dawn was beginning to break outside. But how had it happened then that if the corpse was to be removed at night it had not gone, and that the hearse still waited, when morning was already coming?

“Presently I got out of bed again, and with the sense of strong physical shrinking I went to the window and pulled back the blind. The dawn was coming fast; the whole street was lit by that silver hueless light of morning. But there was no hearse there.

“Once again I looked at my watch. It was just a quarter-past four. But I would swear that not half an hour had passed since it had told me that it was half-past eleven.

“Then a curious double sense, as if I was living in the present and at the same moment had been living in some other time, came over me. It was dawn on June 25th, and the street, as natural, was empty. But a little while ago the driver of a hearse had spoken to me, and it was half-past eleven. What was that driver, to what plane did he belong? And again *what* half-past eleven was it that I had seen recorded on the dial of my watch?

“And then I told myself that the whole thing had been a dream. But if you ask me whether I believed what I told myself, I must confess that I did not.

===Chinese===
「重又是一片死寂。我时时刻刻盼着听见楼梯上传来裹着东西的、沉滞的脚步声——那种在重担之下挪得又慢又小的脚步声——可整所房子里头，一点声响也没有。外头也同样是一片死一般的寂静，那辆灵车还在门口候着。一分一秒地走着，一分一秒地走着，到末了我终于瞧见屋里的光线起了变化，知道外面天开始放亮了。可这是怎么一回事呢？倘若尸首是要趁夜运走的，怎会还没走、灵车怎会还在门口候着，而天都已经亮了？

「过了一会儿，我又下了床，怀着一种极强烈的生理上的畏缩，走到窗前，把窗帘拉了回去。天亮得很快；整条街都被早晨那种银色而无色的光亮照着。可那儿哪有什么灵车。

「我又看了一回表。正是四点一刻。可我敢起誓，自它告诉我十一点半以来，过去的光景绝不到半个钟头。

「于是一种古怪的双重感觉袭上心头，仿佛我既活在当下，与此同时又曾活在另一段时间里。这是6月25日的黎明，街道一如所料，是空荡荡的。可就在方才，一位灵车车夫还跟我开了口，那时是十一点半。那车夫究竟是什么？他属于哪一层界？再者，我在表盘上所看见的，究竟是哪一个十一点半？

「接着我便告诉自己，整件事不过是一场梦。可你若问我，我自己信不信这番自言自语，那我必须坦白：我并不信。

===Original===
“Your man did not appear at breakfast next morning, nor did I see him again before I left that afternoon. I think if I had, I should have told you about all this, but it was still possible, you see, that what I had seen was a real hearse, driven by a real driver, for all the ghastly gaiety of the face that had looked up to mine, and the levity of his pointing hand. I might possibly have fallen asleep soon after seeing him, and slumbered through the removal of the body and the departure of the hearse. So I did not speak of it to you.”

---

===Chinese===
「第二天早上吃早饭时，你那仆人并没有露面，我那天下午离开之前，也没有再见过他。我想，若是见到了，我准会把这一切都告诉你；可你也明白，我所见到的，仍可能是一辆真真切切的灵车、由一个真真切切的车夫赶着——尽管那张仰向我看的脸带着一种可怖的快活，尽管他那只手指点的手那样轻佻。我也许是在看见他之后没多久便睡着了，一路睡过了尸首的运走和灵车的离去。所以我没有跟你提起。」

---

===Original===
There was something wonderfully straightforward and prosaic in all this; here were no Jacobean houses oak-panelled and surrounded by weeping pine-trees, and somehow the very absence of suitable surroundings made the story more impressive. But for a moment a doubt assailed me.

“Don’t tell me it was all a dream,” I said.

“I don’t know whether it was or not. I can only say that I believe myself to have been wide awake. In any case the rest of the story is—odd.”

“I went out of town again that afternoon,” he continued, “and I may say that I don’t think that even for a moment did I get the haunting sense of what I had seen or dreamed that night out of my mind. It was present to me always as some vision unfulfilled. It was as if some clock had struck the four quarters, and I was still waiting to hear what the hour would be.

===Chinese===
这一切里头，有一种妙极了的直截了当与平淡无奇；这里头没有詹姆斯一世时代、镶着橡木护墙板、四周围绕着垂泪松树的宅子，而不知怎的，恰恰是这合宜氛围的缺席，反倒让故事更有慑人之力。可一时间，我也生出一丝疑虑。

「你莫告诉我那全是一场梦。」我说。

「我也不知道是不是。我只能说，我相信自己是彻彻底底地醒着的。无论如何，故事的下半截——是奇特的。」

「那天下午我又出了城，」他接着说，「我也可以说，那一夜我所见、所梦的，那萦绕不去的感觉，我自始至终一刻也没能把它从心头驱散过。它始终在我心头，像一桩尚未应验的异象。就仿佛某座钟已经敲过了那四个一刻钟，而我仍等着听它最终要敲出几点来。

===Original===
“Exactly a month afterwards I was in London again, but only for the day. I arrived at Victoria about eleven, and took the underground to Sloane Square in order to see if you were in town and would give me lunch. It was a baking hot morning, and I intended to take a bus from the King’s Road as far as Graeme Street. There was one standing at the corner just as I came out of the station, but I saw that the top was full, and the inside appeared to be full also. Just as I came up to it the conductor who, I suppose, had been inside, collecting fares or whatnot, came out on to the step within a few feet of me. He wore grey trousers, brown boots, a black coat buttoned, a straw hat, and over his shoulder was a strap on which hung his little machine for punching tickets. I saw his face, too; it was the face of the driver of the hearse, with a mole on the left cheek. Then he spoke to me, jerking his thumb over his shoulder.

“‘Just room for one inside, sir,’ he said.

“At that a sort of panic-terror took possession of me, and I knew I gesticulated wildly with my arms, and cried, ‘No, no!’ But at that moment I was living not in the hour that was then passing, but in that hour which had passed a month ago, when I leaned from the window of your bedroom here just before the dawn broke. At this moment too I knew that my spyhole had been opposite the spyhole into the spiritual world. What I had seen there had some significance, now being fulfilled, beyond the significance of the trivial happenings of today and tomorrow. The Powers of which we know so little were visibly working before me. And I stood there on the pavement shaking and trembling.

===Chinese===
「整整一个月之后，我又到了伦敦，可只待一天。十一点光景我到了维多利亚（Victoria），搭地铁到斯隆广场（Sloane Square），想看看你是不是在城里、能不能请我吃顿午饭。那是一个烤炉般酷热的上午，我打算从国王路（the King’s Road）搭一辆公共汽车到格雷姆街。我刚出地铁站，就有一辆停在拐角，可我看见顶层已经坐满了，里头看上去也坐满了。我正走到车跟前，那售票员——我想他刚才一直待在里头收车费什么的——便跨到了踏板上，离我不过几英尺。他穿着灰裤子、棕色的靴子，一件扣得严严的黑外衣，一顶草帽，肩头搭着一根带子，上头挂着那只打票的小机器。我也看清了他的脸；那正是那辆灵车车夫的脸，左边脸颊上有一颗痣。接着他便冲我开了口，把大拇指朝肩后一挑。

「『里头刚好还有一个空位，先生。』他说。

「这一来，一种惶乱如惊恐般的恐惧攫住了我，我知道自己两只胳膊狂乱地挥舞着，喊了出来：『不，不！』可那一刻，我所活在其中的，并非正在流逝的这个钟点，而是一个月以前那个已经过去了的钟点——那时我正从你这儿卧室的窗口探身出去，正是天将破未破之际。也是在这一刻，我明白过来：我那窥孔，正对着通向灵界的那个窥孔。我在那里所见到的，含有某种意义，如今正在应验，其意义远在今明两日那些琐碎小事的意义之上。我们所知甚少的那种种大能（the Powers），正在我眼前明明地运作着。而我便站在那人行道上，浑身发着抖、打着颤。

===Original===
“I was opposite the post-office at the corner, and just as the bus started my eye fell on the clock in the window there. I need not tell you what the time was.

“Perhaps I need not tell you the rest, for you probably conjecture it, since you will not have forgotten what happened at the corner of Sloane Square at the end of July, the summer before last. The bus pulled out from the pavement into the street in order to get round a van that was standing in front of it. At the moment there came down the King’s Road a big motor going at a hideously dangerous pace. It crashed full into the bus, burrowing into it as a gimlet burrows into a board.”

He paused.

“And that’s my story,” he said.

===Chinese===
「我正站在拐角那家邮局对面，就在那辆公共汽车启动的一刹那，我的目光落在了邮局窗里那只钟上。那时是几点，我用不着告诉你了。

「下面的事，或许我也用不着告诉你了，因为你多半已经猜到了——前年夏天七月底，在斯隆广场的拐角上出了什么事，你是不会忘的。那辆公共汽车从人行道边驶出、拐进街心，好绕过停在它前头的一辆运货车。就在那一刻，国王路上正驶来一辆大汽车，速度骇人地快、危险之极。它一头撞了个正着，钻进了公共汽车里，像一只手钻钻进一块木板那样。」

他停了停。

「这便是我的故事了。」他说。

## The Cat / 猫

===Original===
Many people will, doubtless, remember that exhibition at the Royal Academy, not so many seasons ago, which came to be known as Alingham's year, when Dick Alingham vaulted, with one bound, as it were, out of the crowd of strugglers and seated himself with admirably certain poise on the very topmost pinnacle of contemporary fame. He exhibited three portraits, each a masterpiece, which killed every picture within range. But since that year nobody cared anything for pictures whether in or out of range except those three, it did not signify so greatly. The phenomenon of his appearance was as sudden as that of the meteor, coming from nowhere and sliding large and luminous across the remote and star-sown sky, as inexplicable as the bursting of a spring on some dust-ridden rocky hillside. Some fairy godmother, one might conjecture, had bethought herself of her forgotten godson, and with a wave of her wand bestowed on him this transcendant gift. But, as the Irish say, she held her wand in her left hand, for her gift had another side to it. Or perhaps, again, Jim Merwick is right, and the theory he propounds in his monograph, "On certain obscure lesions of the nerve centres," says the final word on the subject.

Dick Alingham himself, as was indeed natural, was delighted with his fairy godmother or his obscure lesion (whichever was responsible), and (the monograph spoken of above was written after Dick's death) confessed frankly to his friend Merwick, who was still struggling through the crowd of rising young medical practitioners, that it was all quite as inexplicable to himself as it was to anyone else.

"All I know about it," he said, "is that last autumn I went through two months of mental depression so hideous that I thought again and again that I must go off my head. For hours daily, I sat here, waiting for something to crack, which as far as I am concerned would end everything. Yes, there was a cause; you know it."

===Chinese===
毫无疑问，许多人都会记得不多几个季度之前皇家艺术院（Royal Academy）的那次画展——那次画展后来被称作"阿林厄姆之年"，因为就在那一年，迪克·阿林厄姆（Dick Alingham）仿佛只一跃，便从那一群苦苦挣扎的人当中跳了出来，以令人叹服的、笃定从容的姿态，坐上了当今画坛那最高的巅峰。他展出了三幅肖像画，每一幅都是杰作，其光焰所及，令所有近旁的画作都黯然失色。不过，既然那一年除了那三幅之外，再没有人去关心任何画作——无论它们在不在光焰所及的范围之内——那么这一桩也就无关紧要了。他的横空出世，其突兀犹如一颗流星——不知从何处而来，硕大而明亮地划过那辽远而繁星密布的夜空；又如同一汪泉水在尘土满面的石山上汩汩涌出，全无从解释。人们或许会猜想，是某位仙母忽然想起了她那位被遗忘的教子，把魔杖一挥，将这份超凡的天赋赐给了他。然而，正如爱尔兰人所说，她这支魔杖是执于左手的，因为她所赠的礼物另有它的另一面。再不然，也许吉姆·默里克（Jim Merwick）是对的，他在专著《论神经中枢若干隐性损伤》（On certain obscure lesions of the nerve centres）里所阐述的学说，才对这件事下了最终的判词。

迪克·阿林厄姆本人，自然也对这位仙母或那处隐性的损伤（无论罪魁祸首是哪一位）满心欢喜，而且（前述的那部专著是在迪克死后才写成的）他向朋友默里克坦言，这一切对他自己而言，与对任何旁人一样，全然无从解释；而那时默里克还在一群扶摇直上的年轻医师当中苦苦挣扎。

「我对此所知道的全部，」他说，「就是去年秋天，我整整熬过了两个月那样的精神抑郁，情形可怖到了这般地步，以致我一再地想，自己怕是要发疯。每天我一连几个小时坐在这里，等着有什么东西裂开，一旦裂开，对我而言就一切完结。是的，事情自有缘由；你是知道的。」

===Original===
He paused a moment and poured into his glass a fairly liberal allowance of whisky, filled it half up from a syphon, and lit a cigarette. The cause, indeed, had no need to be enlarged on, for Merwick quite well remembered how the girl Dick had been engaged to, threw him over with an abruptness that was almost superb, when a more eligible suitor made his appearance. The latter was certainly very eligible indeed with his good looks, his title, and his million of money, and Lady Madingley﻿—ex-future Mrs. Alingham﻿—was perfectly content with what she had done. She was one of those blonde, lithe, silken girls who, happily for the peace of men's minds, are rather rare, and who remind one of some humanised yet celestial and bestial cat.

"I needn't speak of the cause," Dick continued, "but, as I say, for those two months I soberly thought that the only end to it would be madness. Then one evening when I was sitting here alone﻿—I was always sitting alone﻿—something did snap in my head. I know I wondered, without caring at all, whether this was the madness which I had been expecting, or whether (which would be preferable) some more fatal breakage had happened. And even while I wondered, I was aware that I was not depressed or unhappy any longer."

He paused for so long in a smiling retrospect that Merwick indicated to him that he had a listener.

"Well?" he said.

"It was well indeed. I haven't been unhappy since. I have been riotously happy instead. Some divine doctor, I suppose, just wiped off that stain on my brain that hurt so. Heavens, how it hurt! Have a drink, by the way?"

"No, thanks," said Merwick. "But what has all this got to do with your painting?"

"Why, everything. For I had hardly realised the fact that I was happy again, when I was aware that everything looked different. The colours of all I saw were twice as vivid as they had been, shape and outline were intensified too. The whole visible world had been dusty and blurred before, and seen in a half light. But now the lights were turned up, and there was a new heaven and a new earth. And in the same flash, I knew that I could paint things as I saw them. Which," he concluded, "I have done."

===Chinese===
他停了片刻，往杯子里倒了颇为慷慨的一份威士忌，又用苏打水瓶兑上半杯，然后点燃一支烟。事情的原委其实不必赘述，因为默里克记得很清楚：迪克原先与之订婚的那位姑娘，在一位条件更优的求婚者出现时，以一种近乎绝妙的果决把他一脚踢开了。后面这一位条件的确优越至极——貌美、有头衔、家财百万——而马丁利夫人（Lady Madingley），也就是前准阿林厄姆太太（ex-future Mrs. Alingham），对自己所做之事完全心安理得。她是那种金发、柔软、绸缎般光滑的女子，所幸于男人心境的安宁而言并不多见，令人联想到一只既有人性、又带着神性与兽性的猫。

「缘由我就不必细说了，」迪克接着道，「可正如我刚才所言，那两个月里我认真地想过，结局只会是发疯。后来有一天傍晚，我又独自坐在这里——我总是独自坐着——我脑子里当真有什么东西啪地断了。我记得自己当时满不在乎地纳闷，这究竟是不是我一直等候着的那种发疯，抑或（倒还更可取些）发生了某种更为致命的崩裂。可就在我这么纳闷的工夫，我便发觉自己再也不抑郁、再也不会不快活了。」

他面带笑意地久久沉浸于回想，默里克只好出声提醒他，自己还在听着。

「怎么样？」默里克问。

「结果是再好不过。从那以后我再没有不快活过。倒不如说，我快活得简直要飞上天去。我想，是哪位神医把我脑中那块伤人的污渍擦掉了。老天，那东西可真伤人！对了，来一杯吗？」

「不，谢谢，」默里克说，「可你说的这些和你的绘画又有什么相干？」

「嗳，全都相干。因为就在我意识到自己重又快活起来的那一刻，我便觉察到万事万物看起来都不一样了。我所见的一切，色彩都鲜明了一倍，形状与轮廓也愈发分明起来。整个可见的世界从前是蒙着灰、模糊不清的，仿佛只在半明半暗的光里。可如今灯一下全亮了，便有了新天新地。而就在同一道闪光里，我明白自己能把我所见的画下来了。」他顿了一顿，总结道，「我也就是这么做的。」

===Original===
There was something rather sublime about this, and Merwick laughed.

"I wish something would snap in my brain, if it kindles the perceptions in that way," said he, "but it is just possible that the snapping of things in one's brain does not always produce just that effect."

"That is possible. Also, as I gather, things don't snap unless you have gone through some such hideous period as I have been through. And I tell you frankly that I wouldn't go through that again even to ensure a snap that would make me see things like Titian."

"What did the snapping feel like?" asked Merwick.

Dick considered a moment.

"Do you know when a parcel comes, tied up with string, and you can't find a knife," he said, "and therefore you burn the string through, holding it taut? Well, it was like that: quite painless, only something got weaker and weaker, and then parted, softly without effort. Not very lucid, I'm afraid, but it was just like that. It had been burning a couple of months, you see."

===Chinese===
这话里多少带着一点近乎壮丽的味道，默里克不由笑了。

「但愿我脑子里也能有什么东西断上一断，要是能这般点燃人的感觉的话，」他说，「只不过，脑子里这种『断裂』之事，未必就总是恰好产生这种效果。」

「那倒是可能的。而且，据我所知，除非先熬过我所经历过的那种可怖时日，否则这些东西是不会断的。而且我坦白告诉你，即便能换得一种让我看东西如提香（Titian）般的断裂，我也不愿再把那一切从头经历一遍。」

「那断裂是什么感觉？」默里克问。

迪克想了想。

「你知道的，有时寄来一个包裹，用绳子捆着，你又找不到刀子，」他说，「于是你便把绳子绷紧，用火把它烧断。对，就像那样：一点也不疼，只是有什么东西越绷越弱，随后便轻轻地、毫不费力地分开了。恐怕我说得不够明白，可就是这种感觉。你也看到了，那绳子已经烧了两个月了。」

===Original===
He turned away and hunted among the letters and papers which littered his writing-table till he found an envelope with a coronet on it. He chuckled to himself as he took it up.

"Commend me to Lady Madingley," he said, "for a brazen impudence in comparison with which brass is softer than putty. She wrote to me yesterday, asking me if I would finish the portrait I had begun of her last year, and let her have it at my own price."

"Then I think you have had a lucky escape," remarked Merwick, "I suppose you didn't even answer her."

"Oh, yes, I did: why not? I said the price would be two thousand pounds, and I was ready to go on at once. She has agreed, and sent me a cheque for a thousand this evening."

Merwick stared at him in blank astonishment. "Are you mad?" he asked.

"I hope not, though one can never be sure about little points like that. Even doctors like you don't know exactly what constitutes madness."

===Chinese===
他转过身去，在摊得凌乱的写字台上那一堆信件和文件里翻找，直到找出一封印有冠冕纹章的信封。他拿起信封，自顾自地轻笑起来。

「马丁利夫人那种厚颜无耻，」他说，「真叫人叹为观止——和她一比，黄铜都软得像油灰了。她昨天写信给我，问我肯不肯把去年动笔为她画的那幅肖像画完，价钱由我自己定。」

「那么我想，你能从那场祸事里全身而退，倒是万幸了，」默里克说，「我猜你根本没回她的信。」

「嗳，回了，怎么不回？我说价钱是两千镑，并且随时可以动笔。她已经答应了，今天傍晚还给我寄来了一张一千镑的支票。」

默里克瞠目结舌地盯着他。「你疯了吗？」他问。

「但愿没有罢，不过这种小问题谁也说不准。连你这样的医生，也未必确切知道构成发疯的究竟是什么。」

===Original===
Merwick got up.

"But is it possible that you don't see what a terrible risk you run?" he asked. "To see her again, to be with her like that, having to look at her﻿—I saw her this afternoon by the way, hardly human﻿—may not that so easily revive again all that you felt before? It is too dangerous: much too dangerous."

Dick shook his head.

"There is not the slightest risk," he said, "everything within me is utterly and absolutely indifferent to her. I don't even hate her: if I hated her there might be a possibility of my again loving her. As it is, the thought of her does not arouse in me any emotion of any kind. And really such stupendous calmness deserves to be rewarded. I respect colossal things like that."

He finished his whisky as he spoke, and instantly poured himself out another glass.

"That's the fourth," said his friend.

"Is it? I never count. It shows a sordid attention to uninteresting detail. Funnily enough too, alcohol does not have the smallest effect on me now."

"Why drink then?"

"Because if I give it up this entrancing vividness of colour and clarity of outline is a little diminished."

"Can't be good for you," said the doctor.

Dick laughed.

"My dear fellow, look at me carefully," he said, "and then if you can conscientiously declare that I show any signs of indulging in stimulants, I'll give them up altogether."

===Chinese===
默里克站了起来。

「可你难道看不出，自己正在冒多大的险吗？」他问，「要再见她，要这样和她相处，不得不凝视着她——顺便说一句，今天下午我也见到了她，简直不像是一个人——这不就轻而易举地会把你从前那些感受都重新勾起来吗？太危险了：太危险了。」

迪克摇了摇头。

「没有半分危险，」他说，「我心里对她已是彻头彻尾、绝对地无动于衷。我连恨都不恨她：要是我还恨她，倒说不定还会有再爱她的可能。如今一想到她，我心里勾不起任何一种情绪。说真的，这般惊人的冷静，是理当有所回报的。我敬佩这种了不起的东西。」

他说着把威士忌一饮而尽，紧接着又给自己斟满了一杯。

「这已经是第四杯了。」他的朋友说。

「是吗？我从不计数。计数反映出一种对无趣细节的斤斤计较，未免俗气。说来也怪，如今酒精对我连一丁点作用都没有。」

「那又何必喝？」

「因为一旦戒了，这种令人着迷的色彩之鲜活、轮廓之清晰，便会稍稍减色。」

「对你不会是好事情。」医生说。

迪克笑了起来。

「亲爱的朋友，你仔细瞧瞧我，」他说，「然后，要是你能凭良心说我有半分纵饮的迹象，我就从此戒掉。」

===Original===
Certainly it would have been hard to find a point in which Dick did not present the appearance of perfect health. He had paused, and stood still a moment, his glass in one hand, the whisky-bottle in the other, black against the front of his shirt, and not a tremor of unsteadiness was there. His face of wholesome sunburnt hue was neither puffy nor emaciated, but firm of flesh and of a wonderful clearness of skin. Clear too was his eye, with eyelids neither baggy nor puckered; he looked indeed a model of condition, hard and fit, as if he was in training for some athletic event. Lithe and active too was his figure, his movements were quick and precise, and even Merwick, with his doctor's eye, trained to detect any symptom, however slight, in which the drinker must betray himself, was bound to confess that no such was here present. His appearance contradicted it authoritatively, so also did his manner; he met the eye of the man he was talking to without sideway glances; he showed no signs however small, of any disorder of the nerves. Yet Dick was altogether an abnormal fellow; the history he had just been recounting was abnormal, those weeks of depression, followed by the sudden snap in his brain which had apparently removed, as a wet cloth removes a stain, all the memory of his love, and of the cruel bitterness that resulted from it. Abnormal too was his sudden leap into high artistic achievement from a past of very mediocre performance. Why should there then not be a similar abnormality here?

"Yes, I confess you show no sign of taking excessive stimulant," said Merwick, "but if I attended you professionally﻿—ah, I'm not touting﻿—I should make you give up all stimulant, and go to bed for a month."

"Why in the name of goodness?" asked Dick.

"Because, theoretically, it must be the best thing you could do. You had a shock, how severe, the misery of those weeks of depression tells you. Well, common sense says, 'Go slow after a shock; recoup.' Instead of which you go very fast indeed and produce. I grant it seems to suit you; you also became suddenly capable of feats which﻿—oh, it's sheer nonsense, man."

"What's sheer nonsense?"

"You are. Professionally, I detest you, because you appear to be an exception to a theory that I am sure must be right. Therefore I have got to explain you away, and at present I can't."

"What's the theory?" asked Dick.

"Well, the treatment of shock first of all. And secondly, that in order to do good work, one ought to eat and drink very little and sleep a lot. How long do you sleep by the way?"

Dick considered.

"Oh, I go to bed about three usually," he said; "I suppose I sleep for about four hours."

"And live on whisky, and eat like a Strasburg goose, and are prepared to run a race tomorrow. Go away, or at least I will. Perhaps you'll break down, though. That would satisfy me. But even if you don't, it still remains quite interesting."

===Chinese===
确实，要找出迪克有哪一点不像个十足康健的人，倒是一件难事。他停下话头，静静地站了一会儿，一手举杯，一手持瓶，那瓶子映在他衬衫前襟上黑黝黝的，手却稳得不颤分毫。他的脸晒成健康的色泽，既不虚胖也不消瘦，肌肉结实，肤色异常清润。他的眼睛也是清明的，眼皮既不松弛也不起皱；他看上去确是康健的典范，结实而精干，仿佛正在为某项运动赛事做着训练。他的身姿灵活矫健，动作敏捷而精准，就连默里克以一双训练有素、专能从纵酒者身上察觉哪怕最细微症状的医生之眼，也不得不承认，此处毫无此类征象。他的外表断然否定了这一点，他的神态亦然；他与交谈的对方目光相接，从不躲闪游移；他没有任何神经错乱的迹象，连最小的也没有。然而迪克整个就是个反常之人；他方才所述的那段经历本身就是反常的——那几周的抑郁，继之以脑中那一下突如其来的崩断，仿佛一块湿布抹去一处污渍，竟将他全部恋情的记忆连同随之而来的刻骨酸楚一并抹掉了。他从以往平庸的画作里一跃而臻于这般高超的艺术造诣，这同样反常。那么，此处为何不能有同样的反常呢？
