“Well, the accident happened at night,” he said. “I don’t know the rules, but that may have some bearing on it, I should think.”

I had one question more in the back of my mind, but I did not like to ask it. At least, I wanted information on this subject without appearing to ask for it.

“Neither do I know the rules of motors,” I said; “and I don’t understand you when you say that Guy Elphinstone’s machine was an irritable, cross-grained brute, that liked running over chickens and rabbits. But I think you subsequently said that the irritability may have been the irritability of its owner. Did he mind being checked?”

“It made him blind-mad if it happened often,” said Harry. “I shall never forget a drive I had with him once: there were hay-carts and perambulators every hundred yards. It was perfectly ghastly; it was like being with a madman. And when we got inside his gate, his dog came running out to meet him. He did not go an inch out of his course: it was worse than that—he went for it, just grinding his teeth with rage. I never drove with him again.”

He stopped a moment, guessing what might be in my mind. “I say, you mustn’t think—you mustn’t think—” he began.

“No, of course not,” said I.

===Chinese===
我不得不说，这对我是一种全新的见解，而且越想越觉得它在理。因为绝大多数人，凡借以感知灵界（我认定那灵界就浓密地、熙攘地萦绕在我们周围）的种种玄秘感官，都仿佛被封住了；换言之，绝大多数人根本从未听见过、也从未看见过鬼魂。那么，剩下的那一小部分人——也就是果真有过、或可能有玄秘经历的人——其中能将所有感官全都开启的，岂不是寥寥无几？难道不是有些人的耳是开通的，另一些人的眼是开通的——有些人能通灵耳，有些人能开天眼？

「是，我觉得这话在理，」我说，「你不能带我上那儿去看看吗？」

「当然成！你要是肯留到星期五，我就星期四带你过去。那天别人都走了，咱们可以等天黑以后赶到那儿。」

我摇摇头。「我怕是留不到星期五，」我说，「我星期四非走不可。可明天怎么样？咱们去亨斯坦顿来回的路上，顺道过去一趟不行吗？」

「不成；那要绕出去三十英里。再说，要天黑以后赶到伯彻姆，就意味着我们回到这儿得是半夜了。而作为招待客人的主人——」

「啊！这些东西只有天黑以后才听得见、看得见，是吗？」我问，「那可就无趣多了。这好比一场把所有灯都熄了的降神会。」

「嗳，那场祸事本来就是夜里出的，」他说，「这里的规矩我弄不清，可我想，这一点或许和它有些关系。」

我心里还藏着另一个问题，却不大好意思问出口。至少，我想就这个题目探得一点消息，却又不愿显得是在探问。

「汽车的规矩我也不懂，」我说，「你说盖伊·埃尔芬斯通那部机器是一头暴躁、乖戾的畜生，爱从鸡呀兔呀身上碾过去，这话我也不大明白。可我想你后来又说了，那暴躁或许是其主人的暴躁。他受不了被人拦阻吗？」

「这种事要是多了，能叫他气得发狂，」哈里说，「我永远忘不了有一回坐他的车：每隔一百码就是运草车和婴儿车。那真是可怕极了；就像跟一个疯子在一起。等我们进了他庄园的大门，他的狗跑出来迎他。他连一寸路都不肯让：不，比不让还糟——他直冲着它碾过去，一边气得咬牙切齿。从那以后，我再没坐过他的车。」

他停了片刻，猜到了我心里可能在想什么。「我说，你可千万别以为——千万别以为——」他开口道。

「自然，当然不会。」我说。

===Original===
Harry Combe-Martin’s house stood close to the weather-eaten, sandy cliffs of the Suffolk shore, which are being incessantly gnawed away by the hunger of the insatiable sea. Fathoms deep below it, and now many hundred yards out, lies what was once the second port in England; but now of the ancient town of Dunwich, and of its seven great churches, nothing remains but one, and that ruinous and already half destroyed by the falling cliff and the encroachments of the sea. Foot by foot, it too is disappearing, and of the graveyard which surrounded it more than half is gone, so that from the face of the sandy cliff on which it stands there stick out like straws in glass, as Dante says, the bones of those who were once committed there to the kindly and stable earth.

Whether it was the remembrance of this rather grim spectacle as I had seen it that afternoon, or whether Harry’s story had caused some trouble in my brain, or whether it was merely that the keen bracing air of this place, to one who had just come from the sleepy languor of the Norfolk Broads, kept me sleepless, I do not know; but, anyhow, the moment I put out my light that night and got into bed, I felt that all the footlights and gas-jets in the internal theatre of my mind sprang into flame, and that I was very vividly and alertly awake. It was in vain that I counted a hundred forwards and a hundred backwards, that I pictured to myself a flock of visionary sheep coming singly through a gap in an imaginary hedge, and tried to number their monotonous and uniform countenances, that I played noughts and crosses with myself, that I marked out scores of double lawn-tennis courts—for with each repetition of these supposedly soporific exercises I only became more intensely wakeful. It was not in remote hope of sleep that I continued to repeat these weary performances long after their inefficacy was proved to the hilt, but because I was strangely unwilling in this timeless hour of the night to think about those protruding relics of humanity; also I quite distinctly did not desire to think about that subject with regard to which I had, a few hours ago, promised Harry that I would not make it the subject of reflection. For these reasons I continued during the black hours to practise these narcotic exercises of the mind, knowing well that if I paused on the tedious treadmill my thoughts, like some released spring, would fly back to rather gruesome subjects. I kept my mind, in fact, talking loud to itself, so that it should not hear what other voices were saying.

Then by degrees these absurd mental occupations became impossible; my mind simply refused to occupy itself with them any longer; and next moment I was thinking intently and eagerly, not about the bones protruding from the gnawed section of sand-cliff, but about the subject I had said I would not dwell upon. And like a flash it came upon me why Harry had bidden me not think about it. Surely in order that I should not come to the same conclusion as he had come to.

===Chinese===
哈里·康伯-马丁的宅子紧挨着萨福克郡（Suffolk）海岸那被风蚀的沙崖，而那沙崖正被贪婪无厌的大海一刻不停地啃噬着。在它深处几英寻之下、如今已在好几英百码之外的海里，埋着昔日英格兰第二大港的遗址；可如今，古老的邓维奇（Dunwich）城和它那七座大教堂，只剩下一座，且已倾颓，早被坍塌的崖壁和步步进逼的大海毁去了一半。这一座也在一寸一寸地消失，环绕着它的墓地已有大半塌去了，于是，正如但丁所言，恍如插在玻璃中的稻草一般，那些曾被人交付给这仁慈而安稳的泥土的逝者的骸骨，便从它所矗立的沙崖崖面上森森地伸出来。

不知是因为我还记着那天下午见过的这阴森森的一幕，还是因为哈里的故事在我脑子里搅起了某种不安，抑或仅仅是因为此地的空气凛冽提神，对一个刚从诺福克湖区（the Norfolk Broads）那昏沉困倦的氛围里来的人而言，教人难以成眠——我弄不清究竟是哪个；但无论如何，那天夜里我一熄灯上床，便觉得自己内心那座戏台上的所有脚灯和煤气灯一齐燃了起来，我清醒得很，而且清醒得异常鲜明警觉。我从一数到一百、再从一百倒数到一，我设想有一群虚幻的绵羊一只接一只地从一道 imaginary 的篱笆缺口里钻过来，试图去数它们那千篇一律的面孔，我和自己玩圈叉棋，我在脑海里画出几十片双打的网球场——这些全都是白费劲；因为这些据说是催眠的操练每重复一遍，我反倒更加清醒。我在它们的无效已被证明得淋漓尽致之后，仍长久地重复这些乏味的动作，早已不是指望还能睡着，而是因为在这不知时辰的黑夜里，我莫名地不愿去想那些伸出来的先人的遗骨；同时，我也十分清楚地不愿意去想那个题目——几个小时前，我曾就它向哈里答应过，不以它为思量的对象。由于这些缘故，我在几个黑漆漆的钟头里一味地做着这些麻醉心神的操练，因为我心里明白，只要在这乏味的人行踏车上一停，我的思绪便会如同一根松开的弹簧，嗖地弹回到那些颇可怖的事情上去。说到底，我是让自己的心不停地高声自说自话，好叫它听不见别的声音在说什么。

后来，渐渐地，这些荒唐的心智营生变得再也做不下去了；我的心干脆拒绝再以此自娱；下一刻，我已专心致志、心急火燎地想了起来——想的不是从被啃掉的沙崖断面上伸出来的那些骸骨，而是我说过不去细想的那个题目。一道闪电似的，我猛地明白了哈里为何嘱咐我不要去想它。那自然是为了让我不至于得出他所得到的那个结论。

===Original===
Now the whole question of “haunt”—haunted spots, haunted houses, and so forth—has always seemed to me to be utterly unsolved, and to be neither proved nor disproved to a satisfactory degree. From the earliest times, certainly from the earliest known Egyptian records, there has been a belief that the scene of a crime is often revisited, sometimes by the spirit of him who has committed it—seeking rest, we must suppose, and finding none; sometimes, and more inexplicably, by the spirit of his victim, crying perhaps, like the blood of Abel, for vengeance. And though the stories of these village gossips in the alehouse about noiseless visions and invisible noises were all as yet unsifted and unreliable, yet I could not help wondering if they (such as they were) pointed to something authentic and to be classed under this head of appearances. But more striking than the yarns of the gaffers seemed to me the questions of the lodge-keeper’s children. How should children have imagined the figure of a child that would not speak to them or play with them? Perhaps it was a real child, a sulky child. Yes—perhaps. But perhaps not. Then after this preliminary skirmish I found myself settling down to the question that I had said I would not think about; in other words, the possible origin of these phenomena interested me more than the phenomena themselves. For what exactly had Guy Elphinstone, that savage driver, done? Had or had not the death of the child been entirely an accident, a thing (given he drove a motor at all) outside his own control? Or had he, irritated beyond endurance at the checks and delays of the day, not pulled up when it was just possible he might have, but had run over the child as he would have run over a rabbit or a hen, or even his own dog? And what, in any case, poor wretched brute, must have been his thoughts in that terrible instant that intervened between the child’s death and his own, when a moment later he smashed into the closed gates of his own lodge? Was remorse his—bitter, despairing contrition? That could hardly have been so; or else surely, knowing only for certain that he had knocked a child down, he would have stopped; he would have done his best, whatever that might be, to repair the irreparable harm. But he had not stopped: he had gone on, it seemed, at full speed, for on the collision the car had been smashed into matchwood and steel shavings. Again, with double force, had this dreadful thing been a complete accident, he would have stopped. So then—most terrible question of all—had he, after making murder, rushed on to what proved to be his own death, filled with some hellish glee at what he had done? Indeed, as in the churchyard on the cliff, bones of the buried stuck starkly out into the night.

---

The pale tired light of earliest morning had turned the window-blinds into glimmering squares before I slept; and when I woke, the servant who called me was already rattling them briskly up on their rollers, and letting the calm serenity of the August day stream into the room. Through the open windows poured in sunlight and sea-wind, the scent of flowers and the song of birds; and each and all were wonderfully reassuring, banishing the hooded forms that had haunted the night, and I thought of the disquietude of the dark hours as a traveller may think of the billows and tempests of the ocean over which he has safely journeyed, unable, now that they belong to the limbo of the past, to recall his qualms and tossings with any vivid uneasiness. Not without a feeling of relief, too, did I dwell on the knowledge that I was definitely not going to visit this equivocal spot. Our drive today, as Harry had said, would not take us within thirty miles of it, and tomorrow I but went to the station and away. Though a thorough-paced seeker after truth might, no doubt, have regretted that the laws of time and space did not permit him to visit Bircham after the sinister dark had fallen, and test whether for him there was visible or audible truth in the tales of the village gossips, I was conscious of no such regret. Bircham and its fables had given me a very bad night, and I was perfectly aware that I did not in the least want to go near it, though yesterday I had quite truthfully said I should like to do so. In this brightness, too, of sun and sea-wind I felt none of the malaise at my waking moments which a sleepless night usually gives me; I felt particularly well, particularly pleased to be alive, and also, as I have said, particularly content not to be going to Bircham. I was quite satisfied to leave my curiosity unsatisfied.

===Chinese===
说到「闹鬼」这整个题目——闹鬼的所在、闹鬼的宅子等等——在我看向来是完全未曾解开的，既没有得到令人信服的证实，也没有得到令人信服的反证。从最古的时候起，至少从已知最早的埃及记载起，便流传着一种信念：一桩罪案发生的地点，往往会被人重新造访，有时是凶手亡魂的造访——我们只能设想它是在寻一处安息而不可得；有时——这更费解——是受害者亡魂的造访，也许正像亚伯的血那样，哭喊着要报仇。虽说酒馆里那些村人嚼舌的种种关于无声之幻影、无形之响动的传闻，都还没有经过筛检、不足凭信，我仍不禁要琢磨：它们（就其本身而言）是否指向某种真实的东西，可以归入这一类显灵的异象之下。然而，在我看来，比老头儿们的种种传闻更触目的，是那看门人的几个孩子提出的问题。孩子们怎么会凭空想象出一个不肯跟他们说话、也不肯跟他们玩耍的小孩的身影来呢？也许那是个真孩子，一个脾气的别扭孩子。是——也许。但也也许不是。这般略一交锋之后，我发觉自己已不知不觉地沉到了那个我说过不去想的题目里；换言之，这些异象可能的成因，比异象本身更勾起了我的兴致。因为，盖伊·埃尔芬斯通那个暴烈的驾车人，到底做了什么？那孩子的死，究竟是不是一桩完完全全的意外，一桩（既然他开着汽车）他无力左右的事？还是他因那一整天被人拦阻、延误而忍耐到了极限，在明明还来得及的时候没有踩下刹车，而是像碾过一只兔子、一只母鸡、甚至他自己的狗那样，碾过了那孩子？而无论如何，那可怜又可鄙的畜生，在孩子已死、他自己尚有一瞬可活的那个可怖的刹那——紧接着他便一头撞上了自家门房那两扇紧闭的大门——他心里想的，会是什么？是悔恨吗——苦痛欲绝的痛悔？可那不大像；否则，他既然只确知自己撞倒了一个孩子，总该停下车来；他总该竭尽所能，无论那能耐多么有限，去弥补这无可弥补的伤害。可他没有停：他似乎一路全速冲了下去，因为相撞之时，那车已被撞成了火柴杆和钢刨花。再者，倘若这可怕的事纯属意外，他更会——以加倍的把握——停下来。那么——这是所有问题中最可怕的一个——他究竟是不是在犯下了杀人之后，带着某种地狱般的得意，冲向了那后来证明是他自己葬身之地的所在？当真，一如崖上那座墓园，埋葬者的骸骨森森地伸进了夜色里。

---

临到入睡，已是清晨那一线疲惫的惨白微光把窗帘映成了微微发亮的方格；待我醒来，叫我起床的仆人已在哗啦啦地把窗帘卷上辊去，让八月那一日宁静的晴和涌进房里。阳光与海风、花香与鸟啼从敞开的窗口一齐涌入；这一切都无比地令人安心，把夜里作祟的那些蒙头盖脸的身影驱赶一空。我回想起黑夜里那份不安，就像一个旅人回望他已安全驶过的怒海狂涛——它们既已归入往昔的虚无，便再也不能勾起他任何真切的惶恐与颠簸了。而一想到我确实不会去造访那个暧昧的所在，我也不无如释重负之感。正如哈里所说，我们今天的行程，连离它三十英里之内的路都不会走，而明天我不过是去火车站、一走了之。一个彻头彻尾的求真者，固然可能会遗憾时间和空间的法则不容他在那不祥的黑夜降临之后亲赴伯彻姆，去验证村里的种种风传于他是否有可见可闻的真凭实据；我却并无这种遗憾。伯彻姆和它的种种传说已害我熬过一个极糟的夜晚，我心知肚明，自己压根儿不想走近它，尽管昨天我确曾十分诚恳地说过我想去。在这一片日光的明媚与海风的清朗里，我也没有尝到通常一夜无眠之后在醒来时刻所感到的那种不适；我觉得分外康健，分外觉得活着是件快活事，而且，如我所说，分外心满意足于自己不去伯彻姆。我倒宁可让自己的这份好奇心得不到满足。

===Original===
The motor came round about eleven, and we started at once, Harry and Mrs. Morrison, a cousin of his, sitting behind in the big back seat, large enough to hold a comfortable three, and I on the left of the driver, in a sort of trance—I am not ashamed to confess it—of expectancy and delight. For this was in the early days of motors, when there was still the sense of romance and adventure round them. I did not want to drive, any more than Harry wanted to; for driving, so I hold, is too absorbing; it takes the attention in too firm a grip: the mania of the true motorist is not consciously enjoyed. For the passion for motors is a taste—I had almost said a gift—as distinct and as keenly individual as the passion for music or mathematics. Those who use motors most (merely as a means of getting rapidly from one place to another) are often entirely without it, while those whom adverse circumstances (over which they have no control) compel to use them least may have it to a supreme degree. To those who have it, analysis of their passion is perhaps superfluous; to those who have it not, explanation is almost unintelligible. Pace, however, and the control of pace, and above all the sensuous consciousness of pace, is at the root of it; and pleasure in pace is common to most people, whether it be in the form of a galloping horse, or the pace of the skate hissing over smooth ice, or the pace of a freewheel bicycle humming downhill, or, more impersonally, the pace of the smashed ball at lawn-tennis, the driven ball at golf, or the low boundary hit at cricket. But the sensuous consciousness of pace, as I have said, is needful: one might experience it seated in front of the engine of an express train, though not in a wadded, shut-windowed carriage, where the wind of movement is not felt. Then add to this rapture of the rush through riven air the knowledge that huge relentless force is controlled by a little lever, and directed by a little wheel on which the hands of the driver seem to lie so negligently. A great untamed devil has there his bridle, and he answers to it, as Harry had said, like a horse with a fine mouth. He has hunger and thirst, too, unslakeable, and greedily he laps of his soup of petrol which turns to fire in his mouth: electricity, the force that rends clouds asunder, and causes towers to totter, is the spoon with which he feeds himself; and as he eats he races onward, and the road opens like torn linen in front of him. Yet how obedient, how amenable is he!—for with a touch on his snaffle his speed is redoubled, or melts into thin air, so that before you know you have touched the rein he has exchanged his swallow-flight for a mere saunter through the lanes. But he ever loves to run; and knowing this, you will bid him lift up his voice and tell those who are in his path that he is coming, so that he will not need the touch that checks. Hoarse and jovial is his voice, hooting to the wayfarer; and if his hooting be not heard he has a great guttural falsetto scream that leaps from octave to octave, and echoes from the hedges that are passing in blurred lines of hanging green. And, as you go, the romantic isolation of divers in deep seas is yours; masked and hooded companions may be near you also, in their driving-dress for this plunge through the swift tides of air; but you, like them, are alone and isolated, conscious only of the ripped ribbon of road, the two great lantern-eyes of the wonderful monster that look through drooped eyelids by day, but gleam with fire by night, the two earlaps of splashboards, and the long lean bonnet in front which is the skull and brain-case of that swift, untiring energy that feeds on fire, and whirls its two tons of weight up hill and down dale, as if some new law as everlasting as gravity, and like gravity making it go ever swifter, was its sole control.

For the first hour the essence of these joys, any description of which compared to the real thing is but as a stagnant pond compared to the bright rushing of a mountain stream, was mine. A straight switchback road lay in front of us, and the monster plunged silently down hill, and said below his breath, “Ha-ha—ha-ha—ha-ha,” as, without diminution of speed, he breasted the opposing slope. In my control were his great vocal chords (for in those days hooter and siren were on the driver’s left, and lay convenient to the hand of him who occupied the box-seat), and it rejoiced me to let him hoot to a pony-cart, three hundred yards ahead, with a hand on his falsetto scream if his ordinary tones of conversation were unheard or disregarded. Then came a road crossing ours at right angles, and the dear monster seemed to say, “Yes, yes—see how obedient and careful I am. I stroll with my hands in my pockets.” Then again a puppy from a farmhouse staggered warlike into the road, and the monster said, “Poor little chap! get home to your mother, or I’ll talk to you in earnest.” The poor little chap did not take the hint, so the monster slackened speed and just said, “Whoof!” Then it chuckled to itself as the puppy scuttled into the hedge, seriously alarmed; and next moment our self-made wind screeched and whistled round us again.

===Chinese===
十一点光景汽车开了过来，我们立刻动身，哈里和他的一位表亲莫里森太太（Mrs. Morrison）坐在后面那个大后座上——那座位宽宽敞敞，舒舒服服坐得下三个人——我则坐在司机左首，处于一种满怀期待与欢愉的恍惚之中——我并不讳言这一点。因为那时还是汽车的早年，围绕着它们的，仍是浪漫与冒险的气息。我无意亲自驾驶，正如哈里也无意；因为依我看，开车太叫人全神贯注了；它把人的注意力攥得太紧：真正的汽车狂所沉迷的那份狂热，本人是并不曾自觉享受的。原来对汽车的这份痴迷，是一种趣味——我几乎要说是一种禀赋——它与对音乐或数学的痴迷同样泾渭分明、同样因人而异。那些最常使用汽车的人（仅仅把它当作从一处快速赶到另一处的工具），往往全无这份痴迷；而那些因境遇不顺（且是不由自主的境遇）而最少能使用它的人，倒可能把这份痴迷发展到了极致。对有此痴迷的人，分析这份痴迷或许纯属多余；对没有的人，解释又近乎对牛弹琴。然而，速度，对速度的驾驭，尤其是对速度的那种感官上的自觉，才是它的根本所在；而速度带来的快感，是大多数人都共有的，无论这速度是疾驰的骏马、冰鞋在光洁冰面上嗤嗤滑过的速度、自由飞轮的自行车下坡时嗡嗡作响的速度，抑或更身外一些的，网球中那一记重扣的速度、高尔夫中那一记抽球的速度，或板球中贴地飞出的边界球的速度。然而如我所说，对速度的感官上的自觉是必不可少的：一个人也许可以坐在特快列车车头前体会到它，却断不能在一间四壁贴满软垫、车窗紧闭、感受不到行进之风的车厢里体会到它。那么，再给这劈风疾行的狂喜添上这么一层心思：一股庞大而无情的伟力，只凭一根小小的操纵杆去节制，只凭一只小小的方向盘去驾驭——而驾车人的双手搁在那方向盘上，看着是何等漫不经心。一头未被驯服的伟魔，衔着的便是这样一副嚼子，而它之听命于这副嚼子，正如哈里所说，像一匹嘴嫩的骏马。它还有着无法解的饥渴，贪婪地啜着它的汽油浓汤，那汤一进它口便化作烈火：电——那能撕开乌云、能叫高塔摇摇欲坠的力量——是它喂自己吃饭的汤匙；它一边吃，一边向前飞奔，道路在它面前如被撕裂的亚麻布一般豁然展开。可它又是何等驯服、何等听命！——因为只在它的小嚼子上轻轻一触，它的速度便加倍，或者化为乌有，以致你还没意识到自己碰了缰绳，它已把燕子的飞掠换成了在小路上信步闲逛。可它素来爱跑；你既知道这一点，便会吩咐它扬起嗓门，告诉挡在道上的人它来了，这样就用不着那叫停的一触。它的嗓门粗哑而欢快，一路向行人鸣着喇叭；倘若它的鸣号无人理会，它还有一串洪亮的、喉音的假声尖叫，一个八度一个八度地往上蹿，从一道道在模糊的绿色垂帘中飞掠而过的树篱间撞出回声。而一路上，你便拥有了深海潜水者那种浪漫的孤独；蒙着脸、戴着兜帽的同伴也许就在你身畔，穿着他们为这趟穿越湍急气流的潜行而备的车装；可你和他们一样，是孤独而隔绝的，所意识的不过是那条被撕裂的缎带般的道路，那头神异巨兽两只硕大的灯笼般的眼睛——白日里透过低垂的眼睑向外张望，夜里则灼灼地射出火光，那两片挡泥板的「耳朵」，还有前面那只修长的车头罩——那便是这以火为食、不知疲倦的迅疾伟力的头骨与脑颅，这伟力载着它两吨重的身躯翻山越岭，仿佛有某条与万有引力一般亘古、且和引力一样使它越跑越快的新定律，是它唯一的制衡。

头一个钟头里，上述种种快意的精髓，尽归我所有——任何文字上的描摹较之实物，都不过是死水一潭比之山涧的清流奔泻而已。我们面前是一条起起伏伏的直路，那巨兽无声地俯冲下山，又在下头压低嗓门自语着「哈—哈—哈—哈—哈—哈」，毫无减速地迎着对面的上坡冲了上去。它那副巨大的声带正操在我手里（因为那时喇叭和汽笛都装在驾车人的左首，就在占据副座的人伸手可及之处），而我颇觉得快意，对着三百码开外一辆小马货车让它鸣笛示警，倘若它日常那副说话的腔调无人理会，我手底下便摁住它那串假声的尖叫。接着是一条与我们的路成直角交叉的大道，这可爱的巨兽似乎在说：「是，是——瞧我多听话、多小心。我把两只手插在口袋里溜达着呢。」过了一会儿，农庄里的一只小狗气势汹汹、跌跌撞撞地闯到了路上，巨兽便说：「可怜的小家伙！快回家找你妈妈去吧，不然我可要正经跟你说话了。」那可怜的小家伙没理会这警告，于是巨兽放慢了速度，只说了声：「嗬！」待那小狗吓得赶紧窜进树篱里，它暗自得意地笑了一下；下一刻，我们自己兜起的风又在耳畔尖啸呼啸起来。

===Original===
Napoleon, I believe, said that the power of an army lay in its feet: that is true also of the monster. There was a loud bang, and in thirty seconds we were at a standstill. The monster’s off forefoot troubled it, and the chauffeur said, “Yes, sir—burst.”

So the burst boot was taken off and a new one put on, a boot that had never been on foot before. The foot in question was held up on a jack during this operation, and the new boot laced up with a pump. This took exactly twenty-five minutes. Then the monster got his spoon going again, and said, “Let me run: oh, let me run!” And for fifteen miles on a straight and empty road it ran. I timed the miles, but shall not produce their chronology for the benefit of a forsworn constabulary.

But there were no more dithyrambics that morning. We should have reached Hunstanton in time for lunch. Instead, we waited to repair our fourth puncture at 1:45 p.m., twenty-five miles short of our destination. This fourth puncture was caused by a spicule of flint three-quarters of an inch long—sharp, it is true, but weighing perhaps two pennyweights, while we weighed two tons. It seemed an impertinence. So we lunched at a wayside inn, and during lunch the pundits held a consultation, of which the upshot was this:

We had no more boots for our monster, for his off forefoot had burst once, and punctured once (thus necessitating two socks and one boot). Similarly, but more so, his off hind-foot had burst twice (thus necessitating two boots and two socks). Now, there was no certain shoemaker’s shop at Hunstanton, as far as we knew, but there was a regular universal store at King’s Lynn, which was about equidistant.

And, so said the chauffeur, there was something wrong with the monster’s spoon (ignition), and he didn’t rightly know what, and therefore it seemed the prudent part not to go to Hunstanton (lunch, a thing of the preterite, having been the object), but to the well-supplied King’s Lynn. And we all breathed a pious hope that we might get there.

===Chinese===
我记得拿破仑曾说，一支军队的力量在于它的双脚：这话对这巨兽也同样成立。只听得砰的一声闷响，不出三十秒，我们便停住了。巨兽右前脚出了毛病，司机说：「是的，先生——爆胎了。」

于是那只爆了的外胎被卸下，换上一只新的，一只从未着过地的「鞋」。这工夫里，那只「脚」被千斤顶高高支起，新「鞋」用打气筒「系」紧。这前后恰好花了二十五分钟。随后巨兽又把它的汤匙啜了起来，说道：「让我跑吧：哦，让我跑吧！」于是在一条笔直空旷的大路上，它一连跑了十五英里。我掐了掐每一英里的时间，但那份时刻表我可不打算公布出来，去便宜那帮言而无信的警察。

可那天上午再没有那种酒神颂歌般的狂喜了。我们本该赶在午饭前到亨斯坦顿的。可到了下午一点四十五分，我们还在补第四个洞，离目的地差着二十五英里。这第四个洞，是一片四分之三英寸长的燧石刺——锋利是锋利，分量也许只值两本尼威，而我们足足有两吨重。这简直是放肆。于是我们在一家路旁客栈用了午饭，席间几位行家开了一个会，议决的结果如下：

巨兽再也没有备用的「鞋」了，因为它的右前脚爆过一次、又扎破过一次（这就用去了两条「内袜」和一只「外鞋」）。同样地，而且更糟，它的右后脚爆过两次（这就用去了两只「外鞋」和两条「内袜」）。而据我们所知，亨斯坦顿未必有稳靠的修车铺，可金斯林（King’s Lynn）却有一家应有尽有的综合铺子，两地距离倒是差不多。

司机又说，巨兽的「汤匙」（点火装置）出了点毛病，他也说不准究竟毛病在哪儿，因而看来稳妥之计，是不去亨斯坦顿（午饭既已是过去的事，它原本是此行的目的），而到货色齐全的金斯林去。我们一齐虔诚地盼望着能赶到那儿。

===Original===
Whizz: hoot: purr! The last boot held, the spoon went busily to the monster’s mouth, and we just flowed into King’s Lynn. The return journey, so I vaguely gathered, would be made by other roads; but personally, intoxicated with air and movement, I neither asked nor desired to know what those roads would be. This one small but rather salient fact is necessary to record here, that as we waited at King’s Lynn, and as we buzzed homewards afterwards, no thought of Bircham entered my head at all. The subsequent hallucination, if hallucination it was, was not, as far as I know, self-suggested. That we had gone out of our way for the sake of the garage, I knew, and that was all. Harry also told me that he did not know where our road would take us.

The rest that follows is the baldest possible narrative of what actually occurred. But it seems to me, a humble student of the occult, to be curious.

While we waited we had tea in a hotel looking on to a big empty square of houses, and after tea we waited a very long time for our monster to pick us up. Then the telephone from the garage inquired for “the gentleman on the motor,” and since Harry had strolled out to get a local evening paper with news of the last Test Match, I applied ear and mouth to that elusive instrument. What I heard was not encouraging: the ignition had gone very wrong indeed, and “perhaps” in an hour we should be able to start. It was then about half-past six, and we were just seventy-eight miles from Dunwich.

Harry came back soon after this, and I told him what the message from the garage had been. What he said was this: “Then we shan’t get back till long after dinner. We might just as well have camped out to see your ghost.”

As I have already said, no notion of Bircham was in my mind, and I mention this as evidence that, even if it had been, Harry’s remark would have implied that we were not going through Bircham.

The hour lengthened itself into an hour and a half. Then the monster, quite well again, came hooting round the corner, and we got in.

“Whack her up, Jack,” said Harry to the chauffeur. “The roads will be empty. You had better light up at once.”

The monster, with its eyes agleam, was whacked up, and never in my life have I been carried so cautiously and yet so swiftly. Jack never took a risk or the possibility of a risk, but when the road was clear and open he let the monster run just as fast as it was able. Its eyes made day of the road fifty yards ahead, and the romance of night was fairyland round us. Hares started from the roadside, and raced in front of us for a hundred yards, then just wheeled in time to avoid the earflaps of the great triumphant brute that carried us. Moths flitted across, struck sometimes by the lenses of its eyes, and the miles peeled over our shoulders. When It occurred we were going top-speed. And this was It—quite unsensational, but to us quite inexplicable unless my midnight imaginings happened to be true.

===Chinese===
嗖：叭：嘟！最后一只「鞋」撑住了，那汤匙又殷勤地送到了巨兽嘴边，我们就这样滑进了金斯林。回程走的将是另外几条路——这是我隐约听来的；可就我个人而言，正醉心于这风与奔驰之中，既不曾打听、也不想打听那会是哪几条路。这里有一点虽小、却颇为显眼的事实必须记下：我们在金斯林等候时、以及此后嗡嗡地往回赶时，伯彻姆这个字眼压根儿就没进过我的脑子。至于后来的那一桩幻觉——倘若那真是幻觉的话——就我所知，并不是我自己暗示出来的。我仅仅知道，我们是为了修车铺才绕了道，仅此而已。哈里也告诉我，他不知道我们的路会引向何方。

下面要讲的，便是实际发生之事尽可能平铺直叙的记述。可在我这个玄学的谦卑学徒看来，它是颇可玩味的。

等候的当儿，我们在一家面朝一片空旷的大宅广场的旅馆里用了茶，茶后又等了许久，才盼到我们的巨兽来接我们。这时车行的电话找「汽车上那位先生」，而哈里已踱出去买一份本地的晚报，看看最后一场板球对抗赛的消息，我便把耳朵和嘴巴凑到那支影影绰绰的话筒上。我听来的并不叫人安心：点火装置坏得不轻，「也许」再过一个钟头才能动身。那时大约是六点半，我们离邓维奇恰好七十八英里。

哈里没多久就回来了，我把车行的口信告诉了他。他听了说道：「那我们不到晚餐过后很久是回不去的。咱们倒不如干脆在外头露宿一晚，好看你那鬼呢。」

如我方才所说，我脑子里根本没有伯彻姆的影子；我提及这一点，是想作为一条证据——退一步讲，即便有，哈里这句话也等于在说，我们并不会路过伯彻姆。

一个钟头拖成了一个半钟头。随后那巨兽大好了，一路鸣着喇叭拐过街角来了，我们便上了车。

「把它加足，杰克，」哈里对司机说，「路上会空得很。你最好这就把灯点上。」

巨兽两眼灼灼地被加足了劲，我这辈子从未被人载得如此谨慎、又如此飞快过。杰克从不冒一丝风险，连风险的可能性也不冒，可只要前面路空道畅，他便任那巨兽能跑多快就跑多快。它那两只眼睛把车前五十码照得如同白昼，夜的浪漫在我们周遭化作了仙境。野兔从路旁惊起，在我们前面跑上一百码，然后堪堪在来得及的时候一拐，避开这载着我们的、趾高气扬的巨兽的两片「耳朵」。飞蛾掠过，有时撞在它眼睛的镜片上，而一英里又一英里，被我们从肩头一件件剥落下去。当那桩事发生时，我们正开着全速。而这便是那桩事——毫无耸人听闻之处，可对我们而言，又全然无从解释，除非我午夜的那一番遐想恰巧是真的。

===Original===
As I have said, I was in command of the hooter and of the siren. We were flying along on a straight downgrade, as fast as ever we could go, for the engines were working, though the decline was considerable. Then quite suddenly I saw in front of us a thick cloud of dust, and knew instinctively and on the instant, without thought or reasoning, what that must mean. Evidently something going very fast (or else so large a cloud could not have been raised) was in front of us, and going in the same direction as ourselves. Had it been something on the road coming to meet us, we should of course have seen the vehicle first and run into the dust-cloud afterwards. Had it, again, been something of low speed—a horse and dogcart, for instance—no such dust could have been raised. But, as it was, I knew at once that there was a motor travelling swiftly just ahead of us, also that it was not going as fast as we were, or we should have run into its dust much more gradually. But we went into it as into a suddenly lowered curtain.

Then I shouted to Jack. “Slow down, and put on the brake,” I shrieked. “There’s something just ahead of us.”

As I spoke I wrought a wild concerto on the hooter, and with my right hand groped for the siren, but did not find it. Simultaneously I heard a wild, frightened shriek, just as if I had sounded the siren myself. Jack had felt for it too, and our hands fingered each other. Then we entered the dust-cloud.

We slowed down with extraordinary rapidity, and still peering ahead we went dead-slow through it. I had not put on my goggles after leaving King’s Lynn, and the dust stung and smarted in my eyes. It was not, therefore, a belt of fog, but real road-dust. And at the moment we crept through it I felt Harry’s hands on my shoulder.

“There’s something just ahead,” he said. “Look! don’t you see the tail light?”

As a matter of fact, I did not; and, still going very slow, we came out of that dust-cloud. The broad empty road stretched in front of us; a hedge was on each side, and there was no turning either to right or left. Only, on the right, was a lodge, and gates which were closed. The lodge had no lights in any window.

Then we came to a standstill; the air was dead-calm, not a leaf in the hedgerow trees was moving, not a grain of dust was lifted from the road. But, behind, the dust-cloud still hung in the air, and stopped dead-short at the closed lodge-gates. We had moved very slowly for the last hundred yards: it was difficult to suppose that it was of our making. Then Jack spoke, with a curious crack in his voice.

“It must have been a motor, sir,” he said. “But where is it?”

===Chinese===
如我所说，喇叭与汽笛正归我掌管。我们正顺着一条直直的下坡路飞驰，速度已是不能再快，因为虽是相当陡的下坡，发动机仍在工作着。猛然间，我看见我们前方腾起一团浓密的尘云，并凭着本能，当下便不加思索、不加推演地知道了那意味着什么。显然，前方有什么东西正以极快的速度行进（否则扬不起这么大一团尘），而且和我们同向而行。倘若它是迎面而来的，我们当然会先看见那辆车，再闯进它的尘云里去。倘若它是低速之物——比方说一匹马拉的轻便马车——也断然扬不起这样的尘土。可事情既如此，我便当即明白了：有一辆汽车正紧贴在我们前面飞驰；也明白了：它不如我们快，否则我们闯进它的尘尾时会缓慢得多。可我们闯进去时，那尘尾却像一道猝然落下的帷幕。

我便朝杰克喊了起来。「慢下来，踩刹车，」我尖声叫道，「前面就有东西。」

我一边喊，一边在喇叭上奏起了一支狂乱的协奏曲，右手则去摸汽笛，却没摸着。与此同时，我听见了一声狂乱而惊惶的尖叫，那声音就好像是我自己摁响了汽笛。杰克也在摸它，我们两人的手在汽笛上互相摸到了一起。随后我们便闯进了那团尘云。

我们极其迅猛地慢了下来，仍眯眼朝前张望着，在尘团中死一般慢地挪动着。出了金斯林以后我没有戴上护目镜，那尘土蜇得我眼睛火辣辣地疼。可见那并非一段雾带，而是实实在在的道路扬尘。就在我们钻过尘团的当儿，我觉得哈里的手搭上了我的肩头。

「前面有东西，」他说，「瞧！你没看见那盏尾灯吗？」

事实上，我并没有看见；我们仍旧走得很慢，从那团尘云里钻了出来。宽阔空旷的大路在我们前方延伸；路两旁各是一道树篱，左右都没有岔路。只是右边有一座门房，还有两扇紧闭的大门。门房的哪一扇窗户里都没有灯光。

接着我们停了下来；空气死一般地静，树篱里没有一片树叶在动，路上没有一粒尘土被掀起。可是，在我们身后，那团尘云依然悬在半空，到了那紧闭的门房大门前便戛然而止。我们最后这一百码走得极慢：很难说那尘云是我们扬起来的。这时杰克开了口，嗓音古怪地发着劈。

「那想必是一辆汽车，先生，」他说，「可车在哪儿呢？」

===Original===
I had no reply to this, and from behind another voice, Harry’s voice, spoke. For the moment I did not recognise it, for it was strained and faltering.

“Did you open the siren?” he asked. “It didn’t sound like our siren. It sounded like, like—”

“I didn’t open the siren,” said I.

Then we went on again. Soon we came to scattered lights in houses by the wayside.

“What’s this place?” I asked Jack.

“Bircham, sir,” said he.

===Chinese===
我无言以对，后面传来另一个声音，是哈里的声音。一时之间我没有认出它来，因为它又紧绷又发颤。

「你摁响汽笛了吗？」他问，「那声音听着不像我们的汽笛。它听着像——像——」

「我没有摁汽笛。」我说。

随后我们又继续前行。不久我们便到了路旁几所宅子里零星的灯火前。

「这是什么地方？」我问杰克。

「伯彻姆，先生。」他说。

## The Gardener / 园丁

===Original===
Two friends of mine, Hugh Grainger and his wife, had taken for a month of Christmas holiday the house in which we were to witness such strange manifestations, and when I received an invitation from them to spend a fortnight there I returned them an enthusiastic affirmative. Well already did I know that pleasant heathery countryside, and most intimate was my acquaintance with the subtle hazards of its most charming golf-links. Golf, I was given to understand, was to occupy the solid day for Hugh and me, so that Margaret should never be obliged to set her hand to the implements with which the game, so detestable to her, was conducted.…﻿ ﻿

===Chinese===
我的两位朋友，休·格兰杰（Hugh Grainger）夫妇，为度一个月的圣诞假期，租下了那所我们即将在其中目睹种种异象的宅子。及至收到他们的邀请，请我去盘桓两礼拜，我便回了一封热切的允诺书。那片长满石楠花的悦人乡野我早已熟稔，至于它那迷人的高尔夫球场上种种微妙的陷阱，我与它们也再亲密不过。我得到的安排是：打高尔夫将占去休和我一整个白天，这样玛格丽特（Margaret）便永不必亲手去碰那套她所深恶痛绝的、用来打这种球的器械。……

===Original===
I arrived there while yet the daylight lingered, and as my hosts were out, I took a ramble round the place. The house and garden stood on a plateau facing south; below it were a couple of acres of pasture that sloped down to a vagrant stream crossed by a footbridge, by the side of which stood a thatched cottage with a vegetable patch surrounding it. A path ran close past this across the pasture from a wicket-gate in the garden, conducted you over the footbridge, and, so my remembered sense of geography told me, must constitute a shortcut to the links that lay not half a mile beyond. The cottage itself was clearly on the land of the little estate, and I at once supposed it to be the gardener’s house. What went against so obvious and simple a theory was that it appeared to be untenanted. No wreath of smoke, though the evening was chilly, curled from its chimneys, and, coming closer, I fancied it had that air of “waiting” about it which we so often conjure into unused habitations. There it stood, with no sign of life whatever about it, though ready, as its apparently perfect state of repair seemed to warrant, for fresh tenants to put the breath of life into it again. Its little garden, too, though the palings were neat and newly painted, told the same tale; the beds were untended and unweeded, and in the flower-border by the front door was a row of chrysanthemums, which had withered on their stems. But all this was but the impression of a moment, and I did not pause as I passed it, but crossed the footbridge and went on up the heathery slope that lay beyond. My geography was not at fault, for presently I saw the clubhouse just in front of me. Hugh no doubt would be just about coming in from his afternoon round, and so we would walk back together. On reaching the clubhouse, however, the steward told me that not five minutes before Mrs. Grainger had called in her car for her husband, and I therefore retraced my steps by the path along which I had already come. But I made a detour, as a golfer will, to walk up the fairway of the seventeenth and eighteenth holes just for the pleasure of recognition, and looked respectfully at the yawning sandpit which so inexorably guards the eighteenth green, wondering in what circumstances I should visit it next, whether with a step complacent and superior, knowing that my ball reposed safely on the green beyond, or with the heavy footfall of one who knows that laborious delving lies before him.

===Chinese===
我到达那里时天光尚存，因主人们都不在家，我便在宅子四周闲逛了一圈。宅子和花园坐落在一处朝南的高地上；下方是两英亩牧草地，缓缓倾斜着通向一条蜿蜒无定的小溪，溪上架着一座小木桥，桥边立着一栋茅草小屋，四周圈着一块菜地。花园里一扇小边门外，紧贴着这条小径穿过牧草地，把你引过小木桥——依我所记得的方位感判断——这该是通往球场的一条近路，球场就在不到半英里之外。这小屋分明是这片小产业的地界，我便当即猜想它是园丁的住所。可这再明显不过、再简单不过的推断却有一点说不通：它似乎无人居住。尽管傍晚寒意袭人，烟囱里却不见一缕炊烟。走近了些，我觉得它身上有一种「等待」的神气，那种我们常常自行安加到无人居住的宅子上去的神气。它就那么立着，周身上下不见一丝生息，然而似乎又随时——单看它那显然完好无损的修缮状况便足以担保——只等新房客再往里头注入生命的气息。它那小花园也讲着同样的故事：虽则栅栏整整齐齐、漆色新崭，花畦却无人打理、长满了杂草；前门旁的花境里有一排菊花，早已在枝头枯萎了。但这不过是一瞬的印象，我打它跟前过时并未驻足，而是过了小木桥，径直走上那头长满石楠花的山坡。我的方位感没出差错，因为不一会儿我便看见俱乐部会所就在眼前。休想必刚要打完下午那一局回来，这样我俩便可以一同走回去了。可到了俱乐部会所，管事却告诉我，不出五分钟前，格兰杰太太已开着车来接她丈夫走了，于是我只好顺着我来时的小径折返回去。但我像所有打高尔夫的人那样绕了个弯，特地去走第十七、十八洞的那段球道，不过是为着认认路的乐趣罢了；我又恭恭敬敬地端详了那个张着大口的沙坑——它铁面无情地扼守着第十八洞的果岭——心里盘算着下一回再来光顾它，会是怎样的光景：是迈着志得意满、居高临下的步子过来，因为知道自己的球已稳稳当当地停在沙坑那头的果岭上；还是迈着沉重的步子过来，因为知道自己面前还有一番辛苦的刨挖要做。

===Original===
The light of the winter evening had faded fast, and when I crossed the footbridge on my return the dusk had gathered. To my right, just beside the path, lay the cottage, the whitewashed walls of which gleamed whitely in the gloaming; and as I turned my glance back from it to the rather narrow plank which bridged the stream I thought I caught out of the tail of my eye some light from one of its windows, which thus disproved my theory that it was untenanted. But when I looked directly at it again I saw that I was mistaken: some reflection in the glass of the red lines of sunset in the west must have deceived me, for in the inclement twilight it looked more desolate than ever. Yet I lingered by the wicket gate in its low palings, for though all exterior evidence bore witness to its emptiness, some inexplicable feeling assured me, quite irrationally, that this was not so, and that there was somebody there. Certainly there was nobody visible, but, so this absurd idea informed me, he might be at the back of the cottage concealed from me by the intervening structure, and, still oddly, still unreasonably, it became a matter of importance to my mind to ascertain whether this was so or not, so clearly had my perceptions told me that the place was empty, and so firmly had some conviction assured me that it was tenanted. To cover my inquisitiveness, in case there was someone there, I could inquire whether this path was a shortcut to the house at which I was staying, and, rather rebelling at what I was doing, I went through the small garden, and rapped at the door. There was no answer, and, after waiting for a response to a second summons, and having tried the door and found it locked, I made the circuit of the house. Of course there was no one there, and I told myself that I was just like a man who looks under his bed for a burglar and would be beyond measure astonished if he found one.

===Chinese===
冬日傍晚的天光褪得飞快，等我折返过那座小木桥时，暮色已然四合。右边小径旁便是那栋小屋，它那粉刷过的白墙在暮霭里泛着幽幽的白光；当我把目光从小屋收回、转向那块横跨小溪的颇为狭窄的木板时，我觉得眼角的余光瞥见了它某一扇窗里透出的一点灯光，这便否证了我那「小屋无人居住」的推断。可我再直直地朝它望去时，却发觉自己弄错了：必是玻璃上映着西天日落那一道道红光的反光，把我骗了，因为在凄寒的暮色里，它看上去比先前更加荒凉。然而我仍在它那矮栅栏的小边门前流连了一阵，因为虽说所有外在的迹象都指证着它空无一人，某种不可名状的感觉却叫我相信——全无道理地相信——事情并非如此，那屋里是有人着的。固然看不见人影，可这荒唐的念头却告诉我：他也许就在小屋背面，被那屋子的墙体挡着，没让我瞧见；而依旧古怪地、依旧无理地，弄清楚究竟是否如此，竟成了我心中一桩紧要的事——我的感官已那般明白地告诉我那地方空无一人，而某种信念又那般坚定地告诉我那里头有人。为掩饰我的好奇（万一里头真有人），我可以借口问问这条小径是不是通往我借宿的宅子的近路；我一面为自己正在做的事暗暗抗拒着，一面穿过那小小花园，叩响了屋门。无人应声。我等候着第二次叩门的回音，又试了试门，发觉门是锁着的，便绕屋一周。屋里当然没有人。我暗自好笑，觉得自己活像一个趴在床底下找窃贼的人——真要找出一个来，反倒要大惊失色了。

===Original===
My hosts were at the house when I arrived, and we spent a cheerful two hours before dinner in such desultory and eager conversation as is proper between friends who have not met for some time. Between Hugh Grainger and his wife it is always impossible to light on a subject which does not vividly interest one or other of them, and golf, politics, the needs of Russia, cooking, ghosts, the possible victory over Mount Everest, and the income tax were among the topics which we passionately discussed. With all these plates spinning, it was easy to whip up any one of them, and the subject of spooks generally was lighted upon again and again.

===Chinese===
我到家时主人们已在宅中。晚餐前那两个钟头，我们聊得热热闹闹——久未谋面的朋友之间正该有那样东拉西扯、又兴致勃勃的交谈。休·格兰杰夫妇之间，向来不可能挑出一个引不起他们这一位或那一位强烈兴趣的题目；高尔夫、政治、俄国之急需、烹饪、鬼魂、征服珠穆朗玛峰之可能、所得税，都在我们热烈讨论之列。这么多盘子一齐转着，随手一拨便能挑起任何一个；而鬼魂这一总题目，更是被一次又一次地重新提起。

===Original===
“Margaret is on the high road to madness,” remarked Hugh on one of these occasions, “for she has begun using planchette. If you use planchette for six months, I am told, most careful doctors will conscientiously certify you as insane. She’s got five months more before she goes to Bedlam.”

“Does it work?” I asked.

“Yes, it says most interesting things,” said Margaret. “It says things that never entered my head. We’ll try it tonight.”

“Oh, not tonight,” said Hugh. “Let’s have an evening off.”

Margaret disregarded this.

“It’s no use asking planchette questions,” she went on, “because there is in your mind some sort of answer to them. If I ask whether it will be fine tomorrow, for instance, it is probably I—though indeed I don’t mean to push—who makes the pencil say ‘yes.’”

“And then it usually rains,” remarked Hugh.

“Not always: don’t interrupt. The interesting thing is to let the pencil write what it chooses. Very often it only makes loops and curves—though they may mean something—and every now and then a word comes, of the significance of which I have no idea whatever, so I clearly couldn’t have suggested it. Yesterday evening, for instance, it wrote ‘gardener’ over and over again. Now what did that mean? The gardener here is a Methodist with a chin-beard. Could it have meant him? Oh, it’s time to dress. Please don’t be late, my cook is so sensitive about soup.”

===Chinese===
「玛格丽特正走在通向癫狂的大道上呢，」有一回休这么说道，「因为她开始玩通灵板（planchette）了。听说一连玩上六个月的通灵板，再审慎的大夫也会凭良心给你开具一张精神失常的证明。她离进贝德兰姆（Bedlam）还差五个月。」

「它灵吗？」我问。

「灵的，它说出的话顶有趣，」玛格丽特说，「它说的那些，是我脑子里从未想到过的。今晚我们就来试试。」

「哦，今晚就算了吧，」休说，「让我们歇一晚上。」

玛格丽特没理会这话。

「问通灵板问题是没有用的，」她接着说，「因为你脑子里对那问题总有某种答案。比方说我问明天会不会天晴，那么让铅笔答出『是』来的，多半还是我自己——虽说我自己并不存心使劲。」

「然后通常就下雨了。」休插嘴。

「也不是回回如此：你别打岔。有趣的是让那支铅笔随它高兴，爱写什么就写什么。它常常只画些圈圈弯弯——虽说那些圈圈弯弯也许另有含义——时不时却会写出一个字来，那字的含义我全然摸不着头脑，可见那绝非我能暗示出来的。比方说昨天傍晚，它就把『园丁』写了一遍又一遍。这是什么意思呢？这儿的园丁是个留着下巴胡的循道宗信徒（Methodist）。莫非指的就是他？哦，该更衣赴宴了。请别迟到，我家的厨子对汤可是顶顶计较的。」

===Original===
We rose, and some connection of ideas about “gardener” linked itself up in my mind.

“By the way, what’s that cottage in the field by the footbridge?” I asked. “Is that the gardener’s cottage?”

“It used to be,” said Hugh. “But the chin-beard doesn’t live there: in fact nobody lives there. It’s empty. If I was owner here, I should put the chin-beard into it, and take the rent off his wages. Some people have no idea of economy. Why did you ask?”

I saw Margaret was looking at me rather attentively.

“Curiosity,” I said. “Idle curiosity.”

“I don’t believe it was,” said she.

“But it was,” I said. “It was idle curiosity to know whether the house was inhabited. As I passed it, going down to the clubhouse, I felt sure it was empty, but coming back I felt so sure that there was someone there that I rapped at the door, and indeed walked round it.”

Hugh had preceded us upstairs, as she lingered a little.

“And there was no one there?” she asked. “It’s odd: I had just the same feeling as you about it.”

“That explains planchette writing ‘gardener’ over and over again,” said I. “You had the gardener’s cottage on your mind.”

“How ingenious!” said Margaret. “Hurry up and dress.”

===Chinese===
我们起身，我脑子里「园丁」一词勾连起了某种联想。

「对了，小木桥边田里那栋小屋是怎么回事？」我问，「那是园丁住的屋子吗？」

「从前是的，」休说，「可那位下巴胡并不住那儿：说真的，根本没人住那儿。那屋子空着。要我是这儿的主人，我就把下巴胡塞进去住，再从他的工钱里扣下房租。有些人压根儿不懂得节俭。你问这做什么？」

我看见玛格丽特正颇为留意地打量着我。

「好奇，」我说，「纯粹是好奇。」

「我才不信呢。」她说。

「可确实是这样，」我说，「我想知道那屋子有没有人住，纯粹是出于好奇。我往俱乐部去的时候打它跟前过，满心以为它是空的；可回来时我又那样确信里头有人，竟叩了叩门，还绕着它走了一圈。」

休已先我们上楼去了，她却稍作停留。

「里头没有人？」她问，「奇了：我对那地方的感觉和你一模一样。」

「这倒解释了通灵板为什么把『园丁』写了一遍又一遍，」我说，「你心里惦记着那园丁的小屋。」

「好聪明的一张嘴！」玛格丽特说，「快上去更衣吧。」

===Original===
A gleam of strong moonlight between my drawn curtains when I went up to bed that night led me to look out. My room faced the garden and the fields which I had traversed that afternoon, and all was vividly illuminated by the full moon. The thatched cottage with its white walls close by the stream was very distinct, and once more, I suppose, the reflection of the light on the glass of one of its windows made it appear that the room was lit within. It struck me as odd that twice that day this illusion should have been presented to me, but now a yet odder thing happened. Even as I looked the light was extinguished.

===Chinese===
那天夜里我上楼就寝时，两幅拉拢的窗帘之间漏进一线明亮的月光，引我探头向外望去。我的房间朝着花园和我那天下午走过的那片田野，明月高悬，把它们照得分外分明。那栋白墙茅顶的小屋紧挨着小溪，轮廓十分清晰；我想，又一次是某扇窗玻璃上的反光，让那屋子看上去像里头点着灯似的。同一天里这错觉竟在我眼前出现两回，我觉得有些古怪；可紧接着，一桩更古怪的事发生了。就在我张望的当儿，那灯光熄了。

===Original===
The morning did not at all bear out the fine promise of the clear night, for when I woke the wind was squealing, and sheets of rain from the southwest were dashed against my panes. Golf was wholly out of the question, and, though the violence of the storm abated a little in the afternoon, the rain dripped with a steady sullenness. But I wearied of indoors, and, since the two others entirely refused to set foot outside, I went forth mackintoshed to get a breath of air. By way of an object in my tramp, I took the road to the links in preference to the muddy shortcut through the fields, with the intention of engaging a couple of caddies for Hugh and myself next morning, and lingered awhile over illustrated papers in the smoking-room. I must have read for longer than I knew, for a sudden beam of sunset light suddenly illuminated my page, and looking up, I saw that the rain had ceased, and that evening was fast coming on. So instead of taking the long detour by the road again, I set forth homewards by the path across the fields. That gleam of sunset was the last of the day, and once again, just as twenty-four hours ago, I crossed the footbridge in the gloaming. Till that moment, as far as I was aware, I had not thought at all about the cottage there, but now in a flash the light I had seen there last night, suddenly extinguished, recalled itself to my mind, and at the same moment I felt that invincible conviction that the cottage was tenanted. Simultaneously in these swift processes of thought I looked towards it, and saw standing by the door the figure of a man. In the dusk I could distinguish nothing of his face, if indeed it was turned to me, and only got the impression of a tallish fellow, thickly built. He opened the door, from which there came a dim light as of a lamp, entered, and shut it after him.

===Chinese===
清朗的夜里所作的晴好许诺，到了清晨一点也没有兑现：我醒来时，风正尖啸，一片片从西南方扫来的雨幕砸在我的窗玻璃上。打高尔夫是全然无望了；虽则午后风雨之势稍减，那雨却仍执拗地滴滴答答下个不停。可我在屋里待得腻烦，而另外两位又一字不提踏出门外半步，我便裹上雨衣，出去透一口空气。为使这趟散步有个目的，我没有抄田间那条泥泞的近路，而走了通往球场的大路，打算为休和我自己预订第二天一早的两个球童；我在吸烟室里翻看画报，磨蹭了好一阵。我读的时间一定比自己以为的要久，因为一束突至的夕阳忽然照亮了我眼前的书页，抬头一看，雨已停了，夜色正急急降临。于是我没有再沿大路绕那个长弯，而是取田间小径动身回家。那一抹夕光是白昼最后的一抹；我又一次——正如二十四小时之前一样——在暮霭里走过了那座小木桥。在那之前，就我所知，我压根儿没有想起过那儿的那栋小屋；可这会儿，一闪念间，我昨夜在那儿看见的那道光——那道猝然熄灭的光——又浮上了心头，与此同时，我又感到那不可战胜的信念：那小屋里是有人着的。在这电光石火般的思绪里，我同时朝它望去，只见门前立着一个人影。暮色里我辨不清他的脸——倘若那张脸确是朝着我这边的话——只得了这么一个印象：一个中等偏高、身板厚实的汉子。他推开门——门里透出一缕昏黄如灯的光——走了进去，随手把门带上。

===Original===
So then my conviction was right. Yet I had been distinctly told that the cottage was empty: who, then, was he that entered as if returning home? Once more, this time with a certain qualm of fear, I rapped on the door, intending to put some trivial question; and rapped again, this time more drastically, so that there could be no question that my summons was unheard. But still I got no reply, and finally I tried the handle of the door. It was locked. Then, with difficulty mastering an increasing terror, I made the circuit of the cottage, peering into each unshuttered window. All was dark within, though but two minutes ago I had seen the gleam of light escape from the opened door.

===Chinese===
那么说，我的预感是对的。可别人明明白白告诉我那小屋是空的：那么，这一个像回家似地走进去的人，又是谁呢？我又一次叩响了门——这一回怀着某种胆怯——本想问一个无关紧要的问题；我又叩了一次，这一回叩得更急，好让人没法说没听见我的叫门。可依旧毫无应声，我终于伸手去试门把手。门是锁着的。于是我强自按捺着节节上涨的恐惧，绕着小屋走了一周，朝每一扇没装百叶板的窗子里张望。里头漆黑一片，虽说两分钟前我还分明看见一道光从那敞开的门里透出来。

===Original===
Just because some chain of conjecture was beginning to form itself in my mind, I made no allusion to this odd adventure, and after dinner Margaret, amid protests from Hugh, got out the planchette which had persisted in writing “gardener.” My surmise was, of course, utterly fantastic, but I wanted to convey no suggestion of any sort to Margaret.… For a long time the pencil skated over her paper making loops and curves and peaks like a temperature chart, and she had begun to yawn and weary over her experiment before any coherent word emerged. And then, in the oddest way, her head nodded forward and she seemed to have fallen asleep.

Hugh looked up from his book and spoke in a whisper to me.

“She fell asleep the other night over it,” he said.

Margaret’s eyes were closed, and she breathed the long, quiet breaths of slumber, and then her hand began to move with a curious firmness. Right across the big sheet of paper went a level line of writing, and at the end her hand stopped with a jerk, and she woke.

She looked at the paper.

“Hullo,” she said. “Ah, one of you has been playing a trick on me!”

We assured her that this was not so, and she read what she had written.

“Gardener, gardener,” it ran. “I am the gardener. I want to come in. I can’t find her here.”

“O Lord, that gardener again!” said Hugh.

Looking up from the paper, I saw Margaret’s eyes fixed on mine, and even before she spoke I knew what her thought was.

“Did you come home by the empty cottage?” she asked.

“Yes: why?”

“Still empty?” she said in a low voice. “Or—or anything else?”

I did not want to tell her just what I had seen—or what, at any rate, I thought I had seen. If there was going to be anything odd, anything worth observation, it was far better that our respective impressions should not fortify each other.

“I tapped again, and there was no answer,” I said.

Presently there was a move to bed: Margaret initiated it, and after she had gone upstairs Hugh and I went to the front door to interrogate the weather. Once more the moon shone in a clear sky, and we strolled out along the flagged path that fronted the house. Suddenly Hugh turned quickly and pointed to the angle of the house.

“Who on earth is that?” he said. “Look! There! He has gone round the corner.”

I had but the glimpse of a tallish man of heavy build.

“Didn’t you see him?” asked Hugh. “I’ll just go round the house, and find him; I don’t want anyone prowling round us at night. Wait here, will you, and if he comes round the other corner ask him what his business is.”

Hugh had left me, in our stroll, close by the front door which was open, and there I waited until he should have made his circuit. He had hardly disappeared when I heard, quite distinctly, a rather quick but heavy footfall coming along the paved walk towards me from the opposite direction. But there was absolutely no one to be seen who made this sound of rapid walking. Closer and closer to me came the steps of the invisible one, and then with a shudder of horror I felt somebody unseen push by me as I stood on the threshold. That shudder was not merely of the spirit, for the touch of him was that of ice on my hand. I tried to seize this impalpable intruder, but he slipped from me, and next moment I heard his steps on the parquet of the floor inside. Some door within opened and shut, and I heard no more of him. Next moment Hugh came running round the corner of the house from which the sound of steps had approached.

“But where is he?” he asked. “He was not twenty yards in front of me—a big, tall fellow.”

“I saw nobody,” I said. “I heard his step along the walk, but there was nothing to be seen.”

“And then?” asked Hugh.

“Whatever it was seemed to brush by me, and go into the house,” said I.

There had certainly been no sound of steps on the bare oak stairs, and we searched room after room through the ground floor of the house. The dining-room door and that of the smoking-room were locked, that into the drawing-room was open, and the only other door which could have furnished the impression of an opening and a shutting was that into the kitchen and servants’ quarters. Here again our quest was fruitless; through pantry and scullery and boot-room and servants’ hall we searched, but all was empty and quiet. Finally we came to the kitchen, which too was empty. But by the fire there was set a rocking-chair, and this was oscillating to and fro as if someone, lately sitting there, had just quitted it. There it stood gently rocking, and this seemed to convey the sense of a presence, invisible now, more than even the sight of him who surely had been sitting there could have done. I remember wanting to steady it and stop it, and yet my hand refused to go forth to it.

===Chinese===
正因为脑子里已开始隐隐串起一条猜测的链子，我绝口不提这一桩古怪的遭遇。晚餐之后，玛格丽特不顾休的抗议，拿出了那块屡屡爱写「园丁」的通灵板。我那番猜测自然全然荒诞无稽，可我不愿给玛格丽特任何形式的暗示。……很长一段时间里，那支铅笔在她纸上滑来滑去，画出一个个圈、一道道弯、一座座尖峰，活像一张体温表；她已经打起呵欠、对这实验心生厌倦了，这才终于冒出一句成话。紧接着，她以最古怪的姿态把头一点，像是睡着了。

休从书上抬起眼，低声对我说话。

「前两天晚上她也是这样在它上头睡着的。」他说。

玛格丽特双目紧闭，呼吸悠长而安静，正是酣眠的样子。随后她的手动了起来，带着一种奇异的坚定。那笔直而平稳的一行字划过了那大张的纸，到末了她的手猛地一顿，她便醒了。

她看着那张纸。

「哎呀，」她说，「啊，你们俩哪一个在捉弄我！」

我们一口咬定并无此事，她便念出她所写下的来。

「园丁，园丁，」那上面写着，「我是园丁。我要进来。我在这里找不到她。」

「老天爷，又是那个园丁！」休说。

我从纸上抬起眼，看见玛格丽特正目不转睛地望着我，不等她开口我已知道她想的是什么。

「你回来时是打那栋空屋子跟前过的？」她问。

「是的：怎么？」

「还是空的？」她低声道，「还——还是有了别的什么？」

我不想把我的所见——或者至少是我以为我之所见——原原本本告诉她。倘若真要有什么古怪事、有什么值得观察的，那么我俩各自的印象最好互不相涉、彼此不为佐证。

「我又叩了门，无人应声。」我说。

不久便有人提议就寝：是玛格丽特先起的头。她上楼去之后，休和我走到前门口去探看天气。明月又一次挂在澄澈的天上，我们便信步走出，沿着宅子正门前那条石板路踱着。忽然休猛一转身，指着宅子的墙角。

「那到底是谁？」他说，「瞧！那儿！他拐过墙角了。」

我只来得及瞥见一个中等偏高、身板厚实的男人。

「你没看见他？」休问，「我干脆绕宅一周，把他揪出来；夜里我可不愿意有谁在我们屋外转悠。你在这儿等着，行吗？要是他从另一个墙角绕过来，你就问问他有什么事。」

我们信步时休把我留在了敞开的前门附近，我便在那里等着，等他绕宅一周。他刚一不见，我便清清楚楚地听见一阵颇为急促却又沉重的脚步声，从相反的方向沿着那条石板路朝我而来。可那发出急促脚步声的人，压根儿就看不见一个。那无形之人的脚步离我越来越近，紧接着我浑身一凛，感到一个看不见的人在我站在门槛上时从我身边挤了过去。那一凛不仅仅是出于心神，因为他的触碰落在我手上，冷得像冰。我试图抓住这无形的闯入者，可他已从我手中滑脱，下一刻我听见他的脚步踏上了屋里镶拼木地板。里面某扇门开了又关，我便再听不见他的动静。下一刻休从脚步声原先逼近的那个墙角飞奔过来。

「可他人呢？」他问，「他就在我前头不出二十码——一个大个子、高个子。」

「我什么人也没看见，」我说，「我听见他的脚步沿着石板路过来，可什么也看不见。」

「然后呢？」休问。

「那东西像是擦着我身子过去，进了屋。」我说。

赤裸的橡木楼梯上分明没有任何脚步声，我们便挨间搜过楼下那一层。餐室和吸烟室的门都锁着，客厅的门是开着的，而唯一可能给人「一开一关」之感的那扇门，便是通往厨房和仆人住处的那一扇。这一处我们的搜寻又是徒然；配膳室、洗碗间、鞋帽房、仆人厅，一一搜遍，处处空寂。终于我们来到厨房，那里也是空的。只是炉边摆着一张摇椅，那椅子正一来一回地轻晃着，像是方才坐在上头的人刚刚起身。它就那么立着，轻轻摇晃，这景象比之亲眼瞧见那个想必方才坐在上头的人，更强烈地传达出一种「此间有存在」的感觉——虽说那存在如今已不可见了。我记得自己想伸手去把它按住、让它停下，可我的手却怎么也不肯伸出去。

===Original===
What we had seen, and in especial what we had not seen, would have been sufficient to furnish most people with a broken night, and assuredly I was not among the strong-minded exceptions. Long I lay wide-eyed and open-eared, and when at last I dozed I was plucked from the borderland of sleep by the sound, muffled but unmistakable, of someone moving about the house. It occurred to me that the steps might be those of Hugh conducting a lonely exploration, but even while I wondered a tap came at the door of communication between our rooms, and, in answer to my response, it appeared that he had come to see whether it was I thus uneasily wandering. Even as we spoke the step passed my door, and the stairs leading to the floor above creaked to its ascent. Next moment it sounded directly above our heads in some attics in the roof.

“Those are not the servants’ bedrooms,” said Hugh. “No one sleeps there. Let us look once more: it must be somebody.”

With lit candles we made our stealthy way upstairs, and just when we were at the top of the flight, Hugh, a step ahead of me, uttered a sharp exclamation.

“But something is passing by me!” he said, and he clutched at the empty air. Even as he spoke, I experienced the same sensation, and the moment afterwards the stairs below us creaked again, as the unseen passed down.

All night long that sound of steps moved about the passages, as if someone was searching the house, and as I lay and listened that message which had come through the pencil of the planchette to Margaret’s fingers occurred to me. “I want to come in. I cannot find her here.”… Indeed someone had come in, and was sedulous in his search. He was the gardener, it would seem. But what gardener was this invisible seeker, and for whom did he seek?

===Chinese===
我们之所见，尤其是我们之所未见，已足以叫大多数人彻夜难眠了；而我断然不是那些心志坚毅的例外之人。我睁着眼、支着耳朵躺了很久；及至终于打了个盹，便被一阵闷闷的、却再清楚不过的声响——有人在屋里走动——从睡乡的边缘一把拽醒。我想到这脚步也许是休独自出来探查，可我正这样想着，两间屋相通的那扇门上便响起一下叩门声；我应了一声开门一看，原来他也是来瞧瞧，那不安地四处游走的是不是我。就在我们说话的当儿，那脚步从我门外经过，通往楼上的楼梯随着它的上行吱嘎作响。下一刻它已在我们头顶正上方——屋顶层某几间阁楼里——响了起来。

「那可不是仆人们的卧室，」休说，「没人在那儿睡。我们再去瞧一回：一定是有人的。」

我们擎着点燃的蜡烛，蹑手蹑脚地上楼去。才到楼梯顶，比我高一级的休忽然发出一声短促的惊呼。

「可有东西正从我身边过去！」他说，一边朝空无一物的空中抓了一把。就在他说话的同时，我也感到了同样的触碰；下一刻我们脚下的楼梯又吱嘎作响起来，是那无形之物走了下去。

整整一夜，那脚步声在走廊里来来去去，像是有谁在搜遍整所宅子。我躺着静听，便想起那句从通灵板的铅笔下、流到玛格丽特指尖上的话来：「我要进来。我在这里找不到她。」……果然有人进来了，而且在勤谨不怠地搜寻。这来客似乎正是那位园丁。可这无形的搜寻者究竟是个什么园丁？他所寻的，又是谁？

===Original===
Even as when some bodily pain ceases it is difficult to recall with any vividness what the pain was like, so next morning, as I dressed, I found myself vainly trying to recapture the horror of the spirit which had accompanied these nocturnal adventures. I remembered that something within me had sickened as I watched the movements of the rocking-chair the night before and as I heard the steps along the paved way outside, and by that invisible pressure against me knew that someone had entered the house. But now in the sane and tranquil morning, and all day under the serene winter sun, I could not realise what it had been. The presence, like the bodily pain, had to be there for the realisation of it, and all day it was absent. Hugh felt the same; he was even disposed to be humorous on the subject.

“Well, he’s had a good look,” he said, “whoever he is, and whomever he was looking for. By the way, not a word to Margaret, please. She heard nothing of these perambulations, nor of the entry of—of whatever it was. Not gardener, anyhow: who ever heard of a gardener spending his time walking about the house? If there were steps all over the potato-patch, I might have been with you.”

Margaret had arranged to drive over to have tea with some friends of hers that afternoon, and in consequence Hugh and I refreshed ourselves at the clubhouse after our game, and it was already dusk when for the third day in succession I passed homewards by the whitewashed cottage. But tonight I had no sense of it being subtly occupied; it stood mournfully desolate, as is the way of untenanted houses, and no light nor semblance of such gleamed from its windows. Hugh, to whom I had told the odd impressions I had received there, gave them a reception as flippant as that which he had accorded to the memories of the night, and he was still being humorous about them when we came to the door of the house.

“A psychic disturbance, old boy,” he said. “Like a cold in the head. Hullo, the door’s locked.”

He rang and rapped, and from inside came the noise of a turned key and withdrawn bolts.

“What’s the door locked for?” he asked his servant who opened it.

The man shifted from one foot to the other.

“The bell rang half an hour ago, sir,” he said, “and when I came to answer it there was a man standing outside, and—”

“Well?” asked Hugh.

“I didn’t like the looks of him, sir,” he said, “and I asked him his business. He didn’t say anything, and then he must have gone pretty smartly away, for I never saw him go.”

“Where did he seem to go?” asked Hugh, glancing at me.

“I can’t rightly say, sir. He didn’t seem to go at all. Something seemed to brush by me.”

“That’ll do,” said Hugh rather sharply.

===Chinese===
正如某一阵肉体的疼痛止息之后，便很难再鲜明地记起那疼痛究竟是何滋味；第二天早晨我更衣时，发觉自己正徒劳地想重新抓住昨夜那场冒险所带来的心灵上的恐惧。我记得昨夜我望着摇椅的晃动、听见外头石板路上的脚步、又凭那无形之物压上我身的触感而知道有人进了屋时，我心里有某种东西作呕似的难受。可如今，在这清醒而宁静的早晨，在这一整日肃穆的冬日阳光下，我却怎么也体味不回那番滋味了。那「存在」一如肉体的疼痛，非要它实实在在地在那儿，才能体会它；而这一整日，它都并不在。休也有同感；他甚至还有心思拿这事打趣。

「行啦，他把这宅子瞧了个够了，」他说，「管他是谁，管他找的是谁。对了，请千万莫对玛格丽特提一个字。那些来回踱步的声音她一无所闻，至于那进了屋的——进了屋的什么东西，她也一概不知。反正绝不是园丁：谁听说过园丁把工夫都花在屋里走来走去的？要是一地的脚印都踩在土豆畦上，我也许就跟你一条心了。」

玛格丽特已安排好那天下午坐车去和几位朋友喝茶，因此休和我在打完球后便在俱乐部会所歇脚消遣；待我第三日接连从那粉刷一白的小屋跟前经过、走回家时，天色已然昏黄。可今夜我并不觉得它被什么微妙地占据着；它凄凉而孤寂地立着，正如一切无人居住的屋子那样；窗里也不再有一点灯光或类似的影子闪动。休——我曾把我从那地方所受的古怪印象告诉过他——对那些印象的反应，一如他对昨夜的种种记忆那般轻佻；我们走到宅子门前时，他还在拿这事打趣。

「一种心灵上的骚扰罢了，老兄，」他说，「就像伤风感冒一样。咦，门锁着呢。」

他拉铃、叩门，里头传来钥匙转动、门闩抽开的声响。

「门干吗锁上？」他问开门的仆人。

那人把重心从一只脚挪到另一只脚上。

「半个钟头前铃响了，先生，」他说，「等我出来应门，外头站着个男人，于是——」

「于是？」休问。

「我不大喜欢他那模样，先生，」他说，「便问他是来干什么的。他没吭声，跟着一定是溜得飞快，因为我压根儿没瞧见他怎么走的。」

「他像是往哪儿去的？」休问，朝我瞥了一眼。

「我说不上来，先生。他简直像是压根儿没走。倒像有什么东西从我身边擦过去。」

「行了。」休相当生硬地说。

===Original===
Margaret had not come in from her visit, but when soon after the crunch of the motor wheels was heard Hugh reiterated his wish that nothing should be said to her about the impression which now, apparently, a third person shared with us. She came in with a flush of excitement on her face.

“Never laugh at my planchette again,” she said. “I’ve heard the most extraordinary story from Maud Ashfield—horrible, but so frightfully interesting.”

“Out with it,” said Hugh.

“Well, there was a gardener here,” she said. “He used to live at that little cottage by the footbridge, and when the family were up in London he and his wife used to be caretakers and live here.”

Hugh’s glance and mine met: then he turned away. I knew, as certainly as if I was in his mind, that his thoughts were identical with my own.

“He married a wife much younger than himself,” continued Margaret, “and gradually he became frightfully jealous of her. And one day in a fit of passion he strangled her with his own hands. A little while after someone came to the cottage, and found him sobbing over her, trying to restore her. They went for the police, but before they came he had cut his own throat. Isn’t it all horrible? But surely it’s rather curious that the planchette said Gardener. ‘I am the gardener. I want to come in. I can’t find her here.’ You see I knew nothing about it. I shall do planchette again tonight. Oh dear me, the post goes in half an hour, and I have a whole budget to send. But respect my planchette for the future, Hughie.”

We talked the situation out when she had gone, but Hugh, unwillingly convinced and yet unwilling to admit that something more than coincidence lay behind that “planchette nonsense,” still insisted that Margaret should be told nothing of what we had heard and seen in the house last night, and of the strange visitor who again this evening, so we must conclude, had made his entry.

“She’ll be frightened,” he said, “and she’ll begin imagining things. As for the planchette, as likely as not it will do nothing but scribble and make loops. What’s that? Yes: come in!”

There had come from somewhere in the room one sharp, peremptory rap. I did not think it came from the door, but Hugh, when no response replied to his words of admittance, jumped up and opened it. He took a few steps into the hall outside, and returned.

“Didn’t you hear it?” he asked.

“Certainly. No one there?”

“Not a soul.”

Hugh came back to the fireplace and rather irritably threw a cigarette which he had just lit into the fender.

“That was rather a nasty jar,” he observed; “and if you ask me whether I feel comfortable, I can tell you I never felt less comfortable in my life. I’m frightened, if you want to know, and I believe you are too.”

I hadn’t the smallest intention of denying this, and he went on.

“We’ve got to keep a hand on ourselves,” he said. “There’s nothing so infectious as fear, and Margaret mustn’t catch it from us. But there’s something more than our fear, you know. Something has got into the house and we’re up against it. I never believed in such things before. Let’s face it for a minute. *What* is it anyhow?”

“If you want to know what I think it is,” said I, “I believe it to be the spirit of the man who strangled his wife and then cut his throat. But I don’t see how it can hurt us. We’re afraid of our own fear really.”

“But we’re up against it,” said Hugh. “And what will it do? Good Lord, if I only knew what it would do I shouldn’t mind. It’s the not knowing.… Well, it’s time to dress.”

===Chinese===
玛格丽特串门还未回来。可不久之后，便听得汽车轮子碾过沙地的咯吱声。休重申他的意愿：如今显然有第三个人也与我们共享了那番印象，这事万万不可对玛格丽特提。她走了进来，一脸因兴奋而飞红的颜色。

「往后你再不许取笑我的通灵板了，」她说，「我刚从莫德·阿什菲尔德（Maud Ashfield）那儿听来一桩顶离奇的故事——骇人，可又骇人地有趣。」

「快讲。」休说。

「嗯，从前这儿有过一个园丁，」她说，「他一度住在小木桥边那栋小屋里；一家人上伦敦去的时候，他和他的妻子就做看屋人，住在这宅子里。」

休的目光与我相接：随即他又转开去。我确凿地知道——就像钻进了他脑子里一样确凿——他的心思和我一模一样。

「他娶了一个比自己年轻得多的妻子，」玛格丽特接着说，「渐渐地，他对她妒忌得要发狂。后来有一天，他在一阵盛怒之下，亲手把她掐死了。过后不久，有人到那小屋去，发现他俯在她身上啜泣，想把她救回来。他们去叫警察，可还没等警察赶到，他已割断了自己的喉咙。这整个事儿骇不骇人？可通灵板说的偏偏是园丁，这未免太巧了吧。『我是园丁。我要进来。我在这里找不到她。』要知道，我事先对这事一无所知。今晚我还要再玩一回通灵板。哎呀，邮件半个钟头后就要封发了，我还有一大堆信要寄呢。不过从今往后，你可得尊重我的通灵板了，休伊（Hughie）。」

她走后，我们把这事前前后后讨论了个透。可休虽已被不情愿地说服、却又不肯承认那「通灵板的胡闹」背后还藏着什么超出巧合的东西，依旧坚持不可让玛格丽特知晓我们昨夜在屋里所闻所见的一切，也不可让她知道，今夜——我们只能这样推断——那位古怪的访客又一次进了屋。

「她会害怕的，」他说，「她一害怕，就会开始胡思乱想。至于通灵板嘛，多半只会乱涂乱画几个圈儿罢了。什么声音？是，进来！」

屋里不知何处，响了一下短促、不容分说的叩击声。我并不觉得那声音是从门口来的，可休见没人应他那句「进来」，便一跃而起，拉开门。他向外走进门厅几步，又折了回来。

「你没听见？」他问。

「听见了。外头没人？」

「一个鬼影也没有。」

休回到壁炉前，相当恼怒地把刚点上的一支烟扔进了炉床围栏里。

「这一下可不轻，」他说，「你要是问我舒不舒服，我可以告诉你，我这辈子从来没这么不舒服过。不怕告诉你，我害怕了，我想你也一样。」

我一点不想否认，他便接着说。

「我们得把自己按住，」他说，「再没有比恐惧更传染的东西了，玛格丽特万万不能从我们这儿染上。可是，比我们的恐惧更深的，还有别的什么。有什么东西进了这宅子，我们和它狭路相逢了。从前我从不信这一套。让我们面对它一会儿吧。那到底是个什么？」

「你要是问我的看法，」我说，「我相信那是亲手掐死妻子、又割断自己喉咙的那个男人的亡灵。可我瞧不出它能伤着我们。我们真正怕的，其实是自己的恐惧罢了。」

「可我们和它狭路相逢了，」休说，「它接下来会做什么？老天爷，只要我知道它会做什么，我倒也不在乎了。怕就怕这『不知道』。……算了，该更衣了。」

===Original===
Margaret was in her highest spirits at dinner. Knowing nothing of the manifestations of that presence which had taken place in the last twenty-four hours, she thought it absorbingly interesting that her planchette should have “guessed” (so ran her phrase) about the gardener, and from that topic she flitted to an equally interesting form of patience for three which her friend had showed her, promising to initiate us into it after dinner. This she did, and, not knowing that we both above all things wanted to keep planchette at a distance, she was delighted with the success of her game. But suddenly she observed that the evening was burning rapidly away, and swept the cards together at the conclusion of a hand.

“Now just half an hour of planchette,” she said.

“Oh, mayn’t we play one more hand?” asked Hugh. “It’s the best game I’ve seen for years. Planchette will be dismally slow after this.”

“Darling, if the gardener will only communicate again, it won’t be slow,” said she.

“But it is such drivel,” said Hugh.

“How rude you are! Read your book, then.”

Margaret had already got out her machine and a sheet of paper, when Hugh rose.

“Please don’t do it tonight, Margaret,” he said.

“But why? You needn’t attend.”

“Well, I ask you not to, anyhow,” said he.

Margaret looked at him closely.

“Hughie, you’ve got something on your mind,” she said. “Out with it. I believe you’re nervous. You think there is something queer about. What is it?”

I could see Hugh hesitating as to whether to tell her or not, and I gathered that he chose the chance of her planchette inanely scribbling.

“Go on, then,” he said.

Margaret hesitated: she clearly did not want to vex Hugh, but his insistence must have seemed to her most unreasonable.

“Well, just ten minutes,” she said, “and I promise not to think of gardeners.”

She had hardly laid her hand on the board when her head fell forward, and the machine began moving. I was sitting close to her, and as it rolled steadily along the paper the writing became visible.

“I have come in,” it ran, “but still I can’t find her. Are you hiding her? I will search the room where you are.”

What else was written but still concealed underneath the planchette I did not know, for at that moment a current of icy air swept round the room, and at the door, this time unmistakably, came a loud, peremptory knock. Hugh sprang to his feet.

“Margaret, wake up,” he said, “something is coming!”

The door opened, and there moved in the figure of a man. He stood just within the door, his head bent forward, and he turned it from side to side, peering, it would seem, with eyes staring and infinitely sad, into every corner of the room.

“Margaret, Margaret,” cried Hugh again.

But Margaret’s eyes were open too; they were fixed on this dreadful visitor.

“Be quiet, Hughie,” she said below her breath, rising as she spoke. The ghost was now looking directly at her. Once the lips above the thick, rust-coloured beard moved, but no sound came forth, the mouth only moved and slavered. He raised his head, and, horror upon horror, I saw that one side of his neck was laid open in a red, glistening gash.…

For how long that pause continued, when we all three stood stiff and frozen in some deadly inhibition to move or speak, I have no idea: I suppose that at the utmost it was a dozen seconds. Then the spectre turned, and went out as it had come. We heard his steps pass along the parqueted floor; there was the sound of bolts withdrawn from the front door, and with a crash that shook the house it slammed to.

“It’s all over,” said Margaret. “God have mercy on him!”

===Chinese===
晚餐时玛格丽特兴致勃勃。她对过去二十四小时里那「存在」的种种显形一无所知，只觉得她的通灵板竟「猜中」（她原话如此）了园丁之事，分外引人入胜；从这个题目她又跳到一种同样有趣的三人单人纸牌戏上，那是她朋友教她的，她应允饭后也教我们一手。她果然教了；又因她全然不知我们俩都恨不得让通灵板离得越远越好，便对她这游戏的大获成功满心欢喜。可忽然她发觉这晚上正飞速地烧过去，便在一局结束时把牌一拢。

「现在来玩半个钟头通灵板吧。」她说。

「哦，不能再打一局吗？」休问，「这可是我多年来见着的最有趣的游戏了。打过这个，通灵板就乏味得要命了。」

「亲爱的，只要那园丁肯再通消息过来，就不会乏味。」她说。

「可那尽是些胡言乱语。」休说。

「你好没礼貌！那你看你的书去吧。」

玛格丽特已拿出了她的通灵板和一张纸，休却站起身来。

「今晚别玩了，玛格丽特。」他说。

「可为什么？你不必在旁边看着。」

「不管怎样，我请你别玩。」他说。

玛格丽特定定地望着他。

「休伊，你有心事，」她说，「说出来吧。我看你是害怕了。你觉得这宅子里有什么古怪。到底是什么？」

我看得出休在犹豫要不要告诉她，而我揣度他这是宁可押宝在通灵板只会傻乎乎地乱涂一气上。

「那就玩吧。」他说。

玛格丽特也犹豫了一下：她显然不想惹休不快，可他这般执意反对，在她看来一定颇不合理。

「好吧，就十分钟，」她说，「我答应不去想什么园丁了。」

她的手刚一搭上那板子，头便垂了下去，那板子也动了起来。我坐在她近旁，随着它稳稳地在纸上滚过，字迹便显露出来。

「我进来了，」那上面写着，「可我还是找不到她。你们是不是把她藏起来了？我要搜一搜你们所在的这间屋子。」

底下还写了什么、仍遮在通灵板底下看不见，我不得而知；因为就在那一刻，一股冰冷刺骨的气流绕室而过，门口又响起了一下——这一回断不会错——又响又不容分说的叩击。休一跃而起。

「玛格丽特，快醒醒，」他说，「有东西要来了！」

门开了，一个男人的身影走了进来。他就立在门里，头向前垂着，把头从一边转到另一边，似乎用那一双圆睁的、悲苦无尽无休的眼睛，向屋里每一个角落探视。

「玛格丽特，玛格丽特。」休又叫了一声。

可玛格丽特的眼睛也睁着；她直勾勾地盯着这位可怖的来客。

「别出声，休伊。」她压低嗓门说，一边站起身来。那鬼魂此刻正定定地望着她。那部浓密的铁锈色胡子上方的嘴唇动了一下，却没有发出半点声响，只见那嘴一张一合，淌着涎水。他抬起头来，而一重恐惧叠上一重恐惧，我看见他脖子的一侧豁开着一道红红的、闪着光的伤口。……

我们三个人就这样僵立着，冻住了一般，在某种叫人动弹不得、说不出话的死寂的禁制之中。这一阵僵持持续了多久，我全然不知：我想至多不过十几秒罢了。随后那鬼魂转过身，像来时一样走了出去。我们听见他的脚步声沿着镶拼木地板一路过去；前门传来抽开门闩的声响，紧接着一声震得整所宅子直晃的巨响，那门砰然合上。

「都过去了。」玛格丽特说，「上帝怜悯他吧！」

===Original===
Now the reader may put precisely what construction he pleases on this visitation from the dead. He need not, indeed, consider it to have been a visitation from the dead at all, but say that there had been impressed on the scene, where this murder and suicide happened, some sort of emotional record, which in certain circumstances could translate itself into images visible and invisible. Waves of ether, or whatnot, may conceivably retain the impress of such scenes; they may be held, so to speak, in solution, ready to be precipitated. Or he may hold that the spirit of the dead man indeed made itself manifest, revisiting in some sort of spiritual penance and remorse the place where his crime was committed. Naturally, no materialist will entertain such an explanation for an instant, but then there is no one so obstinately unreasonable as the materialist. Beyond doubt a dreadful deed was done there, and Margaret’s last utterance is not inapplicable.

===Chinese===
至于这一桩来自亡者的造访，读者尽可以随自己的高兴，作怎样的解释都成。他甚至可以根本不认这是亡者的造访，而说在那桩杀人与自戕发生的现场，烙下了某种情绪的记录，在特定的情形下，这记录便能化为可见或不可见的影像。以太的波也好，别的什么也好，保留下这类场景的印痕并非不可想象；可以说，它们仿佛被溶解着、悬置着，只待时机一到便沉淀而出。又或者，他可以认定那死者的亡灵确然显现了，是以某种灵魂上的赎罪与悔恨，重访了他犯下罪行的所在。自然，任何唯物论者都不会对这样的解释买一秒钟的账，可话又说回来，世上再没有谁像唯物论者那样固执得不近情理了。一桩可怖的事在那里发生过，这是毫无疑问的；而玛格丽特最后那句话，用在这里倒也并不为过。

## The Horror-Horn / 恐怖之角

===Original===
For the past ten days Alhubel had basked in the radiant midwinter weather proper to its eminence of over 6,000 feet. From rising to setting the sun (so surprising to those who have hitherto associated it with a pale, tepid plate indistinctly shining through the murky air of England) had blazed its way across the sparkling blue, and every night the serene and windless frost had made the stars sparkle like illuminated diamond dust. Sufficient snow had fallen before Christmas to content the skiers, and the big rink, sprinkled every evening, had given the skaters each morning a fresh surface on which to perform their slippery antics. Bridge and dancing served to while away the greater part of the night, and to me, now for the first time tasting the joys of a winter in the Engadine, it seemed that a new heaven and a new earth had been lighted, warmed, and refrigerated for the special benefit of those who like myself had been wise enough to save up their days of holiday for the winter.

But a break came in these ideal conditions: one afternoon the sun grew vapour-veiled and up the valley from the northwest a wind frozen with miles of travel over icebound hillsides began scouting through the calm halls of the heavens. Soon it grew dusted with snow, first in small flakes driven almost horizontally before its congealing breath and then in larger tufts as of swansdown. And though all day for a fortnight before the fate of nations and life and death had seemed to me of far less importance than to get certain tracings of the skate-blades on the ice of proper shape and size, it now seemed that the one paramount consideration was to hurry back to the hotel for shelter: it was wiser to leave rocking-turns alone than to be frozen in their quest.

===Chinese===
过去十天里，阿尔胡贝尔（Alhubel）一直沉浸在它与 6,000 余英尺海拔相称的明媚隆冬天气里。太阳从升起到落下，一路在那熠熠的碧空中燃烧着行过（这教那些迄今只把它同一轮苍白温吞、朦朦胧胧地透过英格兰浊空气发亮的圆盘联系起来的人大为惊奇）；每夜那宁静无风的严霜，又使繁星如点亮了的金刚砂一般闪烁。圣诞前已落下了足以让滑雪人心满意足的雪，那座大滑冰场每晚洒一遍水，第二天清早便给滑冰的人一面崭新的冰面，由着他们去耍那滑溜溜的把戏。桥牌与舞会消磨了大半个夜晚；而在我这个头一回尝到恩加丁（Engadine）冬日之乐的人看来，仿佛另有一方新天新地，专为像我这般明智地把假期积攒到冬天来用的人而点亮、烘暖、又冰镇过。

可这理想的境况终被打破：一天下午，太阳蒙上了一层水汽，从山谷西北方，顺着那越过多英里冰封山坡而已冻得彻骨的风，开始窥探起天庭寂静的殿堂。不一会儿，风里夹起了雪，先是细小的雪粒，几乎横着被它那凝固的气息刮走，继而便是大朵大朵如天鹅绒般的雪团。虽说此前整整两周，家国命运与生死存亡在我看来越发无足轻重，远不及在冰上划出形状大小都恰到好处的冰刀痕迹要紧，此刻头一等要紧的事，却是赶忙回旅馆避一避：与其为了那几个摇摆弯道把人冻僵，不如不去招惹它们。

===Original===
I had come out here with my cousin, Professor Ingram, the celebrated physiologist and Alpine climber. During the serenity of the last fortnight he had made a couple of notable winter ascents, but this morning his weather-wisdom had mistrusted the signs of the heavens, and instead of attempting the ascent of the Piz Passug he had waited to see whether his misgivings justified themselves. So there he sat now in the hall of the admirable hotel with his feet on the hot-water pipes and the latest delivery of the English post in his hands. This contained a pamphlet concerning the result of the Mount Everest expedition, of which he had just finished the perusal when I entered.

“A very interesting report,” he said, passing it to me, “and they certainly deserve to succeed next year. But who can tell, what that final six thousand feet may entail? Six thousand feet more when you have already accomplished twenty-three thousand does not seem much, but at present no one knows whether the human frame can stand exertion at such a height. It may affect not the lungs and heart only, but possibly the brain. Delirious hallucinations may occur. In fact, if I did not know better, I should have said that one such hallucination had occurred to the climbers already.”

“And what was that?” I asked.

===Chinese===
我和表兄英格拉姆教授（Professor Ingram）——那位著名的生理学家兼登山家——一同来到此地。过去两周风和日丽，他已完成两次了不起的冬季登顶；可今天早晨，他那份看天识天气的本领对天象起了疑心，于是没有去攀登皮茨帕苏格峰（Piz Passug），而是等着看自己的隐忧是否坐实。此刻他便坐在这家出色旅馆的大厅里，脚搁在热水管上，手里拿着刚到的最后一批英国邮件。其中有一本小册子，讲的是珠穆朗玛峰探险队的结果，我进去时他刚把它看完。

「一份很有意思的报告，」他把它递给我，说道，「他们明年当然配得上成功。可谁能说得准，那最后六千英尺会带来什么？在你已经登上了两万三千英尺之后，再多六千英尺似乎不算什么，可如今谁也不知道人体在那样的高度上能否承受得住劳累。它也许不仅影响肺和心，还可能影响脑子。人会陷入谵妄的幻觉。事实上，要不是我有所知闻，我准会说登山的人里已经有一个犯了这样的幻觉。」

「那是什么呢？」我问。

===Original===
“You will find that they thought they came across the tracks of some naked human foot at a great altitude. That looks at first sight like an hallucination. What more natural than that a brain excited and exhilarated by the extreme height should have interpreted certain marks in the snow as the footprints of a human being? Every bodily organ at these altitudes is exerting itself to the utmost to do its work, and the brain seizes on those marks in the snow and says ‘Yes, I’m all right, I’m doing my job, and I perceive marks in the snow which I affirm are human footprints.’ You know, even at this altitude, how restless and eager the brain is, how vividly, as you told me, you dream at night. Multiply that stimulus and that consequent eagerness and restlessness by three, and how natural that the brain should harbour illusions! What after all is the delirium which often accompanies high fever but the effort of the brain to do its work under the pressure of feverish conditions? It is so eager to continue perceiving that it perceives things which have no existence!”

“And yet you don’t think that these naked human footprints were illusions,” said I. “You told me you would have thought so, if you had not known better.”

He shifted in his chair and looked out of the window a moment. The air was thick now with the density of the big snowflakes that were driven along by the squealing northwest gale.

“Quite so,” he said. “In all probability the human footprints were real human footprints. I expect that they were the footprints, anyhow, of a being more nearly a man than anything else. My reason for saying so is that I know such beings exist. I have even seen quite near at hand—and I assure you I did not wish to be nearer in spite of my intense curiosity—the creature, shall we say, which would make such footprints. And if the snow was not so dense, I could show you the place where I saw him.”

===Chinese===
「你会看到，他们说自己在极高的地方遇见了某种赤足人的脚印。乍一看，这像是幻觉。一个被极端的高度刺激得兴奋昂扬的脑子，把雪上某些痕迹当作了人的脚印，还有比这更顺理成章的吗？在这种高度上，身体每个器官都在竭尽全力地履职，而脑子一把抓住了雪上的那些痕迹，便说：『是，我没问题，我干得挺好，我看见雪上有一些痕迹，我断定它们是人的脚印。』你总该知道，即便在这样的高度，脑子是何等躁动而急切，夜里做梦——你曾告诉过我——又何等鲜明。把这种刺激、以及随之而来的急切与躁动再加上三倍，那么脑子滋生出幻觉，岂不是再自然不过！说到底，高烧时常伴生的谵妄，不正是脑子在发烧的状况下拼命履职的挣扎吗？它是那样急切地要继续感知，乃至感知到了根本不存在的东西！」

「可你并不认为那些赤足的脚印是幻觉，」我说，「你告诉过我，要不是你有所知闻，你本会这样以为的。」

他在椅子里挪了挪身子，朝窗外望了一会儿。此刻空气已被呼啸的西北大风卷来的大雪花塞得满满当当。

「正是如此，」他说，「那些人的脚印，十之八九是真的人的脚印。我料想，无论如何，那是某种比任何东西都更接近人的生物的脚印。我这么说的理由是：我知道这种生物是存在的。我甚至近在咫尺地看见过——我向你保证，尽管我好奇心切，却一点也不想再靠近它——那头姑且这么说吧、能留下这种脚印的生灵。要不是雪下得这么密，我还能指给你看，我是在哪儿看见它的。」

===Original===
He pointed straight out of the window, where across the valley lies the huge tower of the Ungeheuerhorn with the carved pinnacle of rock at the top like some gigantic rhinoceros-horn. On one side only, as I knew, was the mountain practicable, and that for none but the finest climbers; on the other three a succession of ledges and precipices rendered it unscalable. Two thousand feet of sheer rock form the tower; below are five hundred feet of fallen boulders, up to the edge of which grow dense woods of larch and pine.

“Upon the Ungeheuerhorn?” I asked.

“Yes. Up till twenty years ago it had never been ascended, and I, like several others, spent a lot of time in trying to find a route up it. My guide and I sometimes spent three nights together at the hut beside the Blumen glacier, prowling round it, and it was by luck really that we found the route, for the mountain looks even more impracticable from the far side than it does from this. But one day we found a long, transverse fissure in the side which led to a negotiable ledge; then there came a slanting ice couloir which you could not see till you got to the foot of it. However, I need not go into that.”

===Chinese===
他径直朝窗外一指：山谷对面，耸立着翁盖莫霍恩峰（Ungeheuerhorn）那座巨大的塔峰，顶端那座嶙峋的岩柱，宛如一根硕大无朋的犀角。据我所知，这山只有一面可登，且非最顶尖的登山好手不能为；其余三面，层层叠叠的岩阶与悬崖使它无从攀登。两千英尺的峭壁构成了那座塔峰；其下是五百英尺的乱石堆，直至落叶松与松树的密林边沿。

「在翁盖莫霍恩峰上？」我问。

「是的。直到二十年前，它还从未被人登顶过，我像另外几个人一样，花了不少工夫想找出一条上山的路。我和我的向导有时一起在布卢门冰川（Blumen glacier）旁的那间小屋里连住三夜，绕着它四处打探，而那条路实在是凭运气找到的，因为从对面看，这山比从这边看还要无可攀援。可有一天，我们在山体侧面发现了一条长长的横向裂隙，通往一处勉强可行的岩阶；接着是一道斜斜的冰沟槽，非得到它脚下才能看得见。不过，这些细节我就不必细说了。」

===Original===
The big room where we sat was filling up with cheerful groups driven indoors by this sudden gale and snowfall, and the cackle of merry tongues grew loud. The band, too, that invariable appanage of teatime at Swiss resorts, had begun to tune up for the usual potpourri from the works of Puccini. Next moment the sugary, sentimental melodies began.

“Strange contrast!” said Ingram. “Here are we sitting warm and cosy, our ears pleasantly tickled with these little baby tunes and outside is the great storm growing more violent every moment, and swirling round the austere cliffs of the Ungeheuerhorn: the Horror-Horn, as indeed it was to me.”

“I want to hear all about it,” I said. “Every detail: make a short story long, if it’s short. I want to know why it’s *your* Horror-Horn?”

===Chinese===
我们坐着的那间大屋子，渐渐被这突如其来的狂风大雪赶进屋来的欢快一群一群的人填满了，叽叽喳喳的谈笑声越来越响。那支乐队——瑞士各处茶时必不可少的附属——也开始调起音来，准备演奏那段惯常的、取自普契尼（Puccini）作品的杂锦选段。下一刻，那甜腻腻的、多愁善感的旋律便响了起来。

「多么奇异的对照！」英格拉姆说，「我们这儿坐着，又暖又惬意，耳朵被这些奶声奶气的小调挠得舒舒服服，外头却是越刮越猛的大风雪，在翁盖莫霍恩峰那冷峻的峭壁间打旋：那恐怖之角（the Horror-Horn），果然于我也是恐怖之角。」

「我想把这事原原本本听一遍，」我说，「每一个细节：原是短故事，也请把它说成长故事。我想知道，为什么它是『你的』恐怖之角？」

===Original===
“Well, Chanton and I (he was my guide) used to spend days prowling about the cliffs, making a little progress on one side and then being stopped, and gaining perhaps five hundred feet on another side and then being confronted by some insuperable obstacle, till the day when by luck we found the route. Chanton never liked the job, for some reason that I could not fathom. It was not because of the difficulty or danger of the climbing, for he was the most fearless man I have ever met when dealing with rocks and ice, but he was always insistent that we should get off the mountain and back to the Blumen hut before sunset. He was scarcely easy even when we had got back to shelter and locked and barred the door, and I well remember one night when, as we ate our supper, we heard some animal, a wolf probably, howling somewhere out in the night. A positive panic seized him, and I don’t think he closed his eyes till morning. It struck me then that there might be some grisly legend about the mountain, connected possibly with its name, and next day I asked him why the peak was called the Horror-Horn. He put the question off at first, and said that, like the Schreckhorn, its name was due to its precipices and falling stones; but when I pressed him further he acknowledged that there was a legend about it, which his father had told him. There were creatures, so it was supposed, that lived in its caves, things human in shape, and covered, except for the face and hands, with long black hair. They were dwarfs in size, four feet high or thereabouts, but of prodigious strength and agility, remnants of some wild primeval race. It seemed that they were still in an upward stage of evolution, or so I guessed, for the story ran that sometimes girls had been carried off by them, not as prey, and not for any such fate as for those captured by cannibals, but to be bred from.
