Young men also had been raped by them, to be mated with the females of their tribe. All this looked as if the creatures, as I said, were tending towards humanity. But naturally I did not believe a word of it, as applied to the conditions of the present day. Centuries ago, conceivably, there may have been such beings, and, with the extraordinary tenacity of tradition, the news of this had been handed down and was still current round the hearths of the peasants. As for their numbers, Chanton told me that three had been once seen together by a man who owing to his swiftness on skis had escaped to tell the tale. This man, he averred, was no other than his grandfather, who had been benighted one winter evening as he passed through the dense woods below the Ungeheuerhorn, and Chanton supposed that they had been driven down to these lower altitudes in search of food during severe winter weather, for otherwise the recorded sights of them had always taken place among the rocks of the peak itself. They had pursued his grandfather, then a young man, at an extraordinarily swift canter, running sometimes upright as men run, sometimes on all-fours in the manner of beasts, and their howls were just such as that we had heard that night in the Blumen hut. Such at any rate was the story Chanton told me, and, like you, I regarded it as the very moonshine of superstition. But the very next day I had reason to reconsider my judgment about it.

===Chinese===
「嗳，香东（Chanton）和我——他是我的向导——从前常常花上整整几天在峭壁间转悠，从这一面攀上一点，便被挡住，又从那一面爬高个五百英尺，接着便遇着某处不可逾越的障碍，直到那一天我们凭着运气找到了路。香东从来不喜欢这桩差事，原因何在，我百思不得其解。并非因为攀登的艰难或危险，因为论到与岩石和冰雪打交道，他是我所见过的最有胆量的人；可他总坚持我们必须在日落前下山、回到布卢门小屋。即便我们已经回到了藏身之处、闩好了门，他也难以安下心来；我清楚地记得有一夜，我们正吃晚饭，听见外头黑夜里有什么野兽——多半是狼——在某处嚎叫。他竟被一阵切切实实的惊惶攫住，我想他直到天亮也没阖过眼。那时我便隐隐觉得，这山也许有什么可怕的传说，说不定与它的名字有关；第二天我便问他，为什么这山峰叫作恐怖之角。他起先搪塞了过去，说它和施雷克霍恩峰（Schreckhorn）一样，名字是因它的悬崖和落石而得；可我再加追问，他便承认关于它确有一个传说，是他父亲讲给他听的。据说山中的洞穴里住着一种生灵，形似人，除了脸和手之外，周身覆盖着长长的黑毛。它们身量矮小，四英尺上下，却力大无穷、矫健异常，是某一支野蛮太古种族的孑遗。据我推测，它们似乎仍处在向人演进的过程中，因为传说里讲，有时姑娘会被它们掳去——并非当作猎物，也并非要遭受被食人族掳去的那类厄运——而是用来繁衍。年轻男子也会被它们强掳，与本族的雌性交合。这一切看起来，正如我所说，这些生灵正趋向于人。可我自然一个字也不信，就今日的情形而言。几个世纪以前，不妨说可能有这种生灵存在，而凭着传说那异乎寻常的顽强，这一消息便传了下来，至今仍流传在农人的炉火边。至于它们的数目，香东告诉我，曾有人一次见过三只聚在一起，那人因为滑雪滑得快，才逃脱了性命、得以把这事讲出来。他断言，那人不是别人，正是他的祖父，有一年冬天的傍晚，他祖父在翁盖莫霍恩峰下那片密林里穿行时被困在了夜色中；香东猜想，它们是被严冬的天气赶到这些较低的地方来觅食的，因为除此之外，有记录的目击都发生在那座山峰本身的岩石之间。它们追赶他祖父——其时还是个年轻人——其疾如飞，时而像人那样直立着跑，时而像野兽那样四脚着地，它们的嚎叫，正与我们那一夜在布卢门小屋听见的一般无二。无论如何，这便是香东讲给我的故事，而我和你一样，把它当作彻头彻尾的迷信妄谈。可就在第二天，我便有了理由，要重新掂量自己的判断。

===Original===
“It was on that day that after a week of exploration we hit on the only route at present known to the top of our peak. We started as soon as there was light enough to climb by, for, as you may guess, on very difficult rocks it is impossible to climb by lantern or moonlight. We hit on the long fissure I have spoken of, we explored the ledge which from below seemed to end in nothingness, and with an hour’s step-cutting ascended the couloir which led upwards from it. From there onwards it was a rock-climb, certainly of considerable difficulty, but with no heartbreaking discoveries ahead, and it was about nine in the morning that we stood on the top. We did not wait there long, for that side of the mountain is raked by falling stones loosened, when the sun grows hot, from the ice that holds them, and we made haste to pass the ledge where the falls are most frequent. After that there was the long fissure to descend, a matter of no great difficulty, and we were at the end of our work by midday, both of us, as you may imagine, in the state of the highest elation.

===Chinese===
「就在那一天，经过一星期的探查，我们撞上了目前所知通往峰顶的唯一路径。天刚亮到能攀爬，我们便动身了，因为你可以想见，在极其险恶的岩石上，提着灯笼、借着月光是没法攀的。我们找到了我说过的那条长裂隙，探查了那处从下面看来似乎通往虚无的岩阶，又花了一个钟头砍出台阶，攀上了从那里向上延伸的冰沟槽。从那儿再往上便是岩石攀登了，固然相当艰难，却再没有令人心碎的新难关横在前头；约莫早上九点，我们便站上了峰顶。我们没有在上面久留，因为那面的山体在太阳晒热之后，便会落石不断——石头是被晒化了托着它们的冰而松脱的——我们便匆匆穿过落石最频繁的那段岩阶。此后的便只是顺着那条长裂隙下撤，这倒不算太难；到了正午，我们的大功便已告成，你我可想而知，两人都处在最高昂的兴奋之中。

===Original===
“A long and tiresome scramble among the huge boulders at the foot of the cliff then lay before us. Here the hillside is very porous and great caves extend far into the mountain. We had unroped at the base of the fissure, and were picking our way as seemed good to either of us among these fallen rocks, many of them bigger than an ordinary house, when, on coming round the corner of one of these, I saw that which made it clear that the stories Chanton had told me were no figment of traditional superstition.

===Chinese===
「接下来等着我们的，是在崖脚那片巨大的乱石间一段又长又乏味的攀爬。这一带的山体极为多孔，巨大的岩洞深深延伸到山腹之中。我们在裂隙脚下便解开了绳索，各自在那些坠石之间拣好走的路走，那些石头有许多比一栋普通的房子还大；就在我绕过其中一块的拐角时，我看见了那样一幕，使我顿时明白，香东讲给我的那些绝非传统迷信的杜撰。

===Original===
“Not twenty yards in front of me lay one of the beings of which he had spoken. There it sprawled naked and basking on its back with face turned up to the sun, which its narrow eyes regarded unwinking. In form it was completely human, but the growth of hair that covered limbs and trunk alike almost completely hid the suntanned skin beneath. But its face, save for the down on its cheeks and chin, was hairless, and I looked on a countenance the sensual and malevolent bestiality of which froze me with horror. Had the creature been an animal, one would have felt scarcely a shudder at the gross animalism of it; the horror lay in the fact that it was a man. There lay by it a couple of gnawed bones, and, its meal finished, it was lazily licking its protuberant lips, from which came a purring murmur of content. With one hand it scratched the thick hair on its belly, in the other it held one of these bones, which presently split in half beneath the pressure of its finger and thumb. But my horror was not based on the information of what happened to those men whom these creatures caught, it was due only to my proximity to a thing so human and so infernal. The peak, of which the ascent had a moment ago filled us with such elated satisfaction, became to me an Ungeheuerhorn indeed, for it was the home of beings more awful than the delirium of nightmare could ever have conceived.

===Chinese===
「离我不过二十码的前方，便躺着一只他所说的那种生灵。它赤身裸体、仰面朝天，懒懒地摊在那里晒太阳，脸朝着日头，那双狭长的眼睛一眨不眨地瞅着它。它的身形完全和人一样，可那一身覆盖着四肢与躯干的毛发，几乎把底下晒成褐色的皮肤遮得严严实实。然而它的脸——除两颊与下巴上那层绒毛之外——却是光溜溜的；我所注视的那张脸上，满是淫邪而恶毒的兽性，把我惊得僵在了原地。倘若它只是一头野兽，人对它那粗鄙的兽性几乎不会有一丝战栗；恐怖之处在于，它是个人。它身旁丢着两根啃过的骨头，饭既吃完，它正懒洋洋地舔着那外凸的嘴唇，口中发出一阵满足的呼噜声。它一只手搔着肚皮上的厚毛，另一只手握着其中一根骨头，不一会儿，那骨头便被它的拇指与食指一捏，裂成了两半。可我的恐惧并非源于得知这些生灵一旦抓到人会怎样处置，而仅仅是因为我离一个如此似人、又如此可怖的东西太近了。这座山峰，刚才攀登它还使我们满心欢喜得意，此刻在我真成了一座名副其实的恐怖之角（Ungeheuerhorn），因为它是比噩梦的谵妄所能想象的更为可怖的生灵的巢穴。

===Original===
“Chanton was a dozen paces behind me, and with a backward wave of my hand I caused him to halt. Then withdrawing myself with infinite precaution, so as not to attract the gaze of that basking creature, I slipped back round the rock, whispered to him what I had seen, and with blanched faces we made a long detour, peering round every corner, and crouching low, not knowing that at any step we might not come upon another of these beings, or that from the mouth of one of these caves in the mountainside there might not appear another of those hairless and dreadful faces, with perhaps this time the breasts and insignia of womanhood. That would have been the worst of all.

===Chinese===
「香东在我身后十几步开外，我朝后摆了摆手，叫他停住。然后我以十二万分的谨慎把自己撤回来，免得招惹那晒太阳的生灵的注意，溜回到岩石后头，悄声把我看见的告诉了他。我们脸色煞白，绕了老大一个弯，每一个拐角都先探头张望，把身子压得低低的，不知下一步会不会又撞见另一只这样的生灵，不知这山壁上哪一处洞穴的洞口会不会又探出另一张无毛的、可怕的脸——这一回也许还带着女人的乳房和特征。那才是最不堪设想的。

===Original===
“Luck favoured us, for we made our way among the boulders and shifting stones, the rattle of which might at any moment have betrayed us, without a repetition of my experience, and once among the trees we ran as if the Furies themselves were in pursuit. Well now did I understand, though I dare say I cannot convey, the qualms of Chanton’s mind when he spoke to me of these creatures. Their very humanity was what made them so terrible, the fact that they were of the same race as ourselves, but of a type so abysmally degraded that the most brutal and inhuman of men would have seemed angelic in comparison.”

===Chinese===
「老天保佑，我们在那些乱石与松动的石块间穿行——那些石头的磕碰声随时可能出卖我们——却没再碰上我那样的遭遇；一钻进树林，我们便撒腿狂奔，仿佛身后有复仇女神（the Furies）们紧紧追赶。直到此刻，我才算真正明白了——虽然我恐怕说不明白——香东对我提起这些生灵时心里那份惊惶。使它们如此可怖的，正是它们那似人之处：它们和我们同属一类，却又堕落到那样一个深渊，相形之下，最残忍、最不像人的人，也显得有如天使。」

===Original===
The music of the small band was over before he had finished the narrative, and the chattering groups round the tea-table had dispersed. He paused a moment.

“There was a horror of the spirit,” he said, “which I experienced then, from which, I verily believe, I have never entirely recovered. I saw then how terrible a living thing could be, and how terrible, in consequence, was life itself. In us all I suppose lurks some inherited germ of that ineffable bestiality, and who knows whether, sterile as it has apparently become in the course of centuries, it might not fructify again. When I saw that creature sun itself, I looked into the abyss out of which we have crawled. And these creatures are trying to crawl out of it now, if they exist any longer. Certainly for the last twenty years there has been no record of their being seen, until we come to this story of the footprint seen by the climbers on Everest. If that is authentic, if the party did not mistake the footprint of some bear, or whatnot, for a human tread, it seems as if still this bestranded remnant of mankind is in existence.”

===Chinese===
他那番讲述还没完，小乐队的演奏便已收了场，茶桌四周那群叽叽喳喳的人也已散去。他停了一停。

「那一次，我经历了一种心灵上的恐怖，」他说，「我相信，我至今不曾完全从中复原。那时我才看见，一个活物可以可怕到什么地步，也因此，生命本身可以可怕到什么地步。我想，我们每一个人身上，都潜伏着某种承袭而来的、那不可名状的兽性的胚芽，谁知它——纵使在这几个世纪的漫长岁月里显然已归于不育——会不会再度结果。我看见那生灵晒太阳的那一刻，便是俯瞰了我们一路爬上来的那道深渊。而这些生灵，倘若它们仍存在于世，此刻正想从那道深渊里爬上来。至少这二十年来，再没有任何关于它们被人目击的记载，直到珠穆朗玛峰上登山者看见脚印的那段传闻。倘若那属实，倘若那一行人并非把某只熊之类的脚印错认成了人的足迹，那么，似乎这一支搁浅在岸的人类孑遗，至今仍存于世间。」

===Original===
Now, Ingram, had told his story well; but sitting in this warm and civilised room, the horror which he had clearly felt had not communicated itself to me in any very vivid manner. Intellectually, I agreed, I could appreciate his horror, but certainly my spirit felt no shudder of interior comprehension.

“But it is odd,” I said, “that your keen interest in physiology did not dispel your qualms. You were looking, so I take it, at some form of man more remote probably than the earliest human remains. Did not something inside you say ‘This is of absorbing significance’?”

He shook his head.

“No: I only wanted to get away,” said he. “It was not, as I have told you, the terror of what according to Chanton’s story, might await us if we were captured; it was sheer horror at the creature itself. I quaked at it.”

---

===Chinese===
英格拉姆这故事讲得很好；然而坐在这间温暖、文明的屋子里，他所明显感到的那种恐怖，并不曾怎样鲜明地传到我身上。理智上，我承认我能领会他的恐怖，可我的内心，却全然没有那种感同身受的战栗。

「不过，有一桩倒奇怪，」我说，「你对生理学的浓厚兴趣，竟没能驱散你的惊惶。依我看，你所注视的，多半是一种比最古的人类遗骸还要久远的人形。你心里难道没有什么在说：『这是极其重要的发现』吗？」

他摇了摇头。

「不：我只想着赶紧脱身，」他说，「这并不是——我已经告诉过你——出于对香东故事里所说的、我们万一被擒会遭遇何等下场的那种恐惧；那完全是对那生灵本身的纯粹恐惧。我在它面前发抖。」

---

===Original===
The snowstorm and the gale increased in violence that night, and I slept uneasily, plucked again and again from slumber by the fierce battling of the wind that shook my windows as if with an imperious demand for admittance. It came in billowy gusts, with strange noises intermingled with it as for a moment it abated, with flutings and moanings that rose to shrieks as the fury of it returned. These noises, no doubt, mingled themselves with my drowsed and sleepy consciousness, and once I tore myself out of nightmare, imagining that the creatures of the Horror-Horn had gained footing on my balcony and were rattling at the window-bolts. But before morning the gale had died away, and I awoke to see the snow falling dense and fast in a windless air. For three days it continued, without intermission, and with its cessation there came a frost such as I have never felt before. Fifty degrees were registered one night, and more the next, and what the cold must have been on the cliffs of the Ungeheuerhorn I cannot imagine. Sufficient, so I thought, to have made an end altogether of its secret inhabitants: my cousin, on that day twenty years ago, had missed an opportunity for study which would probably never fall again either to him or another.

===Chinese===
那天夜里风雪愈演愈烈，我睡得极不安稳，一次又一次被狂风凶猛的扑打从睡梦中拽醒，它摇撼着我的窗子，仿佛强横地要闯进来。它一阵阵地涌来，暂歇的片刻，便夹杂着种种奇怪的声响，那呜呜咽咽的哀吟，待到风势再起，便又拔高成了尖厉的嘶叫。这些声响，想必也渗进了我昏沉困倦的意识；有一回，我猛地从噩梦中挣脱出来，恍惚觉得恐怖之角的那些生灵已经爬上了我的阳台，正哗啦哗啦地摇撼着窗栓。可天亮之前，狂风便平息了下去，我醒来时，只见大雪在无风的空气中又密又急地落着。这场雪下了整整三天，一刻不停；雪一停，便来了一场我这辈子从未经历过的严寒。一夜测到零下五十度，第二夜更冷，至于翁盖莫霍恩峰的悬崖上究竟冷到了什么地步，我都不敢去想。我想，足以把它那些隐秘的居民一总了结了吧：我那位表兄，二十年前的那一日，错过了一次研考的机会，那机会多半再也不会落到他、或任何别的人头上了。

===Original===
I received one morning a letter from a friend saying that he had arrived at the neighbouring winter resort of St. Luigi, and proposing that I should come over for a morning’s skating and lunch afterwards. The place was not more than a couple of miles off, if one took the path over the low, pine-clad foothills above which lay the steep woods below the first rocky slopes of the Ungeheuerhorn; and accordingly, with a knapsack containing skates on my back, I went on skis over the wooded slopes and down by an easy descent again on to St. Luigi. The day was overcast, clouds entirely obscured the higher peaks though the sun was visible, pale and unluminous, through the mists. But as the morning went on, it gained the upper hand, and I slid down into St. Luigi beneath a sparkling firmament. We skated and lunched, and then, since it looked as if thick weather was coming up again, I set out early about three o’clock for my return journey.

===Chinese===
一天早上，我收到一位朋友的来信，说他已到了邻近的冬季度假地圣路易吉（St. Luigi），约我过去滑一上午冰、再一起吃午饭。那地方不过两英里开外，只要走那条越过松林覆盖的低矮丘陵的小径——那丘陵之上，便是翁盖莫霍恩峰最初几道岩石坡麓之下的陡峭林地——于是我背着一只装着冰鞋的背包，踩着滑雪板，穿过林木葱郁的山坡，再顺着一段好走的下坡，滑进了圣路易吉。那天本来阴着，云把更高的几座山峰全遮住了，虽然隔着雾，太阳仍隐约可辨，苍白而不发光。可随着上午一点点过去，太阳渐渐占了上风，我滑进圣路易吉时，头顶已是一片晶莹的蓝天。我们滑了冰、吃了午饭，随后，眼看着天色又要转阴，我便早早地在三点来钟动身往回走。

===Original===
Hardly had I got into the woods when the clouds gathered thick above, and streamers and skeins of them began to descend among the pines through which my path threaded its way. In ten minutes more their opacity had so increased that I could hardly see a couple of yards in front of me. Very soon I became aware that I must have got off the path, for snow-cowled shrubs lay directly in my way, and, casting back to find it again, I got altogether confused as to direction. But, though progress was difficult, I knew I had only to keep on the ascent, and presently I should come to the brow of these low foothills, and descend into the open valley where Alhubel stood. So on I went, stumbling and sliding over obstacles, and unable, owing to the thickness of the snow, to take off my skis, for I should have sunk over the knees at each step. Still the ascent continued, and looking at my watch I saw that I had already been near an hour on my way from St. Luigi, a period more than sufficient to complete my whole journey. But still I stuck to my idea that though I had certainly strayed far from my proper route a few minutes more must surely see me over the top of the upward way, and I should find the ground declining into the next valley. About now, too, I noticed that the mists were growing suffused with rose-colour, and, though the inference was that it must be close on sunset, there was consolation in the fact that they were there and might lift at any moment and disclose to me my whereabouts. But the fact that night would soon be on me made it needful to bar my mind against that despair of loneliness which so eats out the heart of a man who is lost in woods or on mountainside, that, though still there is plenty of vigour in his limbs, his nervous force is sapped, and he can do no more than lie down and abandon himself to whatever fate may await him.… And then I heard that which made the thought of loneliness seem bliss indeed, for there was a worse fate than loneliness. What I heard resembled the howl of a wolf, and it came from not far in front of me where the ridge—was it a ridge?—still rose higher in vestment of pines.

===Chinese===
我一钻进树林，头顶的云便聚得厚了起来，一缕一缕、一团一团的，开始在那条小径所穿行的松林之间沉下来。再过十分钟，云雾浓得我连前面两码都看不清了。我很快就发觉自己一定是走错了路，因为戴着雪兜帽般的灌木丛直直地横在我面前；我回头去找那条路，方向却已全然糊涂了。可路虽然难走，我明白只要一直往上爬，不久总能到这片低矮丘陵的梁上，再下到阿尔胡贝尔所在的那片开阔山谷。于是我只管往前，在障碍物间跌跌撞撞、滑来滑去；雪积得太厚，我又没法脱下滑雪板，否则每一步都要没过膝盖。上坡仍在继续，我一看表，从圣路易吉动身已将近一个钟头，这点时间足够我把全程走完了。可我仍死守着一个念头：虽说确实偏离了正道，再过几分钟总该到这上坡路的顶了吧，到时候地势便会往下一个山谷倾斜了。大约就在这时，我又注意到雾里渐渐泛起了玫瑰色；虽说由此可推断日头已近黄昏，可这点泛红至少说明雾还在，随时可能升起来，露出我身在何处。可夜色很快就要拢上来，我便不得不紧紧锁住心神，抵挡那种孤独的绝望——那种绝望最能掏空一个在林中或山间迷路之人的心，它叫他四肢明明还很有气力，精神的劲头却已被抽干，他只能一躺了之，任凭什么样的命运降临到自己头上。……就在这时，我听见了那样一种声响，它叫我想起孤独反而是桩幸事，因为还有比孤独更糟的命运。我听见的，像是一声狼嚎，它来自我前面不远的地方，那里那道山脊——究竟是不是一道山脊呢？——仍披着松林的衣裳，向上耸得更高。

===Original===
From behind me came a sudden puff of wind, which shook the frozen snow from the drooping pine-branches, and swept away the mists as a broom sweeps the dust from the floor. Radiant above me were the unclouded skies, already charged with the red of the sunset, and in front I saw that I had come to the very edge of the wood through which I had wandered so long. But it was no valley into which I had penetrated, for there right ahead of me rose the steep slope of boulders and rocks soaring upwards to the foot of the Ungeheuerhorn. What, then, was that cry of a wolf which had made my heart stand still? I saw.

Not twenty yards from me was a fallen tree, and leaning against the trunk of it was one of the denizens of the Horror-Horn, and it was a woman. She was enveloped in thick growth of hair grey and tufted, and from her head it streamed down over her shoulders and her bosom, from which hung withered and pendulous breasts. And looking on her face I comprehended not with my mind alone, but with a shudder of my spirit, what Ingram had felt. Never had nightmare fashioned so terrible a countenance; the beauty of sun and stars and of the beasts of the field and the kindly race of men could not atone for so hellish an incarnation of the spirit of life. A fathomless bestiality modelled the slavering mouth and the narrow eyes; I looked into the abyss itself and knew that out of that abyss on the edge of which I leaned the generations of men had climbed. What if that ledge crumbled in front of me and pitched me headlong into its nethermost depths?…

===Chinese===
我身后忽地刮来一阵风，把冻成冰的雪从低垂的松枝上摇落，又像扫帚扫地一般，把雾一扫而空。我头顶是晴朗无云的天，已染上了落日的殷红；面前，我看见自己已到了这片我徘徊许久的树林的边沿。可我所闯入的并不是什么山谷，因为就在我正前方，陡峭的乱石坡拔地而起，一路向上直抵翁盖莫霍恩峰的脚下。那么，那叫我心骤然一停的狼嚎，又是怎么回事呢？我看见了。

离我不到二十码的地方，倒着一棵树，一只恐怖之角的居民正倚在它的树干上——是个女人。她裹着一身灰色的、一簇簇的厚毛，头发从头上顺着肩膀和胸膛披流下来，胸前垂着干瘪松弛的乳房。我端详着她的脸，不只是用脑子，更是用一阵灵魂的战栗，明白了英格拉姆当时的感受。噩梦也从未捏造出如此可怕的一张脸；日月星辰之美、田野走兽之美、人类那善良的种族之美，都无从为生命精神如此地狱般的一次化身赎罪。那无底的兽性，塑出了那张流着涎水的嘴和那双狭长的眼；我直直地望进了深渊本身，明白了世人那一代代的人，便是从我倚着的这道深渊边上爬上来的。万一我面前的这道边沿一松，把我一个倒栽葱摔进它最深的深处，那又如何呢？……

===Original===
In one hand she held by the horns a chamois that kicked and struggled. A blow from its hind-leg caught her withered thigh, and with a grunt of anger she seized the leg in her other hand, and, as a man may pull from its sheath a stem of meadow-grass, she plucked it off the body, leaving the torn skin hanging round the gaping wound. Then putting the red, bleeding member to her mouth she sucked at it as a child sucks a stick of sweetmeat. Through flesh and gristle her short, brown teeth penetrated, and she licked her lips with a sound of purring. Then dropping the leg by her side, she looked again at the body of the prey now quivering in its death-convulsion, and with finger and thumb gouged out one of its eyes. She snapped her teeth on it, and it cracked like a soft-shelled nut.

===Chinese===
她一只手揪着一只小羚羊（chamois）的角，那羚羊还在踢蹬挣扎。羚羊的后腿一蹬，踢中了她干瘪的大腿，她怒哼一声，另一只手便攥住那条腿，像人从草鞘里抽出一根草地里的草茎似的，生生把它从羊身上扯了下来，撕开的皮还挂在豁大的伤口周围。然后她把那条血淋淋、红殷殷的腿凑到嘴边，像孩子吮一根糖棒似的吮了起来。她那短短的褐色牙齿咬穿了肉和软骨，一边还发出呼噜呼噜的响声舔着嘴唇。接着她把那条腿往身边一丢，又看向那猎物的身子——它正在临死的抽搐里颤动——用拇指和食指抠出了它的一只眼睛。她拿牙一咬，那眼珠像一颗软壳坚果似的，咔的一声裂开了。

===Original===
It must have been but a few seconds that I stood watching her, in some indescribable catalepsy of terror, while through my brain there pealed the panic-command of my mind to my stricken limbs, “Begone, begone, while there is time.” Then, recovering the power of my joints and muscles, I tried to slip behind a tree and hide myself from this apparition. But the woman—shall I say?—must have caught my stir of movement, for she raised her eyes from her living feast and saw me. She craned forward her neck, she dropped her prey, and half rising began to move towards me. As she did this, she opened her mouth, and gave forth a howl such as I had heard a moment before. It was answered by another, but faintly and distantly.

===Chinese===
我那样僵立着看她，想必不过几秒钟，却陷入了一种无法形容的、吓僵了的木然里，与此同时，我脑中轰响着我的心神向那瘫软的四肢发出的仓皇号令：「快逃，快逃，趁还来得及。」随后，我重新唤回了关节与筋肉的力量，想悄悄溜到一棵树后，把自己从这副可怖的景象里藏起来。可那女人——我该这么说吗？——一定捕捉到了我这一动，因为她从她那活生生的盛宴上抬起眼，看见了我。她把脖子往前一伸，扔下猎物，半直起身，开始朝我移动。她一边这样，一边张开嘴，发出了一声方才我所听见的那种嚎叫。远远地、隐隐地，另一声嚎叫应和了它。

===Original===
Sliding and slipping, with the toes of my skis tripping in the obstacles below the snow, I plunged forward down the hill between the pine-trunks. The low sun already sinking behind some rampart of mountain in the west reddened the snow and the pines with its ultimate rays. My knapsack with the skates in it swung to and fro on my back, one ski-stock had already been twitched out of my hand by a fallen branch of pine, but not a second’s pause could I allow myself to recover it. I gave no glance behind, and I knew not at what pace my pursuer was on my track, or indeed whether any pursued at all, for my whole mind and energy, now working at full power again under the stress of my panic, was devoted to getting away down the hill and out of the wood as swiftly as my limbs could bear me. For a little while I heard nothing but the hissing snow of my headlong passage, and the rustle of the covered undergrowth beneath my feet, and then, from close at hand behind me, once more the wolf-howl sounded and I heard the plunging of footsteps other than my own.

===Chinese===
我跌跌滑滑地向前冲，滑雪板的板尖被雪下的障碍物绊着，从松树干之间一路往山下扎去。低低的太阳已被西边某一道山垒遮去大半，用它最后的几缕光，把雪和松树都染得通红。我背上装着冰鞋的背包甩来甩去，一只滑雪杖已经被一根落下的松枝从我手里夺走了，可我连停下一秒钟去捡它的工夫也不敢耽搁。我不敢回头看一眼，也不知道追我的人以怎样的速度在我身后追赶，甚或到底有没有人在追，因为我整个的心神与气力——在惊惶的催逼下此刻又全速运转起来——全都扑在了一件事上：尽我这双腿所能，飞快地逃下山、逃出这片林子。有一阵子，我什么也听不见，只有自己一路横冲直撞激起的嗤嗤雪声，和脚下覆着雪的下木丛的窸窣声；然后，从我身后近处，那狼嚎再一次响起，我听见了除我之外另有一双脚在沉重地扑腾。

===Original===
The strap of my knapsack had shifted, and as my skates swung to and fro on my back it chafed and pressed on my throat, hindering free passage of air, of which, God knew, my labouring lungs were in dire need, and without pausing I slipped it free from my neck, and held it in the hand from which my ski-stock had been jerked. I seemed to go a little more easily for this adjustment, and now, not so far distant, I could see below me the path from which I had strayed. If only I could reach that, the smoother going would surely enable me to outdistance my pursuer, who even on the rougher ground was but slowly overhauling me, and at the sight of that ribbon stretching unimpeded downhill, a ray of hope pierced the black panic of my soul. With that came the desire, keen and insistent, to see who or what it was that was on my tracks, and I spared a backward glance. It was she, the hag whom I had seen at her gruesome meal; her long grey hair flew out behind her, her mouth chattered and gibbered, her fingers made grabbing movements, as if already they closed on me.

===Chinese===
我背包的带子滑了位，冰鞋在我背上甩来甩去，磨着、压着我的喉头，挡住了气的去路——上帝知道，我那喘得要命的两片肺正急需气呢——我一边跑一边把它从脖子上褪下来，握在原来被夺走滑雪杖的那只手里。这一调整之后，我似乎跑得顺了些；这时，在不远的下方，我已经能看见我走失的那条小径了。只要能到得了那里，那好走得多的路一定能让我甩开追我的人——纵使在这坑洼的地上，他也不过是慢慢追上我而已；一看见那条缎带似的路畅通无阻地向山下铺展，一线希望便刺穿了我灵魂里那一片漆黑的惊惶。伴随希望而来的，是一股强烈而急切的冲动，想看看追着我的到底是谁、是什么东西，我便回头瞥了一眼。是她，是我看见在那顿骇人饭菜前的那老妖婆；她灰白的长发在身后飞扬，嘴里叽叽咕咕地念念有词，手指一张一合地做出抓攫的动作，仿佛已经攥住了我。

===Original===
But the path was now at hand, and the nearness of it I suppose made me incautious. A hump of snow-covered bush lay in my path, and, thinking I could jump over it, I tripped and fell, smothering myself in snow. I heard a maniac noise, half scream, half laugh, from close behind, and before I could recover myself the grabbing fingers were at my neck, as if a steel vice had closed there. But my right hand in which I held my knapsack of skates was free, and with a blind backhanded movement I whirled it behind me at the full length of its strap, and knew that my desperate blow had found its billet somewhere. Even before I could look round I felt the grip on my neck relax, and something subsided into the very bush which had entangled me. I recovered my feet and turned.

===Chinese===
可那条路已经在眼前了，我想正是它的临近叫我大意了起来。一丛覆着雪的矮灌木横在道上，我自以为能纵身跳过去，却被绊了一跤，一头扎进了雪里。我听见近在咫尺的身后传来一声癫狂的怪响，半是尖叫、半是狂笑，我还没来得及爬起来，那抓攫的手指便搭上了我的脖颈，仿佛一只钢钳钳在了那里。可我那只握着装冰鞋背包的右手还自由，我凭着一种盲目的反手一抡，把它顺着带子的全长朝身后甩了出去，便知道我这一记绝命的打击总归是砸在了什么上面。我还没来得及回头，便觉得脖子上的钳制松了，有什么东西瘫进了刚才绊倒我的那丛灌木里。我爬起来，转过身。

===Original===
There she lay, twitching and quivering. The heel of one of my skates piercing the thin alpaca of the knapsack had hit her full on the temple, from which the blood was pouring, but a hundred yards away I could see another such figure coming downwards on my tracks, leaping and bounding. At that panic rose again within me, and I sped off down the white smooth path that led to the lights of the village already beckoning. Never once did I pause in my headlong going: there was no safety until I was back among the haunts of men. I flung myself against the door of the hotel, and screamed for admittance, though I had but to turn the handle and enter; and once more as when Ingram had told his tale, there was the sound of the band, and the chatter of voices, and there, too, was he himself, who looked up and then rose swiftly to his feet as I made my clattering entrance.

===Chinese===
她躺在那里，一抽一抽地颤动着。我一只冰鞋的鞋跟戳穿了背包那层薄薄的羽绸，正正地砸在她的太阳穴上，血从那里汩汩地淌出来；可是在一百码开外，我看见另一个一模一样的身影正沿着我的来路蹦跳着往下赶来。这一见，惊惶再度在我心里翻涌起来，我顺着那条白色平坦、通向村里那一簇已依稀可见的灯火的路，飞也似的奔了下去。我这一路亡命，一次也没有停下：在回到人烟之中以前，便没有安全可言。我一头撞在旅馆的门上，尖声叫人开门，虽然我只要一拧门把手便能进去；而这一回，正像英格拉姆讲他那番故事时一样，又是乐队的乐声，又是人声的喧哗；他也正在那里，抬头一看，便霍地站起身来——正当我哗啦一声闯了进去。

===Original===
“I have seen them too,” I cried. “Look at my knapsack. Is there not blood on it? It is the blood of one of them, a woman, a hag, who tore off the leg of a chamois as I looked, and pursued me through the accursed wood. I—”

Whether it was I who spun round, or the room which seemed to spin round me, I knew not, but I heard myself falling, collapsed on the floor, and the next time that I was conscious at all I was in bed. There was Ingram there, who told me that I was quite safe, and another man, a stranger, who pricked my arm with the nozzle of a syringe, and reassured me.…

===Chinese===
「我也看见它们了，」我喊道，「瞧瞧我的背包。上面难道没有血吗？那是其中一只的血，一个女的，一个老妖婆，我亲眼看着她把一只小羚羊的腿生扯下来，又在那片可诅咒的林子里追我。我——」

究竟是我自己在打转，还是那间屋子仿佛在围着我打转，我弄不清，我只听见自己倒了下去，瘫在了地板上；等我再有半点知觉，我已经躺在了床上。英格拉姆在那儿，告诉我说我已经十分安全了；还有一个陌生人，用注射器的针头刺了刺我的胳膊，一边宽慰我。……

===Original===
A day or two later I gave a coherent account of my adventure, and three or four men, armed with guns, went over my traces. They found the bush in which I had stumbled, with a pool of blood which had soaked into the snow, and, still following my ski-tracks, they came on the body of a chamois, from which had been torn one of its hind-legs and one eye-socket was empty. That is all the corroboration of my story that I can give the reader, and for myself I imagine that the creature which pursued me was either not killed by my blow or that her fellows removed her body.… Anyhow, it is open to the incredulous to prowl about the caves of the Ungeheuerhorn, and see if anything occurs that may convince them.

===Chinese===
一两天之后，我把我的遭遇原原本本地讲了一遍，三四个带着枪的人，顺着我的足迹走了一趟。他们找到了我绊倒的那丛灌木，灌木下有一摊渗进雪里的血；再顺着我的滑雪板印走下去，他们又看见了一只小羚羊的尸首，它的一条后腿被扯掉了，一只眼眶也是空的。这便是我能给读者的、关于我这番故事的全部佐证了；至于我自己，我想，追我的那个生灵要么并没有被我一击打死，要么便是它的同类挪走了它的尸首。……无论如何，那些不肯轻信的人，大可以到翁盖莫霍恩峰的那些洞穴四周去转一转，看看会不会遇上什么能叫他们信服的事。

## The House with the Brickkiln / 有砖窑的宅子

===Original===
The hamlet of Trevor Major lies very lonely and sequestered in a hollow below the north side of the south downs that stretch westward from Lewes, and run parallel with the coast. It is a hamlet of some three or four dozen inconsiderable houses and cottages much girt about with trees, but the big Norman church and the manor house which stands a little outside the village are evidence of a more conspicuous past. This latter, except for a tenancy of rather less than three weeks, now four years ago, has stood unoccupied since the summer of 1896, and though it could be taken at a rent almost comically small, it is highly improbable that either of its last tenants, even if times were very bad, would think of passing a night in it again. For myself—I was one of the tenants—I would far prefer living in a workhouse to inhabiting those low-pitched oak-panelled rooms, and I would sooner look from my garret windows on to the squalor and grime of Whitechapel than from the diamond-shaped and leaded panes of the Manor of Trevor Major on to the boskage of its cool thickets, and the glimmering of its clear chalk-streams where the quick trout glance among the waving water-weeds and over the chalk and gravel of its sliding rapids.

It was the news of these trout that led Jack Singleton and myself to take the house for the month between mid-May and mid-June, but as I have already mentioned a short three weeks was all the time we passed there, and we had more than a week of our tenancy yet unexpired when we left the place, though on the very last afternoon we enjoyed the finest dry-fly fishing that has ever fallen to my lot. Singleton had originally seen the advertisement of the house in a Sussex paper, with the statement that there was good dry-fly fishing belonging to it, but it was with but faint hopes of the reality of the dry-fly fishing that we went down to look at the place, since we had before this so often inspected depopulated ditches which were offered to the unwary under high-sounding titles. Yet after a half-hour’s stroll by the stream, we went straight back to the agent, and before nightfall had taken it for a month with option of renewal.

===Chinese===
特雷弗·梅杰（Trevor Major）这小村，孤零零地、与世隔绝地藏在一道洼地里，洼地位于从刘易斯（Lewes）向西绵延、与海岸平行的南唐斯丘陵（the South Downs）北麓。这是一个三四十户不起眼的房屋农舍组成的小村落，四周密密匝匝围着树木，但村里那座诺曼式大教堂和坐落在村外一点点的庄园宅邸，却见证着它曾有过的更为显赫的往昔。这座庄园宅邸，除了一次为期不足三周、如今已届四年之久的租住之外，自 1896 年夏天起便一直空置着；虽说它的租金低廉得近乎可笑，它的上两任房客——纵使时境再窘——多半也不肯再去那里头过上一夜了。至于我——我便是那房客之一——我宁肯住进济贫院，也不愿再住进那些低矮的、镶着橡木护墙板的房间；我宁肯从我阁楼的窗子望出去是白教堂（Whitechapel）那肮脏腌臜的景象，也不肯从特雷弗·梅杰庄园那镶铅的菱形小格窗子望出去，去看它那些阴凉密林的幽影，看它那些清澈的白垩溪流粼粼的波光——波光里矫捷的鳟鱼在摇曳的水草间一闪而过，掠过那缓缓流淌的浅滩上白垩与砾石。

正是关于这些鳟鱼的消息，引得杰克·辛格尔顿（Jack Singleton）和我把这座宅子租了下来，租期为五月中到六月中这一个月，可如我方才所言，我们在那里拢共只住了短短三个礼拜，临走时租期还剩一周有余未满；然而就在最后那个下午，我们却享受到了我有生以来最妙不可言的一回干蝇钓（dry-fly fishing）。当初是辛格尔顿在一份萨塞克斯（Sussex）的报纸上看见了这宅子的招租广告，上头说宅子附带有上好的干蝇钓场，可我们动身去看房子时，对那干蝇钓的虚实并无多大指望，因为此前我们已太多次实地踏勘过那些被冠以堂皇名目、兜售给不疑有他之人的、鱼虾绝迹的水沟了。然而沿着溪流闲逛了半小时之后，我们便径直折回经纪人那儿，天黑之前已把它租下了一个月，并约定可以续租。

===Original===
We arrived accordingly from town at about five o’clock on a cloudless afternoon in May, and through the mists of horror that now stand between me and the remembrance of what occurred later, I cannot forget the exquisite loveliness of the impression then conveyed. The garden, it is true, appeared to have been for years untended; weeds half-choked the gravel paths, and the flowerbeds were a congestion of mingled wild and cultivated vegetations. It was set in a wall of mellowed brick, in which snapdragon and stonecrop had found an anchorage to their liking, and beyond that there stood sentinel a ring of ancient pines in which the breeze made music as of a distant sea. Outside that the ground sloped slightly downwards in a bank covered with a jungle of wild-rose to the stream that ran round three sides of the garden, and then followed a meandering course through the two big fields which lay towards the village. Over all this we had fishing-rights; above, the same rights extended for another quarter of a mile to the arched bridge, over which there crossed the road which led to the house. In this field above the house on the fourth side, where the ground had been embanked to carry the road, stood a brickkiln in a ruinous state. A shallow pit, long overgrown with tall grasses and wild field-flowers, showed where the clay had been digged.

The house itself was long and narrow; entering, you passed direct into a square panelled hall, on the left of which was the dining-room which communicated with the passage leading to the kitchen and offices. On the right of the hall were two excellent sitting-rooms looking out, the one on to the gravel in front of the house, the other on to the garden. From the first of these you could see, through the gap in the pines by which the road approached the house, the brickkiln of which I have already spoken. An oak staircase went up from the hall, and round it ran a gallery on to which the three principal bedrooms opened. These were commensurate with the dining-room and the two sitting-rooms below. From this gallery there led a long narrow passage shut off from the rest of the house by a red-baize door, which led to a couple more guestrooms and the servant’s quarters.

Jack Singleton and I share the same flat in town, and we had sent down in the morning Franklyn and his wife, two old and valued servants, to get things ready at Trevor Major, and procure help from the village to look after the house, and Mrs. Franklyn with her stout comfortable face all wreathed in smiles opened the door to us. She had had some previous experience of the “comfortable quarters” which go with fishing, and had come down prepared for the worst, but found it all of the best. The kitchen-boiler was not furred; hot and cold water were laid on in the most convenient fashion, and could be obtained from taps that neither stuck nor leaked. Her husband, it appeared, had gone into the village to buy a few necessaries, and she brought up tea for us, and then went upstairs to the two rooms over the dining-room and bigger sitting-room, which we had chosen for our bedrooms, to unpack. The doors of these were exactly opposite one another to right and left of the gallery, and Jack who chose the bedroom above the sitting-room had thus a smaller room, above the second sitting-room, unoccupied, next his and opening out from it.

We had a couple of hours’ fishing before dinner, each of us catching three or four brace of trout, and came back in the dusk to the house. Franklyn had returned from the village from his errand, reported that he had got a woman to come in to do housework in the mornings, and mentioned that our arrival had seemed to arouse a good deal of interest. The reason for this was obscure; he could only tell us that he was questioned a dozen times as to whether we really intended to live in the house, and his assurance that we did produced silence and a shaking of heads. But the country-folk of Sussex are notable for their silence and chronic attitude of disapproval, and we put this down to local idiosyncrasy.

===Chinese===
于是我们便在一个万里无云的五月午后、约莫五点钟时从城里到了那儿，如今隔着一层后来所发生之事的可怖迷雾，我仍忘不了当时所得的那一印象是何等精绝的可爱。诚然，园子看起来已多年无人打理；杂草半掩了碎石小径，花坛里野草与家花盘根错节、挤作一团。园子外围是一道年深日久、颜色温润的砖墙，金鱼草和景天在墙上寻到了中意的栖身处，再往外，一圈古松如哨兵般伫立，风过其间，奏出恍若远海的乐声。再往外，地势顺着一段覆满野玫瑰丛的土坡微微下倾，通到那条绕着园子三面流过的溪边，溪水随后蜿蜒穿过两片朝着村子方向铺展的大田野。这片水域我们都享有钓权；在上游，同样的钓权又延伸出去四分之一英里，直到一座拱桥，那条通往宅子的路便从桥上跨过。在宅子上方、宅子第四面那片田野里——那里的地被垫高以便修路——立着一座破败不堪的砖窑（brickkiln）。一道浅坑，久已被高高的草丛和野草野花覆满，标出了当初取土的所在。

宅子本身又长又窄；一进门便直接走进一个方形的、镶着护墙板的大厅，大厅左边是餐室，餐室连通着通往厨房和杂役用房的那条过道。大厅右边是两间极好的起居室，一间的窗子朝着宅子前的碎石地，另一间朝着园子。从第一间起居室望出去，透过松树间那条供马车驶近宅子的缺口，可以看见我方才所说的那座砖窑。一道橡木楼梯从大厅往上延伸，楼梯口绕着一圈回廊，三间主要的卧室便开在回廊上。这几间卧室与楼下的餐室和两间起居室大小相当。从这道回廊还通出一条狭长的走廊，以一道红色呢绒门与宅子的其余部分隔开，走廊尽头是两间客房和仆人住的下房。

杰克·辛格尔顿和我在城里合住同一套公寓，那天早上我们已先打发弗兰克林（Franklyn）夫妇下乡——他们两位是我们多年的、极为看重的老仆人——去特雷弗·梅杰把一切打点妥帖，并从村里物色帮手来照管宅子。弗兰克林太太（Mrs. Franklyn）那张胖乎乎、和蔼可亲的脸上笑意盈盈地给我们开了门。她从前也曾领教过钓鱼人家所谓的「舒坦住处」，此番下乡原是做足了最坏的打算，却发现一切都再好不过。厨房的锅炉里没有结上水垢；冷热水都接得极其方便，从水龙头里放得出水来，龙头既不涩也不漏。她丈夫似乎已进村去买几样必需品了，她给我们端上了茶，随后便上楼到餐室和那间大起居室上方的两间房里去——我们挑了那两间作卧室——解开行李。这两间的门在回廊左右正正相对，杰克挑了起居室上方那间作卧室，于是紧挨着他卧室、还有一间开连着的小些的屋子——在第二间起居室的正上方——便空着没用上。

晚饭前我们钓了两个钟头的鱼，两人各钓了三四对鳟鱼，趁着暮色回到宅子。弗兰克林已从村里办完差事回来，报告说他找了一位妇人每天上午来打理家务，又说起我们的到来似乎引起了不小的兴致。这其中的缘故不甚明了；他只能告诉我们，他被人盘问了十来遍，问我们是否当真打算住进这宅子，他一口咬定说是，换来的却是一阵沉默和直摇头。不过萨塞克斯的乡民本就以寡言少语和那仿佛与生俱来的不以为然的态度著称，我们便把这事归到了地方性情上头。

===Original===
The evening was exquisitely warm, and after dinner we pulled out a couple of basket-chairs on to the gravel by the front door, and sat for an hour or so, while the night deepened in throbs of gathering darkness. The moon was not risen and the ring of pines cut off much of the pale starlight, so that when we went in, allured by the shining of the lamp in the sitting-room, it was curiously dark for a clear night in May. And at that moment of stepping from the darkness into the cheerfulness of the lighted house, I had a sudden sensation, to which, during the next fortnight, I became almost accustomed, of there being something unseen and unheard and dreadful near me. In spite of the warmth, I felt myself shiver, and concluded instantly that I had sat out-of-doors long enough, and without mentioning it to Jack, followed him into the smaller sitting-room in which we had scarcely yet set foot. It like the hall was oak-panelled, and in the panels hung some half-dozen of watercolour sketches, which we examined, idly at first, and then with growing interest, for they were executed with extraordinary finish and delicacy, and each represented some aspect of the house or garden. Here you looked up the gap in the fir-trees into a crimson sunset; here the garden, trim and carefully tended, dozed beneath some languid summer noon; here an angry wreath of storm-cloud brooded over the meadow where the trout-stream ran grey and leaden below a threatening sky, while another, the most careful and arresting of all, was a study of the brickkiln. In this, alone of them all, was there a human figure; a man, dressed in grey, peered into the open door from which issued a fierce red glow. The figure was painted with miniature-like elaboration; the face was in profile, and represented a youngish man, clean-shaven with a long aquiline nose and singularly square chin. The sketch was long and narrow in shape, and the chimney of the kiln appeared against a dark sky. From it there issued a thin streamer of grey smoke.

Jack looked at this with attention.

“What a horrible picture,” he said, “and how beautifully painted. I feel as if it meant something, as if it was a representation of something that happened, not a mere sketch. By Jove!—”

He broke off suddenly, and went in turn to each of the other pictures.

“That’s a queer thing,” he said. “See if you notice what I mean.”

With the brickkiln rather vividly impressed on my mind, it was not difficult to see what he had noticed. In each of the pictures appeared the brickkiln, chimney and all, now seen faintly between trees, now in full view, and in each the chimney was smoking.

“And the odd part is that from the garden side, you can’t really see the kiln at all,” observed Jack, “it’s hidden by the house, and yet the artist F. A., as I see by his signature, puts it in just the same.”

“What do you make of that?” I asked.

“Nothing. I suppose he had a fancy for brickkilns. Let’s have a game of picquet.”

===Chinese===
傍晚天气暖和得极妙，饭后我们拖出两把藤椅，放在前门外的碎石地上，坐了个把钟头，眼看夜色一阵紧似一阵地深了下去。月亮还没升起，那圈古松又遮去了大半苍白的星光，于是当我们被起居室里那盏灯的光亮吸引着进屋时，天色对一个晴朗的五月之夜而言，是出奇地黑了。而就在从黑暗踏入灯火可亲的宅子的那一刹那，我忽地生出一种奇异的感觉——在其后的两周里，我对这感觉几乎习以为常——觉得我身畔有什么看不见、听不着、却又可怖的东西。尽管天气暖和，我仍觉自己打了个寒战，当即断定是自己在户外坐得太久了，便也不跟杰克提起，跟着他走进了那间我们几乎还从未涉足的小起居室。这间屋子也和门厅一样镶着橡木护墙板，护墙板间挂着半打水彩速写，我们起初只是漫不经心地看看，后来越看越有兴致，因为那几幅画画得异常工细精妙，每一幅画的都是宅子或园子的某一处景象。这一幅，你从松树的缺口望上去，望见一片殷红的落霞；这一幅，修剪齐整、精心侍弄的园子在某个慵懒的夏日正午打着盹；这一幅，一团怒涛般的雷雨云压在草地上空，鳟鱼溪在阴沉沉的天色下泛着灰铅色的光；还有另一幅，也是所有画里画得最精心、最触目的一幅，画的是那座砖窑。唯独这一幅里画了一个人影；一个穿灰衣的男人，正探身朝那扇敞着的窑门里张望，门里射出猛烈的红光。那人影画得如细密画一般精工细作；脸是侧着的，看得出是个年纪不大的男人，胡须刮得精光，长着一只长长的鹰钩鼻和一方出奇方正的下巴。这幅画狭长，窑的烟囱衬着一片幽暗的天空。从烟囱里飘出一缕细细的灰烟。

杰克细细端详着这一幅。

「多可怕的一幅画，」他说，「可画得又是多美。我觉得它像是在暗示着什么，像是在画一桩真正发生过的事，而不只是随手一幅速写。天哪！——」

他猛地顿住，转身挨个儿去看其余几幅画。

「这就怪了，」他说，「你瞧瞧，看出我说的意思没有。」

那座砖窑在我脑海里印得正深，要看出他所注意到的并不难。原来每一幅画里都画着那座砖窑，连同烟囱，时而在树影间隐隐绰绰，时而又一览无余，而且每一幅里那烟囱都在冒着烟。

「而古怪的是，从园子这一边，你其实根本瞧不见那窑，」杰克说道，「它被宅子挡住了，可这位画家——我从签名看，他叫 F. A.——却把它一模一样地画了进去。」

「你作何解释？」我问。

「没什么。我猜他偏爱砖窑吧。来打一盘皮克牌（picquet）如何？」

===Original===
A fortnight of our three weeks passed without incident, except that again and again the curious feeling of something dreadful being close at hand was present in my mind. In a way, as I said, I got used to it, but on the other hand the feeling itself seemed to gain in poignancy. Once just at the end of the fortnight I mentioned it to Jack.

“Odd you should speak of it,” he said, “because I’ve felt the same. When do you feel it? Do you feel it now for instance?”

We were again sitting out after dinner, and as he spoke I felt it with far greater intensity than ever before. And at the same moment the house-door which had been closed, though probably not latched, swung gently open, letting out a shaft of light from the hall, and as gently swung to again, as if something had stealthily entered.

“Yes,” I said. “I felt it then. I only feel it in the evening. It was rather bad that time.”

Jack was silent a moment.

“Funny thing the door opening and shutting like that,” he said. “Let’s go indoors.”

We got up and I remember seeing at that moment that the windows of my bedroom were lit; Mrs. Franklyn probably was making things ready for the night. Simultaneously, as we crossed the gravel, there came from just inside the house the sound of a hurried footstep on the stairs, and entering we found Mrs. Franklyn in the hall, looking rather white and startled.

“Anything wrong?” I asked.

She took two or three quick breaths before she answered:

“No, sir,” she said, “at least nothing that I can give an account of. I was tidying up in your room, and I thought you came in. But there was nobody, and it gave me a turn. I left my candle there; I must go up for it.”

I waited in the hall a moment, while she again ascended the stairs, and passed along the gallery to my room. At the door, which I could see was open, she paused, not entering.

“What is the matter?” I asked from below.

“I left the candle alight,” she said, “and it’s gone out.”

Jack laughed.

“And you left the door and window open,” said he.

“Yes, sir, but not a breath of wind is stirring,” said Mrs. Franklyn, rather faintly.

This was true, and yet a few moments ago the heavy hall-door had swung open and back again. Jack ran upstairs.

“We’ll brave the dark together, Mrs. Franklyn,” he said.

He went into my room, and I heard the sound of a match struck. Then through the open door came the light of the rekindled candle and simultaneously I heard a bell ring in the servant’s quarters. In a moment came steps, and Franklyn appeared.

“What bell was that?” I asked.

“Mr. Jack’s bedroom, sir,” he said.

===Chinese===
三个礼拜的租期里，头两个礼拜平平静静地过去了，只是一桩怪异的感觉一次又一次地涌上心头：似乎有什么可怕的东西就在近旁。如我所说，在某种意义上我已渐渐习惯了它，可另一方面，那感觉本身却又似乎越发地尖锐了。就在两周将尽的时候，有一次我向杰克提起了它。

「你倒提起这个，真是怪了，」他说，「因为我也觉着一样。你都是什么时候觉着的？比方说，你这会儿觉着没有？」

饭后我们又在外头坐着，他这话一出口，我便觉着那感觉比方才任何一次都要强烈得多。而与此同时，那扇原本关着——只怕没有拴上的——宅门，轻轻地荡了开来，从门厅里泻出一道光柱，又轻轻地荡了回去，仿佛有什么东西悄没声地溜了进来。

「是，」我说，「我这会儿觉着了。我只有到了傍晚才觉着。这一回可来得不轻。」

杰克沉默了一晌。

「门这么一开一合，倒怪有趣的，」他说，「咱们进屋吧。」

我们起身，我记得那时还瞧见我卧室的窗子亮着灯；想必是弗兰克林太太在收拾过夜的东西。与此同时，我们穿过碎石地时，只听得宅子里头、楼梯那边传来一阵匆匆的脚步声，我们一进门，便看见弗兰克林太太站在门厅里，脸色煞白，一副受了惊的样子。

「出什么事了？」我问。

她急急地喘了两三口气，才答上来：

「没事，先生，」她说，「至少我说不上来有什么事。我刚才在您房里拾掇，以为您进来了。可又没个人影，把我吓了一跳。我把蜡烛落在上头了；我得去拿。」

我在门厅里站了一会儿，看她重又上了楼，沿着回廊走到我的房门口。那扇门开着，我看得见她在门口停下，没进去。

「怎么了？」我从楼下问。

「我点的蜡烛，」她说，「灭了。」

杰克笑了起来。

「准是你把门窗都敞着，」他说。

「是的，先生，可外头一丝风也没有啊，」弗兰克林太太有气无力地说。

这话不假，可方才那扇沉重的门厅大门分明荡了开又合上。杰克跑上楼去。

「咱们一块儿壮着胆子摸黑吧，弗兰克林太太，」他说。

他进了我的房间，我听得擦火柴的声响。随后从敞着的房门里透出重新点着的烛光，与此同时，我听见仆人下房那边有一只铃响了。不一会儿便传来脚步声，弗兰克林出现了。

「是哪里的铃？」我问。

「杰克先生的卧室，先生。」他说。

===Original===
I felt there was a marked atmosphere of nerves about for which there was really no adequate cause. All that had happened of a disturbing nature was that Mrs. Franklyn had thought I had come into my bedroom, and had been startled by finding I had not. She had then left the candle in a draught, and it had been blown out. As for a bell ringing, that, even if it had happened, was a very innocuous proceeding.

“Mouse on a wire,” I said. “Mr. Jack is in my room this moment lighting Mrs. Franklyn’s candle for her.”

Jack came down at this juncture, and we went into the sitting-room. But Franklyn apparently was not satisfied, for we heard him in the room above us, which was Jack’s bedroom, moving about with his slow and rather ponderous tread. Then his steps seemed to pass into the bedroom adjoining, and we heard no more.

I remember feeling hugely sleepy that night, and went to bed earlier than usual, to pass rather a broken night with stretches of dreamless sleep interspersed with startled awakenings, in which I passed very suddenly into complete consciousness. Sometimes the house was absolutely still, and the only sound to be heard was the sighing of the night breeze outside in the pines, but sometimes the place seemed full of muffled movements, and once I could have sworn that the handle of my door turned. That required verification, and I lit my candle, but found that my ears must have played me false. Yet even as I stood there, I thought I heard steps just outside, and with a considerable qualm, I must confess, I opened the door and looked out. But the gallery was quite empty, and the house quite still. Then from Jack’s room opposite I heard a sound that was somehow comforting, the snorts of the snorer, and I went back to bed and slept again, and when next I woke, morning was already breaking in red lines on the horizon, and the sense of trouble that had been with me ever since last evening had gone.

===Chinese===
我只觉四下里弥漫着一股子神经过敏的气氛，而其实并无什么站得住脚的由头。要说真正出了什么搅扰人心的事，无非是弗兰克林太太以为我进了卧室，发现并非如此，便吃了一惊。随后她把蜡烛搁在风口里，被吹灭了。至于铃响，纵使当真响过，也是桩顶无害的事。

「是老鼠踩着电线了，」我说，「杰克先生这会儿正在我房里给弗兰克林太太点蜡烛呢。」

恰在这时杰克下了楼，我们便进了起居室。可弗兰克林显然不放心，因为我们听见他在我们头顶上那间——也就是杰克的卧室里——他那缓慢而略嫌沉重的脚步来回走动。随后他的脚步似乎走进了隔壁那间卧室，我们便再听不见什么了。

我记得那一夜格外困倦，比平时早上床许多，然而这一夜睡得颇不安稳，一段段无梦的酣睡之间，夹杂着一惊一乍的醒来，醒来时便一下子完全清醒。有时宅子里静得出奇，能听见的只有屋外松林里夜风的叹息声；可有的时候，这地方似乎又满是掩着的声音、藏着动静，有一回我简直可以起誓，我那扇门的把手转了一下。这事得验证一下，我点了蜡烛，却发现准是我的耳朵捉弄了我。然而即便我站在那儿，也好像听见门外刚刚有脚步声，而且——我必须承认——我心里颇打了个咯噔，我还是开了门往外张望。可回廊里空无一人，宅子里一片寂静。随后，从对门杰克的房里传来一个不知怎地叫人安心的声响——那打鼾的呼噜声，我便回床接着睡，下一次醒来时，天边已泛起一道道红霞，破晓了，而从昨晚起就一直缠着我的那份不安，也已烟消云散。

===Original===
Heavy rain set in after lunch next day, and as I had arrears of letter-writing to do, and the water was soon both muddy and rising, I came home alone about five, leaving Jack still sanguine by the stream, and worked for a couple of hours sitting at a writing-table in the room overlooking the gravel at the front of the house, where hung the watercolours. By seven I had finished, and just as I got up to light candles, since it was already dusk, I saw, as I thought, Jack’s figure emerge from the bushes that bordered the path to the stream, on to the space in front of the house. Then instantaneously and with a sudden queer sinking of the heart, quite unaccountable, I saw that it was not Jack at all, but a stranger. He was only some six yards from the window, and after pausing there a moment he came close up to the window, so that his face nearly touched the glass, looking intently at me. In the light from the freshly-kindled candles I could distinguish his features with great clearness, but though, as far as I knew, I had never seen him before, there was something familiar about both his face and figure. He appeared to smile at me, but the smile was one of inscrutable evil and malevolence, and immediately he walked on, straight towards the house-door opposite him, and out of sight of the sitting-room window.

Now, little though I liked the look of the man, he was, as I have said, familiar to my eye, and I went out into the hall, since he was clearly coming to the front-door, to open it to him and learn his business. So without waiting for him to ring, I opened it, feeling sure I should find him on the step. Instead, I looked out into the empty gravel-sweep, the heavy-falling rain, the thick dusk. And even as I looked, I felt something that I could not see push by me through the half-opened door and pass into the house. Then the stairs creaked, and a moment after a bell rang.

Franklyn is the quickest man to answer a bell I have ever seen, and next instant he passed me going upstairs. He tapped at Jack’s door, entered, and then came down again.

“Mr. Jack still out, sir?” he asked.

“Yes. His bell ringing again?”

“Yes, sir,” said Franklyn, quite imperturbably.

===Chinese===
第二天午饭后下起了大雨，我手头积压了不少待回的信要写，溪水又很快变得浑浊且看涨，便在五点光景独自先回来了，留下杰克还兴致勃勃地守在溪边。我在那间朝着宅子前碎石地的屋子里、坐在书桌前写了两个钟头的信——那屋里挂着那几幅水彩画。到七点我写完了，正要起身点蜡烛——天色已然薄暮——我瞧见，我以为，杰克的身影从通往溪边那条小路两旁的灌木丛里钻出来，走到宅子前的空地上。紧接着，刹那之间，我心里没来由地猛地一沉，古怪极了，我看出那根本不是杰克，而是一个陌生人。他离窗子不过六码光景，在那儿站了一会儿，便径直走到窗前，脸几乎贴上了玻璃，目不转睛地盯着我瞧。在新点的烛光里，我能极清楚地辨认出他的容貌，可虽然——据我所知——我从没见过此人，他的脸和身形却又有几分眼熟。他似乎冲我笑了笑，可那笑里是一种莫测的邪恶与怨毒，随即他便继续往前走，径直朝着他对面那扇宅门走去，走出了起居室窗子的视野。

虽说那人模样我看着不痛快，可他正如我所说，落在我眼里是眼熟的。我走进门厅，既然他分明是奔正门来的，便打算开门迎他、问明来意。于是我也不等他按铃，便把门打开，满心以为能在台阶上撞见他。谁知，映入眼帘的只是空荡荡的碎石车道、瓢泼的大雨、浓重的暮色。而就在我张望的当儿，我觉得有个我看不见的东西从我身边、从半开的门里挤了过去，钻进了宅子。随即楼梯嘎吱一响，紧接着一只铃响了。

弗兰克林是我所见过听铃最快的人，转眼间他便从我身边经过上了楼。他敲了敲杰克的门，进去，又下来了。

「杰克先生还没回来吗，先生？」他问。

「嗯。又是他那屋的铃响？」

「是的，先生。」弗兰克林说，不动声色极了。

===Original===
I went back into the sitting-room, and soon Franklyn brought a lamp. He put it on the table above which hung the careful and curious picture of the brickkiln, and then with a sudden horror I saw why the stranger on the gravel outside had been so familiar to me. In all respects he resembled the figure that peered into the kiln; it was more than a resemblance, it was an identity. And what had happened to this man who had inscrutably and evilly smiled at me? And what had pushed in through the half-closed door?

At that moment I saw the face of Fear; my mouth went dry, and I heard my heart leaping and cracking in my throat. That face was only turned on me for a moment, and then away again, but I knew it to be the genuine thing; not apprehension, not foreboding, not a feeling of being startled, but Fear, cold Fear. And then though nothing had occurred to assuage the Fear, it passed, and a certain sort of reason usurped—for so I must say—its place. I had certainly seen somebody on the gravel outside the house; I had supposed he was going to the front-door. I had opened it, and found he had not come to the front-door. Or—and once again the terror resurged—had the invisible pushing thing been that which I had seen outside? And if so, what was it? And how came it that the face and figure of the man I had seen was the same as that which was so scrupulously painted in the picture of the brickkiln?

I set myself to argue down the Fear for which there was no more foundation than this, this and the repetition of the ringing bell, and my belief is that I did so. I told myself, till I believed it, that a man—a human man—had been walking across the gravel outside, and that he had not come to the front-door but had gone, as he might easily have done, up the drive into the high-road. I told myself that it was mere fancy that was the cause of the belief that Something had pushed in by me, and as for the ringing of the bell, I said to myself, as was true, that this had happened before. And I must ask the reader to believe also that I argued these things away, and looked no longer on the face of Fear itself. I was not comfortable, but I fell short of being terrified.

I sat down again by the window looking on to the gravel in front of the house, and finding another letter that asked, though it did not demand an answer, proceeded to occupy myself with it. Straight in front led the drive through the gap in the pines, and passed through the field where lay the brickkiln. In a pause of page-turning I looked up and saw something unusual about it; at the same moment an unusual smell came to my nostril. What I saw was smoke coming out of the chimney of the kiln, what I smelt was the odour of roasting meat. The wind—such as there was—set from the kiln to the house. But as far as I knew the smell of roast meat probably came from the kitchen where dinner, so I supposed, was cooking. I had to tell myself this: I wanted reassurance, lest the face of Fear should look whitely on me again.

===Chinese===
我回到起居室，不一会儿弗兰克林送来一盏灯。他把灯搁在那幅画着砖窑、画得格外精心的怪画下面那张桌子上，便在这时，我猛地一阵惊恐，恍然明白了碎石地上那个陌生人为何如此眼熟。他分明与那幅探身朝窑里张望的人影一模一样；那已不止是相像，简直是同一张脸。那么，这个莫测地、怨毒地冲我微笑的人，后来遭了什么？而那个从半掩的门里挤进来的，又是什么？

就在那一刻，我看见了「恐惧」的脸；我口干舌燥，听得见自己的心在喉咙口又跳又裂。那张脸只朝我转了一瞬，便又转了开去，可我知道它是货真价实的东西；不是忧虑，不是预感，不是受惊之后的感觉，而是恐惧，冰冷的恐惧。随后，虽然并无任何事发生来平息这份恐惧，它却过去了，而某一种所谓的理智篡夺了——我只能这么说——它的位置。我确乎在宅外的碎石地上看见过什么人；我以为他要去正门。我开了门，却发现他并没有来正门。要不——那股子看不见的、推挤着的东西，就是我在外头瞧见的那个人？——恐惧再度翻涌上来。倘若如此，那它是什么？我所看见的那个人的脸和身形，又怎会与砖窑那幅画里画得那样一丝不苟的人影分毫不差？

我强自按捺，拿道理去压下这份恐惧——它除了上述那些、除了那反复作响的铃，本无更多凭据——我相信我是压下去了。我一遍遍对自己说，说得自己也信了：是有过一个人——一个活生生的人——走过宅外的碎石地，他没去正门，而是顺着车道拐上了大路，这本是轻而易举的事。我对自己说，所谓有什么东西从我身边挤进来，不过是凭空的臆想；至于铃响，我对自己说——这话不假——从前也响过。我也得请读者相信，我便是这般把这一切都排遣开了，再不去看「恐惧」那张脸本身。我心里并不踏实，可也算不上被吓坏了。

我又在窗前坐下，窗子朝着宅前的碎石地，我又翻出一封虽不一定要回、却也盼着回信的信，便埋头写了起来。正前方，车道穿过松树的缺口延伸出去，穿过那片立着砖窑的田野。翻页的间隙我抬起头，瞧出那窑有些异样；与此同时，一股子异样的气味钻进我鼻孔。我所看见的，是从窑的烟囱里冒出的烟；我所闻到的，是烤肉的焦香。风——要说有风的话——是从窑那边朝宅子吹的。可据我所知，这烤肉的香气多半是从厨房里飘来的，晚饭想必正在那儿做着呢。我不得不这样对自己说：我要的是安心，唯恐「恐惧」的脸又惨白地朝我转过来。

===Original===
Then there came a crisp step on the gravel, a rattle at the front-door, and Jack came in.

“Good sport,” he said, “you gave up too soon.”

And he went straight to the table above which hung the picture of the man at the brickkiln, and looked at it. Then there was silence; and eventually I spoke, for I wanted to know one thing.

“Seen anybody?” I asked.

“Yes. Why do you ask?”

“Because I have also; the man in that picture.”

Jack came and sat down near me.

“It’s a ghost, you know,” he said. “He came down to the river about dusk and stood near me for an hour. At first I thought he was—was real, and I warned him that he had better stand further off if he didn’t want to be hooked. And then it struck me he wasn’t real, and I cast, well, right through him, and about seven he walked up towards the house.”

“Were you frightened?”

“No. It was so tremendously interesting. So you saw him here too. Whereabouts?”

“Just outside. I think he is in the house now.”

Jack looked round.

“Did you see him come in?” he asked.

“No, but I felt him. There’s another queer thing too; the chimney of the brickkiln is smoking.”

Jack looked out of the window. It was nearly dark but the wreathing smoke could just be seen.

“So it is,” he said, “fat, greasy smoke. I think I’ll go up and see what’s on. Come too?”

“I think not,” I said.

“Are you frightened? It isn’t worth while. Besides, it is so tremendously interesting.”

Jack came back from his little expedition still interested. He had found nothing stirring at the kiln, but though it was then nearly dark the interior was faintly luminous, and against the black of the sky he could see a wisp of thick white smoke floating northwards. But for the rest of the evening we neither heard nor saw anything of abnormal import, and the next day ran a course of undisturbed hours. Then suddenly a hellish activity was manifested.

===Chinese===
紧接着，碎石地上一阵清脆的脚步声，前门处哗啦一响，杰克回来了。

「钓得痛快，」他说，「你收竿太早啦。」

说着他便径直走到那幅砖窑前站着个男人的画下面那张桌前，端详起那画来。随后便是沉默；终于还是我开了口，因为有一桩事我想弄明白。

「看见什么人没有？」我问。

「看见了。你问这个做什么？」

「因为我也看见了；就是画里那个人。」

杰克走过来，在我身旁坐下。

「那是鬼呢，你知道，」他说，「黄昏时分他下到河边，在我跟前站了一个钟头。起先我还以为他是——是真的，便提醒他，不想被鱼钩挂到的话最好站远些。后来我才琢磨过来他不是真的，我一甩竿，好嘛，径直从他身上穿了过去，约莫七点钟光景他便朝宅子这边走上去了。」

「你害怕了吗？」

「没有。这有趣得要命。这么说，你也在这儿瞧见他了。在哪儿？」

「就在窗外。我想这会儿他人已在宅子里了。」

杰克环顾四周。

「你看见他进来了吗？」他问。

「没有，可我感觉到了。还有一桩怪事；那砖窑的烟囱在冒烟呢。」

杰克朝窗外望去。天几乎全黑了，可那一团团缭绕的烟还能依稀辨出。

「可不是，」他说，「油腻腻、稠乎乎的烟。我想上去瞧瞧是怎么回事。你也来？」

「我不去了。」我说。

「你怕了？犯不着的。再说，这有趣得要命。」

杰克这一趟小探查回来，兴致依旧。他在窑那儿没发现什么动静，可虽说那时天已差不多黑透，窑里头却隐隐透着微光，衬着漆黑的天幕，他看得见一缕浓白的烟朝北边飘去。但那晚余下的时光，我们再没听见、也没看见任何反常的征象，第二天也平平静静地过了一日。谁料猛然间，一股子地狱般的动静冒了出来。

===Original===
That night, while I was undressing for bed, I heard a bell ring furiously, and I thought I heard a shout also. I guessed where the ring came from, since Franklyn and his wife had long ago gone to bed, and went straight to Jack’s room. But as I tapped at the door I heard his voice from inside calling loud to me. “Take care,” it said, “he’s close to the door.”

A sudden qualm of blank fear took hold of me, but mastering it as best I could, I opened the door to enter, and once again something pushed softly by me, though I saw nothing.

Jack was standing by his bed, half-undressed. I saw him wipe his forehead with the back of his hand.

“He’s been here again,” he said. “I was standing just here, a minute ago, when I found him close by me. He came out of the inner room, I think. Did you see what he had in his hand?”

“I saw nothing.”

“It was a knife; a great long carving knife. Do you mind my sleeping on the sofa in your room tonight? I got an awful turn then. There was another thing too. All round the edge of his clothes, at his collar and at his wrists, there were little flames playing, little white licking flames.”

===Chinese===
那天夜里，我正脱衣就寝，听得一只铃狂响起来，似乎还听见一声喊。我猜得到铃是从哪儿响的——弗兰克林夫妇早已睡下——便径直奔到杰克房门口。可我手才敲门，便听见他在里头高声叫我。「当心，」他说，「他就在门口。」

一阵纯粹的恐惧猛地攫住了我，但我尽力把它压下去，推门而入，于是又有什么东西轻轻地从我身边挤了过去，尽管我什么也没看见。

杰克只脱了一半衣裳，站在床边。我看见他用手背抹了抹额头。

「他又来过了，」他说，「方才我就站在这儿，一眨眼工夫便发觉他就在我身边。我想，他是从里间那屋出来的。你瞧见他手里拿着什么没有？」

「我什么也没瞧见。」

「是一把刀；一把又长又大的切肉刀。今夜我去你屋里睡沙发，你不介意吧？方才我可吓得不轻。还有一桩事。他衣服的边沿、衣领那儿、袖口那儿，都有一簇簇的小火苗在跳动，一簇簇舔着的白色小火苗。」

===Original===
But next day, again, we neither heard nor saw anything, nor that night did the sense of that dreadful presence in the house come to us. And then came the last day. We had been out till it was dark, and as I said, had a wonderful day among the fish. On reaching home we sat together in the sitting-room, when suddenly from overhead came a tread of feet, a violent pealing of the bell, and the moment after yell after yell as of someone in mortal agony. The thought occurred to both of us that this might be Mrs. Franklyn in terror of some fearful sight, and together we rushed up and sprang into Jack’s bedroom.

The doorway into the room beyond was open, and just inside it we saw the man bending over some dark huddled object. Though the room was dark we could see him perfectly, for a light stale and impure seemed to come from him. He had again a long knife in his hand, and as we entered he was wiping it on the mass that lay at his feet. Then he took it up, and we saw what it was, a woman with head nearly severed. But it was not Mrs. Franklyn.

And then the whole thing vanished, and we were standing looking into a dark and empty room. We went downstairs without a word, and it was not till we were both in the sitting-room below that Jack spoke.

“And he takes her to the brickkiln,” he said rather unsteadily. “I say, have you had enough of this house? I have. There is hell in it.”

===Chinese===
然而第二天，我们又是既没听见、也没看见什么，那天夜里，那种宅中有可怖之物存在的压迫感也没再来侵扰。接着便是最后一天了。我们在外头一直待到天黑，如我所说，那一天钓鱼快活极了。一回到家，我们便一同坐在起居室里，猛然间，头顶上传来一阵脚步声，一阵猛烈的铃声，紧接着是一声接一声的惨叫，仿佛有人正承受着致命的痛苦。我们俩都闪过一个念头：莫不是弗兰克林太太撞见了什么可怖的景象，吓得叫起来？于是一同冲上楼，闯进了杰克的卧室。

通往里间那屋的门敞着，就在门里头，我们看见那个男人正弯着腰，俯身在一团黑乎乎、蜷缩着的东西上。屋里虽黑，我们却把他瞧得清清楚楚，因为一层幽暗而污浊的光似乎正从他身上散发出来。他手里又拿着一把长刀，我们进屋时，他正把刀在那团摊在他脚边的东西上擦拭。随后他把它扶了起来，我们这才看清那是什么——一个女人，头颅几乎被割断。但那并不是弗兰克林太太。

紧接着这一切都消失了，我们站在那里，望进一间漆黑、空荡的屋子。我们一言不发地下了楼，直到两人都回到楼下起居室，杰克才开了口。

「他把她带到砖窑去了，」他说话时声音颇不稳。「我说，这宅子你受够了吗？我受够了。这宅子里头有地狱。」

===Original===
About a week later Jack put into my hand a guidebook to Sussex open at the description of Trevor Major, and I read:

> "Just outside the village stands the picturesque manor house, once the home of the artist and notorious murderer, Francis Adam. It was here he killed his wife, in a fit, it is believed, of groundless jealousy, cutting her throat and disposing of her remains by burning them in a brickkiln. Certain charred fragments found six months afterwards led to his arrest and execution."

So I prefer to leave the house with the brickkiln and the pictures signed F. A. to others.

===Chinese===
约莫一周之后，杰克把一本萨塞克斯导游手册塞到我手里，翻到介绍特雷弗·梅杰的那一页，我读到：

> 「村庄外不远处，矗立着那座风景如画的庄园宅邸，它曾是画家、亦是臭名昭著的杀人犯弗朗西斯·亚当（Francis Adam）的居所。据信正是在此处，他出于一场毫无来由的嫉妒，杀死了自己的妻子，割断她的喉咙，并将她的尸骸投入一座砖窑中焚毁。半年之后发现的若干焦黑残骸，致使他落网并被处决。」

所以，那座有砖窑的宅子，以及那些署名 F. A. 的画，我宁愿留给旁人去领教。

## The Man Who Went Too Far / 走得太远的人

===Original===
The little village of St. Faith’s nestles in a hollow of wooded hill up on the north bank of the river Fawn in the county of Hampshire, huddling close round its grey Norman church as if for spiritual protection against the fays and fairies, the trolls and “little people,” who might be supposed still to linger in the vast empty spaces of the New Forest, and to come after dusk and do their doubtful businesses. Once outside the hamlet you may walk in any direction (so long as you avoid the high road which leads to Brockenhurst) for the length of a summer afternoon without seeing sign of human habitation, or possibly even catching sight of another human being. Shaggy wild ponies may stop their feeding for a moment as you pass, the white scuts of rabbits will vanish into their burrows, a brown viper perhaps will glide from your path into a clump of heather, and unseen birds will chuckle in the bushes, but it may easily happen that for a long day you will see nothing human. But you will not feel in the least lonely; in summer, at any rate, the sunlight will be gay with butterflies, and the air thick with all those woodland sounds which like instruments in an orchestra combine to play the great symphony of the yearly festival of June. Winds whisper in the birches, and sigh among the firs; bees are busy with their redolent labour among the heather, a myriad birds chirp in the green temples of the forest trees, and the voice of the river prattling over stony places, bubbling into pools, chuckling and gulping round corners, gives you the sense that many presences and companions are near at hand.

Yet, oddly enough, though one would have thought that these benign and cheerful influences of wholesome air and spaciousness of forest were very healthful comrades for a man, in so far as nature can really influence this wonderful human genus which has in these centuries learned to defy her most violent storms in its well-established houses, to bridle her torrents and make them light its streets, to tunnel her mountains and plough her seas, the inhabitants of St. Faith’s will not willingly venture into the forest after dark. For in spite of the silence and loneliness of the hooded night it seems that a man is not sure in what company he may suddenly find himself, and though it is difficult to get from these villagers any very clear story of occult appearances, the feeling is widespread. One story indeed I have heard with some definiteness, the tale of a monstrous goat that has been seen to skip with hellish glee about the woods and shady places, and this perhaps is connected with the story which I have here attempted to piece together. It too is well-known to them; for all remember the young artist who died here not long ago, a young man, or so he struck the beholder, of great personal beauty, with something about him that made men’s faces to smile and brighten when they looked on him. His ghost they will tell you “walks” constantly by the stream and through the woods which he loved so, and in especial it haunts a certain house, the last of the village, where he lived, and its garden in which he was done to death. For my part I am inclined to think that the terror of the Forest dates chiefly from that day. So, such as the story is, I have set it forth in connected form. It is based partly on the accounts of the villagers, but mainly on that of Darcy, a friend of mine and a friend of the man with whom these events were chiefly concerned.

===Chinese===
圣费斯（St. Faith’s）这座小村庄，安卧在汉普郡（Hampshire）福恩河（the river Fawn）北岸一座林木葱茏的山丘凹地里，紧紧依偎着它那座灰色的诺曼式教堂，仿佛在寻求某种灵性上的庇佑，以抵御那些妖精仙子、巨怪与「小人儿」——据说他们仍游荡在新林（the New Forest）那大片空旷的腹地之中，待黄昏一到，便出来做他们那暧昧的勾当。一出村口，你尽可朝任何方向走去（只要避开那条通往布罗肯赫斯特（Brockenhurst）的大路），走满一个夏日午后的时辰，也不会见到半点人烟，甚至可能连一个人影也看不见。毛蓬蓬的野马也许会在你经过时停下吃草，抬眼一望；野兔的白尾梢会一闪便钻进洞穴；一条棕色的蝰蛇或许会从你脚下的路上滑进一丛石楠花；看不见的鸟儿在灌木丛中咯咯地笑——可整整漫长一天，你可能什么人的踪迹也见不着。但你绝不会感到丝毫寂寞；至少在夏天，日光里蝴蝶翩跹，一派欢然，空气中则充盈着林间的种种声响——它们恰如管弦乐队里的各件乐器，汇合起来，奏出这一年一度的六月盛典那宏大的交响。风在白桦树间低语，在松杉间叹息；蜜蜂在石楠丛中忙碌它们芬芳的劳作，千万只鸟儿在林木构成的绿色殿堂里啁啾；河水流过石滩时潺潺絮语，灌进水潭时咕嘟冒泡，绕过弯角时咯咯吞咽——这水声让你觉得，身边有许多在场的灵、许多同伴。

然而，说来也奇——尽管人们原会以为，这清新的空气与森林的旷阔所带来的那些温煦、欣然的影响，对人而言该是极为有益的伙伴；且不论大自然果真能影响这奇妙的人种到何种程度，须知这物种在多少个世纪里已学会在他那稳固的宅子里抵挡她最狂暴的风雨，驯服她的急流并使之照亮他的街衢，凿通她的山岳、犁开她的海洋——然而，圣费斯的居民天黑之后却绝不肯轻易走进那片林子。因为，尽管蒙着头盖的黑夜静寂而空旷，一个人却说不准自己会突然撞见什么样的同伴；虽说很难从这些村民嘴里掏出什么关于灵异显形的清楚说法，可这种心有余悸的感觉却是普遍的。的确有一个故事，我听得相当确切——说有一只硕大无朋的山羊，有人看见它带着地狱般的欢腾，在林间和阴翳之处蹦跳；这传说也许与我这里试图缀合的这桩故事不无关联。这桩故事于他们同样耳熟能详；因为所有人都还记得那位不久前死在这里的年轻画家，一个青年男子——至少观者所得的印象是如此——容貌极其俊美，周身带着某种东西，教人一见他，脸上便不由自主地绽出笑容、焕发出光彩。他们会告诉你，他的鬼魂常在那溪边、在那他如此钟爱的林中「出没」，尤其是某一栋房子——村里最末一栋——他生前所居、及其花园，即他被活活弄死之处，更是频频闹鬼。就我而言，我倒倾向于认为，那林子的恐怖主要是从那一日起的。故而，这故事无论好坏，我已将其缀连成篇，述之于下。它一部分取自村民们的种种说法，但主要取自我的朋友达西（Darcy）的叙述——他既是我的朋友，也是与这些事件关系最深的那位主人公的朋友。

---

===Original===
The day had been one of untarnished midsummer splendour, and as the sun drew near to its setting, the glory of the evening grew every moment more crystalline, more miraculous. Westward from St. Faith’s the beechwood which stretched for some miles toward the heathery upland beyond already cast its veil of clear shadow over the red roofs of the village, but the spire of the grey church, overtopping all, still pointed a flaming orange finger into the sky. The river Fawn, which runs below, lay in sheets of sky-reflected blue, and wound its dreamy devious course round the edge of this wood, where a rough two-planked bridge crossed from the bottom of the garden of the last house in the village, and communicated by means of a little wicker gate with the wood itself. Then once out of the shadow of the wood the stream lay in flaming pools of the molten crimson of the sunset, and lost itself in the haze of woodland distances.

This house at the end of the village stood outside the shadow, and the lawn which sloped down to the river was still flecked with sunlight. Garden-beds of dazzling colour lined its gravel walks, and down the middle of it ran a brick pergola, half-hidden in clusters of rambler-rose and purple with starry clematis. At the bottom end of it, between two of its pillars, was slung a hammock containing a shirt-sleeved figure.

The house itself lay somewhat remote from the rest of the village, and a footpath leading across two fields, now tall and fragrant with hay, was its only communication with the high road. It was low-built, only two stories in height, and like the garden, its walls were a mass of flowering roses. A narrow stone terrace ran along the garden front, over which was stretched an awning, and on the terrace a young silent-footed manservant was busied with the laying of the table for dinner. He was neat-handed and quick with his job, and having finished it he went back into the house, and reappeared again with a large rough bath-towel on his arm. With this he went to the hammock in the pergola.

===Chinese===
这一日是纤尘不染的仲夏盛景；待到夕阳将坠，傍晚的光华每过一刻都愈发晶莹，愈发不可思议。从圣费斯向西望去，那片绵延数英里、直抵远处石楠遍生的岗地的山毛榉林，已将它清朗的阴影之纱投在村庄的红屋顶上，可那座灰色教堂的尖顶高出于一切之上，仍把一根灼灼的橘黄手指指向天空。山下流淌的福恩河，泛着映天的片片蔚蓝，绕着这片林子的边缘，蜿蜒着它那梦幻般迂曲的水路；林子边上，一座粗糙的两板木桥从村里最末一栋宅子的花园尽头横跨而过，借一道小柳条门与林子相通。而一出了林阴，溪水便躺在燃烧着的一汪汪熔金般的落日殷红里，消融在远方林野的薄霭之中。

村庄尽头这栋宅子正立在林阴之外，那向下倾斜、直抵河岸的草坪上，仍斑驳着日光。绚烂夺目的花圃沿着砾石小径一字排开，草坪正中则纵贯着一道砖砌的藤廊，半隐在一簇簇的蔓生蔷薇里，因星点般的铁线莲而染上紫色。藤廊尽头，在两根廊柱之间，吊着一张吊床，上头躺着一个只穿衬衫的人影。

这宅子本身离村子其余的人家稍远，一条小径穿过两片田野——此时田野里干草长得高而芬芳——便是它与大路唯一的通道。房子低矮，不过两层高，而且与花园一样，墙上爬满了盛放的蔷薇。一道窄窄的石砌露台沿花园一侧延伸出去，上头张着一幅凉棚；露台上，一个年轻、脚步轻悄的男仆正忙着摆晚餐的桌子。他手脚麻利，干活利索，摆完之后便回到屋里，胳膊上搭着一条粗大的浴巾又走了出来。他拿着这条浴巾径直走向藤廊里的吊床。

===Original===
“Nearly eight, sir,” he said.

“Has Mr. Darcy come yet?” asked a voice from the hammock.

“No, sir.”

“If I’m not back when he comes, tell him that I’m just having a bathe before dinner.”

The servant went back to the house, and after a moment or two Frank Halton struggled to a sitting posture, and slipped out on to the grass. He was of medium height and rather slender in build, but the supple ease and grace of his movements gave the impression of great physical strength: even his descent from the hammock was not an awkward performance. His face and hands were of very dark complexion, either from constant exposure to wind and sun, or, as his black hair and dark eyes tended to show, from some strain of southern blood. His head was small, his face of an exquisite beauty of modelling, while the smoothness of its contour would have led you to believe that he was a beardless lad still in his teens. But something, some look which living and experience alone can give, seemed to contradict that, and finding yourself completely puzzled as to his age, you would next moment probably cease to think about that, and only look at this glorious specimen of young manhood with wondering satisfaction.

He was dressed as became the season and the heat, and wore only a shirt open at the neck, and a pair of flannel trousers. His head, covered very thickly with a somewhat rebellious crop of short curly hair, was bare as he strolled across the lawn to the bathing-place that lay below. Then for a moment there was silence, then the sound of splashed and divided waters, and presently after, a great shout of ecstatic joy, as he swam upstream with the foamed water standing in a frill round his neck. Then after some five minutes of limb-stretching struggle with the flood, he turned over on his back, and with arms thrown wide, floated downstream, ripple-cradled and inert. His eyes were shut, and between half-parted lips he talked gently to himself.

“I am one with it,” he said to himself, “the river and I, I and the river. The coolness and splash of it is I, and the water-herbs that wave in it are I also. And my strength and my limbs are not mine but the river’s. It is all one, all one, dear Fawn.”

===Chinese===
「快八点了，先生。」他说。

「达西先生到了没有？」吊床里传出一个声音问道。

「没有，先生。」

「要是我还没回来他就到了，告诉他，我饭前先去游个澡。」

仆人回到屋里；过了一会儿，弗兰克·哈尔顿（Frank Halton）挣扎着坐起身来，滑到草地上。他中等身量，身形相当纤瘦，但他的动作那般柔韧从容、那般优雅，给人一种力气极大的印象：就连从吊床里下来这一个动作，也毫不显得笨拙。他的脸和手肤色极深，也许是终年风吹日晒所致，也或许——正如他那黑发黑眼所暗示的——是因为血脉里有某支南方的血统。他头颅小巧，面容轮廓精妙绝伦，那线条的圆润光洁，会令你以为他还是个没长胡子、不过十七八岁的少年。但有某种东西，某种唯有阅历和生活才能赋予的神情，似乎又否定了这一点；你发觉自己全然说不出他究竟多大年纪，下一刻你多半便不再去想这件事，而只是带着惊异而满足的心情，端详这个年轻男子这般光华照人的典范。

他穿得与季节和酷暑相称，只着一件敞开领口的衬衫，一条法兰绒长裤。他穿过草坪朝下方的浴场走去时，没戴帽子，那一头浓密、多少有些桀骜的短卷发尽沐在日光里。随后片刻的寂静，接着是水被劈开溅起的声音，紧接着，是一声心醉神迷的大喊——他逆流而游，泛起白沫的水在他颈间立成一道褶边。又与水流奋力搏击了约莫五分钟，他翻过身来仰面朝天，双臂大张，顺流漂浮而下，被涟漪轻轻摇曳着，身子一动不动。他双眼阖着，在半开的唇间，轻声地自言自语。

「我与它是一体的，」他对自己说，「河水与我，我与河水。它的清凉、它飞溅的水花，便是我；那在水中摇曳的水草，也是我。我的气力、我的四肢，不是我的，是河水的。全是一体的，全是一体的，亲爱的福恩。」

---

===Original===
A quarter of an hour later he appeared again at the bottom of the lawn, dressed as before, his wet hair already drying into its crisp short curls again. There he paused a moment, looking back at the stream with the smile with which men look on the face of a friend, then turned towards the house. Simultaneously his servant came to the door leading on to the terrace, followed by a man who appeared to be some halfway through the fourth decade of his years. Frank and he saw each other across the bushes and garden-beds, and each quickening his step, they met suddenly face to face round an angle of the garden walk, in the fragrance of syringa.

“My dear Darcy,” cried Frank, “I am charmed to see you.”

But the other stared at him in amazement.

“Frank!” he exclaimed.

“Yes, that is my name,” he said laughing, “what is the matter?”

Darcy took his hand.

“What have you done to yourself?” he asked. “You are a boy again.”

“Ah, I have a lot to tell you,” said Frank. “Lots that you will hardly believe, but I shall convince you—”

He broke off suddenly, and held up his hand.

“Hush, there is my nightingale,” he said.

The smile of recognition and welcome with which he had greeted his friend faded from his face, and a look of rapt wonder took its place, as of a lover listening to the voice of his beloved. His mouth parted slightly, showing the white line of teeth, and his eyes looked out and out till they seemed to Darcy to be focused on things beyond the vision of man. Then something perhaps startled the bird, for the song ceased.

“Yes, lots to tell you,” he said. “Really I am delighted to see you. But you look rather white and pulled down; no wonder after that fever. And there is to be no nonsense about this visit. It is June now, you stop here till you are fit to begin work again. Two months at least.”

“Ah, I can’t trespass quite to that extent.”

Frank took his arm and walked him down the grass.

“Trespass? Who talks of trespass? I shall tell you quite openly when I am tired of you, but you know when we had the studio together, we used not to bore each other. However, it is ill talking of going away on the moment of your arrival. Just a stroll to the river, and then it will be dinnertime.”

Darcy took out his cigarette case, and offered it to the other.

Frank laughed.

“No, not for me. Dear me, I suppose I used to smoke once. How very odd!”

“Given it up?”

“I don’t know. I suppose I must have. Anyhow I don’t do it now. I would as soon think of eating meat.”

“Another victim on the smoking altar of vegetarianism?”

“Victim?” asked Frank. “Do I strike you as such?”

He paused on the margin of the stream and whistled softly. Next moment a moorhen made its splashing flight across the river, and ran up the bank. Frank took it very gently in his hands and stroked its head, as the creature lay against his shirt.

“And is the house among the reeds still secure?” he half-crooned to it. “And is the missus quite well, and are the neighbours flourishing? There, dear, home with you,” and he flung it into the air.

“That bird’s very tame,” said Darcy, slightly bewildered.

“It is rather,” said Frank, following its flight.

===Chinese===
一刻钟后，他又出现在草坪尽头，衣着如前，湿发已渐渐干透，又恢复了那短而鬈的发卷。他在那里驻足片刻，回头望了望那条溪流，那神情正如人们望着一张友人的脸时所有的微笑；然后转身朝宅子走去。与此同时，他的仆人出现在通往露台的门口，身后跟着一位男子，年岁瞧着约莫三十有半。弗兰克和他隔着灌木与花圃彼此望见，各人加快脚步，在花园小径的一个拐角处，于山梅花的芬芳里，猝不及防地打了个照面。

「亲爱的达西，」弗兰克喊道，「见到你真是太高兴了。」

可对方却惊异地瞪着他。

「弗兰克！」他叫道。

「是啊，这是我的名字，」他笑着说，「怎么了？」

达西握住了他的手。

「你对自己做了什么？」他问，「你又变回一个少年了。」

「啊，我有许多话要跟你说，」弗兰克说，「有许多你几乎不会相信，可我会说服你——」

他突然住了口，举起一只手。

「嘘，我的夜莺在叫呢。」他说。

方才迎接朋友时脸上那认出与欢迎的微笑淡去了，取而代之的是一种出神而惊奇的神情，宛如一个恋人正在聆听他心上人的声音。他的嘴微微张开，露出一道洁白的齿列；他的目光远远地、远远地望出去，直到在达西看来，那目光所凝注的，是人目所不能见之物。接着，许是什么惊动了那鸟儿，歌声停了。

「是，有许多话要说，」他说，「说真的，见到你我太高兴了。可你瞧着挺苍白、挺憔悴的；那场热病过后，也不足为怪。这一回可由不得你推三阻四。如今是六月了，你就留在这里，养到能重新开始工作的程度再说。至少两个月。」

「啊，我可不能这么长久地叨扰。」

弗兰克挽起他的胳膊，带他顺着草地走下去。

「叨扰？谁谈什么叨扰？等我厌烦了你，我会坦白地告诉你的；可你总记得，当年我们合用一间画室的时候，彼此是从不厌烦对方的。不过，你才进门就谈走，也未免太扫兴。先到河边走走，然后就该开饭了。」

达西掏出烟盒，递了过去。

弗兰克笑了起来。

「不，我不抽。哎呀，我想我从前大概是抽过烟的。多奇怪啊！」

「戒了？」

「我也不知道。想必是戒了吧。反正我现在不抽了。叫我想那个，就跟叫我想吃肉一样。」

「又一位献身于素食主义祭坛的烟客？」

「牺牲品？」弗兰克反问，「我瞧着像么？」

他在溪边停下，轻轻地打了个呼哨。下一刻，一只水鸡扑溅着飞过河面，奔上堤岸。弗兰克极温柔地把它捧在手里，那鸟就贴在他衬衫上，他轻轻抚着它的头。

「芦苇里那间屋子还安稳么？」他对它像是轻声哼着，「太太可好？邻居们都还兴旺？好了，宝贝，回家去吧。」说着便把它往空中一抛。

「这鸟真够驯的。」达西说，有点发懵。

「是挺驯的。」弗兰克说，目光追着它飞远了。

===Original===
During dinner Frank chiefly occupied himself in bringing himself up-to-date in the movements and achievements of this old friend whom he had not seen for six years. Those six years, it now appeared, had been full of incident and success for Darcy; he had made a name for himself as a portrait painter which bade fair to outlast the vogue of a couple of seasons, and his leisure time had been brief. Then some four months previously he had been through a severe attack of typhoid, the result of which as concerns this story was that he had come down to this sequestered place to recruit.

“Yes, you’ve got on,” said Frank at the end. “I always knew you would. A.R.A. with more in prospect. Money? You roll in it, I suppose, and, O Darcy, how much happiness have you had all these years? That is the only imperishable possession. And how much have you learned? Oh, I don’t mean in Art. Even I could have done well in that.”

Darcy laughed.

“Done well? My dear fellow, all I have learned in these six years you knew, so to speak, in your cradle. Your old pictures fetch huge prices. Do you never paint now?”

Frank shook his head.

“No, I’m too busy,” he said.

“Doing what? Please tell me. That is what everyone is forever asking me.”

“Doing? I suppose you would say I do nothing.”

Darcy glanced up at the brilliant young face opposite him.

“It seems to suit you, that way of being busy,” he said. “Now, it’s your turn. Do you read? Do you study? I remember you saying that it would do us all—all us artists, I mean—a great deal of good if we would study any one human face carefully for a year, without recording a line. Have you been doing that?”

Frank shook his head again.

“I mean exactly what I say,” he said, “I have been *doing* nothing. And I have never been so occupied. Look at me; have I not done something to myself to begin with?”

“You are two years younger than I,” said Darcy, “at least you used to be. You therefore are thirty-five. But had I never seen you before I should say you were just twenty. But was it worth while to spend six years of greatly-occupied life in order to look twenty? Seems rather like a woman of fashion.”

Frank laughed boisterously.

“First time I’ve ever been compared to that particular bird of prey,” he said. “No, that has not been my occupation—in fact I am only very rarely conscious that one effect of my occupation has been that. Of course, it must have been if one comes to think of it. It is not very important. Quite true my body has become young. But that is very little; I have become young.”

===Chinese===
席间，弗兰克主要忙着让自己赶上进度，了解这位六年未见的老友近来的行止与成就。原来这六年对达西而言是事故连连、也成功连连的六年；他作为肖像画家已闯出了名头，且这名头看来不会只风光一两季便过去，他的闲暇少得很。约莫四个月前，他又得了一场重的伤寒，至于这场病与本故事的关联，便是他来到了这个幽僻之地调养。

「是啊，你发达了，」临了弗兰克说，「我早就知道你会的。皇家艺术院副院士（A.R.A.），前途还有更高的。钱嘛？我猜你是腰缠万贯了。可是，哦，达西，这些年你有过多少快乐呢？那才是唯一不会朽坏的东西。这些年你又学到了多少？哦，我说的不是艺术。便是我，当年在这上头也能做得不差。」

达西笑了起来。

「做得不差？亲爱的朋友，我这六年所学的一切，可以说你还在摇篮里时就已懂得了。你早年的画如今卖得出大价钱。你现在竟不再动笔了么？」

弗兰克摇了摇头。

「是的，我太忙了。」他说。

「忙什么？请告诉我。这也是人人不停地问我的。」

「忙？你大概会说，我什么也没做。」

达西抬眼看了看对面那张容光焕发的年轻面孔。

「这种忙法儿倒是挺养人的，」他说，「现在，轮到你了。你读书么？你钻研什么么？我还记得你从前说过，如果我们——我指的是我们这些画家——肯花上一年工夫仔仔细细地研究一张人脸，却一笔不落、一字不录，对我们大家都会有莫大的益处。你这些年做的是这个吗？」

弗兰克又摇了摇头。

「我说的正是字面上的意思，」他说，「我什么也没做。可我从未如此忙碌过。你瞧瞧我；单是我对自己所做的，难道还不足以说明问题吗？」

「你比我小两岁，」达西说，「至少从前是。这么说来你今年三十五。可要是从前没见过你，我会说你刚好二十岁。但花六年大忙特忙的光阴，只为了看起来像二十岁，值得么？这倒有点儿像时髦的贵妇了。」

弗兰克纵声大笑。

「我还是头一回被比作那种猛禽呢，」他说，「不，那并非我忙碌的内容——事实上，我极难得才会意识到我这份营生竟有这一桩副作用。当然了，仔细一想，必是如此。这并不打紧。我的身体变年轻了，这没错。但那是小事；是我整个人变年轻了。」

===Original===
Darcy pushed back his chair and sat sideways to the table looking at the other.

“Has that been your occupation then?” he asked.

“Yes, that anyhow is one aspect of it. Think what youth means! It is the capacity for growth, mind, body, spirit, all grow, all get stronger, all have a fuller, firmer life every day. That is something, considering that every day that passes after the ordinary man reaches the full-blown flower of his strength, weakens his hold on life. A man reaches his prime, and remains, we say, in his prime, for ten years, or perhaps twenty. But after his primest prime is reached, he slowly, insensibly weakens. These are the signs of age in you, in your body, in your art probably, in your mind. You are less electric than you were. But I, when I reach my prime—I am nearing it—ah, you shall see.”

The stars had begun to appear in the blue velvet of the sky, and to the east the horizon seen above the black silhouette of the village was growing dove-coloured with the approach of moonrise. White moths hovered dimly over the garden-beds, and the footsteps of night tiptoed through the bushes. Suddenly Frank rose.

“Ah, it is the supreme moment,” he said softly. “Now more than at any other time the current of life, the eternal imperishable current runs so close to me that I am almost enveloped in it. Be silent a minute.”

He advanced to the edge of the terrace and looked out standing stretched with arms outspread. Darcy heard him draw a long breath into his lungs, and after many seconds expel it again. Six or eight times he did this, then turned back into the lamplight.

“It will sound to you quite mad, I expect,” he said, “but if you want to hear the soberest truth I have ever spoken and shall ever speak, I will tell you about myself. But come into the garden if it is not too damp for you. I have never told anyone yet, but I shall like to tell you. It is long, in fact, since I have even tried to classify what I have learned.”

They wandered into the fragrant dimness of the pergola, and sat down. Then Frank began:
