我是怎么下的楼，自己也说不清。一种可怖的战栗与恶心——与其说是肉体的，不如说是灵魂的——攫住了我；不止一回，得由他把我的脚搬到台阶上，而他一边走，一边不时朝楼梯上方投去恐惧而忧虑的目光。不过我们终于到了楼下他那间更衣室；在那里，我把此处所写的一切都告诉了他。

---

后事可以长话短说；事实上，我的一些读者或许已经猜到了是怎么回事——如果他们还记得大约八年前西福利（West Fawley）墓园那桩说不清道不明的旧事：有个自杀身亡的女人的尸首，曾三次试图下葬，都未能成事。每一次，不出几天，那口棺材就又从土里拱了出来。第三次之后，为了免得这事被人议论，那尸首便被另葬他处，埋在了未经祝圣的不洁之地。下葬的地方，就在这个女人生前所住那宅子的花园、那扇铁门外头。她是在那宅子塔楼顶层的一间屋子里寻的死。她的名字，叫朱莉娅·斯通。

后来，这尸首又被人偷偷挖了出来，人们发现，那口棺材里盛满了血。

## The Shootings of Achnaleish / 阿赫纳利什的猎场

===Original===
The dining-room windows, both front and back, the one looking into Oakley Street, the other into a small backyard with three sooty shrubs in it (known as the garden), were all open, so that the table stood in midstream of such air as there was. But in spite of this the heat was stifling, since, for once in a way, July had remembered that it was the duty of good little summers to be hot. Hot in consequence it had been: heat reverberated from the house-walls, it rose through the boot from the paving-stones, it poured down from a large superheated sun that walked the sky all day long in a benignant and golden manner. Dinner was over, but the small party of four who had eaten it still lingered.

Mabel Armytage﻿—it was she who had laid down the duty of good little summers﻿—spoke first.

“Oh, Jim, it sounds too heavenly,” she said. “It makes me feel cool to think of it. Just fancy, in a fortnight’s time we shall all four of us be there, in our own shooting-lodge﻿—”

“Farmhouse,” said Jim.

“Well, I didn’t suppose it was Balmoral, with our own coffee-coloured salmon river roaring down to join the waters of our own loch.”

===Chinese===
餐室前后两面的窗都敞着，一面临奥克利街（Oakley Street），一面临一个后院小得很，院里有三株沾满煤灰的灌木（这便叫作「花园」），好让餐桌摆在仅有的那点穿堂风的中流。可纵然如此，闷热仍叫人喘不过气来，因为七月这一回总算记起了，乖巧的小夏日本分原是应当热的。于是它便果然热了起来：暑气从四围房屋的墙上映回来，从铺路石透过靴底蒸上来，又从一轮过热的大太阳倾泻而下，那太阳整日以一副慈祥而金黄的姿态在天上踱步。晚饭既毕，用过饭的那四人小组却仍恋坐着不肯散。

梅布尔·阿米蒂奇（Mabel Armytage）——正是她定下了乖巧小夏日的本分——先开了口。

「哦，吉姆（Jim），听起来简直太美妙了，」她说，「一想起来便觉着凉快。你想啊，再过两周，我们四个就都到那儿了，在我们自家的猎墅里——」

「农舍。」吉姆说。

「嗳，我又没当它是巴尔莫勒尔（Balmoral），有我们自家那条咖啡色的鲑鱼河哗哗地奔下来，汇进我们自家的湖里去。」

===Original===
Jim lit a cigarette.

“Mabel, you mustn’t think of shooting-lodges and salmon rivers and lochs,” he said. “It’s a farmhouse, rather a big one, though I’m sure we shall find it hard enough to fit in. The salmon river you speak of is a big burn, no more, though it appears that salmon have been caught there. But when I saw it, it would have required as much cleverness on the part of a salmon to fit into it as it will require on our parts to fit into our farmhouse. And the loch is a tarn.”

Mabel snatched the *Guide to Highland Shootings* out of my hand with a rudeness that even a sister should not show her elder brother, and pointed a withering finger at her husband.

“ ‘Achnaleish,’ ” she declaimed, “ ‘is situated in one of the grandest and most remote parts of Sutherlandshire. To be let from August 12 till the end of October, the lodge with shooting and fishing belonging. Proprietor supplies two keepers, fishing-gillie, boat on loch, and dogs. Tenant should secure about 500 head of grouse and 500 head of mixed game, including partridge, black-game, woodcock, snipe, roe deer; also rabbits in very large number, especially by ferreting. Large baskets of brown trout can be taken from the loch, and whenever the water is high sea-trout and occasional salmon. Lodge contains’﻿—I can’t go on; it’s too hot, and you know the rest. Rent only £350!”

Jim listened patiently.

“Well?” he said. “What then?”

===Chinese===
吉姆点起一支烟。

「梅布尔，你还是别去想什么猎墅啦鲑鱼河啦湖泊了吧，」他说，「那是一座农舍，倒算是挺大的一座，不过我敢肯定，我们一家子要塞进去也得费好一番周折。你说的那条鲑鱼河，不过是一条略大些的山涧罢了，虽说据说里面确曾捕到过鲑鱼。可我瞧见它那会儿，一条鲑鱼要把自己挤进去所需的心计，怕是不亚于我们一家子挤进那座农舍所需的心计。至于那湖，也不过是一口山潭。」

梅布尔以一种就连做妹妹的也不该对哥哥流露的粗暴，一把从我手里夺去了《高地狩猎指南》（*Guide to Highland Shootings*），用一根几乎要把人灼伤的手指直指她丈夫。

「『阿赫纳利什（Achnaleish），』」她朗诵起来，「『坐落于萨瑟兰郡（Sutherlandshire）最壮丽、最偏僻的地区之一。自八月十二日起至十月底出租，小屋连同附带的狩猎与渔猎之权。地主供应两名猎场看守、一名垂钓侍从、湖上用船及猎犬。租户约可猎获松鸡五百只，及各色猎物五百只，包括鹧鸪、黑松鸡、山鹬、鹬、獐；另有极多之兔，尤以雪貂驱猎时为最。湖中可得大筐大筐之棕鳟，涨水之时又有海鳟，间或有鲑鱼。小屋共有』——我念不下去了；天太热了，剩下的你自己也知道。租金只要三百五十镑！」

吉姆耐着性子听着。

「嗯？」他说，「那又怎样？」

===Original===
Mabel rose with dignity.

“It *is* a shooting-lodge with a salmon river and a loch, just as I have said. Come, Madge, let’s go out. It is too hot to sit in the house.”

“You’ll be calling Buxton ‘the majordomo’ next,” remarked Jim, as his wife passed him.

I had picked up the *Guide to Highland Shootings* again which my sister had so unceremoniously plucked from me, and idly compared the rent and attractions of Achnaleish with other places that were to let.

“Seems cheap, too,” I said. “Why, here’s another place, just the same sort of size and bag, for which they ask £500; here’s another at £550.”

Jim helped himself to coffee.

“Yes, it does seem cheap,” he said. “But, of course, it’s very remote: it took me a good three hours from Lairg, and I don’t suppose I was driving very noticeably below the legal limit. But it’s cheap, as you say.”

===Chinese===
梅布尔端端地站了起来。

「它就是一座带鲑鱼河带湖泊的猎墅，正像我说的一样。来，玛吉（Madge），咱们出去吧。屋里太热，坐不住。」

「下回你该把巴克斯顿（Buxton）叫作『大总管』了。」吉姆在他妻子经过时说道。

我又把妹妹那样蛮横地从我手里夺去的《高地狩猎指南》拾了起来，信手把阿赫纳利什的租金与种种诱人之处，与别处招租的地方比了一比。

「也似乎便宜了点儿，」我说，「瞧，这儿另一处，规模和猎获量全相同，要价五百镑；这儿还有一处，五百五十镑。」

吉姆给自己斟了一杯咖啡。

「是呀，确乎便宜，」他说，「可当然喽，那地方极偏僻：我从莱尔格（Lairg）去，足足花了三个钟头，我自问车速也不见得比法定限度低到哪里去。不过你也说对了，确是便宜。」

===Original===
Now, Madge (who is my wife) has her prejudices. One of them﻿—an extremely expensive one﻿—is that anything cheap has always some hidden and subtle drawback, which you discover when it is too late. And the drawback to cheap houses is drains or offices﻿—the presence, so to speak, of the former, and the absence of the latter. So I hazarded these.

“No, the drains are all right,” said Jim, “because I got the certificate of the inspector, and as for offices, really I think the servants’ parts are better than ours. No﻿—why it’s so cheap, I can’t imagine.”

“Perhaps the bag is overstated,” I suggested.

Jim again shook his head.

“No, that’s the funny thing about it,” he said. “The bag, I am sure, is understated. At least, I walked over the moor for a couple of hours, and the whole place is simply crawling with hares. Why, you could shoot five hundred hares alone on it.”

“Hares?” I asked. “That’s rather queer, so far up, isn’t it?”

Jim laughed.

“So I thought. And the hares are queer, too; big beasts, very dark in colour. Let’s join the others outside. Jove! what a hot night!”

===Chinese===
玛吉（即我妻子）素有她的偏见。其中一条——代价极昂贵的一条——是：凡便宜的东西，必有其隐而不露、微妙难言的弊端，等你发觉时已悔之晚矣。而便宜宅子的弊端，不是排水沟便是杂役房——前者不该有倒有了，后者该有倒没有，可这么粗粗地说。我便拿这两桩来猜。

「不，排水沟没问题，」吉姆说，「因为我拿到了查验官的证书；至于杂役房嘛，说实话，我觉得下人们住的那一片比咱们自个儿住的还强。不——它何以这么便宜，我可摸不着头脑了。」

「也许是那猎获量说得太大了些吧。」我提议道。

吉姆又摇摇头。

「不，可笑之处恰恰在这里，」他说，「那猎获量，我敢保是说小了的。至少，我在那片荒原上走了两个钟头，整片地简直是野兔成灾。嘿，光野兔你就能在那上面打它五百只。」

「野兔？」我问，「这么北的地方，这倒有点儿古怪，是不是？」

吉姆笑了起来。

「我也这么想。而且那些兔子也古怪；个头大，毛色很深。咱们出去跟他们一块儿坐坐吧。天哪！好一个闷热的晚上！」

---

===Original===
Even as Mabel had said, that day fortnight found us all four, the four who had stifled and sweltered in Chelsea, flying through the cool and invigorating winds of the north. The road was in admirable condition, and I should not wonder if for the second time Jim’s big Napier went not noticeably below the legal limit. The servants had gone straight up, starting the same day as we, while we had got out at Perth, motored to Inverness, and were now, on the second day, nearing our goal. Never have I seen so depopulated a road. I do not suppose there was a man to a mile of it.

We had left Lairg about five that afternoon, expecting to arrive at Achnaleish by eight, but one disaster after another overtook us. Now it was the engine, and now a tyre that delayed us, till finally we stopped some eight miles short of our destination, to light up, for with evening had come a huge wrack of cloud out of the west, so that we were cheated of the clear post-sunset twilight of the north. Then on again, till, with a little dancing of the car over a bridge, Jim said:

“That’s the bridge of our salmon river; so look out for the turning up to the lodge. It is to the right, and only a narrow track. You can send her along, Sefton,” he called to the chauffeur; “we shan’t meet a soul.”

===Chinese===
正应了梅布尔所言，两周后的那一天，我们四个——那四个在切尔西（Chelsea）闷得透不过气、热得汗如雨下的人——正疾驰在北方凉爽提神的风里。路面极佳，吉姆那辆大纳皮尔（Napier）车若再一次开得不明显低于法定限度，我也不会觉得奇怪。仆人们与我们同一天动身，径直前往；我们则在珀斯（Perth）下了火车，驱车至因弗内斯（Inverness），如今第二天，眼看就要到目的地了。我从未见过人烟如此稀少的路。我想一路上每一英里恐怕也摊不到一个人。

那天下午五点光景我们离开了莱尔格，原指望八点便可抵达阿赫纳利什，不料一桩接一桩的祸事追上了我们。一会儿是发动机，一会儿是轮胎，耽搁个不住，最后我们在离目的地约八英里之处停了下来点亮车灯——因为入夜时分，一大片乱云从西天卷来，把北方日落之后那清明的暮色夺了去。再往前开，待到车子在一座桥上微微一颠，吉姆说道：

「这就是咱们那条鲑鱼河上的桥了；留神看拐上去往猎墅的那条岔路。就在右边，只是一条窄道儿。你只管放开跑，塞夫顿（Sefton），」他冲司机喊道，「咱们一路遇不上一个人影儿。」

===Original===
I was sitting in front, finding the speed and the darkness extraordinarily exhilarating. A bright circle of light was cast by our lamps, fading into darkness in front, while at the sides, cut off by the casing of the lamps, the transition into blackness was sharp and sudden. Every now and then, across this circle of illumination some wild thing would pass: now a bird, with hurried flutter of wings when it saw the speed of the luminous monster, would just save itself from being knocked over; now a rabbit feeding by the side of the road would dash onto it and then bounce back again; but more frequently it would be a hare that sprang up from its feeding and raced in front of us. They seemed dazed and scared by the light, unable to wheel into the darkness again, until time and again I thought we must run over one, so narrowly, in giving a sort of desperate sideways leap, did it miss our wheels. Then it seemed that one started up almost from under us, and I saw, to my surprise, it was enormous in size, and in colour apparently quite black. For some hundred yards it raced in front of us, fascinated by the bright light pursuing it, then, like the rest, it dashed for the darkness. But it was too late, and with a horrid jolt we ran over it. At once Sefton slowed down and stopped, for Jim’s rule is to go back always and make sure that any poor run-over is dead. So, when we stopped, the chauffeur jumped down and ran back.

“What was it?” Jim asked me, as we waited.

“A hare.”

Sefton came running back.

“Yes, sir, quite dead,” he said. “I picked it up, sir.”

“What for?”

“Thought you might like to see it, sir. It’s the biggest hare I ever see, and it’s quite black.”

===Chinese===
我坐在前座，觉得这般车速、这般夜色，格外令人精神振奋。车灯投出一圈明亮的光，在前方渐渐溶入黑暗；两侧则被灯罩截断，由明入黑的过渡突兀而干脆。不时有野物横穿这一圈光地：一会儿是一只鸟，一见这头发光巨兽的速度，便急忙扑棱着翅膀险险躲过被撞翻的命运；一会儿是一只正在路边觅食的兔子窜上路面、又蹦了回去；但更常见的，是从觅食处惊起、在我们车前一路飞奔的野兔。它们似乎被灯光弄得又呆又怕，没法再拐回黑暗里去，一次又一次，我以为我们必定要从某一只身上碾过去了——它斜斜一跳，拼了命地闪避，堪堪擦过我们的车轮。后来有一只几乎是从我们车底下蹿起来的，我一看之下吃了一惊：它个头大得惊人，颜色像是全黑的。它在车前奔了约莫一百码，被那束追着它的强光摄住了魂似的，接着又如别的兔子一样朝黑暗里冲去。可太晚了，只觉一阵可怖的颠簸，我们从它身上碾了过去。塞夫顿立刻放慢车速停了下来，因为吉姆有个规矩：凡是碾着了什么可怜的小牲口，总得回头去看个分明，确认它已经死了才罢。于是车一停，司机便跳下车跑了回去。

「是什么？」吉姆等的时候问我。

「一只野兔。」

塞夫顿跑了回来。

「是，先生，死透了，」他说，「我把它捡来了，先生。」

「捡来做什么？」

「想您也许想瞧一瞧，先生。我生平见过的最大的兔子，而且通体乌黑。」

===Original===
It was immediately after this that we came to the track up to the house, and in a few minutes we were within doors. There we found that if “shooting-lodge” was a term unsuitable, so also was “farmhouse,” so roomy, excellently proportioned, and well furnished was our dwelling, while the contentment that beamed from Buxton’s face was sufficient testimonial for the offices. In the hall, too, with its big open fireplace, were a couple of big solemn bookcases, full of serious works, such as some educated minister might have left, and, coming down dressed for dinner before the others, I dipped into the shelves. Then﻿—something must long have been vaguely simmering in my brain, for I pounced on the book as soon as I saw it﻿—I came upon Elwes’s *Folklore of the North West Highlands*, and looked out “Hare” in the index. Then I read:

“Nor is it only witches that are believed to have the power of changing themselves into animals.﻿ ﻿… Men and women on whom no suspicion of the sort lies are thought to be able to do this, and to don the bodies of certain animals, notably hares.﻿ ﻿… Such, according to local superstition, are easily distinguishable by their size and colour, which approaches jet black.”

===Chinese===
就在这之后不久，我们便拐上了通往宅子的那条小道，再过几分钟便进了门。进门一瞧，才发觉「猎墅」这称呼固不相宜，「农舍」这称呼也同样不称——我们这住所竟是这般宽敞，比例这般合宜，陈设这般齐全；而从巴克斯顿脸上洋溢出来的那份满意，已足为杂役房作最好的保证了。门厅里有一口大敞开的壁炉，还有两只庄重的大书橱，满满的尽是些严肃的典籍，仿佛某位有学问的牧师留下来的；我比旁人先换好赴晚餐的礼服下了楼，便到书橱前随手翻翻。后来——必有某种念头早已在我脑子里隐约地翻腾了许久，因为我一瞧见那书便扑了过去——我翻到了埃尔韦斯（Elwes）的《西北高地民俗志》（*Folklore of the North West Highlands*），从索引里查了「野兔」一条。随后我读到：

「世人相信，能将自身化作禽兽者，并不仅仅是女巫。……有些男女，平日并不见有何可疑之处，也被认为能行此事，能穿上某些禽兽的躯壳，尤其是野兔的躯壳......据当地的迷信说，此类变怪之物，可凭其体型与毛色轻易辨识：其色近乎纯黑。」

===Original===
I was up and out early next morning, prey to the vivid desire that attacks many folk in new places﻿—namely, to look on the fresh country and the new horizons﻿—and, on going out, certainly the surprise was great. For I had imagined an utterly lonely and solitary habitation; instead, scarce half a mile away, down the steep brae-side at the top of which stood our commodious farmhouse, ran a typically Scotch village street, the hamlet no doubt of Achnaleish. So steep was this hillside that the village was really remote; if it was half a mile away in crow-flying measurement, it must have been a couple of hundred yards below us. But its existence was the odd thing to me: there were some four dozen houses, at the least, while we had not seen half that number since leaving Lairg. A mile away, perhaps, lay the shining shield of the western sea; to the other side, away from the village, I had no difficulty in recognising the river and the loch. The house, in fact, was set on a hog’s back; from all sides it must needs be climbed to. But, as is the custom of the Scots, no house, however small, should be without its due brightness of flowers, and the walls of this were purple with clematis and orange with tropaeolum. It all looked very placid and serene and homelike.

===Chinese===
第二天一早我便起了床，出门去——许多人在新地方都会被那种热切的渴望攫住，便是要去看一看那新鲜的乡野、那新的天际线——一走出去，我着实吃了一惊。因为我原以为这是一处绝偏绝孤的住所；谁知顺着我们这座宽敞农舍所踞的山顶往下，那陡坡（brae）上不到半英里处，便躺着一条典型的苏格兰乡村街市，那村落自是阿赫纳利什了。这山坡陡得很，村子其实也极偏僻；若说它离我们按直线算还有半英里，那么在我们脚底下怕有二百码深。可它的存在本身已叫我纳罕：少说也有四五十栋房子，而我们自打出了莱尔格，还没见过这一半数目的人家。西边一英里外，大概便是那面闪亮的西方大海的盾牌；另一侧，远离村子的方向，那条河和那口湖我一眼便认了出来。这宅子其实是盖在一道山脊（hog’s back）的脊背上；从哪一面来都得爬山才能到。可正如苏格兰人的习俗，无论房子多小，都该有它那一份花朵应有的明丽，这座房子的墙面便被铁线莲染成紫色，又被金莲花染成橙色。一切看上去都非常安详、宁谧、像家。

===Original===
I continued my tour of exploration, and came back rather late for breakfast. A slight check in the day’s arrangements had occurred, for the head keeper, Maclaren, had not come up, and the second, Sandie Ross, reported that the reason for this had been the sudden death of his mother the evening before. She was not known to be ill, but just as she was going to bed she had thrown up her arms, screamed suddenly as if with fright, and was found to be dead. Sandie, who repeated this news to me after breakfast, was just a slow, polite Scotchman, rather shy, rather awkward. Just as he finished﻿—we were standing about outside the backdoor﻿—there came up from the stables the smart, very English-looking Sefton. In one hand he carried the black hare.

He touched his hat to me as he went in.

“Just to show it to Mr. Armytage, sir,” he said. “She’s as black as a boot.”

He turned into the door, but not before Sandie Ross had seen what he carried, and the slow, polite Scotchman was instantly turned into some furtive, frightened-looking man.

“And where might it be that you found that, sir?” he asked.

===Chinese===
我继续四处踏看，回来时早餐已有点儿迟了。当日的安排略略出了点岔子：猎场总看守麦克拉伦（Maclaren）没有上来，二把手桑迪·罗斯（Sandie Ross）禀报说，缘由是他母亲昨夜骤然去世了。她素日并无为人所知的病症，可正要上床就寝之时，忽然两臂一甩，像受了惊似的尖叫了一声，便已气绝。早饭之后，桑迪又把这消息向我复述了一遍。他是个慢性子、彬彬有礼的苏格兰人，有些腼腆，有些笨拙。他话音刚落——我们正站在后门外闲立着——从马房那边走上来了整洁利落、一副十足英国人派头的塞夫顿。他一只手提着那只黑兔。

他进屋时朝我抬了抬帽子。

「给阿米蒂奇先生瞧一瞧，先生，」他说，「它黑得像只靴子。」

他转身进了门，可还没进去，桑迪·罗斯已经看见他手里拎的是什么了；这慢性子、彬彬有礼的苏格兰人，一转眼便换上了一副鬼鬼祟祟、面露惧色的模样。

「敢问先生是在哪儿捡到那只的？」他问。

===Original===
Now, the black-hare superstition had already begun to intrigue me.

“Why does that interest you?” I asked.

The slow Scotch look was resumed with an effort.

“It’ll no interest me,” he said. “I just asked. There are unco many black hares in Achnaleish.”

Then his curiosity got the better of him.

“She’d have been nigh to where the road passes by and on to Achnaleish?” he asked.

“The hare? Yes, we found her on the road there.”

Sandie turned away.

“She aye sat there,” he said.

===Chinese===
说到这里，黑兔的迷信已开始勾起我的好奇了。

「你怎么会对这个有兴趣？」我问。

他费了点劲，才又恢复了那副慢吞吞的苏格兰人的神情。

「我没兴趣，」他说，「我不过是问问。阿赫纳利什的黑兔，多得没数儿。」

紧接着，他的好奇压倒了他。

「它——大约是在那条大路从旁边经过、通往阿赫纳利什去的那一带？」他问。

「那只兔子？是，我们是在那段路上捡到它的。」

桑迪转过脸去。

「它一向就坐在那儿。」他说。

===Original===
There were a number of little plantations climbing up the steep hillside from Achnaleish to the moor above, and we had a pleasant slack sort of morning shooting there, walking through and round them with a nondescript tribe of beaters, among whom the serious Buxton figured. We had fair enough sport, but of the hares which Jim had seen in such profusion none that morning came to the gun, till at last, just before lunch, there came out of the apex of one of these plantations, some thirty yards from where Jim was standing, a very large, dark-coloured hare. For one moment I saw him hesitate﻿—for he holds the correct view about long or doubtful shots at hares﻿—then he put up his gun to fire. Sandie, who had walked round outside, after giving the beaters their instructions, was at this moment close to him, and with incredible quickness rushed upon him and with his stick struck up the barrels of the gun before he could fire.

“Black hare!” he cried. “Ye’d shoot a black hare? There’s no shooting of hares at all in Achnaleish, and mark that.”

Never have I seen so sudden and extraordinary a change in a man’s face: it was as if he had just prevented some blackguard of the street from murdering his wife.

“An’ the sickness about an’ all,” he added indignantly. “When the puir folk escape from their peching fevered bodies an hour or two, to the caller muirs.”

Then he seemed to recover himself.

“I ask your pardon, sir,” he said to Jim. “I was upset with ane thing an’ anither, an’ the black hare ye found deid last night﻿—eh, I’m blatherin’ again. But there’s no a hare shot on Achnaleish, that’s sure.”

Jim was still looking in mere speechless astonishment at Sandie when I came up. And, though shooting is dear to me, so too is folklore.

“But we’ve taken the shooting of Achnaleish, Sandie,” I said. “There was nothing there about not shooting hares.”

Sandie suddenly boiled up again for a minute.

“An’ mebbe there was nothing there about shooting the bairns and the weemen!” he cried.

===Chinese===
从阿赫纳利什到上方荒原之间那片陡坡上，散布着好些小片的人造林，我们便在那儿度过了上午一段愉快而松散的射猎时光，在一群杂七杂八的轰兽人（beaters）簇拥下穿行于林间、绕着林缘走，严肃的巴克斯顿也夹杂在其中。我们的收获还算可观，只是吉姆曾看见铺天盖地那么多的野兔，这一上午竟没有一只进了枪口。直到临午饭前，从其中一片林子的顶尖处——离吉姆所站的地方不过三十来码——蹿出了一只个头极大、毛色深暗的野兔。我瞧见他犹豫了一下——因为他一向所持的是关于远距离或无把握之兔击的正统看法——随后端起枪要放。桑迪方才在外面绕了一圈，给轰兽人们分派过指示，这会儿正挨在他身边，只见他以惊人的迅疾扑了上去，用手里的棍子一挑，赶在他开枪之前把枪管挑向了天。

「黑兔！」他叫道，「你要打一只黑兔？在阿赫纳利什，压根儿就不兴打野兔，你记住。」

我从未见过谁的脸色有这般突兀、这般异乎寻常的变化：那神情仿佛他刚刚拦住了一个街上行凶的流氓、阻止了他杀害自己的妻子。

「这会儿病疫还在到处闹呢，」他愤然又道，「那些可怜的人，好不容易从他们那气喘吁吁发烧的身子骨里挣出来一两个钟头，到那清凉的荒原上去。」

接着他似乎醒了过来。

「请先生见恕，」他对吉姆说，「我这一阵被这桩那桩的事搅得心神不宁，再说昨儿晚上你们捡到的那只死黑兔——呃，我又在瞎扯了。不过阿赫纳利什不打野兔，这是断然的。」

我走过去的时候，吉姆还在那里无言地、不胜错愕地望着桑迪。虽说射猎为我所钟爱，民俗也是我所钟爱。

「可是我们已经租下了阿赫纳利什的猎场啊，桑迪，」我说，「那上头可没写着不许打野兔。」

桑迪霎时又发起急来。

「许是那上头也没写着不许打孩子和女人呢！」他叫道。

===Original===
I looked round, and saw that by now the beaters had all come through the wood: of them Buxton and Jim’s valet, who was also among them, stood apart: all the rest were standing round us two with gleaming eyes and open mouths, hanging on the debate, and forced, so I imagined, from their imperfect knowledge of English to attend closely in order to catch the drift of what went on. Every now and then a murmur of Gaelic passed between them, and this somehow I found peculiarly disconcerting.

“But what have the hares to do with the children or women of Achnaleish?” I asked.

There was no reply to this beyond the reiterated sentence: “There’s na shooting of hares in Achnaleish whatever,” and then Sandie turned to Jim.

“That’s the end of the bit wood, sir,” he said. “We’ve been a’ roound.”

Certainly the beat had been very satisfactory. A roe had fallen to Jim (one ought also to have fallen to me, but remained, if not standing, at any rate running away). We had a dozen of black-game, four pigeons, six brace of grouse (these were, of course, but outliers, as we had not gone on to the moor proper at all), some thirty rabbits, and four couple of woodcock. This, it must be understood, was just from the fringe of plantations about the house, but this was all we meant to do today, making only a morning of it, since our ladies had expressly desired first lessons in the art of angling in the afternoon, so that they too could be busy. Excellently too had Sandie worked the beat, leaving us now, after going, as he said, all round, a couple of hundred yards only from the house, at a few minutes to two.

So, after a little private signalling from Jim to me, he spoke to Sandie, dropping the hare-question altogether.

“Well, the beat has gone excellently,” he said, “and this afternoon we’ll be fishing. Please settle with the beaters every evening, and tell me what you have paid out. Good morning to you all.”

We walked back to the house, but the moment we had turned a hum of confabulation began behind us, and, looking back, I saw Sandie and all the beaters in close whispering conclave. Then Jim spoke.

===Chinese===
我环顾四周，见这时轰兽人已尽数穿过林子出来了：其中的巴克斯顿和吉姆的贴身男仆——他也夹在轰兽人之中——站得稍远些；其余的全都围拢在我们两人身边，目灼灼、口张张地，屏息听着这场争执，我猜他们英文不大通，不得不凑近了仔细听，才能抓住事情的大意。他们之间不时地有一阵盖尔语（Gaelic）的低语传过，这种情形不知怎的，我觉得分外叫人发毛。

「可是野兔与阿赫纳利什的孩子和女人有什么相干？」我问。

对此并无别的回答，只有那句反复重申的话：「阿赫纳利什压根儿不许打野兔。」接着桑迪转向吉姆。

「这片小林子到底了，先生，」他说，「咱们已经统统绕了一圈。」

方才这一程轰猎无疑很叫人满意。吉姆打到一只獐（本来我也该打到一只的，可那只虽说不算站着，至少也是跑着逃了）。我们还猎得黑松鸡十二只、野鸽四只、松鸡六对（这些当然只是些散兵游勇，因为我们根本还没上到真正的荒原上去）、约莫三十只兔子，以及山鹬四对。须知，这还只是宅子周围那些林缘地带的收获；可今日我们也只打算做这么多，只消一个上午便罢，因为太太们已明言要在下午学垂钓的初步手艺，好叫她们也有事可忙。桑迪这一程轰猎调度得也极漂亮：照他所说绕了一圈下来，此刻离宅子不过两百码远近，时间是两点差几分。

于是，吉姆向我略略使了个眼色，便对桑迪开口了，把野兔的事全然撇开不提。

「嗯，这一程打得极好，」他说，「今儿下午我们去钓鱼。请你每晚跟轰兽人们结清工钱，告诉我你付出了多少。各位早安。」

我们走回宅子去，可一转过身，身后便起了一阵嘁嘁喳喳的密议声；我回头看，只见桑迪和所有轰兽人凑在一处低声商议。然后吉姆说道：

===Original===
“More in your line than mine,” he said; “I prefer shooting a hare to routing out some cock-and-bull story as to why I shouldn’t. What does it all mean?”

I mentioned what I had found in Elwes last night.

“Then do they think it was we who killed the old lady on the road, and that I was going to kill somebody else this morning?” he asked. “How does one know that they won’t say that rabbits are their aunts, and woodcock their uncles, and grouse their children? I never heard such rot, and tomorrow we’ll have a hare drive. Blow the grouse! We’ll settle this hare-question first.”

Jim by this time was in the frame of mind typical of the English when their rights are threatened. He had the shooting of Achnaleish, on which were hares, sir, hares. And if he chose to shoot hares, neither papal bull nor royal charter could stop him.

“Then there’ll be a row,” said I, and Jim sniffed scornfully.

At lunch Sandie’s remark about the “sickness,” which I had forgotten till that moment, was explained.

“Fancy that horrible influenza getting here,” said Madge. “Mabel and I went down to the village this morning, and, oh, Ted, you can get all sorts of things, from mackintoshes to peppermints, at the most heavenly shop, and there was a child there looking awfully ill and feverish. So we inquired: it was the ‘sickness’﻿—that was all they knew. But, from what the woman said, it’s clearly influenza. Sudden fever, and all the rest of it.”

“Bad type?” I asked.

“Yes; there have been several deaths already among the old people from pneumonia following it.”

===Chinese===
「这倒更对你的路数，不对我的，」他说，「我宁可去打一只兔子，也不愿刨出什么天方夜谭，来解释我为何不该打。这一切究竟是怎么回事？」

我便把昨夜在埃尔韦斯的书里所见，向他说了。

「这么说，他们以为是我们在路上打死了那位老太太，今儿早上我又要去打死别的人喽？」他问，「你怎么知道他们不会说兔子是他们的姨妈，山鹬是他们的舅舅，松鸡是他们的孩子呢？我从没听过这种胡说八道，明天咱们就搞一场赶兔。去它的松鸡！咱们先把这野兔的事儿弄弄清楚。」

吉姆此时已陷入那种典型的英格兰人心态——一旦自己所享的权利受到威胁便油然而生的那种心态。他租下了阿赫纳利什的猎场，那上面有的是兔子，先生，兔子。只要他高兴打野兔，无论教皇的训谕还是钦赐的特许状，都拦他不住。

「那就要闹起来了。」我说。吉姆不屑地哼了一声。

午饭时，桑迪所说的「病疫」——我此前一直忘了——也得到了解释。

「想不到这可怕的流感竟蔓延到了这儿，」玛吉说，「今早我和梅布尔下了村子，哦，特德（Ted），在一家美得像天堂似的小铺子里，你什么都能买到，从胶布雨衣到薄荷糖都有；铺子里有个孩子，看着病得很重，烧得厉害。我们就打听了一下：那是『病疫』——他们只晓得这么多。不过听那妇人的口气，分明就是流感。忽然发高烧，诸如此类。」

「来势凶吗？」我问。

「凶。已经有好几个老人跟着发了肺炎，死掉了。」

===Original===
Now, I hope that as an Englishman I too have a notion of my rights, and attempt anyhow to enforce them, as a general rule, if they are wantonly threatened. But if a mad bull wishes to prevent my going across a certain field, I do not insist on my rights, but go round instead, since I see no reasonable hope of convincing the bull that according to the constitution of my country I may walk in this field unmolested. And that afternoon, as Madge and I drifted about the loch, while I was not employed in disentangling her flies from each other or her hair or my coat, I pondered over our position with regard to the hares and men of Achnaleish, and thought that the question of the bull and the field represented our standpoint pretty accurately. Jim *had* the shooting of Achnaleish, and that undoubtedly included the right to shoot hares: so too he might have the right to walk over a field in which was a mad bull. But it seemed to me not more futile to argue with the bull than to hope to convince these folk of Achnaleish that the hares were﻿—as was assuredly the case﻿—only hares, and not the embodiments of their friends and relations. For that, beyond all doubt, was their belief, and it would take, not half an hour’s talk, but perhaps a couple of generations of education to kill that belief, or even to reduce it to the level of a superstition. At present it was no superstition﻿—the terror and incredulous horror on Sandie’s face when Jim raised his gun to fire at the hare told me that﻿—it was a belief as sober and commonplace as our own belief that the hares were not incarnations of living folk in Achnaleish. Also, virulent influenza was raging in the place, and Jim proposed to have a hare-drive tomorrow! What would happen?

===Chinese===
我希望，身为一个英格兰人，我也还算懂得我自己的权利，并且大凡这权利被人无端侵犯之时，多少总试图加以维护。可倘若一头疯牛要阻止我穿过某一片田地，我便不坚持我的权利，宁可绕着走，因为我看不出有什么指望能说服那头牛，让它明白按照我国的宪法，我可以在这片田里通行无阻。那天下午，玛吉和我在湖上随波漂荡，我凡是——不必把她的假蝇钓钩从它们彼此之间、从她的头发里、从我上衣上解开的时候——便琢磨着我们与阿赫纳利什的兔子们和人们之间的情势，觉得那疯牛与田地之喻，倒相当准确地代表了我们的处境。吉姆确是租下了阿赫纳利什的猎场，这毫无疑问地包括打野兔的权利：正如他也可能有权利走进一片关着疯牛的田地。可在我看来，要说服阿赫纳利什的这些百姓，让他们相信那些兔子——这一点确凿无疑——不过是兔子而已，并非他们的亲朋故旧投胎转世，其徒劳无益，正不下于跟那头牛理论。因为那是他们笃信不疑的事，要灭绝这种信念，光靠半个钟头的谈话是没用的，怕是要两代人的教育才行，甚至不能把它削弱到一种「迷信」的程度。眼下这还算不得迷信——吉姆端枪要打那只兔子时，桑迪脸上那种惊恐、那种难以置信的骇然，已经告诉了我——这是一种信仰，和我们之坚信这些兔子并非阿赫纳利什活人投胎一样，清醒而平常。况且当地正流行着凶猛的流感，而吉姆竟打算明日去赶兔！会发生什么事呢？

===Original===
That evening Jim raved about it in the smoking-room.

“But, good gracious, man, what can they *do*?” he cried. “What’s the use of an old gaffer from Achnaleish saying I’ve shot his granddaughter and, when he is asked to produce the corpse, telling the jury that we’ve eaten it, but that he has got the skin as evidence? What skin? A hare-skin! Oh, folklore is all very well in its way, a nice subject for discussion when topics are scarce, but don’t tell me it can enter into practical life. What can they do?”

“They can shoot us,” I remarked.

“The canny, God-fearing Scotchmen shoot us for shooting hares?” he asked.

“Well, it’s a possibility. However, I don’t think you’ll have much of a hare-drive in any case.”

“Why not?”

“Because you won’t get a single native beater, and you won’t get a keeper to come either. You’ll have to go with Buxton and your man.”

“Then I’ll discharge Sandie,” snapped Jim.

“That would be a pity: he knows his work.”

Jim got up.

“Well, his work tomorrow will be to drive hares for you and me,” said Jim. “Or do you funk?”

“I funk,” I replied.

===Chinese===
当晚吉姆在吸烟室里为这事大发牢骚。

「可是，老天爷，老兄，他们能做什么呢？」他嚷道，「阿赫纳利什一个老头儿说我打死了他外孙女，等人家要他拿出尸首来，他却跟陪审团说我们已经把它吃下肚了，不过他留了一张皮作证——这有什么用？什么皮？一张兔皮！哦，民俗学也自有其妙处，话题稀少的时候倒是个好谈资，可你别跟我说它能当真搅进实际生活里来。他们能做什么？」

「他们可以拿枪打我们。」我说。

「那些精明而敬畏上帝的苏格兰人，会因为我们打了兔子就拿枪打我们？」他问。

「嗯，这是一种可能。不过无论如何，我想你这场赶兔是赶不成了。」

「为什么？」

「因为你一个当地的轰兽人也雇不到，你也休想再有一个看守肯来。你只好带着巴克斯顿和你的男仆去。」

「那我就辞掉桑迪。」吉姆没好气地说。

「那未免可惜：他是懂行的。」

吉姆站起身来。

「好，他明儿的活儿就是给你我轰兔子，」吉姆说，「难道你害怕了？」

「我害怕。」我答道。

===Original===
The scene next morning was extremely short. Jim and I went out before breakfast, and found Sandie at the back door, silent and respectful. In the yard were a dozen young Highlanders, who had beaten for us the day before.

“Morning, Sandie,” said Jim shortly. “We’ll drive hares today. We ought to get a lot in those narrow gorges up above. Get a dozen beaters more, can you?”

“There will be na hare-drive here,” said Sandie quietly.

“I have given you your orders,” said Jim.

Sandie turned to the group of beaters outside and spoke half a dozen words in Gaelic. Next moment the yard was empty, and they were all running down the hillside towards Achnaleish. One stood on the skyline a moment, waving his arms, making some signal, as I supposed, to the village below. Then Sandie turned again.

“An’ whaur are your beaters, sir?” he asked.

For the moment I was afraid Jim was going to strike him. But he controlled himself.

“You are discharged,” he said.

===Chinese===
第二天早上那一场极其短促。吉姆和我早饭前出去，便在后门口看见桑迪，沉默而恭顺。院里站着头一天为我们轰兽的十几个高地小伙子。

「早，桑迪，」吉姆简短地说，「今天我们要赶兔子。上面那些窄窄的山沟里，应该能赶出不少。你再去找十几个轰兽人来，行不行？」

「这里不会有赶兔这回事。」桑迪平静地说。

「我已经给你下了命令。」吉姆道。

桑迪转向外头那一群轰兽人，用盖尔语说了六七个字。下一瞬间院子里便空了，他们一齐顺着山坡往阿赫纳利什跑下去了。有一个在山脊线上站了一会儿，挥动两臂，我猜是给下头村子打什么信号。然后桑迪又转过身来。

「那您的轰兽人在哪儿呢，先生？」他问。

一时之间，我怕吉姆要动手打他。但他按捺住了。

「你被辞退了。」他说。

===Original===
The hare-drive, therefore, since there were neither beaters nor keeper﻿—Maclaren, the head-keeper, having been given this “day-off” to bury his mother﻿—was clearly out of the question, and Jim, still blustering rather, but a good bit taken aback at the sudden disciplined defection of the beaters, was in betting humour that they would all return by tomorrow morning. Meanwhile the post which should have arrived before now had not come, though Mabel from her bedroom window had seen the post-cart on its way up the drive a quarter of an hour ago. At that a sudden idea struck me, and I ran to the edge of the hog’s back on which the house was set. It was even as I thought: the post-cart was just striking the high-road below, going away from the house and back to the village, without having left our letters.

I went back to the dining-room. Everything apparently was going wrong this morning: the bread was stale, the milk was not fresh, and the bell was rung for Buxton. Quite so: neither milkman nor baker had called.

From the point of view of folklore this was admirable.

“There’s another cock-and-bull story called ‘taboo,’ ” I said. “It means that nobody will supply you with anything.”

“My dear fellow, a little knowledge is a dangerous thing,” said Jim, helping himself to marmalade.

I laughed.

“You are irritated,” I said, “because you are beginning to be afraid that there is something in it.”

“Yes, that’s quite true,” he said. “But who could have supposed there was anything in it? Ah, dash it! there *can’t* be. A hare is a hare.”

“Except when it is your first cousin,” said I.

“Then I shall go out and shoot first cousins by myself,” he said.

===Chinese===
既然既无轰兽人又无看守——总看守麦克拉伦已被准了这天假去安葬他的母亲——赶兔之事自是显然办不成了。吉姆嘴上还硬撑着，可这一众轰兽人这般训练有素地一齐反水，到底叫他颇为吃惊，他便与人打赌，说他们到明儿早上必统统回来。与此同时，本该早到了的邮差却还没有到，虽说一刻钟之前梅布尔从她卧室的窗口看见运邮小车已经驶上了宅门前那条车道。我顿时心生一计，跑到宅子所踞的那道山脊的边沿上一望。果不其然：那辆运邮小车刚刚拐到下面的公路上，正背着宅子、朝村子的方向开回去，根本没把我们的信留下。

我回到餐室。今儿早上显见诸事都不对劲：面包是陈的，牛奶不新鲜，于是拉铃叫巴克斯顿。果然：送奶的和送面包的都没上门。

从民俗学的观点来看，这可真叫人叹为观止。

「还有一种天方夜谭，叫做『塔布』（taboo），」我说，「意思是，谁也不肯供给你任何东西了。」

「老兄，一知半解最是危险。」吉姆一面给自己涂橘子酱，一面说。

我笑了起来。

「你恼火，」我说，「是因为你开始害怕这里面真有点儿名堂了。」

「是，一点不错，」他说，「可谁能想到这里面真有名堂呢？啊，见鬼！不可能有的。兔子就是兔子。」

「除非它是你的表亲。」我说。

「那我就自个儿出去打表亲。」他说。

===Original===
That, I am glad to say, in the light of what followed, we dissuaded him from doing, and instead he went off with Madge down the burn. And I, I may confess, occupied myself the whole morning, ensconced in a thick piece of scrub on the edge of the steep brae above Achnaleish, in watching through a field-glass what went on there. One could see as from a balloon almost: the street with its houses was spread like a map below.

First, then, there was a funeral﻿—the funeral, I suppose, of the mother of Maclaren, attended, I should say, by the whole village. But after that there was no dispersal of the folk to their work: it was as if it was the Sabbath; they hung about the street talking. Now one group would break up, but it would only go to swell another, and no one went either to his house or to the fields. Then, shortly before lunch, another idea occurred to me, and I ran down the hillside, appearing suddenly in the street, to put it to the test. Sandie was there, but he turned his back square on me, as did everybody else, and as I approached any group talk fell dead. But a certain movement seemed to be going on; where they stood and talked before, they now moved and were silent. Soon I saw what that meant. None would remain in the street with me: every man was going to his house.

The end house of the street was clearly the “heavenly shop” we had been told of yesterday. The door was open and a small child was looking round it as I approached, for my plan was to go in, order something, and try to get into conversation. But, while I was still a yard or two off, I saw through the glass of the door a man inside come quickly up and pull the child roughly away, banging the door and locking it. I knocked and rang, but there was no response: only from inside came the crying of the child.

===Chinese===
这一点，鉴于后来所发生的事，我很高兴地说，我们到底劝住了他没去；他便与玛吉一道顺着那条山涧（burn）下去了。而我呢——我可以承认——整个上午都蜷伏在阿赫纳利什上方那陡坡边沿上一片茂密的灌木丛里，拿一副望远镜瞧着下面村子里的一举一动。那景象几乎如同从气球上俯瞰一般：那条街连同它的房子便像一张地图似的铺在底下。

先是，有一场葬礼——我想那是麦克拉伦母亲的葬礼——据我看是全村的人都到了。可葬礼过后，人们却不散去各干各的活计：那情形仿佛是安息日；他们三三两两地聚在街上谈讲。这一圈散了，也只是去壮大另一圈，谁也不回自己的家，谁也不下田去。后来，快到午饭的时候，我又起了一个念头，便跑下山坡，蓦地出现在那条街上，要把这念头试上一试。桑迪在那里，可他把背正对着我，旁人也都如此；我一走近哪一群，那一群的谈话便戛然而止。但某种动静似乎正在进行着：方才他们站着说话之处，如今他们走动起来，并且默不作声。不久我明白了这是什么意思。谁也不肯和我一同留在街上：每一个人都往自个儿家里走。

街头尽头那栋房子，显然就是我们昨儿听说的那家「天堂似的小铺子」。门开着，一个小孩正从门后探出头来张望，我走过去——因为我打的主意是进去买点东西、设法搭上几句话。可离门口还有一两码的时候，我隔着门玻璃看见里面有个男人急步走上前，粗暴地把那孩子拉开，砰地关上门，落了锁。我敲门、按铃，都无人应声：只有那孩子从里头传出来的哭声。

===Original===
The street which had been so busy and populous was now completely empty; it might have been the street of some long-deserted place, but that thin smoke curled here and there above the houses. It was as silent, too, as the grave, but, for all that, I knew it was watching. From every house, I felt sure, I was being watched by eyes of mistrust and hate, yet no sign of living being could I see. There was to me something rather eerie about this: to know one is watched by invisible eyes is never, I suppose, quite a comfortable sensation; to know that those eyes are all hostile does not increase the sense of security. So I just climbed back up the hillside again, and from my thicket above the brae again I peered down. Once more the street was full.

Now, all this made me uneasy: the taboo had been started, and﻿—since not a soul had been near us since Sandie gave the word, whatever it was, that morning﻿—was in excellent working order. Then what was the purport of these meetings and colloquies? What else threatened? The afternoon told me.

===Chinese===
方才那样热闹、那样挤满了人的街，此刻已空空如也；它简直像一条早已荒废的古镇之街，要不是各家的屋顶上这里那里飘着一缕细细的炊烟。它也像坟墓一般寂静，可尽管如此，我知道它在窥视着我。我敢断定，从每一栋房子里，都有不信任的、怀恨的眼睛在盯着我，然而我一个活人的影子也看不见。这其中颇有某种叫人发毛的东西：知道自己被一双双看不见的眼睛盯着，这种感觉想必从来就不大舒服；知道那些眼睛全都是怀有敌意的，更不会增添几分安全感。于是我便爬回山坡上去，再从我那片陡坡上面的灌木丛里朝下窥望。街上又满了。

这一切使我颇不自在：塔布已经启动，而且——自从桑迪那天早上下了那道不知什么内容的命令之后，没有一个人靠近过我们——进行得十分顺遂。那么，这些集会和密议，所为何来？还有什么别的祸事在酝酿？下午给了我答案。

===Original===
It was about two o’clock when these meetings finally broke up, and at once the whole village left the street for the hillsides, much as if they were all returning to work. The only odd thing indeed was that no one remained behind: women and children alike went out, all in little parties of two and three. Some of these I watched rather idly, for I had formed the hasty conclusion that they were all going back to their usual employments, and saw that here a woman and girl were cutting dead bracken and heather. That was reasonable enough, and I turned my glass on others. Group after group I examined; all were doing the same thing, cutting fuel﻿ ﻿… fuel.

Then vaguely, with a sense of impossibility, a thought flashed across me; again it flashed, more vividly. This time I left my hiding-place with considerable alacrity and went to find Jim down by the burn. I told him exactly what I had seen and what I believed it meant, and I fancy that his belief in the possibility of folklore entering the domain of practical life was very considerably quickened. In any case, it was not a quarter of an hour afterwards that the chauffeur and I were going, precisely as fast as the Napier was able, along the road to Lairg. We had not told the women what my conjecture was, because we believed that, making the dispositions we were making, there was no cause for alarm-sounding. One private signal only existed between Jim within the house that night and me outside. If my conjecture proved to be correct, he was to place a light in the window of my room, which I should see returning after dark from Lairg. My ostensible reason for going was to get some local fishing-flies.

===Chinese===
大约两点钟光景，这些集会终于散了，随即全村的人都离开了街道、往山坡上去，情形颇像他们都要重新去做活。唯一古怪的是，没有一个人留下来：妇女和孩子也一样出去，都是两人一组、三人一伙的。其中几伙我颇无聊地望着，因为我草草下了结论，以为他们都不过是回去做各自的日常营生，便瞧见这一处一个女人和一个女孩在割枯死的蕨草和帚石楠。这倒合情合理，我便把望远镜转向别处。一伙又一伙，我看过去；他们全在做同一件事，割柴火......柴火。

随后，模糊地，带着一种不可思议之感，一个念头闪过我心头；它又一次闪过，愈发鲜明。这一回我相当敏捷地离开了藏身之处，下山涧去找吉姆。我把我所见的、以及我猜测它意味着什么，原原本本地告诉了他，我想，他之于民俗学可能闯进实际生活领域这一信念，是被大大地加深了。总之，不到一刻钟之后，司机和我便已沿着通往莱尔格的公路，以那辆纳皮尔所能开出的最快速度，飞驰而去了。我们没有把我的猜测告诉太太们，因为我们相信，只要按我们正在部署的去做，便没有理由拉响警报。当夜，在屋内的吉姆和在屋外的我之间，只存在一个私下的暗号。倘若我的猜测得到证实，他便在我房间的窗台上放一盏灯，我夜里从莱尔格赶回来时便可看见。我此行的明面理由，是要去买几枚本地的假蝇钓钩。

===Original===
As we flowed﻿—there is no other word for the movement of these big cars but that﻿—over the road to Lairg, I ran over everything in my mind. I felt no doubt whatever that all the brushwood and kindling I had seen being gathered in was to be piled after nightfall round our walls and set on fire. This certainly would not be done till after dark; indeed, we both felt sure that it would not be done till it was supposed that we were all abed. It remained to see whether the police at Lairg agreed with my conjecture, and it was to ascertain this that I was now flowing there.

I told my story to the chief constable as soon as I got there, omitting nothing and, I think, exaggerating nothing. His face got graver and graver as I proceeded.

“Yes, sir, you did right to come,” he said. “The folk at Achnaleish are the dourest and the most savage in all Scotland. You’ll have to give up this hare-hunting, though, whatever,” he added.

He rang up his telephone.

“I’ll get five men,” he said, “and I’ll be with you in ten minutes.”

===Chinese===
我们就这样滑行着——这些大车的行进，除了「滑行」二字，没有别的词可形容——驰往莱尔格的公路上，我把一切又在脑中过了一遍。我毫不怀疑，我所见到的、被搜集起来的那些灌木和引火物，入夜之后便要堆到我们宅子的四墙根下，付之一炬。此事当然要等到天黑之后才会进行；说实在的，我们俩都深信，要等到他们以为我们都已上床就寝之时才会进行。剩下的便是看莱尔格的警察是否赞同我的猜测，而我此刻「滑行」到那里去，正是为了确证这一点。

我一到便把事情的经过告诉了警察局长，一桩也没漏，我想也没有一桩夸大。我讲下去的时候，他的脸色愈发凝重起来。

「是，先生，您来报案报得对，」他说，「阿赫纳利什那一带的百姓，是全苏格兰最阴鸷、最凶悍的。不过，打野兔这件事，您是怎么也得放手的了。」他又道。

他拨通了电话。

「我调五个人，」他说，「十分钟后我跟您一起动身。」

===Original===
Our plan of campaign was simple. We were to leave the car well out of sight of Achnaleish, and﻿—supposing the signal was in my window﻿—steal up from all sides to command the house from every direction. It would not be difficult to make our way unseen through the plantations that ran up close to the house, and hidden at their margins we could see whether the brushwood and heather was piled up round the lodge. There we should wait to see if anybody attempted to fire it. That somebody, whenever he showed his light, would be instantly covered by a rifle and challenged.

It was about ten when we dismounted and stalked our way up to the house. The light burned in my window; all else was quiet. Personally, I was unarmed, and so, when I had planted the men in places of advantageous concealment round the house, my work was over. Then I returned to Sergeant Duncan, the chief constable, at the corner of the hedge by the garden, and waited.

How long we waited I do not know, but it seemed as if aeons slipped by over us. Now and then an owl would hoot, now and then a rabbit ran out from cover and nibbled the short sweet grass of the lawn. The night was thickly overcast with clouds, and the house seemed no more than a black blot, with slits of light where windows were lit within. By and by even these slits of illumination were extinguished, and other lights appeared in the top story. After a while they, too, vanished; no sign of life appeared on the quiet house. Then suddenly the end came: I heard a foot grate on the gravel; I saw the gleam of a lantern, and heard Duncan’s voice.

“Man,” he shouted, “if you move hand or foot I fire. My rifle-bead is dead on you.”

Then I blew the whistle; the others ran up, and in less than a minute it was all over. The man we closed in on was Maclaren.

“They killed my mither with that hell-carriage,” he said, “as she juist sat on the road, puir body, who had niver hurt them.”

And that seemed to him an excellent reason for attempting to burn us all to death.

===Chinese===
我们的作战方案很简单。把汽车停在阿赫纳利什看不见的地方，然后——倘若我窗上的暗号亮着——从四面八方悄悄摸上去，把宅子从各个方向控制起来。要不被察觉地穿过那几片一直延伸到宅子跟前的人造林，并不困难；藏在林缘，我们便可看清猎墅四周是否堆满了灌木和帚石楠。我们便在那里守着，看是否有人来点火。那个人，只要他一露出灯火，立刻便会被步枪瞄准，并遭大声喝止。

大约十点钟，我们下了车，悄悄地摸到宅子跟前。那盏灯在我窗上亮着；其余一切寂然。我个人是手无寸铁的，因此，等我把那几个警员一一安置到宅子四周便于隐蔽的有利位置上之后，我的活儿便完了。于是我回到花园边树篱拐角处的邓肯巡官（Sergeant Duncan）——即那位警察局长——身旁，等着。

我们等了多久，我不知道，只觉得仿佛一个个世代从我们身上滑了过去。时而有一只猫头鹰叫上一两声，时而有一只兔子从藏身处蹿出来啃那草坪上短而甜的青草。夜空浓云密布，那宅子不过是黑暗中一块墨迹，只在窗内有灯之处透出几线光。渐渐地连这几线光也熄了，三楼上又亮起了别的灯。过了一会儿，那些灯也熄了；这座寂静的宅子上再无生命的迹象。然后，突然地，结局来了：我听见一只脚在砾石上碾了一下；我看见一只灯笼一闪，听见了邓肯的声音。

「老兄，」他喊道，「你敢动一动手、动一动脚，我就开枪。我的枪星正正地压在你身上。」

然后我吹响了哨子；其余的人跑了上来，不出一分钟，一切都结束了。我们围住的那个人是麦克拉伦。

「他们用那辆地狱般的马车，杀了我母亲，」他说，「她不过是坐在路边罢了，可怜的人，从未害过他们分毫。」

而这件事，在他看来，已是把我们统统烧死的充足理由。

===Original===
But it took time to get into the house: their preparations had been singularly workmanlike, for every window and door on the ground floor was wired up.

Now, we had Achnaleish for two months, but we had no wish to be burned or otherwise murdered. What we wanted was not a prosecution of our head-keeper, but peace, the necessaries of life, and beaters. For that we were willing to shoot no hares, and release Maclaren. An hour’s conclave next morning settled these things; the ensuing two months were most enjoyable, and relations were the friendliest.

But if anybody wants to test how far what Jim still calls cock-and-bull stories can enter into practical life, I should suggest to him to go a-shooting hares at Achnaleish.

===Chinese===
可要进宅子却花了不少工夫：他们的准备工作极为在行——底楼每一扇窗、每一道门都用铁丝拧死了。

我们租下了阿赫纳利什两个月，可并不愿被烧死、或以别的方式被谋害。我们所求的，不是起诉我们的总看守，而是太平、日用必需品，以及轰兽人。为此我们愿意不再打野兔，并释放麦克拉伦。第二天早上一个钟头的会谈便把这些事定了下来；接下来的两个月极是愉快，双方的关系最为融洽。

可倘若有人想要试探一番，被吉姆至今称作天方夜谭的那些事情，究竟能在多大程度上闯进实际生活里来，我会建议他到阿赫纳利什去打一回野兔。

## The Terror by Night / 夜之恐惧

===Original===
The transference of emotion is a phenomenon so common, so constantly witnessed, that mankind in general have long ceased to be conscious of its existence, as a thing worth our wonder or consideration, regarding it as being as natural and commonplace as the transference of things that act by the ascertained laws of matter. Nobody, for instance, is surprised, if, when the room is too hot, the opening of a window causes the cold fresh air of outside to be transferred into the room, and in the same way no one is surprised when into the same room, perhaps, which we will imagine as being peopled with dull and gloomy persons, there enters someone of fresh and sunny mind, who instantly brings into the stuffy mental atmosphere a change analogous to that of the opened windows. Exactly how this infection is conveyed we do not know; considering the wireless wonders (that act by material laws) which are already beginning to lose their wonder now that we have our newspaper brought as a matter of course every morning in mid-Atlantic, it would not perhaps be rash to conjecture that in some subtle and occult way the transference of emotion is in reality material too. Certainly (to take another instance) the sight of definitely material things, like writing on a page, conveys emotion apparently direct to our minds, as when our pleasure or pity is stirred by a book, and it is therefore possible that mind may act on mind by means as material as that.

Occasionally, however, we come across phenomena, which, though they may easily be as material as any of these things, are rarer, and therefore more astounding. Some people call them ghosts, some conjuring tricks, and some nonsense. It seems simpler to group them under the head of transferred emotions, and they may appeal to any of the senses. Some ghosts are seen, some heard, some felt, and though I know of no instance of a ghost being tasted, yet it will seem in the following pages that these occult phenomenon may appeal at any rate to the senses that perceive heat, cold, or smell. For, to take the analogy of wireless telegraphy, we are all of us probably “receivers” to some extent, and catch now and then a message or part of a message that the eternal waves of emotion are ceaselessly shouting aloud to those who have ears to hear, and materializing themselves for those who have eyes to see. Not being, as a rule, perfectly tuned, we grasp but pieces and fragments of such messages, a few coherent words it may be, or a few words which seem to have no sense. The following story, however, to my mind, is interesting, because it shows how different pieces of what no doubt was one message were received and recorded by several different people simultaneously. Ten years have elapsed since the events recorded took place, but they were written down at the time.

===Chinese===
情感的传递（the transference of emotion）是一种如此寻常、如此屡见不鲜的现象，以至于世人早已不再意识到它的存在，不再觉得它值得我们惊奇或思量，只把它看得和那些依已知物质法则运作之物的传递一样自然、一样寻常。譬如，屋里太热时，打开一扇窗便能使外面的清冽冷空气传进屋里，谁也不觉得奇怪；同样，姑且设想这间屋子里坐满了沉闷阴郁的人，这时走进来一位心境明快、阳光灿烂的人，他立时便为这沉闷的精神氛围带来了一种改变，其性质正与那敞开的窗户相仿，谁也不会对此觉得奇怪。这种感染究竟是怎样传递的，我们并不清楚；想想无线电的种种奇迹（那也是依物质法则运作的）——如今我们身在大西洋中部，每天早晨也理所当然地能读到送来的报纸，那些奇迹便已开始失去其奇迹的意味了——那么，揣想情感的传递在某种微妙而玄秘的意义上其实也是物质的，也许并非冒昧之举。当然（再举一例），看那分明是物质的东西，比如一页纸上的文字，似乎也能把情感直接传到我们心里，比如一本书能激起我们的喜悦或怜悯；因此，心灵与心灵之间，未尝不可以凭借同样物质的手段彼此作用。

然而，我们偶尔也会遇见一些现象，它们即便同样可能是物质的，却更为罕见，因而也更令人骇异。有人称之为鬼魂，有人称之为戏法，又有人称之为无稽之谈。把它们归到「传递的情感」这一名目下来看，似乎要简单些；而它们可以诉诸任何一种感官。有些鬼是被看见的，有些是被听见的，有些是被感觉到的；我虽不曾听说过有谁尝过鬼的滋味，但在下文里将会看到，这些玄秘的现象至少可以诉诸那些感知冷、热或气味的感官。因为，拿无线电报作比，我们大家多半在某种程度上都是「接收器」，不时捕捉到一道讯息、或一道讯息的某一部分——那永恒的情感之波一刻不停地向有耳能听者高声呼喊，向有目能视者凝成形体。由于通常调谐得并不完美，我们只能抓到这些讯息的零碎片断，也许是几个连贯的字，也许是几个看似毫无意义的字。然而在我看来，下面这则故事颇有意思，因为它显示了一道无疑本是同一整体的讯息，其各个不同的片段是如何在同一个时刻被几个不同的人接收并记录下来的。所记之事距今已有十年，但当时便已一一笔录在案。

===Original===
Jack Lorimer and I were very old friends before he married, and his marriage to a first cousin of mine did not make, as so often happens, a slackening in our intimacy. Within a few months after, it was found out that his wife had consumption, and, without any loss of time, she was sent off to Davos, with her sister to look after her. The disease had evidently been detected at a very early stage, and there was excellent ground for hoping that with proper care and strict regime she would be cured by the life-giving frosts of that wonderful valley.

The two had gone out in the November of which I am speaking, and Jack and I joined them for a month at Christmas, and found that week after week she was steadily and quickly gaining ground. We had to be back in town by the end of January, but it was settled that Ida should remain out with her sister for a week or two more. They both, I remember, came down to the station to see us off, and I am not likely to forget the last words that passed:

“Oh, don’t look so woebegone Jack,” his wife had said; “you’ll see me again before long.”

Then the fussy little mountain engine squeaked, as a puppy squeaks when its toe is trodden on, and we puffed our way up the pass.

London was in its usual desperate February plight when we got back, full of fogs and stillborn frosts that seemed to produce a cold far more bitter than the piercing temperature of those sunny altitudes from which we had come. We both, I think, felt rather lonely, and even before we had got to our journey’s end we had settled that for the present it was ridiculous that we should keep open two houses when one would suffice, and would also be far more cheerful for us both. So, as we both lived in almost identical houses in the same street in Chelsea, we decided to “toss,” live in the house which the coin indicated (heads mine, tails his) share expenses, attempt to let the other house, and, if successful, share the proceeds. A French five-franc piece of the second empire told us it was “heads.”

===Chinese===
杰克·洛里默（Jack Lorimer）和我自他婚前便是极老的朋友，他娶了我的一个表妹，这桩婚事并未像常有的情形那样使我们的情分疏淡下来。婚后不出几个月，他妻子便被查出患有肺痨，于是毫不耽搁地被送往达沃斯（Davos），由她妹妹照看她。病显然是在极早的阶段便被察觉的，因而大可指望：只要悉心照料、严守起居，她必能被那座奇妙山谷里赐予生命的霜寒所治愈。

她们二人是在我所说的那年十一月动身去的，圣诞节期间，杰克和我去那儿陪了她们一个月，眼看她一周接一周地稳步而迅速地好转起来。我们一月底之前必须回到城里，但议定艾达（Ida）和她妹妹再留在外头一两个星期。我记得她们俩都下到火车站来送我们，而临别最后那几句话，我大概是不会忘记的：

「哦，别这么一副愁眉苦脸的样子，杰克，」他妻子说，「你不久就会再见到我的。」

随后那辆吵吵嚷嚷的小小山间机车吱地一叫，活像一只被人踩了脚趾的小狗，我们便噗噗地翻山越岭而去。

我们回到伦敦时，正赶上它二月里惯常的那副凄惨光景：到处是大雾，还有那胎死腹中的霜寒，似乎酿出了一种比我们方才离开的那些阳光灿烂的高海拔地区那砭人肌骨的气温还要苦寒得多的冷。我们俩，我想，都颇觉孤寂，甚至还没到旅程终点，便已议定：眼下我们各自撑着两处宅子实属荒唐，合在一处便尽够了，对我们俩也要快活得多。于是，既然我们俩在切尔西（Chelsea）同一条街上住着几乎一模一样的两所房子，我们便决定「掷钱」，住在钱币所指的那一所（正面归我，反面归他），共摊开销，把另一所设法租出去，若租成了，租金也平分。一枚法兰西第二帝国时期的五法郎银币告诉我们：是「正面」。

===Original===
We had been back some ten days, receiving every day the most excellent accounts from Davos, when, first on him, then on me, there descended like some tropical storm, a feeling of indefinable fear. Very possibly this sense of apprehension (for there is nothing in the world so virulently infectious) reached me through him: on the other hand both these attacks of vague foreboding may have come from the same source. But it is true that it did not attack me till he spoke of it, so the possibility perhaps inclines to my having caught it from him. He spoke of it first, I remember, one evening when we had met for a good night talk, after having come back from separate houses where we had dined.

“I have felt most awfully down all day,” he said; “and just after receiving this splendid account from Daisy, I can’t think what is the matter.”

He poured himself out some whisky and soda as he spoke.

“Oh, touch of liver,” I said. “I shouldn’t drink that if I were you. Give it me instead.”

“I was never better in my life,” he said.

I was opening letters, as we talked, and came across one from the house agent, which, with trembling eagerness I read.

“Hurrah,” I cried, “offer of five guas—why can’t he write it in proper English—five guineas a week till Easter for number 31. We shall roll in guineas!”

“Oh, but I can’t stop here till Easter,” he said.

“I don’t see why not. Nor by the way does Daisy. I heard from her this morning, and she told me to persuade you to stop. That’s to say, if you like. It really is more cheerful for you here. I forgot, you were telling me something.”

The glorious news about the weekly guineas did not cheer him up in the least.

“Thanks awfully. Of course I’ll stop.”

He moved up and down the room once or twice.

“No, it’s not me that is wrong,” he said, “it’s It, whatever It is. The terror by night.”

“Which you are commanded not to be afraid of,” I remarked.

“I know: it’s easy commanding. I’m frightened: something’s coming.”

“Five guineas a week are coming,” I said. “I shan’t sit up and be infected by your fears. All that matters, Davos, is going as well as it can. What was the last report? Incredibly better. Take that to bed with you.”

===Chinese===
我们回来大约十天，天天都收到达沃斯寄来最叫人放心的佳音，这时，先是他，接着是我，像一场热带的暴风雨一般，袭来了一阵无法名状的恐惧。这种忧惧之感（世上再没有比它传染得更猛烈的东西了）很可能是从他那里传给我的：但另一方面，我们这两场隐隐的预感之袭也可能来自同一个源头。不过，他确是先说起、它才找上我的，所以可能性也许偏向我那一端——我是从他那儿染上的。我记得他头一回提起它，是在某天傍晚，我们各自在外头宅子里吃了饭，回来碰在一起作临睡前一叙的时候。

「我一整天都提不起劲，糟透了，」他说，「刚收到黛西寄来这么好的一封信，我竟是这样，真想不出是哪儿不对。」

他一边说，一边给自己斟了一杯威士忌苏打。

「哦，有点儿肝火罢，」我说，「换了是我，就不喝这个。给我好了。」

「我这辈子从没这么好过。」他说。

我们一边谈着，我一边拆信，翻出一封房屋经手人来的信，我便哆嗦着、迫不及待地读了起来。

「好哇，」我叫道，「出价五几尼——他干吗不用像样的英文写——五几尼一星期，租到复活节，要的是 31 号那所。我们要发几尼财啦！」

「哦，可我在这儿待不到复活节呀。」他说。

「我看不出有什么待不到的。黛西也这么看呢。今早我接到她的信，她让我劝你留下。当然，这是说，要是你愿意。你在这儿到底要快活些。我倒忘了，你方才要跟我说什么来着。」

每周几尼进账这桩大好消息，丝毫没能叫他宽心。

「多谢了。我当然留下。」

他在屋里来回踱了一两趟。

「不，不是我自己不对劲，」他说，「是它，不管它是什么。夜之恐惧。」

「《诗篇》里可吩咐你不必怕它呢。」我说。

「我知道：吩咐是容易的。我怕：有什么事要来了。」

「五几尼一星期的事要来了，」我说，「我可不要熬夜来给你的恐惧染上。要紧的事——达沃斯那边——好得不能再好了。上回的报告怎么说？好得出奇。把这个带去睡觉罢。」

===Original===
The infection—if infection it was—did not take hold of me then, for I remember going to sleep feeling quite cheerful, but I awoke in some dark still hour and It, the terror by night, had come while I slept. Fear and misgiving, blind, unreasonable, and paralysing, had taken and gripped me. What was it? Just as by an aneroid we can foretell the approach of storm, so by this sinking of the spirit, unlike anything I had ever felt before, I felt sure that disaster of some sort was presaged.

Jack saw it at once when we met at breakfast next morning, in the brown haggard light of a foggy day, not dark enough for candles, but dismal beyond all telling.

“So it has come to you too,” he said.

And I had not even the fighting-power left to tell him that I was merely slightly unwell. Besides, never in my life had I felt better.

All next day, all the day after that fear lay like a black cloak over my mind; I did not know what I dreaded, but it was something very acute, something that was very near. It was coming nearer every moment, spreading like a pall of clouds over the sky; but on the third day, after miserably cowering under it, I suppose some sort of courage came back to me: either this was pure imagination, some trick of disordered nerves or whatnot, in which case we were both “disquieting ourselves in vain,” or from the immeasurable waves of emotion that beat upon the minds of men, something within both of us had caught a current, a pressure. In either case it was infinitely better to try, however ineffectively, to stand up against it. For these two days I had neither worked nor played; I had only shrunk and shuddered; I planned for myself a busy day, with diversion for us both in the evening.

“We will dine early,” I said, “and go to the Man from Blankley’s. I have already asked Philip to come, and he is coming, and I have telephoned for tickets. Dinner at seven.”

Philip, I may remark, is an old friend of ours, neighbour in this street, and by profession a much-respected doctor.

Jack laid down his paper.

“Yes, I expect you’re right,” he said. “It’s no use doing nothing, it doesn’t help things. Did you sleep well?”

“Yes, beautifully,” I said rather snappishly, for I was all on edge with the added burden of an almost sleepless night.

“I wish I had,” said he.

This would not do at all.

“We have got to play up!” I said. “Here are we two strong and stalwart persons, with as much cause for satisfaction with life as any you can mention, letting ourselves behave like worms. Our fear may be over things imaginary or over things that are real, but it is the fact of being afraid that is so despicable. There is nothing in the world to fear except fear. You know that as well as I do. Now let’s read our papers with interest. Which do you back, Mr. Druce, or the Duke of Portland, or the *Times* Book Club?”

That day, therefore, passed very busily for me; and there were enough events moving in front of that black background, which I was conscious was there all the time, to enable me to keep my eyes away from it, and I was detained rather late at the office, and had to drive back to Chelsea, in order to be in time to dress for dinner, instead of walking back as I had intended.

Then the message, which for these three days, had been twittering in our minds, the receivers, just making them quiver and rattle came through.

===Chinese===
那感染——倘若它真是感染——当时并没有缠上我，因为我记得上床睡觉时心情还相当轻快；可我在某个幽暗寂静的时辰醒来，它——那夜之恐惧——已趁我睡着时来了。恐惧与忧疑，盲目的、无端的、使人瘫痪的，已经攫住了我、扼住了我。这是什么？正如凭一只无液气压表便可预知风暴将至，凭这种我前所未尝的心神的下沉，我也确信：必有某种灾祸已被预示了出来。

第二天早晨我们在早餐桌上碰面时，杰克一眼便看了出来——那是一个雾天的褐色、憔悴的天光里，暗得还不够点蜡烛，却阴郁得无以复加。

「原来也找上你了。」他说。

而我连一点还击的气力都没剩下，没能告诉他我只是略感不适。况且，我这辈子从没觉得身子更好过。

第二天一整天、第三天一整天，那恐惧像一件黑色的斗篷罩在我心上；我不知道自己怕的是什么，只知那是某种极锐利的东西，某种已极近的东西。它每一刻都在逼近，像一片殡殓的云在天上铺展开来；可到了第三天，在凄惨地蜷伏于它之下以后，我想我是鼓起了某种勇气：要么这纯粹是臆想，是紊乱的神经之类的什么花招，那样的话，我们俩便是「徒然自扰」；要么，从那拍击着人心的无垠的情感波涛里，我们两人心底的某种东西截住了一股潮流、一股压力。无论哪一种，奋力地、哪怕是徒劳地站起来抵挡它，都要好上无数倍。这两天里我既没做事，也没消遣；我只是蜷缩着、战栗着；我给自己安排了一个忙碌的白昼，晚上还要给我们俩寻些消遣。

「我们早点吃晚饭，」我说，「去看《来自布兰克利的来客》。我已经请了菲利普，他会来，我也已经打电话订了票。七点开饭。」

菲利普（Philip），容我补一句，是我们的老朋友，就住在这条街上，是个颇受人敬重的医生。

杰克放下了报纸。

「是，我想你说得对，」他说，「无所事事没有用，于事无补。你睡得好吗？」

「好，好极了。」我颇为暴躁地说，因为我整夜几乎没睡，又添了这副担子，神经全绷紧了。

「我要是也睡好了就好啦。」他说。

这可不行。

「我们得打起精神来！」我说，「咱们俩这么两个壮健结实的人，对人生有那么多的可以满足的理由，不亚于你能举出的任何人，却由着自己像虫子一样行事。我们所怕的，也许是虚妄之事，也许是真实之事，可真正可鄙的，是害怕这一桩事实本身。世上无可畏惧之物，唯有恐惧。这一点你和我一样清楚。现在咱们打起精神来读报罢。你押哪一个，德鲁斯先生，还是波特兰公爵，还是《泰晤士报》读书会？」

于是那天我过得颇为忙碌；在那片黑色背景前头——我始终意识到它在那里——有足够多的事件在流转，足以让我把目光从它身上移开；我在事务所被耽搁得颇晚，只好赶马车回切尔西，好来得及换赴宴的衣裳，没如我原打算的那样走回去。

这时，那道三日来一直在我们这些接收器——我们的心里——啁啾着，只叫它们微微颤动、咯咯作响的讯息，通了过来。

---

===Original===
I found Jack already dressed, since it was within a minute or two of seven when I got in, and sitting in the drawing-room. The day had been warm and muggy, but when I looked in on the way up to my room, it seemed to me to have grown suddenly and bitterly cold, not with the dampness of English frost, but with the clear and stinging exhilaration of such days as we had recently spent in Switzerland. Fire was laid in the grate but not lit, and I went down on my knees on the hearthrug to light it.

“Why, it’s freezing in here,” I said. “What donkeys servants are! It never occurs to them that you want fires in cold weather, and no fires in hot weather.”

“Oh, for heaven’s sake don’t light the fire,” said he, “it’s the warmest muggiest evening I ever remember.”

I stared at him in astonishment. My hands were shaking with the cold. He saw this.

“Why, you are shivering!” he said. “Have you caught a chill? But as to the room being cold let us look at the thermometer.”

There was one on the writing-table.

“Sixty-five,” he said.

There was no disputing that, nor did I want to, for at that moment, it suddenly struck us, dimly and distantly that It was “coming through.” I felt it like some curious internal vibration.

“Hot or cold, I must go and dress,” I said.

Still shivering, but feeling as if I was breathing some rarefied exhilarating air, I went up to my room. My clothes were already laid out, but, by an oversight, no hot water had been brought up, and I rang for my man. He came up almost at once, but he looked scared, or, to my already-startled senses, he appeared so.

“What’s the matter?” I asked.

“Nothing, sir,” he said, and he could hardly articulate the words. “I thought you rang.”

“Yes. Hot water. But what’s the matter?”

He shifted from one foot to the other.

“I thought I saw a lady on the stairs,” he said, “coming up close behind me. And the front door bell hadn’t rung that I heard.”

“Where did you think you saw her?” I asked.

“On the stairs. Then on the landing outside the drawing-room door, sir,” he said. “She stood there as if she didn’t know whether to go in or not.”

“One—one of the servants,” I said. But again I felt that It was coming through.

“No, sir. It was none of the servants,” he said.

“Who was it then?”

“Couldn’t see distinctly sir, it was dim-like. But I thought it was Mrs. Lorimer.”

“Oh, go and get me some hot water,” I said.

But he lingered; he was quite clearly frightened.

===Chinese===
我到家时离七点只差一两分钟，杰克已经穿戴整齐，正坐在客厅里。这一日原本又暖又闷，可我上楼回房时朝客厅里一望，只觉屋子里骤然冷得刺骨，那冷不是英国霜寒的那股潮气，而是我们在瑞士最近所过的那种日子里那种清冽、砭人、提神的冷。炉栅里生好了火却没点着，我便跪在炉前毡上去点火。

「哎哟，这儿冷得结冰似的，」我说，「仆人真是蠢驴！天冷时你想生火他们想不到，天热时你不想生火他们也想不到。」

「哦，看在老天爷份上，别点火，」他说，「这是我所记得的最暖最闷的一个晚上。」

我惊异地瞪着他。我的手正冻得发抖。他看见了。

「哎哟，你在打哆嗦！」他说，「你着凉了吗？至于说屋里冷，咱们来看看温度计罢。」

书桌上正有一只。

「六十五度。」他说。

这一点无可争辩，我也不想争辩，因为就在那一刻，我们隐约而遥遥地忽然觉察：它要「过来了」。我像感到某种古怪的内在震颤一般地感到了它。

「管它冷还是热，我得去换衣裳了。」我说。

我仍哆嗦着，却仿佛呼吸着某种稀薄而提神的空气，上楼回了我的房间。我的衣裳已铺摆好了，可是一时疏忽，热水没送上楼来，我便按铃叫我的贴身男仆。他几乎立刻就上来了，可他一脸惊恐——至少在我那早已受惊的感官看来是如此。

「怎么啦？」我问。

「没什么，先生，」他说，几乎说不出句囫囵话，「我以为您按铃了。」

「是的。要热水。可怎么啦？」

他把重心从一只脚换到另一只脚。

「我好像在楼梯上看见一位太太，」他说，「紧紧跟在我身后上来。可前门的铃并没响，我没听见。」

「你以为你在哪儿看见她的？」我问。

「在楼梯上。后来在客厅门外那块楼梯口，先生，」他说，「她站在那里，好像不知该进去还是不该进去。」

「是——是一个仆人罢。」我说。但我又感到它要过来了。

「不是，先生。不是任何一个仆人。」他说。

「那又是谁呢？」

「看不大真切，先生，影影绰绰的。可我觉得像是洛里默太太。」

「哦，去给我弄点热水来罢。」我说。

可他磨蹭着不走；他分明是吓坏了。

===Original===
At this moment the front-door bell rang. It was just seven, and already Philip had come with brutal punctuality while I was not yet half-dressed.

“That’s Dr. Enderly,” I said. “Perhaps if he is on the stairs you may be able to pass the place where you saw the lady.”

Then quite suddenly there rang through the house a scream, so terrible, so appalling in its agony and supreme terror, that I simply stood still and shuddered, unable to move. Then by an effort so violent that I felt as if something must break, I recalled the power of motion, and ran downstairs, my man at my heels, to meet Philip who was running up from the ground floor. He had heard it too.

“What’s the matter?” he said. “What was that?”

===Chinese===
正在这时，前门的铃响了。刚到七点，菲利普已以毫不通融的准时赶到，而我衣服还没穿到一半。

「是恩德利医生。」我说，「也许他这会儿正在楼梯上，你便敢从你看见那位太太的地方走过去了罢。」

接着，屋子里骤然响起了一声尖叫，那尖叫在其苦痛与极致的恐怖上如此骇人、如此可怖，我只木然地立着、浑身打颤，动弹不得。随后，凭一股猛烈得我以为身上必有某处要崩断的努力，我才重新唤回了行动的能力，奔下楼去，我的男仆紧随我身后，迎面遇上正从底层跑上来的菲利普。他也听见了。

「怎么啦？」他说，「那是什么？」

===Original===
Together we went into the drawing-room, Jack was lying in front of the fireplace, with the chair in which he had been sitting a few minutes before overturned. Philip went straight to him and bent over him, tearing open his white shirt.

“Open all the windows,” he said, “the place reeks.”

We flung open the windows, and there poured in, so it seemed to me, a stream of hot air into the bitter cold. Eventually Philip got up.

“He is dead,” he said. “Keep the windows open. The place is still thick with chloroform.”

Gradually to my sense the room got warmer, to Philip’s the drug-laden atmosphere dispersed. But neither my servant nor I had smelt anything at all.

A couple of hours later there came a telegram from Davos for me. It was to tell me to break the news of Daisy’s death to Jack, and was sent by her sister. She supposed he would come out immediately. But he had been gone two hours now.

I left for Davos next day, and learned what had happened. Daisy had been suffering for three days from a little abscess which had to be opened, and, though the operation was of the slightest, she had been so nervous about it that the doctor gave her chloroform. She made a good recovery from the anaesthetic, but an hour later had a sudden attack of syncope, and had died that night at a few minutes before eight, by central European time, corresponding to seven in English time. She had insisted that Jack should be told nothing about this little operation till it was over, since the matter was quite unconnected with her general health, and she did not wish to cause him needless anxiety.

And there the story ends. To my servant there came the sight of a woman outside the drawing-room door, where Jack was, hesitating about her entrance, at the moment when Daisy’s soul hovered between the two worlds; to me there came—I do not think it is fanciful to suppose this—the keen exhilarating cold of Davos; to Philip there came the fumes of chloroform. And to Jack, I must suppose, came his wife. So he joined her.

===Chinese===
我们一起走进客厅，杰克躺在壁炉前面，几分钟前他还坐着的那张椅子翻在一旁。菲利普径直走到他跟前，俯下身去，撕开他的白衬衣。

「把所有的窗子都打开，」他说，「这屋里味儿重得很。」

我们敞开窗子，在我看来，便有一股热气涌进了那砭骨的寒冷里。末了菲利普直起身来。

「他死了，」他说，「让窗子开着。这屋里仍是满满的氯仿味。」

渐渐地，在我感觉里屋子暖和起来；在菲利普感觉里，那弥漫着药味的空气散去了。可是我和我的男仆，谁都一点儿也没闻到什么。

两小时后，来了一份从达沃斯打给我的电报。是要我把黛西的死讯告知杰克，由她妹妹拍来。她料想他必会立刻赶去。可他已走了两个钟头了。

第二天我动身去达沃斯，得知了事情的经过。黛西三天来患着一个小脓肿，须得开刀，虽然手术极轻，她却为此十分紧张，医生便给她施了氯仿。她从麻醉中恢复得很好，可一小时后突然晕厥，当夜在欧洲中部时间八点差几分——换作英国时间即七点——去世。她坚持，在这场小手术做完之前，什么也不要告诉杰克，因为这事和她总体健康毫不相干，她也不愿叫他无端操心。

故事到此便告结束。在我的男仆，是看见了客厅门外——杰克所在之处——一位踌躇着是否进门的女子，那正是黛西的灵魂徘徊于两个世界之间的时刻；在我，我并不以为这是多情之想——是达沃斯那砭骨提神的寒意传来了；在菲利普，是氯仿的气味传来了。而在杰克，我不得不设想，是他妻子来了。于是他追随她而去了。

## The Thing in the Hall / 厅中之物

===Original===
The following pages are the account given me by Dr. Assheton of the Thing in the Hall. I took notes, as copious as my quickness of hand allowed me, from his dictation, and subsequently read to him this narrative in its transcribed and connected form. This was on the day before his death, which indeed probably occurred within an hour after I had left him, and, as readers of inquests and such atrocious literature may remember, I had to give evidence before the coroner’s jury. Only a week before Dr. Assheton had to give similar evidence, but as a medical expert, with regard to the death of his friend, Louis Fielder, which occurred in a manner identical with his own. As a specialist, he said he believed that his friend had committed suicide while of unsound mind, and the verdict was brought in accordingly. But in the inquest held over Dr. Assheton’s body, though the verdict eventually returned was the same, there was more room for doubt.

For I was bound to state that only shortly before his death, I read what follows to him; that he corrected me with extreme precision on a few points of detail, that he seemed perfectly himself, and that at the end he used these words:

“I am quite certain as a brain specialist that I am completely sane, and that these things happened not merely in my imagination, but in the external world. If I had to give evidence again about poor Louis, I should be compelled to take a different line. Please put that down at the end of your account, or at the beginning, if it arranges itself better so.”

There will be a few words I must add at the end of this story, and a few words of explanation must precede it. Briefly, they are these.

Francis Assheton and Louis Fielder were up at Cambridge together, and there formed the friendship that lasted nearly till their death. In general attributes no two men could have been less alike, for while Dr. Assheton had become at the age of thirty-five the first and final authority on his subject, which was the functions and diseases of the brain, Louis Fielder at the same age was still on the threshold of achievement. Assheton, apparently without any brilliance at all, had by careful and incessant work arrived at the top of his profession, while Fielder, brilliant at school, brilliant at college and brilliant ever afterwards, had never done anything. He was too eager, so it seemed to his friends, to set about the dreary work of patient investigation and logical deductions; he was forever guessing and prying, and striking out luminous ideas, which he left burning, so to speak, to illumine the work of others. But at bottom, the two men had this compelling interest in common, namely, an insatiable curiosity after the unknown, perhaps the most potent bond yet devised between the solitary units that make up the race of man. Both—till the end—were absolutely fearless, and Dr. Assheton would sit by the bedside of the man stricken with bubonic plague to note the gradual surge of the tide of disease to the reasoning faculty with the same absorption as Fielder would study X-rays one week, flying machines the next, and spiritualism the third. The rest of the story, I think, explains itself—or does not quite do so. This, anyhow, is what I read to Dr. Assheton, being the connected narrative of what he had himself told me. It is he, of course, who speaks.

===Chinese===
以下几页，是阿什顿医生（Dr. Assheton）向我讲述的关于「厅中之物」的记述。我凭手快所能，从他的口述中尽可能详尽地记下笔记，随后将这份记述整理成连贯的文字，又读给他听。那是在他去世的前一天——事实上，他大约在我离开他之后不到一个钟头便死去了——而且，凡是读惯了验尸报道之类劣等文字的读者或许还记得，我不得不在死因陪审团前作证。就在一周之前，阿什顿医生还不得不就他朋友路易斯·菲尔德（Louis Fielder）之死，以医学专家的身份提供类似的证词；而他那位朋友的死法，与他本人的死法如出一辙。他以专家的身份表示，他认为他的朋友是在精神失常的状态下自尽的，陪审团据此作出了裁定。但在就阿什顿医生尸体所进行的验尸庭审中，尽管最终作出的裁定相同，却留下了更多可疑之处。

因为我必须声明：就在他去世前不久，我把下文读给他听过；他就若干细节极精确地纠正了我；他看上去神智完全清醒；末了他用了这样几句话：

「作为一名脑科专家，我十分确信自己神智完全健全，而这些事并非仅仅发生在我的想象之中，它们发生在外部世界里。倘若要我重新就可怜的路易斯作证，我将不得不换一种说法。请把这段话附在你这篇记述的末尾，或者放在开头——要是这样安排更顺当的话。」

在这篇故事的末尾，我还得再添上几句话；而在它之前，也必须有几句说明。简言之，说明如下。

弗朗西斯·阿什顿（Francis Assheton）与路易斯·菲尔德当年一同在剑桥（Cambridge）读书，在那里结下了几乎延续到他们去世的友谊。就一般的才具而论，再没有哪两个人比他们更不相像的了：阿什顿在三十五岁上，已成为他那一门——即大脑的功能与疾病——首屈一指、一言九鼎的权威；而路易斯·菲尔德到了同一年纪，却仍滞留在成就的门槛之外。阿什顿显然并无任何过人的天分，单凭勤谨不辍的工作攀上了他这一行的巅峰；菲尔德则不然，求学时才华横溢，大学里才华横溢，此后也一直才华横溢，却从未做成过任何一件事。在朋友们看来，他太不肯安下心去做那点埋头苦干、耐心求证、逻辑推演的乏味功夫；他总是在猜测、在窥探，在迸发出灵光乍现的主意，而这些主意——可以这么说——他便任其燃着，丢下不管，由它们去照亮别人的工作。但在骨子里，这两人却有同一种压倒一切的爱好，那便是对未知之物无法餍足的好奇心——这也许是迄今所知的、把组成人类的那些孤零零的个体联结在一起的最强韧的纽带。他俩——直到最后——都是绝对无所畏惧的：阿什顿会坐在染上腺鼠疫的病人床畔，凝神记录病潮是如何一寸寸地漫上病人的理智机能，那份专注，正与菲尔德这周研究X射线、下周研究飞行器、第三周研究通灵术（spiritualism）的专注一般无二。我想，这故事的余下部分自己会作出交代——或者说，并不完全作出交代。无论如何，下面我所读给阿什顿医生听的，便是他自己讲给我听的、经连贯整理后的记述。当然，开口说话的是他。

===Original===
“After I returned from Paris, where I had studied under Charcot, I set up practice at home. The general doctrine of hypnotism, suggestion, and cure by such means had been accepted even in London by this time, and, owing to a few papers I had written on the subject, together with my foreign diplomas, I found that I was a busy man almost as soon as I had arrived in town. Louis Fielder had his ideas about how I should make my début (for he had ideas on every subject, and all of them original), and entreated me to come and live not in the stronghold of doctors, ‘Chloroform Square,’ as he called it, but down in Chelsea, where there was a house vacant next his own.

“‘Who cares where a doctor lives,’ he said, ‘so long as he cures people? Besides you don’t believe in old methods; why believe in old localities? Oh, there is an atmosphere of painless death in Chloroform Square! Come and make people live instead! And on most evenings I shall have so much to tell you; I can’t “drop in” across half London.’

“Now if you have been abroad for five years, it is a great deal to know that you have any intimate friend at all still left in the metropolis, and, as Louis said, to have that intimate friend next door, is an excellent reason for going next door. Above all, I remembered from Cambridge days, what Louis’ ‘dropping in’ meant. Towards bedtime, when work was over, there would come a rapid step on the landing, and for an hour, or two hours, he would gush with ideas. He simply diffused life, which is ideas, wherever he went. He fed one’s brain, which is the one thing which matters. Most people who are ill, are ill because their brain is starving, and the body rebels, and gets lumbago or cancer. That is the chief doctrine of my work such as it has been. All bodily disease springs from the brain. It is merely the brain that has to be fed and rested and exercised properly to make the body absolutely healthy, and immune from all disease. But when the brain is affected, it is as useful to pour medicines down the sink, as make your patient swallow them, unless—and this is a paramount limitation—unless he believes in them.

===Chinese===
我从巴黎（Paris）回来——在那边我曾师从沙尔科（Charcot）——之后，便在国内开业行医。此时，催眠术（hypnotism）、暗示（suggestion）及以此类手段治病的一般学说，连伦敦（London）也已经接受；加之我写过几篇这方面的论文，又有外国的文凭，所以发现自己几乎刚一进城，便已是个大忙人。关于我应当如何初露锋芒，路易斯·菲尔德有他的一套主意（因为无论什么题目他都有主意，而且全都是别出心裁的主意），力劝我不要住到医生扎堆的堡垒里去——他管那里叫『氯仿广场』——而要住到切尔西（Chelsea）去，他自家隔壁正空着一所房子。

「一个医生住在哪里有什么要紧，」他说，「只要他能把人治好就行？况且你本来就不信那套老法子，又何必信那套老地段？嗐，氯仿广场那一带弥漫着一股无痛而死的气息！你倒是上这儿来，教人好好活下去吧！再说，多半的晚上我都有那么多话要跟你说；隔着大半个伦敦，我可没法『顺道串门』。」

一个人若在国外待上五年，还能确知自己在首都有任何一位至交留存，这已属难得；而正如路易斯所言，这位至交又恰好在隔壁，更成了登门造访的绝佳理由。更何况，我从剑桥时代起便记得路易斯所说的「串门」意味着什么：临近就寝时分，一日的工作既毕，楼梯平台上便会响起一阵急促的脚步声，接下来一个钟头、或是两个钟头，他便滔滔不绝地倾泻着种种主意。他走到哪里，便把生命力——也就是主意——播撒到哪里。他喂养人的大脑，而大脑才是唯一要紧的东西。大多数病人之所以生病，是因为他们的大脑在挨饿，于是身体起而反叛，便得了腰痛或者癌症。这便是我那点微薄工作所得的主要学说。一切躯体的疾病，皆发源于大脑。只要把大脑喂养得当、休歇得当、调遣得当，身体便可绝对康健、百病不侵。然而一旦大脑受了损，那么把药倒进下水道，与让病人把它吞下去，功效是一样的——除非——这是一条至为要紧的限制——除非他信这药。

===Original===
“I said something of the kind to Louis one night, when, at the end of a busy day, I had dined with him. We were sitting over coffee in the hall, or so it is called, where he takes his meals. Outside, his house is just like mine, and ten thousand other small houses in London, but on entering, instead of finding a narrow passage with a door on one side, leading into the dining-room, which again communicates with a small back room called ‘the study,’ he has had the sense to eliminate all unnecessary walls, and consequently the whole ground floor of his house is one room, with stairs leading up to the first floor. Study, dining-room and passage have been knocked into one; you enter a big room from the front door. The only drawback is that the postman makes loud noises close to you, as you dine, and just as I made these commonplace observations to him about the effect of the brain on the body and the senses, there came a loud rap, somewhere close to me, that was startling.

“‘You ought to muffle your knocker,’ I said, ‘anyhow during the time of meals.’

“Louis leaned back and laughed.

“‘There isn’t a knocker,’ he said. ‘You were startled a week ago, and said the same thing. So I took the knocker off. The letters slide in now. But you heard a knock, did you?’

“‘Didn’t you?’ said I.

“‘Why, certainly. But it wasn’t the postman. It was the Thing. I don’t know what it is. That makes it so interesting.’

===Chinese===
一天晚上，我忙了一整天之后，在他那里用饭，便对路易斯说了些这类意思的话。我们坐在厅里喝咖啡——那间屋子如此称呼，他的饭也就在那里吃。从外面看，他的房子与我的、与伦敦成千上万所小房子并无二致；可一进门，却不是一条窄窄的过道，一边开着一扇门通向餐室、餐室又连着一间叫做『书房』的后室——他颇有见地，把所有不必要的隔墙都拆了，于是他家整个底楼便成了一大间屋子，中间有楼梯通向二楼。书房、餐室、过道全打通了；从前门进去，便是一间大屋。唯一的缺点是用餐时邮差就在你身旁弄出很大的声响；而正当我对他就大脑对身体和感官的影响发着这番老生常谈时，我近旁某处忽然传来一下响亮的叩门声，吓了我一跳。

「你该把门环裹上点，」我说，「至少在用饭的时候。」

路易斯往后一仰，笑了起来。

「根本没有门环，」他说，「一周前你吓了一跳，说的也是这话。所以我把门环卸了。如今信件是从门缝里滑进来的。可你确实听到了一下叩门声，是吗？」

「你没听见？」我说。

「嗳，当然听见了。可那不是邮差。那是那个东西。我不知道它是什么。正因如此，它才这么有趣。」

===Original===
“Now if there is one thing that the hypnotist, the believer in unexplained influences, detests and despises, it is the whole root-notion of spiritualism. Drugs are not more opposed to his belief than the exploded, discredited idea of the influence of spirits on our lives. And both are discredited for the same reason; it is easy to understand how brain can act on brain, just as it is easy to understand how body can act on body, so that there is no more difficulty in the reception of the idea that the strong mind can direct the weak one, than there is in the fact of a wrestler of greater strength overcoming one of less. But that spirits should rap at furniture and divert the course of events is as absurd as administering phosphorus to strengthen the brain. That was what I thought then.

“However, I felt sure it was the postman, and instantly rose and went to the door. There were no letters in the box, and I opened the door. The postman was just ascending the steps. He gave the letters into my hand.

“Louis was sipping his coffee when I came back to the table.

“‘Have you ever tried table-turning?’ he asked. ‘It’s rather odd.’

“‘No, and I have not tried violet-leaves as a cure for cancer,’ I said.

“‘Oh, try everything,’ he said. ‘I know that that is your plan, just as it is mine. All these years that you have been away, you have tried all sorts of things, first with no faith, then with just a little faith, and finally with mountain-moving faith. Why, you didn’t believe in hypnotism at all when you went to Paris.’

===Chinese===
倘若有一件事是催眠术家——相信有未经解释的影响之存在的人——所最厌恶、最鄙夷的，那便是通灵术的那一整套根本观念。亡灵干预我们生活这一已被戳穿、名誉扫地的说法，与他所信之事的相抵触程度，再没有别的能出其右了。而这两者之所以名誉扫地，是出于同一个理由：人凭理智便不难理解大脑如何作用于大脑，一如不难理解身体如何作用于身体；因此，接受『强者的心智可以支配弱者的心智』这一观念，并不比接受『力气更大的摔跤手能制服力气较小的摔跤手』这一事实更费气力。但是，说什么亡灵会敲打家具、会左右事变的进程，则如同服磷以补脑一样荒谬。这便是我当时的想法。

不过，我仍确信那是邮差，便立即起身走到门前。信箱里没有信，我便开了门。邮差正拾级而上。他把信交到我手里。

我回到桌边时，路易斯正在小口啜着他的咖啡。

「你试过转桌术（table-turning）吗？」他问，「相当古怪。」

「没有，我也没有试过紫罗兰叶治癌。」我说。

「哦，什么都试试嘛，」他说，「我知道这是你的章法，一如这是我的章法。你出门在外的这些年里，你什么都试过，先是毫无信心，后来有了那么一点信心，最后便有了移山填海的信心。嗐，你刚去巴黎那会儿，压根儿就不信催眠术。」

===Original===
“He rang the bell as he spoke, and his servant came up and cleared the table. While this was being done we strolled about the room, looking at prints, with applause for a Bartolozzi that Louis had bought in the New Cut, and dead silence over a Perdita which he had acquired at considerable cost. Then he sat down again at the table on which we had dined. It was round, and mahogany-heavy, with a central foot divided into claws.

“‘Try its weight,’ he said; ‘see if you can push it about.’

“So I held the edge of it in my hands, and found that I could just move it. But that was all; it required the exercise of a good deal of strength to stir it.

“‘Now put your hands on the top of it,’ he said, ‘and see what you can do.’

“I could not do anything, my fingers merely slipped about on it. But I protested at the idea of spending the evening thus.

“‘I would much sooner play chess or noughts and crosses with you,’ I said, ‘or even talk about politics, than turn tables. You won’t mean to push, nor shall I, but we shall push without meaning to.’

“Louis nodded.

“‘Just a minute,’ he said, ‘let us both put our fingers only on the top of the table and push for all we are worth, from right to left.’

“We pushed. At least I pushed, and I observed his fingernails. From pink they grew to white, because of the pressure he exercised. So I must assume that he pushed too. Once, as we tried this, the table creaked. But it did not move.

===Chinese===
他一边说一边摇了铃，他的仆人进来收拾了桌子。这当儿我们在屋里踱来踱去，赏看那些版画：路易斯在纽卡特（the New Cut）买来的一幅巴托洛齐（Bartolozzi）的作品，我们齐声喝彩；而一幅他花了大价钱弄来的《珀迪塔》（Perdita），我们却哑然无语。随后他又在我们刚才用饭的那张桌前坐下。桌子是圆的，红木所制，分量沉重，中央一只底座分出几只爪足。

「掂掂它的分量，」他说，「看你能不能推得动它。」

于是我双手握住桌沿，发觉勉强能推动它。但也仅此而已；要撼动它，非得费上相当一把力气不可。

「这回把两手放在桌面上，」他说，「看你能做什么。」

我什么也做不了，手指只不过在桌面上滑来滑去。可我不愿意就这样消磨一晚上。

「我宁可跟你下棋或者玩圈叉棋，」我说，「甚至宁可谈谈政治，也不愿搞什么转桌。你不会有意去推，我也不会，可我们会无意之中推起来。」

路易斯点了点头。

「就一分钟，」他说，「咱俩都只把手指放在桌面上，使出吃奶的劲儿，从右往左推。」

我们推了。至少我推了，而我观察着他的指甲。指甲由粉红转为惨白，因为他正用力按着。可见他也必然在推。有一回，我们正这般试着，桌子咯吱响了一声。可它并没有动。

===Original===
“Then there came a quick peremptory rap, not I thought on the front door, but somewhere in the room.

“‘It’s the Thing,’ said he.

“Today, as I speak to you, I suppose it was. But on that evening it seemed only like a challenge. I wanted to demonstrate its absurdity.

“‘For five years, on and off, I’ve been studying rank spiritualism,’ he said. ‘I haven’t told you before, because I wanted to lay before you certain phenomena, which I can’t explain, but which now seem to me to be at my command. You shall see and hear, and then decide if you will help me.’

“‘And in order to let me see better, you are proposing to put out the lights,’ I said.

“‘Yes; you will see why.’

“‘I am here as a sceptic,’ said I.

“‘Scep away,’ said he.

===Chinese===
接着便响起了一下急促而专横的叩击声，我觉得那不是在前门上，而是在屋里某处。

「就是那个东西。」他说。

今天我对你们讲起这事，想必那确实是它。可那天晚上，那不过像是一次挑衅。我想演示它的荒谬。

「断断续续五年了，我一直在研究那套通灵术，」他说，「我先前没告诉你，是因为我想先让你看一些现象，这些现象我解释不了，可如今在我看来，已能由我驾驭。你且看、且听，然后再决定愿不愿意帮我。」

「为了让我看得更清楚，你打算把灯熄了。」我说。

「是的；你会明白缘由。」

「我是作为一个怀疑者来这儿的。」我说。

「那你就尽情怀疑吧。」他说。

===Original===
“Next moment the room was in darkness, except for a very faint glow of firelight. The window-curtains were thick, and no street-illumination penetrated them, and the familiar, cheerful sounds of pedestrians and wheeled traffic came in muffled. I was at the side of the table towards the door; Louis was opposite me, for I could see his figure dimly silhouetted against the glow from the smouldering fire.

“‘Put your hands on the table,’ he said, ‘quite lightly, and—how shall I say it—expect.’

“Still protesting in spirit, I expected. I could hear his breathing rather quickened, and it seemed to me odd that anybody could find excitement in standing in the dark over a large mahogany table, expecting. Then—through my fingertips, laid lightly on the table, there began to come a faint vibration, like nothing so much as the vibration through the handle of a kettle when water is beginning to boil inside it. This got gradually more pronounced and violent till it was like the throbbing of a motorcar. It seemed to give off a low humming note. Then quite suddenly the table seemed to slip from under my fingers and began very slowly to revolve.

“‘Keep your hands on it and move with it,’ said Louis, and as he spoke I saw his silhouette pass away from in front of the fire, moving as the table moved.

“For some moments there was silence, and we continued, rather absurdly, to circle round keeping step, so to speak, with the table. Then Louis spoke again, and his voice was trembling with excitement.
